meaning: To win every battle one fights, achieving victory in each and every engagement. The phrase describes an invincible force or commander who never suffers defeat. It emphasizes absolute and consistent success through superior preparation or skill.
origin: This idiom originates from "Guanzi: Qi Fa" (Seven Methods), a text attributed to Guan Zhong, the celebrated chancellor of the State of Qi during the Spring and Autumn period. The passage argues that a well-trained army striking an untrained one will prevail every time—ten battles, ten victories, a hundred battles, a hundred victories. It later appears in Sima Qian's "Records of the Grand Historian" (Shiji), in the "Treatise on Tortoise Divination," where it describes the infallible foresight of a sacred tortoise whose predictions always come true.
example_zh: 这支精锐部队训练有素，在战场上十战十胜，令敌人闻风丧胆。
example_en: This elite force, rigorously trained, won every battle it fought, making its enemies tremble at the mere mention of its name.

meaning: To have everything turn out exactly as one's heart desires; to be fully satisfied and content. It describes a situation where one's wishes and expectations are completely met without disappointment.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦), Chapter 46, written by Cao Xueqin (曹雪芹). In the original text, a character remarks that things under heaven do not always turn out as satisfactorily as one might wish. The phrase conveys the ideal of complete contentment, though the original usage carries a note of irony—acknowledging that such perfect satisfaction is rare. The modern writer Duanmu Hongliang (端木蕻良) also employed it in his work Nostalgia (乡愁).
example_zh: 她终于找到了一份遂心如意的工作，每天都过得很开心。
example_en: She finally found a job that fully satisfied her, and she is happy every day.

meaning: As solid as a large boulder. Used as a metaphor for something unshakable, immovable, or steadfast in its firmness. Often describes alliances, relationships, or resolve that cannot be swayed by external forces.
origin: From the Han dynasty yuefu poem "古诗为焦仲卿妻作," commonly known as "孔雀东南飞" (The Peacock Flies Southeast), preserved in the Southern Dynasties anthology "玉台新咏." The poem recounts the tragic love of Jiao Zhongqing and his wife Liu Lanzhi, whose marriage was torn apart by his mother's interference. In one famous passage the wife vows, "You shall be the great rock, I shall be the reed; the reed is tough as silk, the rock never shifts," pledging her unwavering devotion.
example_zh: 两国之间的友谊坚如盘石，历经风雨而不变。
example_en: The friendship between the two nations is as solid as a rock, enduring through trials without ever changing.

meaning: Refers to the life and experience of a prisoner behind bars. The phrase evokes the grim reality of imprisonment, where iron-barred windows are the defining feature of one's daily existence. It is often used to describe the hardship and confinement of serving a prison sentence.
origin: There is no single classical literary source for this idiom. It arose from the vivid imagery of prison windows fitted with iron bars, a feature common to jails and detention facilities throughout Chinese history. The expression gained popularity in modern Chinese literature and vernacular writing to convey the bleakness of incarceration. By combining 'iron window' with 'flavor' (in the sense of a taste or experience of life), it encapsulates the entire atmosphere of prison existence.
example_zh: 数十载的监牢生涯，使他遍尝铁窗风味的苦涩。
example_en: Decades of prison life made him taste the full bitterness of confinement behind iron bars.

meaning: A beautiful and lovable young girl. The phrase originates from the Jin dynasty poet Zuo Si's fond description of his own daughter and became a literary epithet for a charming, adorable young woman. It conveys both physical beauty and endearing innocence.
origin: The idiom traces to the Jin dynasty poet Zuo Si, who wrote the poem 'Jiao Nü Shi' (Poem on My Lovely Daughter), opening with the line 'In our family there is a lovely daughter, bright and fair-skinned.' Centuries later, the Tang dynasty poet Li Shangyin alluded to Zuo Si's daughter in his poem, writing 'The young son of the Ji family is still pitiable; how can one forget the lovely daughter of the Zuo family?' The expression '左家娇女' thus became a cultivated way to refer to a beautiful, cherished young girl, carrying the literary prestige of two celebrated poets.
example_zh: 邻家的小姑娘宛如左家娇女，聪慧可爱，人见人夸。
example_en: The little girl next door is like a lovely daughter of a literary family—clever, adorable, and praised by everyone who meets her.

meaning: To study something with concentrated effort and deliberate with all one's mental energy. It describes someone who devotes themselves wholeheartedly to research and thinking, sparing no effort in pursuit of understanding.
origin: This idiom originates from the Song dynasty work 'Yungu Zaji' (云谷杂记) by Zhang Bian (张渂). It recounts how the great historian Sima Guang (司马温公) was deeply fond of the Han dynasty philosopher Yang Xiong's work 'Tai Xuan' (太玄). Sima Guang himself said that ever since his youth he had loved the book, studying it exhaustively and deliberating over it with all his effort for many years, and only then did he dare to write a commentary on it.
example_zh: 他为了攻克这道难题，研精竭虑，连续数月不曾懈怠。
example_en: To crack this difficult problem, he studied and deliberated exhaustively, never slacking off for months on end.

meaning: Literally meaning 'morally there is no turning back,' this idiom describes a situation where one is morally obligated to press forward with courage and determination. It conveys that righteousness demands perseverance, making retreat impossible.
origin: This idiom originates from the Book of Jin (晋书), in the biography of Wen Qiao (温峤). During the Eastern Jin dynasty, Wen Qiao found himself in a perilous political and military situation where retreating was not an option. He compared his predicament to riding a fierce beast—one cannot simply dismount mid-ride. The phrase captures the moral imperative to forge ahead when circumstances demand it, as turning back would be both dishonorable and impractical.
example_zh: 国家存亡之际，将士们义无旋踵，誓死保卫疆土。
example_en: At the moment of national survival, the soldiers pressed forward without retreat, vowing to defend the territory to the death.

meaning: To not follow prevailing vulgar customs or popular trends. It describes someone of noble character who refuses to conform to the common, base practices of society. The term conveys moral integrity and independence of spirit.
origin: The phrase originates from the 'Book of Rites' (《礼记·射义》), a foundational Confucian text compiled during the Han dynasty, which states 'one should not follow the flow of vulgar customs.' The work records Confucian teachings on ritual archery and moral conduct. It emphasizes that a gentleman cultivates inner virtue rather than bending to the popular fashions of the masses. The idiom later became widely used in literature to praise individuals of upright character.
example_zh: 他一生不同流俗，始终坚守自己的学术理想。
example_en: Throughout his life he refused to follow the crowd, always holding fast to his scholarly ideals.

meaning: To grind an iron pestle down into a needle. It is a metaphor for achieving difficult goals through persistent effort and unwavering perseverance. With enough dedication and hard work, even the most daunting tasks can be accomplished.
origin: The story originates from the Ming dynasty encyclopedia Qianque Leishu. As a young boy, the Tang dynasty poet Li Bai was studying but made little progress, so he abandoned his books and left. On the road he encountered an old woman grinding a thick iron pestle against a stone. When Li Bai asked what she was doing, she replied that she intended to grind it into a needle. Deeply moved by her determination, Li Bai returned to his studies and eventually completed his education.
example_zh: 做学问要有磨杵成针的精神，才能有所成就。
example_en: To achieve success in scholarship, one must possess the spirit of grinding a pestle into a needle.

meaning: Describes a state of extreme terror and fright, where one feels as though their very soul has flown away and their spirit has fled. It is a variant of the more common idiom 魂飞魄散 (hún fēi pò sàn). The expression conveys an overwhelming, paralyzing fear that overtakes the entire body and mind.
origin: This idiom is a variant of the widely used 魂飞魄散, both rooted in ancient Chinese folk beliefs that the soul (魂) and spirit (魄) could separate from the body under extreme shock or terror. The imagery of a soul flying away and a spirit leaping out draws on traditional dual-soul concepts found in early Chinese cosmology and medicine. While no single definitive classical text is uniquely associated with this exact wording, the phrase appears in vernacular fiction and storytelling of the Ming and Qing dynasties as a dramatic intensifier for scenes of sudden fright. It functions interchangeably with its better-known counterpart in most literary contexts.
example_zh: 那声巨响让她魂飞魄越，半天说不出一句话。
example_en: That loud crash left her so terrified that she could not utter a single word for a long while.

meaning: To donate money or resources generously and without hesitation, especially to help society or the public. The phrase emphasizes willingness to give for the greater good rather than personal gain.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a single definitive classical source. It is a compound expression: 慷慨 conveys fervent generosity of spirit, while 输将 historically referred to transporting and delivering goods or funds. In later Chinese usage the two combined to denote the act of contributing wealth cheerfully and in substantial amounts. It is most commonly applied to large-scale charitable giving for public welfare or disaster relief.
example_zh: 面对灾区人民的困境，社会各界慷慨输将，纷纷捐款捐物。
example_en: Faced with the plight of the disaster-stricken people, all sectors of society contributed generously, donating money and supplies one after another.

meaning: Food cannot be swallowed. It describes being so worried or anxious that one loses all appetite and cannot bring oneself to eat. The phrase conveys deep distress that physically prevents eating.
origin: This idiom originates from a Tang dynasty essay, the 'Afterword to the Biography of Zhang Zhongcheng' (《张中丞传后叙》) by the renowned writer Han Yu. In it, the loyal general Nan Jiyun makes a passionate declaration: when he arrived at the besieged city of Suiyang, its people had gone without food for over a month. Although he wanted to eat alone, his sense of righteousness would not allow it; and even if he tried to eat, he could not bring himself to swallow. The phrase 'food not down swallow' thus became a vivid expression of grief and moral anguish that makes eating impossible.
example_zh: 得知母亲病重的消息，他整日食不下咽，憔悴了许多。
example_en: After learning that his mother was seriously ill, he could not bring himself to eat day after day and grew visibly haggard.

meaning: To accomplish a task by relying on or borrowing the strength and resources of others rather than one's own. It describes leveraging external help to achieve a goal. The term can carry a neutral or slightly negative connotation, implying a lack of self-reliance.
origin: This idiom originates from the classical text Liezi (《列子·汤问》), dated to the Warring States period. The passage tells of a man named Lai Dan whose father was killed by Heiluan. When someone offered to help him exact revenge using supernatural power, Lai Dan felt ashamed to borrow another's strength, vowing instead to slay Heiluan with his own sword. The phrase '耻假力于人' (ashamed to borrow others' strength) captures his determination to act independently. Over time, '假力于人' came to denote the general act of relying on outside assistance to get things done.
example_zh: 这项工程难度极大，他不得不假力于人，请来了多位专家协助完成。
example_en: The project was extremely difficult, so he had to rely on others' strength and invited several experts to help complete it.

meaning: One's true form or original nature is exposed. It describes a situation where a disguise or deception is uncovered, revealing what someone truly is. Often used when a fraud or impostor's real identity comes to light.
origin: This idiom originates from Tang Haoming's historical novel 'Zeng Guofan' (曾国藩), Part 1, Chapter 9. In the story, a scar-faced man first tried to pass through a tax checkpoint by pretending to be an honest, timid small merchant. When his true identity was exposed, he realized that pleading would be useless and resorted to paying a large bribe to get through. The phrase has since been used to describe the unmasking of one's disguised true nature.
example_zh: 那个骗子在警察的盘问下原形败露，不得不交代了全部罪行。
example_en: The scammer's true nature was exposed under police questioning, and he had to confess to all his crimes.

meaning: Originally referring to a brave warrior who immediately cuts off his own wrist after being bitten by a venomous snake, to prevent the poison from spreading throughout the body. It metaphorically means making a prompt and decisive decision without hesitation or compromise, even at a significant cost.
origin: This idiom originates from the Tang dynasty text 'Shu Shu Fu Xia' (述书赋下) by Dou Gao (窦皐). The original passage draws a parallel: 'A gentleman overlooks flaws to promote talent, just as a brave warrior cuts off his wrist to preserve his life.' The imagery conveys the idea that a courageous person will sacrifice a part of themselves to save the whole, symbolizing the need for resolute action when facing a crisis.
example_zh: 面对亏损不断的子公司，董事会决定以壮士断腕的魄力将其剥离。
example_en: Faced with a perpetually losing subsidiary, the board of directors resolved to divest it with the decisive resolve of a warrior severing his own wrist.

meaning: A metaphor for great longevity, likening a person's lifespan to the long lives traditionally attributed to tortoises and cranes. It is commonly used as a congratulatory expression at birthday celebrations to wish someone a long and healthy life. It is a variant of the idiom '龟年鹤寿'.
origin: The phrase appears in a Song dynasty ci poem by Wei Xiang (韦骧), titled '醉蓬莱·廷评庆寿' (Drunk in Lotus Lane: Celebrating the Birthday of the Court Judge). In the poem, the author expresses wishes for the honoree's longevity, writing '惟愿增高，龟年鹤算，鸿恩紫诏' — hoping only for greater advancement, long life like tortoise and crane, and imperial favor. The tortoise and crane are traditional Chinese symbols of long life, as both were believed to live for many centuries. Over time the expression became a standard term for wishing someone a long life.
example_zh: 祝祖父龟年鹤算，福寿康宁。
example_en: I wish Grandfather a long life like the tortoise and crane, blessed with happiness, longevity, health, and peace.

meaning: This idiom means to work together with one heart and united effort toward a common goal. It is a variant of the more common form 同心戮力, expressing the idea of people joining forces with shared determination and resolve.
origin: No specific origin story is recorded for this variant. It is equivalent to 同心戮力, a phrase found in classical Chinese texts such as the Book of Han (汉书), where it described officials and soldiers uniting their efforts to defend the state or accomplish a difficult task. The character 僯 serves as an archaic variant of 戮 in this context, both conveying the sense of joined exertion. The expression emphasizes shared commitment and collective strength applied toward a single purpose.
example_zh: 面对困难，大家同心僯力，终于完成了任务。
example_en: Facing difficulties, everyone united their efforts with one heart and finally completed the task.

meaning: The price is low and the quality is good. It describes products or services that offer excellent value for money. This is a highly positive characterization of something both affordable and well-made.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing Dynasty novel 近十年之怪现状 (Strange Situations of the Past Decade) by Wu Jianren (吴趼人), Chapter 10. In the story, a friend from Suzhou writes to a printing house saying he has long admired their reputation for being both affordable and of fine quality, and thus comes to seek their services. The phrase became a common expression in commerce and daily life. Lu Xun also used it in his short story 祝福 (New Year's Sacrifice) when describing a restaurant's inexpensive yet excellent fish fin dish.
example_zh: 这家超市的商品价廉物美，深受附近居民喜爱。
example_en: The products at this supermarket are inexpensive and of high quality, making it a favorite among nearby residents.

meaning: Like sitting or lying on a needle-studded felt mat. It describes being extremely restless and anxious, unable to find peace in any position. The idiom conveys a deep sense of unease and psychological torment.
origin: The phrase originates from the Ming Dynasty play "The Righteous Dog" (《义犬》) by Chen Yujiao (陈与郊), specifically the fourth act. In the story, a character named Di Lingqing narrowly escapes death and returns home, counting himself extremely fortunate. Yet his mind remains in such turmoil that he feels as though he is sitting or lying on a mat of needles, unable to settle. The idiom is a variant of the more common "如坐针毡" (like sitting on a needle mat), extending the imagery of discomfort to both sitting and reclining.
example_zh: 自从得知那则消息后，他坐卧针毡，整夜未能合眼。
example_en: Ever since hearing that news, he has been on pins and needles, unable to sleep a wink all night.

meaning: To be unable to devise any plan or solution; to be completely at a loss for ideas. It describes a situation where all options have been exhausted and no strategy can be found.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Records of the Three Kingdoms' (三国志), in the Biography of Qiao Zhou from the Shu section. When the Shu kingdom faced the invading Wei army, the Later Lord Liu Shan summoned his ministers to a council, but no one could produce a workable strategy. Qiao Zhou ultimately advised surrender. The phrase thus evokes a moment of collective helplessness in the face of crisis.
example_zh: 面对如此棘手的局面，众人计无所出，只得暂且按兵不动。
example_en: Faced with such a thorny situation, everyone could devise no plan and had no choice but to hold their position for the time being.

meaning: Literally describing weather clearing as clouds part and fog lifts. Metaphorically, it means that grievances, suspicions, or misunderstandings have been resolved and the truth comes to light, restoring clarity and trust.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty work 'Daoxian Huanhai Jianwen Lu' (Observations from Officialdom in the Daoguang-Xianfeng Era) by Zhang Jixing. The author reflects on how great ministers throughout history often suffered slander and false accusations, yet in a fleeting moment the clouds would clear and the fog disperse — meaning truth prevailed and their names were vindicated. The imagery of sunlight and moonlight breaking through symbolizes the restoration of justice and clarity after a period of darkness and doubt.
example_zh: 经过一番诚恳的交谈，两人之间的误会终于云开雾释，重归于好。
example_en: After an earnest conversation, the misunderstandings between them finally cleared like clouds parting, and they reconciled.

meaning: A metaphor for a person who only eats and drinks but accomplishes nothing useful. It describes someone who is utterly idle and incompetent, serving no purpose beyond consuming food and wine. The term conveys strong contempt for such worthlessness.
origin: The phrase originates from the Song dynasty poet Wang Yucheng's poem 'In Reply to Secretary An's Song Collection,' where he writes that one sleeps at night and rushes by day without noticing aging, and that being a mere rice bag and wine jar is hardly worth mentioning. Later, the Southern Song poet Lu You also referenced it in his poem 'Imitating Sichuanese Tea Brewing,' lamenting that rice bags and wine jars are everywhere while few truly appreciate the fine Mengshan purple bamboo shoot tea. The expression thus became a classical literary condemnation of idle, useless individuals.
example_zh: 这些饭囊酒瓮之徒整日吃喝玩乐，于国于民毫无用处。
example_en: These worthless good-for-nothings spend their days eating, drinking, and playing, serving neither the country nor the people.

meaning: Describes windows adorned with pearls and doors with intricate lattice work. It refers to extremely luxurious and ornate palace architecture, symbolizing extravagance and opulence in royal construction.
origin: From the 'Nan Shi' (History of the Southern Dynasties) compiled by Li Yanshou of the Tang Dynasty. The passage describes Emperor Xiaowu of the Liu Song dynasty who, upon ascending the throne, vastly expanded palace construction beyond previous limits. He built grand halls such as Zhengguang, Yuzhu, and Ziji, decorating them with carved beams, ornate joints, pearl-adorned windows, and latticed doors. The phrase illustrates the extreme luxury and extravagance of his reign.
example_zh: 这座皇家园林珠窗网户，极尽奢华之能事。
example_en: This royal garden features pearl-adorned windows and latticed doors, embodying the utmost in extravagance.

meaning: To not consider something shameful; to feel no sense of disgrace. It describes someone who lacks a proper sense of shame or morality, often behaving improperly without any remorse.
origin: The phrase originates from the philosophical text《邓析子·转辞》(Deng Xi Zi: Turning Words), attributed to Deng Xi, a thinker of the Spring and Autumn period. The original passage observes that when people subjected to punishment such as tattooing or nose-cutting no longer feel ashamed, society falls into chaos with more disorder than order. The idiom thus critiques the erosion of moral standards and the loss of a sense of shame in society.
example_zh: 他抄袭别人的文章还四处炫耀，真是不以为耻。
example_en: He plagiarized someone else's article and even showed it off everywhere, truly feeling no shame about it.

meaning: Describes an appearance of extreme anxiety and impatience. It depicts someone rubbing their hands together and stamping their feet, unable to stay calm when faced with a difficult situation.
origin: From the Qing dynasty novel "Wenming Xiao Shi" (A Short History of Civilization) by Li Baojia, Chapter 34. In the story, the county magistrate grew so anxious that he rubbed his hands and stamped his feet, summoning his clerks and legal advisors to brainstorm a solution. Despite everyone's deliberation, no one could think of a way out. The phrase vividly captures a person in great distress and agitation.
example_zh: 眼看火车就要开了，他急得搓手顿脚，却怎么也找不到车票。
example_en: Seeing the train about to depart, he grew so anxious that he rubbed his hands and stamped his feet, yet still could not find his ticket.

meaning: This idiom means to exhaust troops in vain and squander military provisions. It describes a futile military campaign that drains both manpower and financial resources without achieving any result. The phrase criticizes leadership that commits forces and money to an effort with no tangible gain.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a single specific literary source but is a compound expression from classical Chinese military vocabulary. The character 劳 means to toil or wear out, 师 refers to an army or troops, 糜 means to waste or squander, and 饷 denotes military pay or provisions. The full phrase appears in Qing-era and later military commentaries as a critique of ill-advised campaigns. It reflects the traditional Chinese strategic principle that military action must be decisive and justified, lest one exhaust both soldiers and treasury for nothing.
example_zh: 这场战争劳师糜饷，毫无收获。
example_en: This war exhausted the troops and wasted provisions, achieving nothing at all.

literal: turn against the public, pursue the private
meaning: To betray public duty in pursuit of private gain; to abuse one's position for personal profit. It describes corrupt behavior where an official or person in power puts self-interest above the common good, often in violation of law or ethics.
origin: The phrase originates from the Song Dynasty text 'On Protecting the Dharma' (护法论) by Zhang Shangying, where he lamented that those who betray public duty for private gain endlessly encroach upon others' interests. The term was later cited in Qing Dynasty writings, such as Zhao Lian's 'Notes from the Howling Pavilion' (啸亭杂录), in political memoranda accusing officials of corruption. It has served as a standard condemnation of official misconduct throughout Chinese history.
example_zh: 他因背公营私被革职查办。
example_en: He was dismissed and investigated for betraying public duty for private gain.

meaning: Like ice melting and fog dissipating, this idiom describes the complete disappearance or collapse of something. It is used to indicate that obstacles, enmities, or troubles have vanished entirely without a trace.
origin: The phrase originates from an epitaph written by Yu Xin of the Northern Zhou dynasty, titled 'Epitaph for Sima Yi, Duke of Langya and Grand General of Zhou.' The text describes a military campaign in rugged frontier terrain where hostile tribesmen relied on natural defenses to resist. Once the general overcame the perilous landscape and secured the region, the valleys fell silent and the mountains emptied, with all resistance melting away 'like ice dissolving and fog scattering.'
example_zh: 经过耐心的沟通，双方之间的误会终于冰消雾散。
example_en: After patient communication, the misunderstandings between the two sides finally melted away like ice and fog.

meaning: Following old routines and being content with the way things are. It describes someone who clings to established customs and resists change or innovation.
origin: This idiom does not have a specific literary origin tied to a particular text or historical figure. It is a compound of two ideas: '踏故' (treading the old path) and '习常' (being accustomed to the usual). Together they convey a conservative mindset critical of complacency. The expression reflects a traditional Chinese cultural attitude that cautions against stubbornly adhering to outdated practices.
example_zh: 他踏故习常，不愿尝试任何新方法。
example_en: He stubbornly follows old routines and refuses to try any new methods.

meaning: Means having absolutely no news or information about someone or something. It describes a situation where all communication has ceased and no trace or word can be found. It is commonly used when someone has gone missing or lost contact entirely.
origin: This phrase appears in Wu Yunduo's autobiographical work 'Dedicate Everything to the Party' (把一切献给党), in the chapter 'New Task.' Wu Yunduo was a renowned weapons engineer during the Chinese revolutionary era. In the passage, after sunset, comrades lit lanterns and torches, parting clusters of wild grass to search, yet the artillery shells remained completely without trace. The idiom conveys the sense of something vanishing without the slightest clue or word.
example_zh: 他离家出走后便渺无音讯，家人四处寻找也毫无头绪。
example_en: After he ran away from home, there was no news of him at all, and his family searched everywhere without a clue.

meaning: To shut one's door and sweep away the cart tracks in front of it. It means to cut off all social contact and refuse to receive guests. The idiom describes a deliberate choice of seclusion and withdrawal from social life.
origin: The idiom employs the archaic character 埽, a variant of 扫 (to sweep). The vivid image is of closing one's gate and sweeping away the ruts left by visitors' carriages, signaling that no guests are welcome. This concept of intentional seclusion pervades classical Chinese literature, particularly in accounts of recluses and scholar-officials who withdrew from public life to preserve their integrity. No single definitive source text is widely cited for this exact formulation. It reflects the traditional Chinese ideal of the hermit-scholar who chooses solitude over worldly entanglement.
example_zh: 他退休后便闭门埽轨，不再与昔日同僚来往。
example_en: After retiring, he shut his door and severed all ties, no longer associating with his former colleagues.

meaning: To pursue benefit without compromising righteousness. It describes the principle that one can seek advantage while still upholding moral integrity. The idiom emphasizes that material gain should never come at the expense of justice.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Record of Rites' (礼记·儒行), a Confucian classic compiled during the Han dynasty from earlier Zhou-era sources. In the passage, Confucius describes the character of a true scholar (儒), stating that even when entrusted with wealth and immersed in pleasures, a gentleman sees profit yet does not impair righteousness. The text was part of a larger discourse on the moral standards expected of Confucian scholars, dating back to the Spring and Autumn period.
example_zh: 真正的商人逐利却不昧心，始终坚守利不亏义的底线。
example_en: A true merchant pursues profit without compromising conscience, always holding fast to the principle of seeking gain without impairing righteousness.

meaning: A genre of literature that emerged in the later feudal period of China, created to meet the cultural needs of urban residents. It typically depicts the lives, joys, sorrows, and aspirations of the townspeople class. Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasty huaben (vernacular short stories) are its representative works.
origin: This term refers to a literary tradition that developed during the Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties as cities grew and a prosperous urban merchant class emerged. Unlike classical literature written for the elite, this genre addressed the tastes and concerns of ordinary city dwellers. Its hallmark works are the huaben short stories, which dramatized everyday urban life, romance, commerce, and social conflict. The genre reflects the rising consciousness and desires of the bourgeoisie-like townspeople within the feudal order.
example_zh: 宋元时期的话本是市民文学的代表作，生动描绘了当时城市百姓的日常生活。
example_en: The Song and Yuan dynasty huaben are representative works of townspeople literature, vividly depicting the daily life of urban commoners at the time.

literal: look up, it, even more, high
meaning: The more one looks up at it, the higher it appears. It expresses profound admiration and reverence for someone's virtue, knowledge, or accomplishment that seems beyond reach.
origin: This idiom originates from the Analects (论语·子罕), recording the words of Yan Yuan, the favorite disciple of Confucius. Yan Yuan sighed in praise, saying that the more he looked up to his master's virtue, the higher it seemed, and the more he delved into it, the firmer it appeared. He marveled at how Confucius guided students step by step with culture and ritual, yet the depth of his teaching remained inexhaustible. The phrase has since been used to express deep reverence for a person of extraordinary stature.
example_zh: 面对这位学术大师的深厚学养，学生们仰之弥高，心生敬仰。
example_en: Faced with the profound scholarship of this academic master, the students felt that the more they looked up to him, the higher he stood, and their hearts filled with reverence.

meaning: Not being constrained by trivial matters or petty rules. It describes someone who is broad-minded and does not fuss over minor details, especially in daily life. Often used positively to indicate a generous and unconstrained personality.
origin: The phrase comes from the 'Book of Later Han' (后汉书), in the biography of Yu Yan (虞延). Yu Yan was described as having a simple and honest nature, not bound by petty conventions. During the Eastern Han period, he served as an official known for his straightforwardness and integrity, disregarding trivial formalities. The expression later became widely used to describe people of open and magnanimous character.
example_zh: 他为人豁达大度，不拘小节，深受朋友们的喜爱。
example_en: He is open-minded and does not fuss over trivial matters, and is deeply loved by his friends.

meaning: To be smugly self-satisfied and visibly pleased with oneself. It describes someone who shows off an air of triumphant complacency, as if overflowing with pride over their own achievements or perceived superiority.
origin: This idiom is a variant of the earlier expression 洋洋得意 (yáng yáng dé yì), which dates back to classical Chinese literature where 洋洋 originally conveyed a sense of overflowing abundance or sweeping grandeur. Over time the phrase came to characterize the inflated, self-congratulatory demeanor of someone basking in their own success. No single definitive source text is attributed to 洋洋自得 specifically; it evolved as a colloquial refinement of the older form, emphasizing the inward, self-regarding quality of the satisfaction.
example_zh: 他考了第一名后便洋洋自得，走路都昂着头。
example_en: After placing first in the exam, he grew smugly self-satisfied and walked around with his head held high.

meaning: When the autumn wind arrives, fans are cast aside and no longer used. This idiom is a metaphor for a woman losing her lord's favor once her beauty has faded, much like a fan discarded when the weather turns cold. It conveys the sorrow and helplessness of being abandoned after once being cherished.
origin: The idiom originates from the Qing dynasty playwright Li Yu's work '意中缘·先订' (The Fated Romance: Prior Engagement), in which a character voices her fear that after marriage her husband might be tempted by other beauties and abandon her, leaving her with 'the sorrow of an autumn silk fan.' The imagery draws upon a classical motif dating back to the Han dynasty poetess Ban Jieyu, who compared herself to an autumn fan—treasured in summer but discarded once the cold winds come. Over centuries, this evocative image became a standard literary metaphor for a woman cast aside after losing favor.
example_zh: 后宫佳丽三千，不少嫔妃皆有秋风纨扇之悲。
example_en: In a harem of three thousand beauties, many concubines suffered the sorrow of being cast aside like an autumn fan.

meaning: Describes moving at tremendous speed, like wind sweeping past and clouds racing by. It is commonly used to depict horses, troops, or vehicles moving swiftly and relentlessly.
origin: The phrase originates from the Tang Dynasty work 'Xuan Guai Lu' (Records of the Mysterious and Strange) by Niu Sengru, in the tale 'Cen Shun'. It depicts a vivid military scene where drums sounded three times and troops poured out of four gates, with countless banners flying as soldiers moved as swiftly as wind and clouds, both sides arraying their formations for battle.
example_zh: 骑手们风驰云走，转眼间便冲过了终点线。
example_en: The riders raced like wind and clouds, flashing past the finish line in the blink of an eye.

meaning: Describes being in a dazed, befuddled state, as if intoxicated or dreaming and unable to think clearly. It conveys a loss of mental clarity and awareness of one's surroundings.
origin: The phrase originates from the Song dynasty scholar Zhu Xi's letter 'Reply to Lü Ziyue' (答吕子约). In the letter, Zhu Xi mentions that his elder brother's petition had already been submitted to the authorities, but the people involved were so muddled—'like drunk, like a dream'—that they could not even manage affairs right in front of them, let alone be expected to handle anything greater. The expression thus characterizes a state of mental confusion and incapacity.
example_zh: 他整日如醉如梦，连身边最亲近的人也认不出来。
example_en: He spent his days in a daze, like drunk and dreaming, unable to recognize even those closest to him.

meaning: Refers to a young or inexperienced scholar who has only recently begun their studies, with limited knowledge and shallow experience. It describes a newcomer to a field of learning who lacks depth and seasoning.
origin: No single classical source is recorded for this idiom; it is a descriptive compound formed from the idea of someone newly undertaking study (新学) and a young junior scholar (小生). Such terms were common in traditional Chinese scholarly culture, where seniority and years of accumulated learning were highly valued. The phrase captures the Confucian emphasis on humility before elders and the recognition that mastery requires long dedication.
example_zh: 他自称新学小生，不敢在诸位前辈面前班门弄斧。
example_en: Calling himself a novice scholar, he dared not show off before his distinguished elders.

meaning: Describes a mournful, chilling sound of wailing and crying. The imagery of howling wolves and weeping ghosts conveys an atmosphere of despair and suffering. It is used to depict cries so pitiful and terrifying that they unsettle the listener.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦) by Cao Xueqin, Chapter 58. In the passage, a character rebukes someone for beating a person so severely that their cries were as mournful and eerie as wolves howling and ghosts weeping. The phrase uses the unsettling imagery of wolves and ghosts to emphasize the terrifying and pitiful nature of the sounds produced.
example_zh: 深夜的山村里传来狼号鬼哭的声音，让人毛骨悚然。
example_en: In the mountain village deep at night came sounds of mournful wailing like wolves and ghosts, making one's hair stand on end.

meaning: Originally a metaphor for brotherly love and mutual support, this idiom later came to mean substituting one thing or person for another, or taking the blame on behalf of someone else. It is a variant of the more common idiom 李代桃僵. The image evokes a peach tree dying so that a plum tree may take its place.
origin: The idiom derives from an ancient Han dynasty folk poem in the anthology Yuefu (乐府), titled 'Song of the Plums' (鸡鸣). The poem describes how a peach tree dies and a plum tree stands in its place, originally praising the deep bond of brotherhood and willingness to sacrifice for one another. Over centuries, the metaphor shifted from brotherly devotion to the broader concept of substitution or scapegoating. The variant form 桃僵李代 reverses the character order but carries the same meaning as 李代桃僵.
example_zh: 出了问题他总让别人桃僵李代，自己从不担责。
example_en: When problems arise, he always makes others take the fall for him and never takes responsibility himself.

meaning: A vulgar or conventional view held by ordinary people. It refers to shallow, commonplace opinions that lack independent judgment. The term carries a dismissive tone toward unremarkable mainstream thinking.
origin: This idiom does not trace back to a single literary source but emerged from common usage in classical and vernacular Chinese. It contrasts worldly, conventional opinions with more enlightened or principled perspectives. The phrase appears in various literary works and essays throughout Chinese history where authors criticized shallow majority views. It remains widely used in modern Chinese to describe unreflective, herd-like attitudes.
example_zh: 他不愿以世俗之见来评判一个人的价值。
example_en: He refuses to judge a person's worth by conventional worldly opinions.

meaning: Wherever the carriage goes, timely rain follows. It is a traditional phrase of praise for a virtuous local official whose governance brings blessings to the people, as if rain accompanies him wherever he travels.
origin: The phrase originates from the 'Taiping Yulan' (Imperial Readings of the Taiping Era), which quotes the 'Book of the Later Han' by Xie Cheng of the Three Kingdoms Wu dynasty. The original text states that when officials returned to their posts, rain followed their carriages down. It was used to commend officials whose administration was so benevolent that nature itself seemed to bless the regions they governed.
example_zh: 百姓感念这位县令政绩斐然，甘雨随车，五谷丰登。
example_en: The people were grateful to this county magistrate whose excellent governance brought blessings like timely rain wherever he went, ensuring abundant harvests.

meaning: To sigh and groan out of sadness, frustration, or depression. It describes someone expressing dejection or helplessness through repeated sighing rather than taking action.
origin: The phrase traces back to Ming dynasty vernacular fiction, notably Ling Mengchu's 'Slapping the Table in Amazement, Second Collection' (二刻拍案惊奇), where a character is described as sighing and lamenting all day in distress. It later appeared in Qing dynasty literature such as Cao Xueqin's 'Dream of the Red Chamber,' where characters sigh repeatedly when troubled by unfulfilled desires or worries. Over time it became a common expression for helpless, mournful sighing.
example_zh: 遇到困难就唉声叹气是解决不了问题的。
example_en: Sighing in frustration won't solve the problem when you encounter difficulties.

meaning: This idiom means to deliberately make trouble, play tricks, or create difficulties for others. It describes someone who engages in mischief or acts in an obstructive manner. The phrase draws on Yuan dynasty theatrical terminology to convey deliberate scheming and troublemaking.
origin: This idiom originates from the Yuan dynasty anonymous play 'Hundred Flower Pavilion' (《百花亭》), specifically the first act. In the original context, it describes people who scheme, stir up trouble, and play tricks. The term combines '捏怪' (fabricating strangeness) and '排科' (staging theatrical routines or gags), both rooted in the dramatic conventions of Yuan theater where '科' referred to stage directions. Together they convey the idea of deliberate mischief-making and obstruction.
example_zh: 这伙人专爱捏怪排科，四处惹是生非。
example_en: This gang loves to play tricks and make trouble, stirring up conflict wherever they go.

meaning: The threshold of the door is worn through from excessive foot traffic. It describes a place with an extremely large number of visitors coming and going, so many that the threshold gets trampled and broken. Used to indicate a constant stream of callers or visitors.
origin: This idiom originates from the Tang Dynasty text 'Fa Shu Yao Lu' (Records of Calligraphy) by Zhang Yanyuan. It tells the story of the monk Zhiyong, who resided at Yongxin Temple in Wuxing during the Sui-Tang era. Zhiyong was a renowned calligrapher, and people seeking his calligraphy flocked to the temple like a marketplace. So many visitors came seeking his work that the threshold of his dwelling was worn through with holes from all the foot traffic.
example_zh: 这家新开的火锅店生意火爆，每天都有食客户限为穿。
example_en: This newly opened hotpot restaurant is doing booming business, with so many diners coming daily that the threshold is worn through.

meaning: This idiom means to harm one's own body and damage one's health. It describes self-destructive behaviors such as overindulgence, reckless living, or harmful habits that ruin physical well-being. It serves as a stern warning against conduct that undermines one's vitality.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a single specific literary source. The character 戕 (to kill or injure) and 伐 (to attack or strike) are both classical Chinese verbs denoting harm and destruction, frequently appearing in ancient texts. Combined as a four-character phrase, they emphasize the severity of self-inflicted damage to both body and life. The expression likely emerged from traditional Chinese medical and philosophical traditions that stressed preserving health and cautioned against reckless conduct.
example_zh: 长期熬夜酗酒，无异于戕身伐命，终将毁掉健康。
example_en: Staying up late and drinking excessively over the long term amounts to harming your body and ruining your life, ultimately destroying your health.

meaning: This idiom refers to a nemesis from a past life, describing a relationship marked by extraordinarily deep-seated enmity or resentment. Paradoxically, it is also used as an affectionate term for someone deeply beloved, treating the bond as a karmic entanglement that fate has woven across lifetimes. It is a variant of the more common phrase 夙世冤家.
origin: The concept draws on Buddhist notions of karma and reincarnation, where grievances and debts from past lives carry over into present existence. In classical Chinese literature—particularly Song and Ming dynasty vernacular stories and drama—the word 冤家 carried a double meaning: a bitter enemy and, in a playful twist, a beloved one whose hold on the heart feels almost like a curse. The variant 夙世冤业 substitutes 业 (karmic deed) to emphasize the inescapable karmic weight of the bond. No single definitive source text is recorded for this exact phrasing.
example_zh: 他们两人一见面就争吵不休，简直是夙世冤业。
example_en: The two of them bicker endlessly the moment they meet, as if they were karmic foes from a past life.

meaning: Describes a scene of fleeing in panic and disarray, like rats scurrying and wolves running. It conveys a desperate, chaotic escape from danger or defeat.
origin: This idiom originates from "Water Margin" (水浒传) by Shi Nai'an of the Ming Dynasty, appearing in Chapter 66. It depicts the chaotic scene inside Daming Prefecture when it came under attack, where common citizens fled in terror. The phrase uses the imagery of startled rats and wolves to vividly portray people scattering desperately in every direction.
example_zh: 敌军被打得鼠窜狼奔，丢盔弃甲。
example_en: The enemy troops were beaten into a chaotic rout, fleeing in panic and abandoning their armor.

meaning: This idiom describes a family whose financial situation is moderately comfortable. It indicates that a household has enough resources to live without hardship, though not necessarily wealthy.
origin: The term combines '家道' (family circumstances) with '小康' (moderate prosperity), a concept rooted in classical Chinese texts such as the Book of Rites, where '小康' referred to a society of modest well-being after the decline of the legendary golden age. Over time, the phrase came to describe individual families enjoying a stable, decent standard of living. No single literary source is credited as the definitive origin of this four-character idiom.
example_zh: 他靠多年辛苦劳作，如今也算家道小康了。
example_en: Through years of hard work, his family has now reached a modest level of prosperity.

meaning: Describes things arranged in neat, orderly fashion with clear sequence and logic. The term conveys a state of being well-organized, methodical, and tidy. It is commonly used to praise systems, arrangements, or conduct that follow a clear, sensible order.
origin: The phrase traces to the Qing dynasty scholar Wang Fuzhi (王夫之), appearing in his work 'Xitang Yongri Xulun Waibian' (夕堂永日绪论外编), Volume 26. There, Wang Fuzhi commented on an essay by You Gongying analyzing the classical chapter 'The Ruler of a State's Love for His People' (寡人之于国也), noting that the essay neatly divided its subject into three matters—establishing production, emphasizing agriculture, and relieving famine—in a manner that was orderly and well-arranged. The phrase '井然有序' thus became a standard expression for orderly, systematic arrangement.
example_zh: 图书室的书架被整理得井然有序，找书非常方便。
example_en: The bookshelves in the reading room were arranged in perfect order, making it very easy to find books.

meaning: Oranges grown south of the Huai River turn into bitter trifoliate oranges when transplanted north of it. The idiom metaphorically describes how a change in environment can alter the very nature of a thing. It is often used to explain why the same practice yields different results in different settings.
origin: The idiom comes from 'Yanzi Chunqiu' (Annals of Master Yan), a work recording the words and deeds of Yan Ying, a celebrated minister of the Qi state during the Spring and Autumn period. During a diplomatic mission to the state of Chu, the King of Chu attempted to humiliate Yanzi by parading a man accused of theft who happened to be from Qi. Yanzi replied that oranges grown south of the Huai River are sweet, but when transplanted to the north they become bitter trifoliate oranges, because the soil and water differ — implying that it was Chu's environment, not Qi's, that bred the criminal. The exchange turned the King's mockery back upon himself and became a classic illustration of environment shaping character.
example_zh: 同样的管理方法，换个公司就淮橘为枳，效果大不相同。
example_en: The same management approach yields very different results when moved to another company, like oranges turning bitter across the river.

meaning: To have an exaggeratedly high opinion of oneself. It describes someone who is arrogantly conceited and looks down on everyone else, refusing to acknowledge others' worth or abilities.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Book of Later Han' (《后汉书·马援传》), specifically the biography of Ma Yuan, a famous Eastern Han dynasty general. When Ma Yuan visited the warlord Gongsun Shu (courtesy name Ziyang) who had declared himself emperor in Shu, Ma Yuan remarked that Ziyang was like a frog at the bottom of a well—blind to the wider world—yet presumptuously elevated himself above others. Ma Yuan concluded it would be better to focus attention on the east, where Emperor Guangwu of Han held power. The phrase thus became a lasting metaphor for baseless self-aggrandizement.
example_zh: 他刚取得一点成绩就妄自尊大，连老前辈的话都听不进去了。
example_en: After achieving just a little success, he grew arrogantly conceited and wouldn't even listen to the veterans' advice.

meaning: A sensation of dizziness and blurred vision, as if everything around you is spinning. It describes a physical state where one feels lightheaded and the eyes see things unclearly, often caused by fatigue, illness, shock, or sensory overload.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing Dynasty novel 'Dream of the Red Chamber' (红楼梦) by Cao Xueqin. In the sixth chapter, the protagonist Liu Lao Lao (Granny Liu), a poor country woman, enters the opulent Rong Mansion for the first time. The dazzling display of wealth and luxurious furnishings overwhelms her senses, making her feel dizzy and dazzled. The phrase vividly captures the disorientation of someone unaccustomed to grandeur.
example_zh: 他连续加了三天班，站起来时只觉得头晕目眩，差点摔倒。
example_en: After working overtime for three straight days, he felt so dizzy and lightheaded when he stood up that he nearly fell over.

literal: exhaust the root, trace the source
meaning: To thoroughly investigate and trace something back to its ultimate origin or root cause. It emphasizes leaving no stone unturned in the pursuit of fundamental understanding. The idiom conveys a rigorous, exhaustive approach to uncovering where something truly begins.
origin: This idiom is a classical compound formed from two near-synonymous pairs: 极本 (to exhaust the root) and 穷源 (to trace the source to its end). Both 极 and 穷 carry the sense of pushing inquiry to its furthest limit. The phrase reflects the traditional Chinese scholarly ideal of tracing any phenomenon back to its fundamental cause. It does not derive from a single identifiable text but echoes the investigative spirit found in Song-dynasty Neo-Confucian discourse, where scholars prized exhaustive inquiry into principle (理).
example_zh: 研究历史要极本穷源，才能理清事件的来龙去脉。
example_en: In studying history one must trace every matter back to its very root before the full sequence of events becomes clear.

meaning: To be stingy and miserly toward others while enriching oneself. The idiom uses 'thin' (瘠) as a metaphor for stinginess and 'fat' (肥) as a metaphor for greed, describing someone who exploits others for personal gain.
origin: This idiom originates from the Ming dynasty play 'Record of the Epiphyllum Flower' (昙花记) by Tu Long (屠隆), specifically the scene 'Judgment in the Underworld' (冥司断案). In the play, the underworld judge examines the sins of the dead, noting that many committed offenses of greed and covetousousness—seizing and occupying others' property, enriching themselves at others' expense, unwilling to part with even a single cent. The phrase vividly captures the moral failing of those who impoverish others to fatten themselves.
example_zh: 他靠瘠人肥己的手段发家致富，最终被人举报而身败名裂。
example_en: He made his fortune by enriching himself at others' expense, only to be reported and ruined in the end.

meaning: To make a law that ultimately brings harm to oneself. It refers to a situation where a person's own rules or actions backfire and cause their own downfall. The idiom describes someone who suffers the consequences of their own designs.
origin: The idiom originates from the Records of the Grand Historian (《史记·商君列传》), recounting the story of Shang Yang, a Legalist reformer of the State of Qin during the Warring States period. After Shang Yang's reforms, he fell out of favor and tried to flee. When he sought lodging at an inn, the innkeeper refused him, citing Shang Yang's own law that required all guests to carry identification. Shang Yang sighed deeply, lamenting that the very laws he created had become his own undoing. This gave rise to the expression of suffering from one's own legislation.
example_zh: 他制定的苛刻考勤制度最终作法自毙，自己因迟到被扣光了工资。
example_en: The harsh attendance policy he created ultimately backfired on him—he lost his entire salary to his own penalties for being late.

meaning: To put something behind one's head and forget about it entirely. It describes disregarding or ignoring something as if it no longer matters, dismissing it from one's mind completely.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Wenming Xiao Shi' (A Brief History of Civilization) by Li Baojia, Chapter 14. In the story, three brothers of the Jia family had originally studied under Master Meng. However, after they became disciples of Yao Bogong, they abandoned their former teacher and put him completely out of their minds. The phrase vividly conveys the act of casting aside someone or something as though it were tucked behind one's head, out of sight and out of thought.
example_zh: 他把老师的嘱咐置之脑后，又犯了同样的错误。
example_en: He cast his teacher's warnings aside and made the same mistake again.

meaning: To scheme and plot using clever calculations. It describes someone who uses cunning and stratagems to achieve their goals, often at others' expense. The term carries a negative connotation of manipulation and deceit.
origin: This idiom appears in classical Chinese literature as a variant of the more common form 使心用倖. It reflects the traditional Chinese moral view that using schemes and trickery to gain advantage is beneath a person of integrity. No single definitive origin story is recorded, but the expression embodies the age-old Confucian critique of cunning behavior.
example_zh: 他处处使心作倖，到头来机关算尽反误了自身前程。
example_en: He schemed and plotted everywhere, only to have his calculations backfire and ruin his own future.

literal: move toward good, distance from crime
meaning: To turn toward goodness and stay far from wrongdoing. It describes a moral attitude of actively cultivating virtue while deliberately avoiding sinful or wrongful conduct. The phrase embodies the Confucian ideal of continuous self-improvement in ethical character.
origin: This phrase has no single definitive origin source but draws from classical Confucian moral philosophy. The concept of '迁善' (moving toward goodness) appears in the Book of Changes (易经) and various Confucian texts that emphasize moral cultivation. The combined expression encapsulates the dual Confucian imperative to actively pursue virtue and shun evil, reflecting a core tenet of traditional Chinese ethical thought.
example_zh: 教育的根本目的在于引导人们迁善远罪，成为有道德的人。
example_en: The fundamental purpose of education is to guide people toward goodness and away from wrongdoing, helping them become moral individuals.

meaning: A metaphor for diligent and self-motivated study. It describes someone who, despite poverty and hardship, finds any means available to keep learning—even burning chaff for light. The idiom praises extraordinary perseverance and devotion to education.
origin: This idiom originates from the Biography of Gu Huan in the History of the Southern Dynasties (Nan Shi). Gu Huan, a scholar of the Southern Dynasties period, was born into poverty and could not afford school tuition. He would lean against the wall behind a village school to listen to lessons, never forgetting what he heard. At night, lacking lamp oil, he burned pine knots to read or burned chaff to light his studies. His relentless dedication to learning amid hardship became a lasting symbol of scholarly perseverance.
example_zh: 古人燃糠自照的精神，值得每一个求学的人学习。
example_en: The spirit of the ancients who burned chaff to illuminate their studies deserves to be emulated by everyone pursuing knowledge.

meaning: Literally meaning to harness the wind as one's carriage and drive the rosy clouds as one's steeds, this idiom describes Daoist immortals roaming freely through the heavens. It is used metaphorically to refer to wandering freely across the world in a carefree, unrestrained manner.
origin: This idiom originates from a letter titled 'To Xiao Weidou' written by Jie Xisi, a scholar of the Yuan dynasty. In the letter, Jie Xisi tells Xiao Weidou that if he truly wishes to withdraw from worldly affairs and live in seclusion in the mountains, he could follow the example of ancient hermits like Chao Fu, Xu You, Wu Guang, and Juan Lu. He could also emulate recluses like Yan Ling and Lu Zhonglian. Furthermore, even if he wished to ride the wind and clouds like legendary immortals such as Wo Quan, An Qisheng, Xian Men, Lu Ao, and Xu Fu, that too would be acceptable.
example_zh: 他辞官归隐后，整日骖风驷霞，游历名山大川，好不自在。
example_en: After resigning from his official post and retiring to seclusion, he spent his days roaming the famous mountains and great rivers as freely as an immortal riding the wind and clouds.

meaning: The lone phoenix (孤鸾) is a metaphor for a man who has lost his spouse, while the widowed swan (寡鹄) represents a widow. Together, the idiom refers to men and women who have lost their partners and live in solitude. It conveys the sorrow and loneliness of bereaved spouses.
origin: The idiom traces back to the Han dynasty scholar Wang Bao's 'Ode to the Bamboo Flute' (洞箫赋), which describes 'the lone female and widowed crane finding solace below' (孤雌寡鹤，娱优乎其下兮). The original imagery depicted solitary birds drawn to the melancholic music of the bamboo flute. Over time, the expression evolved into '孤鸾寡鹄' (lone phoenix and widowed swan), using these symbols of fidelity to specifically denote bereaved spouses.
example_zh: 这对孤鸾寡鹄在晚年相遇，彼此慰藉，重新找到了生活的温暖。
example_en: These two lonely souls, both having lost their spouses, met in their later years and found comfort in each other, rediscovering the warmth of life.

meaning: A traditional Chinese system for designating the birth order among brothers: bo (伯) is the eldest, zhong (仲) is the second, shu (叔) is the third, and ji (季) is the youngest. It is used to clearly distinguish siblings by seniority.
origin: The phrase originates from the Zuo Zhuan (左传), a historical text compiled by Zuo Qiuming of the pre-Qin period. In the twenty-sixth year of Duke Zhao's reign, the text records the line '亦唯伯仲叔季图之,' referencing the four birth-order terms used to organize brothers. These designations were a standard convention in ancient China for naming and ranking male siblings within a family.
example_zh: 古代兄弟排行用伯仲叔季区分长幼，一目了然。
example_en: In ancient times, brothers were ranked using the bo-zhong-shu-ji system to distinguish elder from younger, making the order clear at a glance.

meaning: A gentle breeze that does not cause branches to rustle. It metaphorically describes a peaceful, stable society where the climate is mild and harmonious. The phrase evokes an ideal state of governance under which nature itself seems benign.
origin: The phrase originates from Han dynasty texts. Huan Kuan's 'Yantie Lun' (Discourses on Salt and Iron) describes the era of the Duke of Zhou, when the world was at peace, the nation suffered no premature deaths, and no years of famine; at that time, rain did not break clods of earth and wind did not make branches sing. Wang Chong's 'Lunheng' echoes the same image, portraying ideal governance where winds are gentle enough not to rustle branches and rain falls softly enough not to break the soil, with a favorable wind every five days and rain every ten days.
example_zh: 在这风不鸣条的太平盛世里，百姓安居乐业，共享太平。
example_en: In this peaceful and prosperous age where gentle breezes never stir the branches, the people live in harmony and enjoy the tranquility.

meaning: A metaphor for forgetting or discarding the means once the goal has been achieved. The character 荃 (quán) refers to a bamboo fish trap, also written as 筌. It teaches that tools and methods are merely instruments for reaching an end and should not be clung to once their purpose is fulfilled.
origin: This idiom originates from the Daoist text Zhuangzi (《庄子》), specifically the chapter Wai Wu (外物, 'External Things'), written by the philosopher Zhuangzi (庄子) during the Warring States period. The original passage states: 'The trap exists for the fish; once the fish is caught, the trap is forgotten.' Zhuangzi used the analogy of a bamboo fish trap to illustrate that words and methods are merely tools for conveying meaning—once the meaning is grasped, the tools should be discarded rather than fixated upon. This reflects a core Daoist principle of transcending form to attain essence.
example_zh: 研究学问切忌得鱼忘荃，方法与结论同等重要。
example_en: In scholarly pursuit, one must not forget the methods once conclusions are reached; the approach and the result are equally important.

meaning: Literally 'breath like an orchid,' this idiom describes a beautiful woman whose breath is as fragrant as orchid flowers. It is also used metaphorically to praise writing or speech that is elegant and exquisitely refined.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty work 'Tingyan Xiaolu' by Chen Peizhi, specifically in the preface to 'Runxiang Jushi.' In the preface, the author describes a woman whose breath was as fragrant as orchids and whose conduct was as pure as jade. The expression later gained wider circulation through Wang Zhuo's 'Jinshi Shuo,' where Wang Yanting praised the poet Peng Xianmen's lyrical writing using this very phrase.
example_zh: 她启齿微吟，吹气如兰，令在场宾客无不心醉。
example_en: As she softly recited her poem, her breath was as fragrant as orchids, enchanting every guest present.

meaning: This idiom metaphorically describes someone who harbors sinister and treacherous intentions deep within. Like having sharp scales and armor concealed in one's chest, it suggests a person is dangerously calculating and should not be trusted or approached closely.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Records of the Three Kingdoms' (三国志), in the biography of Chen Zhen of Shu. Before departing on a diplomatic mission to Wu, Chen Zhen (style name Xiaoqi) warned the Shu chancellor Zhuge Liang about his fellow official Li Yan (style name Zhengfang), saying he 'had scales and armor in his belly.' Zhuge Liang later relayed this in a letter to Chief Clerk Jiang Wan and Palace Attendant Dong Yun, noting that Li Yan's own townsfolk considered him too dangerous to approach. The phrase thus became a metaphor for harboring deeply malicious intent.
example_zh: 此人胸有鳞甲，不可深交。
example_en: This person harbors sinister intentions and should not be befriended too closely.

meaning: This idiom describes a state of widespread chaos and turmoil across the land. The phrase draws on the ancient Chinese belief that seas surrounded the country, making 'four seas' a metonym for the whole realm, while 'cauldron boiling' vividly evokes bubbling unrest. It is typically used to depict a period of great upheaval or rebellion.
origin: The idiom appears in the 'Biography of Qiao Zhou' in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, where it is contrasted with the chaotic boiling times of the late Qin dynasty and the fragmented landscape of six competing states. It also appears in the 'Biography of Zu Ti' in the Book of Jin, where Zu Ti tells his friend that if the realm falls into chaos and heroes rise up together, they should avoid clashing in the Central Plains. These passages reflect the turbulent political climate of the third and fourth centuries, when warlords vied for control. Over time the expression became a standard metaphor for nationwide disorder.
example_zh: 汉末四海鼎沸，群雄割据，百姓流离失所。
example_en: At the end of the Han dynasty the whole realm was in turmoil, warlords carved up the territory, and the common people were driven from their homes.

meaning: Things of the same kind naturally gather together. It refers to people of similar character or interests associating with one another, often implying that bad people share the same corrupt tastes and collude together. It is synonymous with the more common idiom 物以类聚.
origin: This idiom is a variant of the well-known phrase 物以类聚 (things gather by kind), which expresses the ancient Chinese philosophical observation that like attracts like. The concept reflects the natural tendency for beings of similar nature to associate with one another. Over time, the phrase came to carry a derogatory connotation, often used to describe wrongdoers who flock together due to shared vices. It appears in classical Chinese literature as an expression of this universal principle of affinity.
example_zh: 这几个骗子经常混在一起，真是物以群分。
example_en: These swindlers always hang out together—truly, birds of a feather flock together.

meaning: A gentle spring breeze blowing over people. It is used metaphorically to describe someone who treats others with a warm, amiable, and approachable attitude. The idiom conveys a sense of kindness and friendliness in interpersonal conduct.
origin: The idiom originates from the Ming dynasty anonymous play 'Si Ma Tou Tang' (Four Horses Joining the Tang), specifically the second act. In the scene, a character urges another to set aside past grievances and instead receive a visitor with the warmth and gentleness of a spring breeze, rather than dwelling on old enmities. The metaphor likens a gracious, forgiving demeanor to the soothing caress of spring winds. It has since become a classical expression for amiable and kindhearted behavior toward others.
example_zh: 这位老教师对学生总是春风和气，深受大家敬爱。
example_en: The veteran teacher always treats his students with the warmth of a gentle spring breeze, and is deeply respected and loved by all.

meaning: A metaphor for brilliant fireworks or dazzling lights. It depicts a spectacular scene of illumination, often used to describe festive nighttime celebrations or gorgeous light displays.
origin: This idiom has no single recorded origin text and is a variation of the more common 火树银花, with the character order reversed. The imagery evokes silver flowers blooming among fire-lit trees, painting a picture of magnificent nighttime illuminations. It has been used in classical and modern literature to describe lantern festivals and fireworks displays during celebrations.
example_zh: 元宵之夜，城中银花火树，万民同庆。
example_en: On the night of the Lantern Festival, the city blazed with brilliant lights and fireworks as all the people celebrated together.

meaning: To be as different as water and fire. It describes two things or people that are completely opposite and fundamentally incompatible with each other. The idiom emphasizes a stark contrast or irreconcilable difference.
origin: The phrase originates from Qing dynasty scholar Qian Yong's work 'Lüyuan Conghua' (履园丛话), in the section discussing poetry. It describes the heated disagreement between the prominent official and poetry critic Shen Guiyu and the historian Yuan Jianzhai over their views on poetry. Their contrasting literary opinions were likened to the opposition of water and fire, utterly incompatible and unable to coexist.
example_zh: 这两人的性格判若水火，根本无法共事。
example_en: The two people's personalities are as incompatible as water and fire, making it impossible for them to work together.

meaning: This matter is of great importance and carries significant consequences. It is used to emphasize that something should not be taken lightly due to its substantial weight and implications.
origin: The phrase originates from the Han dynasty scholar Ban Gu's work 'Dian Yin' (典引), where he wrote '兹事体大而允，寤寐次于圣心.' Ban Gu was a prominent historian and poet of the Eastern Han dynasty, best known for compiling the 'Book of Han' (汉书). In this context, he was describing a matter of such gravity that it occupied the emperor's thoughts day and night, underscoring its profound significance to governance and state affairs.
example_zh: 此次改革兹事体大，我们必须慎重考虑每一个细节。
example_en: This reform is a matter of great importance; we must carefully consider every detail.

meaning: Even with a hundred mouths, one would find it difficult to explain or defend oneself. It describes a situation where someone is falsely accused or misunderstood and has no way to clear their name regardless of how hard they try to argue.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Huayue Hen' (花月痕) by Wei Xiuren. In the third chapter, the protagonist laments being labeled 'fickle' (薄幸), exclaiming that even with a hundred mouths he could not argue his way out of the accusation. The phrase conveys the helplessness of being unable to vindicate oneself when faced with overwhelming misunderstanding or false charges.
example_zh: 面对众人的指责，他百口难分，只能默默承受委屈。
example_en: Facing everyone's accusations, he was unable to defend himself and could only silently bear the injustice.

meaning: To analyze and probe so deeply that one penetrates to the innermost layer of a subject. It describes thorough, rigorous inquiry that reaches the most subtle and essential aspects of an issue or text. The phrase conveys depth of understanding rather than surface-level acquaintance.
origin: This phrase originates from the Qing dynasty scholar Li Yong's work Nanxiang Huiyu (南庠汇语). Li Yong, a prominent early Qing Confucian thinker, warned that knowledge and insight gained merely from external texts and hearsay amounts to borrowing ideas without true internalization. He argued that without whipping one's understanding through to the innermost layer—that is, without genuine contemplation and real realization—learning remains shallow and unrooted. The metaphor of driving a whip inward captures the discipline needed to reach the core of a matter.
example_zh: 他对这部经典的解读鞭辟着里，令人深受启发。
example_en: His interpretation of this classic penetrates to the very core, leaving readers deeply inspired.

meaning: Literally 'a single horse taking the lead.' It means to charge ahead at the forefront, to be the first to rush into battle or take initiative. The idiom describes someone who bravely leads the way in a dangerous or challenging situation.
origin: The phrase originates from Yuan dynasty playwright Guan Hanqing's work 'Wuhou Yan' (五侯宴), Act Three, which describes a fierce battle scene: 'The blade sweeps across the universe, three armies perish, a single horse charges to the front fighting a hundred bouts.' The imagery evokes a lone warrior on horseback boldly leading the assault against enemy forces. Over time, it became a metaphor for taking the lead with courage and determination in any endeavor.
example_zh: 冲锋号一响，连长匹马当先，带领战士们冲向敌阵。
example_en: As the charge bugle sounded, the company commander charged to the forefront, leading his soldiers toward the enemy lines.

meaning: To have grand ambitions that soar to the clouds. It describes someone with magnificent and far-reaching ideals or aspirations. The idiom conveys a powerful sense of determination and vision.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Han Dynasty, recorded in the Book of Han (汉书·扬雄传下). Emperor Wu of Han was fond of immortals and the supernatural. The poet Sima Xiangru presented his 'Rhapsody on the Great Man' (大人赋) intending to subtly critique the emperor's obsession, but Emperor Wu instead became inspired and felt his own ambitions soaring to the clouds. The anecdote gave rise to the expression of having 'ambitions that reach the clouds.'
example_zh: 他年纪轻轻就壮志凌云，立志要创办一家改变世界的科技公司。
example_en: Though young, he harbors soaring ambitions and is determined to found a technology company that will change the world.

meaning: The soul has detached from the body. It describes a state of extreme terror or losing one's composure under shock or temptation. The idiom conveys being frightened out of one's wits.
origin: The phrase originates from the Yuan dynasty play 'Jin Qian Ji' (The Money Tale) by Qiao Mengfu, where Act 1 contains the line 'causing the young scholar's soul to leave his body.' It depicts a person so overwhelmed—by fear or desire—that they lose all self-control, as if their very spirit has fled. The idiom was later widely used in classical novels such as Luo Guanzhong's 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms,' where characters experience it in moments of sudden alarm.
example_zh: 听到那声巨响，他吓得魂不附体，半天说不出话来。
example_en: Hearing that loud crash, he was scared out of his wits and could not speak for a long time.

meaning: This idiom metaphorically describes someone with grand ambitions who fearlessly pushes forward through difficulties. It evokes the image of a ship riding strong winds and cleaving through towering waves to reach its distant destination. It is most often used to express confidence and determination in the pursuit of lofty goals.
origin: The idiom originates from the Biography of Zong Que in the Book of Song (南朝宋). When Zong Que was young, his uncle Zong Bing asked him about his aspirations. Zong Que boldly replied, 'I wish to ride the long wind and break through ten thousand li of waves.' The Tang poet Li Bai later immortalized the phrase in his famous poem 'Hard Roads of Shu' (行路难), writing 'The time will come to ride the long wind and break the waves, then hoist the cloud-sail to cross the vast sea.'
example_zh: 年轻人要有长风破浪的志向，才能在逆境中不断前行。
example_en: Young people should have the ambition to ride the wind and break the waves, so they can keep forging ahead through adversity.

meaning: To publicly denounce or condemn someone by openly declaring their faults. It originates from the practice of beating drums to rally support before launching a public attack or criticism. The idiom implies a collective, righteous condemnation of wrongdoing.
origin: This idiom originates from the Analects (论语) of Confucius, compiled during the pre-Qin period. The Ji family, a powerful aristocratic clan in the state of Lu, was wealthier than the Duke of Zhou, and Ran Qiu, a disciple of Confucius, helped them collect taxes and increase their wealth. Confucius, angered by this exploitation of the people, declared that Ran Qiu was no longer his disciple and told his other students they could beat drums and openly attack him for his wrongdoing.
example_zh: 面对这种公然违背原则的行为，我们必须鸣鼓而攻之。
example_en: Faced with this blatant violation of principles, we must publicly condemn it with righteous outrage.

meaning: Literally meaning to chase after waves and drift with the current, this idiom metaphorically describes a person who lacks independent judgment and simply goes along with whatever is popular or fashionable. Such a person echoes others' opinions without forming their own views.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Han dynasty writer Chen Lin's 'Call to Arms for Wu Generals and Their Subordinates' (檄吴将校部曲文), which criticized officials who mired themselves in complacency and drifted along with the tide without realizing it, noting that many who drifted with the currents perished alongside everyone else. Over time, the imagery of chasing waves and following currents came to symbolize those who lack conviction and blindly conform to prevailing trends.
example_zh: 他毫无主见，凡事逐浪随波，从不表达自己的真实想法。
example_en: He has no opinions of his own, always drifting with the crowd and never expressing what he truly thinks.

meaning: To come up with a unique approach or design that differs from convention. It describes creative thinking that produces something original and unconventional.
origin: The phrase comes from Ming dynasty scholar Li Zhi's preface to 'Water Margin' (《水浒全书发凡》), where he explained his editorial approach to the novel. Li Zhi stated he deliberately departed from the original format, adding his own unique design—either marking headings outside chapters or layering commentary within the text. Over time, the phrase came to mean any idea or method that is ingeniously different from the ordinary.
example_zh: 这位设计师别出心裁，将传统旗袍与现代剪裁结合，推出了一系列令人惊艳的作品。
example_en: The designer took an unconventional approach, blending traditional qipao with modern tailoring to launch a stunning collection.

meaning: Like a white crane soaring among the clouds. A metaphor for a person of noble character and lofty conduct whose integrity and aspirations rise above the ordinary world. It conveys admiration for someone unreachable by vulgar entanglements.
origin: From Pei Songzhi's annotation to the Biography of Bing Yuan in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguo Zhi), quoting the 'Yuan Biezhuan'. Bing Yuan was a scholar of the late Eastern Han dynasty renowned for his moral integrity and learning. The phrase likens him to a white crane among the clouds, declaring that no net meant for quails could ever ensnare such a lofty spirit. The comparison emphasizes his extraordinary nobility and the impossibility of binding him to worldly snares.
example_zh: 他为人清高，宛如云中白鹤，超然于世俗之外。
example_en: His character is pure and aloof, like a white crane among the clouds, rising above the mundane world.

literal: take, book, as, driving a chariot
meaning: To drive a horse carriage solely according to what one learned from books. It is a metaphor for rigidly adhering to book learning and doctrine without adapting to real circumstances, which makes it difficult to accomplish anything. The idiom warns against treating theoretical knowledge as a substitute for practical experience.
origin: This idiom originates from a proverb recorded in 'Strategies of the Warring States' (战国策·赵策二), a text from the Warring States period. The full proverb reads: 'He who drives horses according to books cannot fully grasp the nature of horses; he who governs the present by ancient rules cannot understand the changes of affairs.' It was cited to argue against mechanically applying old precedents to new situations. The metaphor criticizes those who rely entirely on written knowledge rather than observing and adapting to actual conditions.
example_zh: 做学问不能以书为御，必须结合实际经验才能有所成就。
example_en: In scholarship one must not rely solely on book learning; only by combining it with practical experience can one achieve real success.

meaning: A metaphor for continually adding on or appending extra details without end. It describes how people embellish or pile on additional elements, often making something more complicated than it needs to be. Commonly used to describe someone who exaggerates or pads out a story.
origin: The idiom originates from a letter by the Song dynasty Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi titled 'Reply to Huang Zigeng.' In the letter, Zhu Xi lamented that people of his time created endless obstacles for themselves, constantly adding branches and attaching leaves without any end in sight. The metaphor of adding branches and leaves to a tree vividly conveys the idea of piling on unnecessary complications. Over time, the phrase came to describe the act of continuously appending or embellishing something.
example_zh: 他讲故事总爱添枝接叶，把简单的事说得天花乱坠。
example_en: He always loves to embellish when telling stories, turning simple matters into wildly exaggerated tales.

meaning: To suddenly come up with a clever idea or solution in a moment of urgency or crisis. It describes the ability to think quickly and resourcefully when under pressure. The phrase highlights how difficult circumstances can stimulate sharp, spontaneous thinking.
origin: This idiom originates from the preface to the Tang dynasty poet Bai Juyi's 'Twenty-Three Poems Matching Wei Zhi.' In the preface, Bai Juyi reflects on a friendly poetry contest with his fellow poet Yuan Zhen (courtesy name Wei Zhi), writing that when challenged by a worthy opponent, one's spirit rises and wisdom emerges in moments of urgency. The passage captures the idea that pressure and competition can sharpen the mind and spark ingenuity.
example_zh: 大火封住了楼道，他急中生智，用湿棉被裹住身体冲了出去。
example_en: The fire had blocked the stairwell, but thinking quickly, he wrapped himself in a wet quilt and dashed to safety.
