example_en: Through every hardship, he held fast to his unwavering resolve and never bowed to difficulty.

meaning: This idiom describes the act of embellishing or exaggerating when recounting events or relaying someone else's words, adding details that were not originally present. It is similar to the English expression 'adding branches and leaves,' meaning to pad a story with fabricated elements. The phrase conveys a mildly critical tone toward those who distort facts through embellishment.
origin: This idiom draws from the natural imagery of a tree: when one already has branches, adding leaves makes the whole appear more lush and elaborate than it truly is. It uses this botanical metaphor to describe how people inflate stories by grafting on fictitious details. Unlike many classical idioms, it does not trace back to a single literary source or historical anecdote. It belongs to vernacular folk speech that crystallized into a fixed expression over time. Its logic parallels other Chinese idioms that use tree imagery to represent the growth of embellishment.
example_zh: 他讲起这件事来有枝添叶，把原本简单的小事说得惊天动地。
example_en: He told the story with added embellishments, blowing a simple matter up into something earth-shattering.

meaning: A phrase referring to rare and unusual flowers and plants. It is also used metaphorically to describe beautiful and outstanding literary or artistic works. The expression evokes imagery of a garden filled with extraordinary botanical specimens.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Northern Wei dynasty work 'Luoyang Qielan Ji' (A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang) by Yang Xuanzhi, which describes the White Horse Temple as having tall bamboo in its courtyards and high pines brushing its eaves, with rare flowers and exotic plants crowding the steps. A similar concept appears in 'Xijing Zajji' (Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital), which notes that extraordinary trees and unusual grasses were all planted there. Over time, the expression expanded beyond literal botany to also symbolize exceptional literary and artistic creations.
example_zh: 御花园中种满了奇花异卉，一年四季都有花开。
example_en: The imperial garden is filled with rare flowers and exotic plants, with blossoms in every season.

meaning: To show tender affection and deep cherishing toward someone in every possible way. It describes lavishing love and care on a person, treating them with the utmost tenderness and regard. The pairing of 'light' and 'heavy' conveys that affection is shown in all measures.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a single classical text or named historical figure; it is a parallel-structured phrase assembled from common classical Chinese vocabulary. The pattern pairs the adverbs 轻 (gently) and 重 (deeply) with the verbs 怜 (to pity or show tender affection) and 惜 (to cherish or value), a rhetorical device favored in literary Chinese. It appears in later vernacular and romance literature to depict doting care. No authoritative source documents a specific origin story for it.
example_zh: 她对幼女轻怜重惜，唯恐有任何闪失。
example_en: She doted on her young daughter with tender, all-encompassing affection, terrified that any mishap might befall her.

meaning: To follow someone's words and heed their plans, signifying complete trust in a person. It describes a relationship where one accepts another's advice and proposals without question. The idiom is a variant of the more common expression 言听计从.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty playwright Hong Sheng's (洪昇) dramatic work The Palace of Eternal Life (长生殿), in the scene titled Bribery for Power (贿权). In the play, a character states that someone follows their words and heeds their schemes, implying they wield subtle influence behind the scenes. The phrase captures the dynamic of placing deep trust in a person so that all their counsel is adopted without hesitation.
example_zh: 经理对他言从计听，公司大事全凭他定夺。
example_en: The manager followed his words and heeded his plans, leaving all major company decisions to him.

meaning: Describes a place so vast and empty that not a single human trace can be seen. It conveys an atmosphere of desolate silence and solitude, often used for remote or abandoned locations.
origin: This idiom originates from modern Chinese literature, specifically from the short story 'The Big Carpenter' (《大木匠》) by the contemporary writer Wang Wenshi (王汶石). In the story, the author describes the fields and roads as quiet and deserted, with no trace of people to be found. The phrase captures the stillness and emptiness of the rural landscape. Unlike many classical idioms, this one does not trace back to an ancient historical text but instead comes from 20th-century literary writing.
example_zh: 深夜的山谷里渺无人踪，只有风声在耳边回荡。
example_en: In the mountain valley deep at night, not a single trace of people could be found, with only the sound of wind echoing in one's ears.

meaning: A wedding blessing wishing the couple a lifelong harmonious union. It expresses the hope that husband and wife will remain loving and devoted to each other for a hundred years. The phrase is commonly used in marriage congratulations and ceremonies.
origin: The phrase appears in the Qing dynasty novel 《粉妆楼》(The Powder Pavilion), traditionally attributed to Luo Guanzhong. In its first chapter, the congratulatory exclamation "百年和合，千载团圆" (a hundred years of harmony, a thousand years of reunion) is used to bless a union. Over time the expression settled into the four-character form 百年好合, becoming a standard wedding benediction in Chinese culture. It reflects the traditional value placed on marital fidelity and lifelong companionship.
example_zh: 在婚礼上，长辈们衷心祝福新人百年好合，白头偕老。
example_en: At the wedding, the elders sincerely wished the newlyweds a hundred years of harmony, to grow old together.

meaning: A trivial or insignificant skill; petty cleverness not worth serious pursuit. It is a variant of the more common idiom 雕虫小技, often used to modestly belittle one's own abilities or to dismiss something as shallow and unworthy.
origin: The phrase comes from the Song-era work 《全唐诗话》 attributed to You Mao, in a commentary on the Tang dynasty poet Zhang Hu. Zhang Hu was known for technically skillful but ornate verse, which was dismissed with the remark that such 'trivial cleverness' (雕虫小巧) was something a serious-minded man (壮夫) would not bother with. This reflects the traditional literati contempt for superficially clever but ultimately shallow literary craft.
example_zh: 这点雕虫小巧算不得什么真本事，别拿出来炫耀了。
example_en: Such petty cleverness is no real skill—don't go showing it off.

meaning: To stand out from the crowd and rise above one's peers. It describes someone whose abilities or qualities are far superior to those of ordinary people in the same group.
origin: The phrase appears in Qing dynasty literature, notably in Xia Jingqu's novel 'Yesou Puyan' (A Rustic's Cudgel), where it describes a character whose literary talents are so extraordinary that they transcend the normal category of talented individuals. The expression combines the ideas of 'exceeding the multitude' and 'standing out from one's class.' It has been used by later writers such as Mao Dun to praise exceptional figures.
example_zh: 他在学术界的成就超群拔类，令人钦佩不已。
example_en: His achievements in academia are outstanding, beyond comparison with his peers, earning him deep admiration.

meaning: A classical idiom mocking people who speak difficult-to-understand southern dialects. The shrike (鴂) is a bird whose harsh call is hard to decipher, and its tongue metaphorically represents incomprehensible speech. It reflects the historical cultural and linguistic divide between northern and southern China.
origin: This idium originates from classical Chinese texts where northern scholars disparaged speakers of southern dialects, whose languages were perceived as unintelligible gibberish. The term 南蛮 (southern barbarians) was a pejorative used by people of the Central Plains to refer to peoples living south of the Yellow River region. The comparison to a shrike's tongue (鴂舌) suggests that southern speech sounded like bird calls—incomprehensible to outsiders. It vividly captures the linguistic chauvinism and regional prejudice prevalent during the Spring and Autumn period and later dynasties, when northern Chinese culture considered itself the standard of civilization.
example_zh: 古时北人常以南蛮鴂舌讥笑南方士子的方言口音。
example_en: In ancient times, northerners often mocked the dialectal accents of southern scholars as 'barbarian shrike tongues.'

literal: tall, commander's banner, great, military flag
meaning: Literally refers to the tall banners and great flags used in the armies of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties. It denotes the imposing military standards of a commander's camp. By extension, it is a metaphor for ostentatious power, prestige, and a grand display of authority.
origin: The phrase comes from the Song dynasty essay 'Record of the Embroidered Robe Hall at Xiangzhou' (相州昼锦堂记) by the renowned scholar-official Ouyang Xiu. The essay was written in praise of Han Qi, a distinguished statesman and military leader, who returned in glory to his hometown of Xiangzhou. Ouyang Xiu reflected that compared to Han Qi's true virtue and achievements, even the tall banners and great military flags were not enough to be counted as his glory.
example_zh: 将军高牙大纛，率师出征，威震四方。
example_en: With tall banners and great flags flying, the general led his army on campaign, his might shaking all directions.

meaning: Flowers reflected in a mirror and the moon reflected in water. Originally referring to an elusive, ethereal artistic mood in poetry, it now metaphorically describes illusions or unreal phenomena that appear real but cannot be grasped. It conveys the sense of something beautiful yet insubstantial.
origin: The phrase originates from a Tang dynasty inscription by Pei Xiu, written for the stela of the eminent Buddhist monk Duan Da (Da Da Fa Shi) at Anguo Temple. The inscription describes how magnificent pillars collapsed in a single day, and speaks of 'water, moon, mirror images'—things without intention to come or go. The Buddhist metaphor reflects the idea that all worldly phenomena are like reflections in a mirror or moon in water: visible yet untouchable, ultimately illusory. Over time the expression entered literary usage to describe any beautiful but unreal vision.
example_zh: 他那些美好的承诺不过是镜花水月，终究无法实现。
example_en: Those beautiful promises of his were nothing but an illusion, ultimately impossible to fulfill.

meaning: This idiom describes a restless and unsettled state of mind. The imagery of playing with shadows and gathering wind—things intangible and impossible to grasp—symbolizes inner turmoil and a spirit that cannot find peace.
origin: The exact origin of this idiom is not clearly documented in surviving classical texts. The phrase employs vivid imagery of shadows and wind, both ephemeral and ungraspable, to convey psychological restlessness. It likely arose from poetic or literary descriptions of an unsettled mental state rather than from a specific historical anecdote. No particular dynasty or historical figure is definitively associated with its coinage.
example_zh: 他近来弄影团风，做什么事都静不下心。
example_en: He has been restless and unsettled lately, unable to calm his mind no matter what he does.

meaning: To promise official positions, titles, and wealth in order to entice others into helping achieve improper or selfish goals. It describes buying loyalty through offers of power and profit rather than genuine merit.
origin: This idiom originates from Tao Juyin's 'History of the Warlord Period of the Northern Government' (北洋军阀统治时期史话), Chapter 71. It depicts how warlords during the Beiyang era would promise promotions and rewards to motivate their soldiers. Despite repeatedly setting deadlines to capture Huailai and using the method of conferring titles and making promises to encourage troops, their front lines never advanced a single step.
example_zh: 他到处封官许愿，拉拢人心，企图夺取权力。
example_en: He went around promising official positions and rewards to win people over, scheming to seize power.

meaning: One after another, in continuous succession. It describes events or people arriving repeatedly without break. The idiom conveys a sense of unceasing, sequential occurrence.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Dream of the Red Chamber' (红楼梦) by Cao Xueqin, first chapter. In the original scene, a fire breaks out and spreads rapidly along an entire street, burning fiercely like the 'Flaming Mountain.' The phrase describes how the fire jumped from house to house in rapid succession. Over time, it came to be used broadly for any series of events happening one after another.
example_zh: 接二连三的坏消息让他几乎崩溃。
example_en: The bad news came one after another, nearly driving him to collapse.

meaning: Peerless and unparalleled in the world. Describes talent, martial skill, or ability so extraordinary that no one in one's era can match it. Conveys the idea of being the absolute best of one's time.
origin: The phrase traces back to《韩非子·解老》, a commentary by the Legalist philosopher Han Feizi (Warring States period) on the Laozi. In the original passage, Han Feizi argues that one who can master all things will easily triumph over enemies in battle, and such repeated victories make one's reputation surpass the entire world. Over time, the expression evolved into an idiom praising someone whose abilities are unmatched in their generation. It was later used in novels such as Qing-era《说岳全传》to describe legendary heroes like Yue Fei.
example_zh: 他的武艺盖世无双，天下无人能与之匹敌。
example_en: His martial arts skills are peerless, and no one in the world can rival him.

meaning: A thief resents the very owner of the property he steals from. This idiom is a metaphor for wicked people hating upright, righteous people who oppose or expose them.
origin: This idiom originates from the Zuo Zhuan (左传), a historical chronicle of the Spring and Autumn period, in the record of Duke Cheng's 15th year. The original passage reads: 'A thief hates the owner; the people resent their superiors. If you are fond of speaking bluntly, you will inevitably meet with disaster.' It was spoken as a warning to someone who valued forthright counsel, cautioning that honesty provokes the enmity of the wicked.
example_zh: 他为人正直，却遭到小人陷害，这正是盗憎主人的写照。
example_en: He was an upright man yet was framed by petty people—this is a perfect illustration of how the wicked hate the righteous.

literal: cannot, be able to, exhaust, speak
meaning: Too numerous to be fully recounted or expressed; impossible to exhaust in telling. It describes an overwhelming abundance of people, events, or things that defy complete enumeration.
origin: This idiom originates from the autobiographical preface of Sima Qian's 'Records of the Grand Historian' (史记·太史公自序), written during the Western Han Dynasty. Sima Qian recounted that peoples from distant foreign lands with differing customs, passing through layers of interpreters, came to the imperial frontiers to offer tribute and request audiences with the court. Their number, he wrote, 'could not be fully recounted,' emphasizing the vast multitude of those who came to submit. The phrase later became a classical expression for anything too numerous to mention.
example_zh: 历代为国捐躯的忠义之士不可胜道。
example_en: Throughout the dynasties, the loyal and righteous souls who sacrificed their lives for the nation are too numerous to count.

meaning: To have no scruples, hesitation, or fear about one's words or actions. It describes someone who acts boldly without worrying about consequences or social norms. It is synonymous with 无所顾忌.
origin: The idiom is a classical four-character compound formed from 无所 (having nothing) and 顾惮 (scruple and fear). 顾 means to take into consideration, while 惮 means to dread or fear. Together they denote a state of being entirely unencumbered by apprehension. It appears in various classical texts as a variant of the more common 无所顾忌, carrying the same sense of acting without restraint or worry.
example_zh: 他仗着家族势力，做事无所顾惮，得罪了许多人。
example_en: Relying on his family's power, he acted without any scruples and offended many people.

meaning: To beat someone with fists and kick with feet. It describes a thorough physical beating or assault. The phrase vividly portrays a violent attack using both hands and feet.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Yuan dynasty playwright Li Shouqing's play 'Wu Yuan Plays the Flute' (伍员吹箫), Act 1, where the original form was '拳撞脚踢' (fists ramming, feet kicking). It was later standardized to '拳打脚踢' in common usage. The phrase gained wider circulation through its appearance in Qing dynasty author Wu Jingzi's novel 'The Scholars' (儒林外史), Chapter 9, where a character complains of being beaten on account of two other people.
example_zh: 他被几个歹徒拳打脚踢了一顿，伤得不轻。
example_en: He was beaten black and blue by several thugs who punched and kicked him mercilessly.

meaning: This idiom describes a beautiful woman becoming thin and haggard, losing her former grace and vitality. It uses jade and fragrance as metaphors for feminine beauty, which diminishes like a fading flower.
origin: The idiom originates from the Yuan dynasty, specifically from a suite of songs titled 'Ji Xian Bin: Lament of Parting' by the playwright Gao Shi. The line describes a woman who, during these times of separation, has grown thin and lost her beauty while falling ill, left alone in cold loneliness. It became a poetic expression for a woman wasting away from sorrow or longing.
example_zh: 自丈夫出征后，她日夜思念，渐渐玉减香消，令人心疼。
example_en: Since her husband went off to war, she has pined for him day and night, gradually wasting away until she is a mere shadow of her former self.

meaning: To swallow one's tears and stifle one's sobs. It describes enduring suffering or oppression in silence, unable to openly express grief or resentment. The image is of tears flowing inward into the belly while suppressing any audible cry.
origin: The phrase originates from Ming dynasty author Shi Nai'an's novel 'Water Margin' (水浒全传), Chapter 98. In the story, the character Qiongying learns devastating news about her parents and is struck with grief like ten thousand arrows piercing her heart. She swallows her sobs and sheds tears in secret, nursing a relentless desire for revenge. The expression has since become a classical idiom for silent suffering under oppression.
example_zh: 她受了委屈只能饮泣吞声，不敢向任何人诉说。
example_en: Wronged, she could only swallow her tears in silence, daring not to confide in anyone.

meaning: This idiom describes pretending to be ghosts or spirits to deceive or frighten others. It also refers to secretly playing tricks, manipulating situations, or cheating through deceptive means. A variant form is 弄神弄鬼.
origin: The idiom draws from folk traditions in which shamans, charlatans, and frauds would impersonate ghosts and deities to swindle or intimidate the superstitious. Such practices were common throughout Chinese history, from village spirit mediums to palace fortune-tellers. Over time the phrase broadened to describe anyone who resorts to trickery and manipulation behind the scenes rather than acting openly.
example_zh: 这个巫婆弄鬼弄神，骗了不少人的钱财。
example_en: This old witch pretended to commune with spirits and swindled many people out of their money.

meaning: A metaphor for fierce, unstoppable impact and momentum. It evokes the image of a dragon soaring and a tiger leaping to describe powerful, courageous forward movement that cannot be withstood. It is a variant of the idiom 龙腾虎蹴.
origin: This idiom does not have a single well-documented origin story in classical literature. It belongs to a family of dragon-and-tiger metaphors that have been used since antiquity to convey overwhelming martial vigor. The pairing of dragon and tiger as symbols of supreme power and ferocity dates back to early Chinese cosmological and military writings. Over time, poets and military commentators adopted such imagery to describe unstoppable battlefield charges.
example_zh: 解放军以龙腾虎踯之势突破了敌军防线。
example_en: The liberation army broke through the enemy's defense line with the unstoppable momentum of soaring dragons and leaping tigers.

literal: in order to, guard against, ten thousand, one
meaning: Used to describe taking precautions against unlikely but possible accidents or emergencies. The term conveys the wisdom of being prepared for any contingency, no matter how improbable. It is commonly used when advising someone to keep a backup plan ready.
origin: This idiom has no specific literary origin or associated historical anecdote. The component '万一' refers to a one-in-ten-thousand chance, symbolizing an extremely unlikely event. Combined with '以防' meaning 'in order to guard against,' the phrase literally denotes preparing for that remote possibility. It has circulated as common folk wisdom in everyday Chinese for centuries without attribution to any particular dynasty or figure.
example_zh: 出门时多带把伞，以防万一下雨。
example_en: Bring an extra umbrella when you go out, just in case it rains.

literal: giant turtle calls, softshell turtle responds
meaning: A metaphor for mutual resonance and sympathetic response between parties. It describes a situation where one party speaks or acts and another responds in kind, showing a close, instinctive connection and mutual understanding.
origin: This idiom draws on the imagery of the mythical giant turtle (鳌) and the common softshell turtle (鳖). In classical Chinese cosmology, creatures of the same kind were believed to communicate and respond to one another across great distances. When the giant turtle calls out, the softshell turtle answers—a natural echo among kindred beings. The expression thus became a literary metaphor for kindred spirits responding to each other. No single classical text is cited as its definitive source.
example_zh: 他们兄弟俩心意相通，一个提出想法，另一个立刻赞同，真是鳌鸣鳖应。
example_en: The two brothers share such a deep rapport that when one proposes an idea, the other immediately agrees—it's a perfect case of mutual resonance.

meaning: Literally meaning 'not worth a single coin,' this idiom describes something or someone as completely worthless or valueless. It is used to express utter contempt or dismissal of a person's worth, opinions, or achievements.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Records of the Grand Historian' (史记·魏其安侯列传) by Sima Qian of the Han dynasty. The text records the phrase '生平毁程不识不直一钱,' describing how someone disparaged the general Cheng Bushi (程不识) as being worth less than a single coin. Cheng Bushi was a respected Han dynasty military commander known for his strict discipline. The expression later became a common metaphor for declaring someone or something to be entirely without value.
example_zh: 他那些所谓的发明，在专家眼里根本不值一钱。
example_en: His so-called inventions are not worth a single coin in the eyes of experts.

meaning: Literally placing a bed on top of a bed and building a roof under a roof. It describes redundant, repetitive actions or overly cumbersome structures. The idiom is used to criticize unnecessary duplication that adds complexity without value.
origin: The phrase originates from the preface of Yan Zhitui's 'Yanshi Jiaxun' (Family Instructions of Master Yan), written during the Northern Qi dynasty. Yan Zhitui observed that since the Wei and Jin dynasties, the philosophical works produced by various scholars were repetitive in reasoning and redundant in content, with each author merely imitating the previous ones. He compared this trend to building a roof beneath an existing roof or placing a bed on top of a bed—pointless duplication that adds nothing new.
example_zh: 写文章应力求简明扼要，切忌叠床架屋，否则读者不得要领。
example_en: In writing, one should strive for conciseness and avoid unnecessary redundancy, otherwise readers will fail to grasp the main point.

meaning: Describes a situation where every matter is arranged with complete thoroughness and propriety, leaving nothing undone. The expression emphasizes that all aspects have been settled in a well-balanced, orderly fashion. It is a variant of the more common form '四亭八当'.
origin: This idiom belongs to a family of expressions built on the numerological pattern of 'four and eight,' which in classical Chinese connotes completeness and balance. The phrase does not trace to a single literary source or historical anecdote; rather, it emerged as a colloquial variant of the related form '四亭八当,' with '停' (to halt, to settle) substituting for '亭' (pavilion, also suggesting a resting point). Both forms convey the idea that affairs have reached a point of settled perfection.
example_zh: 他把婚事的各项事宜都安排得四停八当，只等吉日到了。
example_en: He arranged every detail of the wedding preparations in perfect order, simply waiting for the auspicious day to arrive.

meaning: The common people bring food in baskets and drink in pitchers to welcome an army they love and support. It describes a situation where troops are warmly received and enthusiastically supported by the populace. The idiom conveys genuine popular acclaim for a benevolent or liberating force.
origin: The phrase originates from the 'Mencius' (《孟子·梁惠王上》), a foundational Confucian text of the Warring States period. Mencius advised King Hui of Liang that a truly righteous ruler's army would be greeted by百姓 carrying food in bamboo baskets and drink in pitchers, eager to welcome the king's forces. The image became a classic metaphor for popular support of a just cause. It was later quoted in Luo Guanzhong's 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms' to describe local people welcoming Cao Cao's victorious troops.
example_zh: 解放军进城时，百姓箪食壶浆，夹道欢迎。
example_en: When the liberation army entered the city, the common people came out with food and drink to welcome them along the streets.

meaning: A legendary reference to a painted dragon breaking through a wall and flying away once its eyes were dotted. It is used metaphorically to describe a person whose status, wealth, or official rank suddenly soars to great heights.
origin: During the Liang dynasty, the renowned painter Zhang Sengyou painted four white dragons on the wall of Anle Temple in Jinling but left them without eyes, claiming they would fly away if dotted. People thought this absurd and urged him to dot the eyes. Soon after, thunder and lightning cracked the wall, and two dragons mounted the clouds and ascended to heaven, while the two without eyes remained on the wall. The story is recorded in Tang dynasty Zhang Yanyuan's 'Lidai Minghua Ji' (Records of Famous Painters of All Dynasties).
example_zh: 他这几年破壁飞去，从一个普通职员一跃成为公司总裁。
example_en: In recent years he broke through the wall and flew away, rising from an ordinary clerk to the company's CEO.

meaning: Cooking sand cannot produce rice, and carving ice cannot make a vessel. This idiom metaphorically describes efforts that are completely futile and will never yield any result, no matter how hard one tries.
origin: This idiom originates from the Song Dynasty scholar Zhang Min's (张渂) work 'Yungu Zaji' (云谷杂记), a collection of miscellaneous notes on scholarship and literature. In the preface, Zhang lamented that trying to reconstruct knowledge from ruined and broken texts was like cooking sand and carving ice — it brought no real accomplishment. The phrase criticizes pursuits that waste energy on inherently impossible tasks, urging readers to recognize when effort is misdirected.
example_zh: 不掌握正确方法就盲目努力，无异于炊沙镂冰，终究白费力气。
example_en: Working blindly without the right method is no different from cooking sand and carving ice — a complete waste of effort.

meaning: This idiom means losing a greater benefit because of coveting a small gain. It serves as a metaphor for seeking only immediate advantages while neglecting long-term interests. The phrase warns against being short-sighted and greedy.
origin: This idiom originates from 'Lüshi Chunqiu' (《吕氏春秋》), compiled during the Warring States period. The chapter 'Quan Xun' recounts how General Dazi of the state of Qi requested gold from the King of Qi to reward soldiers before a critical battle against Yan, but the king angrily refused, calling Dazi a worthless fellow. Qi suffered a devastating defeat—Dazi was killed in battle and the king fled to Ju. Afterwards, Yan soldiers poured into the Qi capital and fought over the vast gold hoards in the treasury. The king's petty refusal to spend a small amount of gold ultimately cost him his entire kingdom, perfectly illustrating the folly of coveting small gains at the expense of great ones.
example_zh: 为省几块钱买了劣质品，结果没用两天就坏了，真是贪小失大。
example_en: He bought a shoddy product to save a few bucks, only for it to break in two days—truly a case of losing big by coveting small.

literal: harness the luan, drive the crane
meaning: To ride upon mythical phoenix-like birds and divine cranes. It is a metaphor for attaining immortality and transcending the mortal world. The idiom evokes the Daoist ideal of becoming a celestial being.
origin: This idiom draws on Daoist imagery of immortals riding auspicious birds such as the luan (a phoenix-like creature) and the crane to ascend to the heavens. Cranes and luans were regarded in Chinese mythology as mounts of the immortals, symbolizing purity, longevity, and transcendence. The phrase reflects the ancient aspiration to escape worldly concerns and achieve divine status, a theme common in poetry and Daoist literature across various dynasties.
example_zh: 诗人向往骖鸾驭鹤的仙人生活，常在诗中寄托出世的情怀。
example_en: The poet longed for the immortal life of riding cranes and phoenixes, often expressing his desire to leave the worldly realm in his verse.

meaning: This idiom metaphorically describes a situation where many things or events emerge rapidly and abundantly, much like fog rising and clouds surging across the sky. It is often used to depict a flourishing or dynamic scene where new developments appear one after another.
origin: No specific classical text is recorded as the origin of this idiom. It is constructed from the vivid imagery of natural phenomena—fog rising and clouds rolling in—which together convey a sense of rapid, overwhelming emergence. The phrase follows the common four-character structure of Chinese idioms and draws on the traditional literary association between clouds and mist with abundance and momentum.
example_zh: 互联网时代，各类创业公司雾起云涌，竞争异常激烈。
example_en: In the internet era, startups have emerged in rapid succession, and competition has become exceptionally fierce.

meaning: Greed for personal gain clouds one's judgment and makes one lose all sense of reason. It is a variant of the more common idiom '利令智昏', both warning that the desire for profit can muddle the mind. The idiom describes someone who, in the face of temptation, forgets about consequences and right from wrong.
origin: The idiom appears in the Qing Dynasty novel '镜花缘' (Flowers in the Mirror), Chapter 92, authored by Li Ruzhen (李汝珍). In the original passage, a character laments that when profit is placed right before one's eyes, one forgets the word 'harm'—this is precisely what is called '利令志惛,' prompting a deep sigh. The expression draws on a long tradition of moral philosophy cautioning that greed impairs rational judgment.
example_zh: 他利令志惛，竟为一点小利出卖了多年的好友。
example_en: Blinded by greed, he actually betrayed his longtime friend for a trifling profit.

meaning: No one picks up lost items left on the road. It describes a society with excellent moral conduct and public order. It is equivalent to the more common idiom 道不拾遗.
origin: The phrase appears in the New Book of Tang (新唐书), in the biography of Kan Qin (阚祾). Kan Qin was a military official whose troops were former bandits who plundered each other. He enforced discipline by executing offenders without exception, even among relatives and old friends. His strict governance was so effective that people would not even pick up lost belongings in the street, reflecting a well-ordered society.
example_zh: 明初法令严明，乡里道不举遗，夜不闭户。
example_en: In the early Ming Dynasty, laws were strictly enforced, and the countryside was so orderly that no one picked up lost items on the road and doors were left unbarred at night.

meaning: Describes a scene where people are constantly coming and going, creating a lively and crowded atmosphere. It conveys a sense of busy thoroughfare filled with foot traffic and commercial activity.
origin: The phrase traces back to Sima Qian's 'Records of the Grand Historian' (史记·货殖列传), written during the Western Han dynasty. The original text states: 'The world bustles for profit; the world hurries for profit.' Sima Qian observed that all human activity—people coming and going in great numbers—is ultimately driven by the pursuit of material gain. Over time, the expression '熙来攘往' evolved to describe any bustling, crowded scene of people moving about.
example_zh: 节日的商业街上熙来攘往，十分热闹。
example_en: The commercial street was bustling with people coming and going on the festival day, very lively.

meaning: 要害 refers to a vital or vulnerable spot that can be fatal. The idiom means to strike the most critical point, either literally in combat or figuratively by addressing the crux of a problem or exposing someone's key weakness.
origin: This phrase originates from the Book of Later Han (后汉书), in the Biography of Lai Xi (来歙). Lai Xi was a prominent general and diplomat of the Eastern Han dynasty serving under Emperor Guangwu. He was ambushed and fatally wounded by an assassin at night, and in his final report he wrote that the attacker had struck his vital spot (中臣要害). Over time the expression came to describe hitting upon the most crucial point of any matter.
example_zh: 他的这番话击中要害，让对方无言以对。
example_en: His remarks hit the nail on the head, leaving his opponent speechless.

meaning: Like thunder that is fierce and wind that is swift. It describes carrying out policies or orders with severity and speed. It also characterizes doing things with great momentum and rapid action.
origin: This idiom is a variant of the more common phrase 雷厉风行, which has been used in Chinese literature since at least the Tang dynasty. The imagery draws from natural forces—thunder's overwhelming power and wind's instantaneous movement—to convey authoritative and decisive action. Over time, writers used 雷令风行 as an interchangeable phrasing to emphasize the commanding aspect of swift execution. It frequently appears in contexts describing governance, military campaigns, and administrative reform.
example_zh: 新局长上任后雷令风行，迅速整顿了长期混乱的衙门纪律。
example_en: After taking office, the new bureau chief acted with thunderous authority and swift resolve, quickly rectifying the long-disordered office discipline.

meaning: To aid those in peril and rescue those who are drowning. It is a metaphor for doing one's utmost to help others in distress or danger. The idiom conveys a spirit of selfless compassion and timely intervention.
origin: The idiom draws on the vivid imagery of pulling a drowning person from water and supporting someone in a precarious situation. While no single classical text is cited as its definitive source, the phrase echoes themes found throughout Chinese moral philosophy, where saving the imperiled is regarded as a cardinal virtue. It reflects the Confucian ideal of benevolence and the duty to assist those facing life-threatening circumstances. Over time it became a common expression for humanitarian rescue and charitable relief.
example_zh: 洪水来袭时，他奋不顾身地扶危拯溺，救出了十几位被困村民。
example_en: When the flood struck, he threw himself into rescuing the imperiled and drowning, saving over a dozen trapped villagers.

meaning: To face death as calmly as returning home. It describes someone who is fearless in the face of death and willing to sacrifice their life without hesitation. The idiom conveys supreme courage and unwavering resolve.
origin: The phrase first appears in the Han Feizi (《韩非子·外储说左下》), a Legalist text from the late Warring States period compiled by the philosopher Han Fei. It quotes a minister comparing himself to the noble lord Gongzi Chengfu, who could inspire soldiers to regard death as going home. The idiom also appears in the Lüshi Chunqiu (《吕氏春秋·勿躬》), a compendium sponsored by Lü Buwei during the Qin dynasty, which similarly praises troops who faced death without fear. Both sources use the metaphor to extol extraordinary martial valor.
example_zh: 战士们视死如归，在战场上英勇杀敌。
example_en: The soldiers faced death as if returning home, fighting valiantly on the battlefield.

meaning: To value what one hears while despising what one sees. It describes a mindset of trusting hearsay and rumor over direct observation and concrete facts. The idiom criticizes those who blindly accept secondhand accounts rather than verifying reality with their own eyes.
origin: The phrase originates from the Eastern Han dynasty scholar Zhang Heng's work 'Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital' (东京赋). In the text, Zhang Heng uses it to mock superficial scholars who rely on hearsay and shallow learning rather than firsthand knowledge. He calls such people '末学肤受，贵耳而贱目者也' — students of shallow learning who esteem the ear and deprecate the eye. The idiom has since been widely cited in classical literature, including the Song dynasty Buddhist text 'Wudeng Huiyuan' (五灯会元).
example_zh: 做学问切忌贵耳贱目，应以事实为依据。
example_en: In scholarship, one must avoid trusting hearsay over firsthand observation; conclusions should be based on facts.

meaning: To monopolize and control a particular area or region, typically referring to a powerful figure or tyrant who dominates locally. It usually carries a negative connotation, describing someone who holds exclusive power over a territory.
origin: This idiom originates from 'Gu Jin Xiao Shuo' (古今小说) by Feng Menglong of the Ming Dynasty, in the chapter 'Lin'an Li Qian Poliufa Fa Ji'. It refers to Qian Liu (later King Qian of Wuyue), who was born during the chaotic late Tang period and came to dominate a region, eventually ruling over fourteen prefectures. The phrase describes how a powerful figure established exclusive control over a territory during times of turmoil.
example_zh: 这个恶霸独霸一方，欺压百姓数十年之久。
example_en: This local tyrant dominated the region and oppressed the common people for decades.

meaning: A fish swimming in a cauldron and a swallow nesting on a suspended curtain. It is a metaphor for someone living in an extremely precarious and imperiled situation, unaware of the imminent danger. The image conveys how fragile one's safety is when the very foundation beneath them could give way at any moment.
origin: This phrase originates from a famous letter written by Qiu Chi of the Liang Dynasty (Southern Dynasties) to the general Chen Bozhi, urging him to surrender to the Liang court. Qiu Chi wrote, 'Your generalship is like a fish swimming in a boiling cauldron, or a swallow nesting on a fluttering curtain—is this not folly?' The vivid imagery was meant to warn Chen Bozhi that his current allegiance placed him in mortal peril. The letter is celebrated as a masterpiece of Classical Chinese persuasive prose. Over time, '釜鱼幕燕' became a fixed idiom denoting a gravely insecure处境.
example_zh: 大厦将倾，众人犹自歌舞，恰似釜鱼幕燕，不知死期将至。
example_en: The mansion was about to collapse, yet the crowd still sang and danced—like a fish in a cauldron and a swallow on a curtain, oblivious that their end was near.

meaning: A metaphor for cruel and tyrannical powerful ministers. The idiom evokes the image of fierce tigers and leopards guarding the nine gates of the imperial palace. It describes corrupt officials who abuse their authority and obstruct access to the ruler.
origin: This idiom draws on ancient imagery of the nine gates of the imperial palace being guarded by fierce beasts such as tigers and leopards. It symbolizes how cruel and powerful ministers stand between the common people and the emperor, preventing grievances from reaching the throne. The phrase is synonymous with the idiom 九关虎豹 (jiǔ guān hǔ bào). Both expressions capture the danger and difficulty of passing through layers of oppressive officials.
example_zh: 朝中九阍虎豹当道，忠臣难进一言。
example_en: With cruel and powerful ministers blocking the way at court, loyal officials found it impossible to voice a single word of counsel.

meaning: Literally meaning 'hair standing on end,' this idiom describes a state where one's hair appears to stand straight up. It is used metaphorically in two ways: to express overwhelming fury and indignation, or to describe intense fear, tension, and alarm. Variants include 毛发皆竖, 毛发尽竖, and 毛发为竖.
origin: This idiom draws from the ancient physiological observation that extreme emotion causes one's hair to stand erect, a phenomenon noted in Chinese literature since early times. The image of hair standing on end as a sign of terror or rage appears in texts from the Han dynasty onward. No single canonical source story is attributed to this particular phrasing, though similar descriptions appear in works such as Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian when depicting figures in moments of extreme fright or fury. Over time, the expression became a standard literary device for conveying visceral emotional intensity.
example_zh: 听闻那声凄厉的惨叫，众人无不毛发倒竖，吓得不敢动弹。
example_en: Hearing that blood-curdling shriek, everyone's hair stood on end and they were too terrified to move.

meaning: To adopt a conciliatory policy toward enemies and win them over, while attracting distant peoples to submit and pledge allegiance. It describes a governing strategy of using gentle, accommodating methods rather than force to bring adversaries and far-off populations into submission.
origin: This idiom originates from the Han dynasty scholar Jia Yi's memorial 'On the Accumulation of Grain' (论积贮疏), presented to Emperor Wen of Han. In the essay, Jia Yi argued that with sufficient grain reserves, the state could use soft power to win over enemies and attract distant peoples—asking rhetorically what could not be accomplished with such an approach. The phrase reflects the classical Chinese political philosophy that benevolence and material prosperity can pacify adversaries and draw faraway populations into allegiance, a strategy favored over military conquest.
example_zh: 古代明君常以怀敌附远之策治理天下。
example_en: Wise rulers of antiquity often governed the realm with the strategy of winning over enemies and attracting distant peoples.

meaning: An unchanging rule or principle. It refers to a law or standard that remains constant and should not be altered over time.
origin: This idiom originates from the essay 'Zhebai Ma Fu' (赭白马赋) by Yan Yanzhi, a literary figure of the Liu Song dynasty during the Southern Dynasties. The original text reads '教敬不易之典，训人必书之举,' meaning that teaching respect follows an unchanging principle, and instructing people is a deed that must be recorded. The phrase has since been used to describe enduring rules or laws that stand the test of time.
example_zh: 治国之道，当遵循不易之典，方能安定天下。
example_en: The way of governing a state should follow unchanging principles so that the realm may be kept at peace.

meaning: To be impoverished, distressed, and thoroughly dejected in spirit. It originally described scholars of meager means who had fallen into hardship and lost their ambition. The idiom conveys both material destitution and the emotional collapse that accompanies it.
origin: The phrase comes from a Qing dynasty anonymous work, 'Dumen Bamboo Branch Lyrics: Ten Poems for Instructors' (《都门竹枝词·教官十首》), which satirized the plight of minor education officials. One poem describes an instructor so broke he has no travel money to return home, stuck lingering in the capital in utter destitution. The line '盘费全无怎去家，穷愁潦倒驻京华' gave the idiom its enduring form. The novelist Zeng Pu later used it memorably in 'Flowers in a Sea of Sin' (《孽海花》).
example_zh: 他晚年穷愁潦倒，连买药的钱都凑不齐。
example_en: In his later years he fell into poverty and despair, unable even to scrape together money for medicine.

meaning: Describes a household thrown into complete turmoil and uproar, with family members quarreling or making a commotion so that no one can find peace. It conveys the image of a home turned upside down by noise and conflict.
origin: This idiom originates from Chapter 116 of 'Dream of the Red Chamber' (红楼梦), written by Cao Xueqin during the Qing Dynasty. In the passage, a character recalls how, when it was once said that Lin Daiyu would return to the south, Baoyu was nearly frightened to death, and the entire household was thrown into chaos. The phrase vividly captures the domestic upheaval caused by Baoyu's frantic reaction, making it a lasting expression for a household in disorder.
example_zh: 兄弟俩为分家产闹得家翻宅乱，连邻居都惊动了。
example_en: The two brothers quarreled so fiercely over the inheritance that the whole household was thrown into chaos, even alarming the neighbors.

meaning: To laugh something off and let it go, dismissing it with a smile rather than taking it seriously. It indicates that one does not attach much importance to the matter at hand.
origin: This idiom originates from the modern Chinese novel 淘金记 (The Gold Rush) by the writer Sha Ting (沙汀), published in the 1940s. In the story, a character delivers a viciously sarcastic remark aimed at another, yet the target merely laughs it off without further reaction. The phrase captures an attitude of treating something as unworthy of serious attention or retaliation.
example_zh: 面对别人的冷嘲热讽，他总是一笑了之，从不放在心上。
example_en: He always laughs off others' sarcastic remarks, never taking them to heart.

meaning: To defend the country's borders and let the people live in peace. It describes a policy of maintaining security at the frontiers while ensuring the populace can settle and prosper without the disruption of war. The phrase emphasizes that a ruler's foremost duty is to safeguard territory and give citizens repose.
origin: The phrase originates from the Biography of Liu Xiong in the Book of Zhou (周书·刘雄传), a history of the Northern Zhou dynasty compiled in the Tang era. It records that the Northern Zhou state had established diplomatic relations with the Northern Qi, agreeing that each side would protect its own borders and let its people rest, refraining from mutual invasion or harassment. Later writers, such as those compiling the Ming History (明史·外国五), reused the phrase to advise rulers that keeping the borders secure and the people at peace was the key to lasting fortune.
example_zh: 王能保境息民，则福可长享。
example_en: If the king can defend the borders and let the people rest in peace, then good fortune may be enjoyed for a long time.

meaning: To endure humiliation and swallow disgrace with patience. It describes someone who bears insults and shame without complaint, often to achieve a greater purpose or maintain composure under adversity.
origin: This phrase originates from the 'Book of the Later Han' (《后汉书》), in the biography of Cao Shishu's wife, the renowned scholar Ban Zhao. The passage instructs that a virtuous woman should accept praise silently, never shirk blame, endure humiliation and disgrace, and always appear fearful and humble—this was regarded as the proper conduct of the lowly and weak. The text reflects traditional Confucian ideals of humility, forbearance, and submission to social hierarchy.
example_zh: 他忍辱含垢多年，终于等来了洗清冤屈的那一天。
example_en: He endured humiliation and disgrace for many years, finally awaiting the day to clear his name.

meaning: Holding hands at a river bridge, a poetic image of bidding farewell to a dear friend. It evokes the sorrow and reluctance of parting, especially between close companions. The phrase is used to describe a deeply emotional send-off.
origin: The idiom originates from a poem by Li Ling of the Han Dynasty, titled 'To Su Wu.' Li Ling and Su Wu had been close friends held captive among the Xiongnu; when Su Wu was finally allowed to return to Han, Li Ling accompanied him to a river bridge to say goodbye. The poem reads, 'Hand in hand we climb the river bridge—where will the wanderer go at dusk?' capturing the anguish of an uncertain farewell between lifelong friends.
example_zh: 老友河梁携手，依依不舍地话别。
example_en: Old friends held hands at the river bridge, reluctantly bidding each other farewell.

meaning: This idiom refers to making every possible effort to rescue or aid someone in distress. The image of crawling (匍匐) conveys urgency and total dedication, suggesting one would go to any length to save another person. It emphasizes wholehearted, selfless assistance in times of crisis.
origin: The idiom traces back to the Classic of Poetry (诗经·邶风·谷风), compiled during the Zhou Dynasty (c. 11th–7th century BCE). The original line reads '凡民有丧，匍匐救之' — 'whenever people suffer misfortune, one should crawl to rescue them' — describing the moral obligation to aid others with all possible effort. Over centuries, the phrase evolved into the four-character idiom '匍匐之救' to denote urgent, wholehearted rescue. It reflects the Confucian virtue of benevolence (仁) and the duty to help those in need without hesitation.
example_zh: 地震发生后，各方力量对灾区施以匍匐之救。
example_en: After the earthquake struck, various forces made every effort to rescue the disaster zone.

meaning: To be of one heart and one virtue, meaning all people share the same mind and work together toward a common goal. It describes a state of unity where everyone is wholeheartedly committed to the same purpose without internal discord.
origin: The idiom originates from the 'Tai Shi' (Great Declaration) chapter, Middle section, of the Shangshu (Book of Documents), one of China's most ancient classics. The text records King Wu of Zhou rallying his forces before marching against the tyrant King Zhou of Shang. He declared that only by being of one heart and one virtue could they establish lasting achievement and endure for generations. The phrase thus became a enduring expression of collective unity and shared moral purpose in the face of a great undertaking.
example_zh: 只要大家一心一德，就没有克服不了的困难。
example_en: As long as everyone is of one heart and one purpose, there is no difficulty that cannot be overcome.

meaning: This idiom describes acting rashly or taking action without careful deliberation. It warns against making hasty decisions driven by impulse rather than sound judgment. It is commonly used as a caution against reckless behavior in uncertain or volatile situations.
origin: This phrase originates from 'Han Feizi: Explaining Laozi' (《韩非子·解老》), a work by the Legalist philosopher Han Fei of the late Warring States period. Han Fei observed that ordinary people easily abandon principles and act recklessly, unaware of how profound and far-reaching the consequences of fortune and misfortune can be. The idiom thus serves as a timeless warning against disregarding reason and acting on impulse.
example_zh: 在局势未明之前，我们不可轻举妄动，以免陷入被动。
example_en: Before the situation becomes clear, we must not act rashly, lest we be forced into a passive position.

meaning: Literally 'dumb mouth, no words' — to be rendered speechless like a mute person. It describes being at a complete loss for words, typically because one's argument has been refuted and one can no longer defend one's position.
origin: This idiom originates from the Ming dynasty collection Stories to Awaken the World (醒世恒言), Volume 8, by Feng Menglong (冯梦龙). In the story, a woman delivers a sharp, well-reasoned speech about proper wedding customs and family obligations. Her words are so compelling that the matchmaker Zhang Liusao (张六嫂) is left completely speechless, unable to offer any reply. The phrase has since been used to describe someone who cannot respond when their argument has been thoroughly dismantled.
example_zh: 面对铁证如山，他哑口无言，无法辩解。
example_en: Faced with irrefutable evidence, he was rendered speechless and unable to defend himself.

meaning: The idiom refers to light spilling through from a neighbor's eastern wall, symbolizing a benefit or favor one receives from others at no cost to the giver. It describes a kind of care or advantage that helps the recipient while causing no loss or inconvenience to the provider.
origin: The phrase evokes the imagery of a poor scholar reading by lamplight that spills through from a neighboring wall, drawing on a cultural motif popularized by the Han dynasty story of Kuang Heng (匡衡), who was too impoverished to afford candles and chiseled a hole in his wall to study by his neighbor's light. While the specific expression '东壁余光' does not trace to a single canonical text, it shares this tradition of deriving benefit from another's resources without diminishing them. The eastern wall (东壁) denotes the neighbor's side, and the surplus light (余光) represents the incidental, costless benefit shared between them. Over time, the phrase came to signify any generous gesture or favorable circumstance that aids one person while leaving the other wholly unaffected.
example_zh: 能借东壁余光完成学业，他心中充满感激。
example_en: He was filled with gratitude for being able to complete his studies by borrowing the surplus light from a neighbor's wall.

meaning: White teeth and red lips. It describes a beautiful, attractive facial appearance, especially used to praise someone's good looks. The phrase highlights the vivid contrast of bright teeth against rosy lips as a mark of beauty.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Ming dynasty play 'Qiong Ju Ji' (琼琚记) by Hu Wenhuan, specifically the scene 'Teasing the Wife Under the Mulberry Tree' (桑下戏妻). In the play, a character describes a woman's beauty by noting her red lips and white teeth, her peach-blossom face, and her green-black hair with willow-leaf eyebrows, and thus could not bear to leave her. The idiom was later popularized in classical vernacular novels such as 'Water Margin' (水浒传) by Shi Nai'an, where it was used to depict handsome young men.
example_zh: 那少年生得齿白唇红，眉清目秀，端的是一表人才。
example_en: That young man had white teeth and red lips, with clear brows and bright eyes—truly a fine figure of a person.

meaning: To be able to draw analogies from one's own nearby experience. It describes the virtue of putting oneself in others' shoes and considering things from one's own perspective to empathize with others. Confucius called this the very method of practicing benevolence.
origin: This idiom originates from the Analerta (《论语·雍也》), compiled during the Spring and Autumn period. Confucius said, 'Being able to draw analogies from what is near at hand can be called the method of benevolence.' He meant that the path to ren (benevolence) begins with self-reflection and empathy—using one's own feelings and situations as a reference point to understand and care for others. The phrase later became a well-known expression for the practice of sympathetic understanding.
example_zh: 教育孩子若能近取譬，以自身经历为喻，效果往往更好。
example_en: If one can draw analogies from one's own experience when educating children, the results are often better.

meaning: The day is growing late and the road has come to an end. It metaphorically describes a situation where one has reached a dead end, with no way forward and resources or options completely exhausted. Often used to depict a person or organization in an extremely dire and hopeless predicament.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), where Wu Zixu of the Spring and Autumn period lamented, 'The day is late and the road is long,' explaining why he resorted to desperate, unconventional actions to avenge his father. The expression was later refined into its current four-character form by the Tang dynasty poet Du Fu in his poem 'Twenty Couplets Presented to Governor Ge Shuhan,' where he wrote that after years of fading prospects like spring grass dying away, he had finally reached the end of his road at dusk. Over the centuries, the idiom came to symbolize being cornered with no remaining options.
example_zh: 这个曾经辉煌的企业如今日暮途穷，濒临破产的边缘。
example_en: This once-glorious enterprise has now reached the end of its road, on the verge of bankruptcy.

meaning: This idiom describes someone or something that is small, delicate, and cleverly cute in appearance. It is most commonly used to describe a person with a petite and lovely figure. The term conveys a sense of endearing charm and refined daintiness.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Tang Dynasty poet Li Bai, who in his work 'Jiangxia Xing' (《江夏行》) wrote fondly of a young woman's petite and charming figure. The word '玲珑' originally referred to the clarity and delicate craftsmanship of carved jade or stone, suggesting exquisite workmanship. Over time, the expression came to be used more broadly to describe anyone or anything small, delicate, and endearingly lovely. It has since become a common literary term in classical and modern Chinese writing.
example_zh: 她身材娇小玲珑，穿上旗袍更显优雅动人。
example_en: With her petite and delicate figure, she looked even more graceful and charming in a qipao.

meaning: Idle chatter and fragmented gossip; trifling remarks unrelated to the matter at hand. It describes rambling, unfocused talk that wanders from the main subject.
origin: This idiom is a close variant of the more common 闲言碎语, with no single definitive literary source. The characters 散 (scattered) and 碎 (fragmented) emphasize the broken, unstructured quality of the speech. It circulated in vernacular Chinese literature as a colloquial expression for aimless gossip. No specific dynasty or historical figure is definitively credited with its coinage.
example_zh: 他只顾散言碎语，正经事却一字不提。
example_en: He only rambled on with idle chatter and never mentioned the real business at hand.

meaning: To cultivate and nurture one's temperament and emotional well-being through refined pursuits. It refers to the practice of engaging in literature, art, or other elevated activities to soothe the mind and refine one's character. Often associated with the leisurely intellectual pursuits of the literati.
origin: The phrase appears in Mao Dun's essay 'How to Appreciate Literary Works,' where he describes how traditional scholar-officials regarded classical poetry, lyrics, rhapsodies, songs, tales, and unofficial histories as 'miscellaneous reading.' After thoroughly studying the Confucian classics and histories, these gentlemen would read such works to 'delight the emotions and nurture the temperament' as well as to broaden their knowledge. The phrase reflects the traditional Chinese literati ideal that literary pursuits serve not merely for entertainment but for moral and spiritual cultivation.
example_zh: 退休后他每日读书练字，怡情养性，日子过得十分充实。
example_en: After retiring, he reads and practices calligraphy every day to cultivate his temperament, living a very fulfilling life.

meaning: To assess a person by examining both what they say and what they do. It emphasizes that true character is revealed only by comparing speech with actual behavior, not by words alone.
origin: The phrase originates from the Chronicle of the Later Han (后汉纪) by Yuan Hong of the Jin Dynasty (265–420). The text records that in ancient times, rulers would examine a person's words and observe their conduct, so that good and evil would become plainly evident. The Tang Dynasty work Old Book of Tang further employed the idiom in the biography of Xue Deng, who argued that officials should be evaluated by first observing their words and deeds, then holding them accountable by comparing reputation with actual performance. The idiom reflects the enduring Chinese principle that judging character requires consistent attention to both speech and action.
example_zh: 用人之道在于察言观行，方能知人善任。
example_en: The key to employing people lies in examining both their words and their conduct; only then can one understand them and assign the right roles.

meaning: To use glib speech to argue cleverly or to sow discord by spreading gossip. It describes someone who manipulates words to cover up faults or stir up trouble through idle talk.
origin: The phrase originates from a memorial written by Ren Fang of the Liang Dynasty during the Southern Dynasties, titled 'Zou Tan Fan Zhen' (Memorial Impeaching Fan Zhen). Fan Zhen was a scholar notorious for his argumentative and contentious nature. In the memorial, Ren Fang accused him of 'playing with his mouth and sounding his tongue' merely to gloss over his own wrongdoings. The expression has since been used to criticize those who employ clever rhetoric to deceive or to sow discord among others.
example_zh: 他整日弄口鸣舌，挑拨同事之间的关系，最终被众人疏远。
example_en: He spent all day using glib words to sow discord among his colleagues, and was eventually shunned by everyone.

literal: hair, bone, stand on end, thus
meaning: Describes a state of extreme fear and alarm. Literally, one's hair stands on end and one's bones feel chilled to the core. It is used when someone is deeply terrified or horrified by something they hear, see, or experience.
origin: This phrase originates from the Ming dynasty vernacular short-story collection 'Stories to Awaken the World' (醒世恒言) by Feng Menglong, in the tale 'Three Filial Brothers Yield Their Inheritance to Gain Renown.' A character named Xu Wu recounts events so vividly and startlingly that his listeners are struck with horror—their hair standing on end and their bones turning cold. The modern writer Mao Dun also employed this idiom in his short story 'New Year,' where a laugh heard by the character Old Zhao leaves him terrified. The expression has since become a common way to describe being chilled to the bone with fright.
example_zh: 听完那个鬼故事，他毛骨耸然，整夜无法入睡。
example_en: After hearing that ghost story, he was chilled to the bone with fear and could not sleep all night.

meaning: To enter a mountain full of treasures but return empty-handed. It is a metaphor for failing to gain anything despite having excellent conditions or opportunities, most often used in the context of seeking knowledge.
origin: The phrase traces to the Buddhist sutra Mahayana Sutra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground (《大乘本生心地观经》), in the chapter Leaving the Worldly Realm (《离世间品》). The original passage reads, 'Like a person without hands, though they reach a treasure mountain, they ultimately gain nothing.' The sutra uses the analogy to show that without the right ability or method, one cannot benefit even when surrounded by opportunity. Over the centuries the expression evolved into the idiom 宝山空回, used to describe someone who wastes favorable circumstances and achieves nothing, especially in the pursuit of learning.
example_zh: 图书馆藏书丰富，若不认真研读，岂非宝山空回？
example_en: The library has a rich collection of books; if you don't study earnestly, wouldn't you be returning empty-handed from a treasure mountain?

meaning: To be stunned as though one were a wooden chicken. It describes a person who is frozen in shock, fear, or bewilderment, unable to react or speak. The idiom conveys a state of being completely dumbfounded.
origin: The idiom originates from the ancient Daoist text Zhuangzi (《庄子·达生》), written during the Warring States period by the philosopher Zhuang Zhou. In the story, a man named Ji Xingzi trains a fighting rooster for King Xuan of Zhou. After forty days of training, the rooster no longer reacts to other chickens' challenges or calls—it stands motionless like a wooden chicken. Its inner composure is so complete that other birds flee in fear without daring to fight. While the original Daoist metaphor praised complete inner stillness and spiritual mastery, later usage shifted to describe being dumbfounded from fear or astonishment.
example_zh: 听到这个噩耗，他呆似木鸡地站在原地，半晌说不出话来。
example_en: Upon hearing the terrible news, he stood rooted to the spot like a wooden chicken, speechless for a long moment.

meaning: Describes tossing and turning in bed, unable to fall asleep. The pounding of the bed and slapping of the pillow expresses restless frustration and agitation when sleep will not come. It conveys intense inner distress that keeps one awake through the night.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Nie Hai Hua' (孽海花) by Zeng Pu, Chapter 3. The original text describes a character whose temper grew increasingly worse — when unable to sleep, he would either pound the bed and slap the pillow, or curse heaven and earth. The phrase vividly captures the restless agitation and sleeplessness born of anger or distress, painting a picture of someone so tormented by inner turmoil that sleep becomes impossible.
example_zh: 他整夜捶床拍枕，怎么也睡不着。
example_en: He spent the whole night pounding the bed and slapping the pillow, unable to fall asleep at all.

meaning: To set up a home and establish residence in a new place, settling there permanently. It describes the act of moving to a new location and making it one's long-term home.
origin: The phrase appears in Guo Moruo's historical novel 'Zheng Chenggong' (郑成功), Chapter 4, where it is used to describe the prospect of settlers moving to Taiwan. Guo Moruo, a prominent 20th-century Chinese writer and historian, depicted the early colonists who could harvest multiple crops per year in Taiwan. The idiom reflects the encouragement for people to settle and build lasting homes in newly developed frontier lands.
example_zh: 他大学毕业后决定在南方这座小城安家落户。
example_en: After graduating from college, he decided to settle down and make this small southern city his permanent home.

meaning: This idiom describes officials who levy and collect wealth from the common people despite their bitter resentment, in order to flatter and curry favor with their superiors. It condemns corrupt governance that sacrifices the welfare of the populace for personal advancement and political gain.
origin: The phrase reflects a pattern observed throughout Chinese imperial history, where venal local officials exploited ordinary subjects by imposing excessive taxes and levies, then used the extracted wealth to bribe and ingratiate themselves with higher authorities. Such behavior was repeatedly criticized in memorials to the throne and historical chronicles, particularly during the late Tang, Song, and Ming dynasties when bureaucratic corruption was rampant. The expression encapsulates the moral condemnation found in Confucian political thought toward those who abuse public office for private gain.
example_zh: 贪官敛怨求媚，最终被朝廷革职查办。
example_en: The corrupt official exploited the people to flatter his superiors, but was ultimately stripped of his post and prosecuted by the imperial court.

meaning: Literally 'to have personally experienced a hundred battles.' It describes someone who has been through many battles or hardships and is therefore highly experienced and battle-hardened. The idiom is commonly used to praise veterans or people with extensive practical experience in their field.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Zizhi Tongjian' (Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance), in the annals of the Later Tang dynasty, during the Tongguang era of Emperor Zhuangzong (925 CE). The passage notes that some ministers had followed the emperor for many years and personally experienced a hundred battles, yet their rewards amounted to no more than a single prefecture. The phrase was used to highlight the disparity between the ministers' long, arduous service and their meager compensation, emphasizing their extensive military experience.
example_zh: 这位身经百战的老将军依然坚守在国防第一线。
example_en: This battle-hardened old general still stands firm on the front line of national defense.

meaning: Literally meaning to personally take the lead among soldiers. It is a metaphor for a leader setting an example by being the first to step forward, standing at the forefront of the people. Similar to 身先士卒, it describes leading by personal example rather than by command.
origin: The phrase originates from a Tang Dynasty text by Zhang Yue (张说), titled 'A Proclamation on the Suppression of the Khitan Rebels in Jizhou for the Prince of Henei, Wu Yizong.' In the proclamation, the author declared the determination to personally brave the enemy's blades and take the lead at the front lines of the soldiers, relying on divine military power to defeat the enemy. The expression highlights a commander's commitment to leading from the front rather than directing from behind.
example_zh: 作为团队的负责人，他在每个项目中都躬先士卒，带领大家攻坚克难。
example_en: As the team leader, he personally took the lead in every project, guiding everyone to overcome difficulties.

meaning: Literally meaning that a mere breath or light touch could break it. It describes skin—especially facial skin—as being so delicate, fine, and tender that it seems it would burst at the slightest puff or tap. The idiom is commonly used to praise exceptionally smooth and youthful complexion.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty novel Qilu Yuan (《歧路灯》) by Li Lüyuan, specifically in its seventy-seventh chapter. In the original passage, a character's face is described as fair as a white snowball, flushing with the color of peach blossoms, and so delicate that it seemed it could be broken by a breath or a flick—'真乃吹弹得破.' The expression has since become a classical poetic descriptor for flawlessly smooth skin.
example_zh: 她那吹弹得破的肌肤令在场的宾客赞叹不已。
example_en: Her skin, so delicate it seemed it could break at a breath, drew admiration from all the guests present.

meaning: Describes a martial and imposing appearance, evoking the image of a powerful warrior. It is commonly used to refer to brave military commanders or heroic fighters who possess a commanding physical presence.
origin: This phrase appears in Chapter 4 of the Qing dynasty novel 'Sui Tang Yanyi' (Romance of Sui and Tang) by Chu Renhuo, where it is used to depict a heroic figure with a commanding aura and formidable bearing. The imagery combines a swallow's chin and a tiger's head, both classical markers of a valiant martial appearance. Such descriptions were a staple of classical Chinese historical fiction for portraying formidable generals and warriors.
example_zh: 只见他燕颔虎头，体格魁梧，一看便是个习武之人。
example_en: With his imposing features and burly frame, he looked at first glance like a seasoned martial artist.

meaning: To change established customs and social habits. It is a variant of the more common idiom 移风易俗, conveying the same idea of reforming outdated traditions to bring about social progress.
origin: This idiom does not have a single well-documented origin story in classical literature. It is a variant phrasing of 移风易俗, a concept that appears in early texts such as the Book of Rites (礼记) and the Han Feizi (韩非子). The idea of transforming social customs was a recurring theme in ancient Chinese governance philosophy, reflecting the belief that rulers and reformers should guide the people toward better practices.
example_zh: 新政府推行迁风移俗的政策，努力改变落后的社会风气。
example_en: The new government implemented policies to change customs and transform backward social attitudes.

meaning: Describes a person growing increasingly emaciated due to old age and illness. The image evokes a leather belt whose buckle must be moved to a tighter hole as the wearer's waist shrinks from wasting away. It conveys a gradual, visible decline in health and physical condition.
origin: The idiom originates from the 'Biography of Shen Yue' in the History of the Southern Dynasties (南史·沈约传). Shen Yue (441–513) was a prominent scholar and official of the Southern Liang Dynasty, renowned for his literary achievements. In his later years he suffered from chronic illness, and he described himself as old and sickly, recounting that over the course of a hundred days he constantly had to shift the buckle of his leather belt to a tighter hole as his body wasted away. This vivid image of a loosening belt became a lasting metaphor for progressive emaciation.
example_zh: 他久病缠身，革带移孔，已不复当年的健壮体魄。
example_en: Ravaged by chronic illness, he grew so gaunt that his belt had to be tightened hole by hole, no longer the robust figure he once was.

meaning: To band closely together and act as one unified group. It describes people who maintain a tight-knit alliance, often implying exclusivity or cliquish behavior in their relationships.
origin: This idiom originates from the novel 'College Years' (大学时代) by the modern writer Cheng Shuzhen (程树榛). In the story, a character named Liu Xiangming and two others banded together to pursue fanciful scientific research, creating a bad influence among their classmates. The phrase vividly captures the image of people embracing tightly into a single mass, symbolizing close-knit solidarity that can carry either positive or negative connotations.
example_zh: 公司里的几个部门经理抱成一团，排挤其他同事。
example_en: Several department managers in the company banded together to ostracize their other colleagues.

meaning: To find a way to survive when in the most desperate and dangerous situation. It describes the moment when all hope seems lost but a path to survival suddenly appears. The idiom emphasizes the unexpected turnaround from certain doom to deliverance.
origin: The phrase derives from a saying recorded in the Ming dynasty work 'Jingshi Tongyan' (警世通言) by Feng Menglong (冯梦龙), in the chapter 'Gui Yuanwai Tuqiong Chanhui' (桂员外途穷忏悔). The original expression used is '吉人天相，绝处逢生' — 'fortunate people are protected by heaven, and those in desperate straits may yet find life.' Over time, '绝路逢生' emerged as a variant, substituting '处' (place/situation) with '路' (road/path) while preserving the same meaning of finding survival at a dead end.
example_zh: 被困山洞三天后，救援队终于赶到，大家绝路逢生。
example_en: After being trapped in the cave for three days, the rescue team finally arrived and everyone found life at a dead end.

meaning: To swear that two opposing parties cannot coexist. It describes a situation where the hatred or enmity between two sides is so deep that they cannot exist at the same time. It expresses an uncompromising determination to defeat one's enemy.
origin: This idiom originates from 'Strategies of the Warring States' (战国策·楚策一), where a strategist explained to the King of Chu that the states of Qin and Chu were fundamentally antagonistic — when Chu was strong, Qin was weak, and vice versa, so the two could not stand simultaneously. The phrase was later popularized in Luo Guanzhong's 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms,' where the general Zhou Yu declares his sworn enmity against the warlord Cao Cao, refusing to coexist with him.
example_zh: 在国家危难之时，他与敌人誓不两立。
example_en: In a time of national crisis, he swore never to coexist with the enemy.

meaning: To build up a household and establish a career. It describes the process of achieving both domestic stability and professional success, often through hard work and prudent management. The phrase emphasizes the dual goals of family prosperity and career accomplishment.
origin: The idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel Qilu Deng (歧路灯) by Li Luyuan, where it appears in Chapter 12. In the original context, it is used to describe the ideal outcome of a capable person managing their affairs well—building a thriving family and establishing a solid livelihood. The phrase later gained wider currency through works like Li Baojia's Guanchang Xianxing Ji (官场现形记), where it described someone who accumulated wealth and established a business through their position.
example_zh: 他靠自己的勤奋和节俭，终于兴家立业，过上了安稳的日子。
example_en: Through his own diligence and frugality, he finally built up his household and established a career, living a stable life.

meaning: A metaphor for two parties locked in a standoff, each refusing to yield, while a third party reaps the benefit. It warns that mutual conflict often leaves both sides weakened and opens the door for an outsider to profit. The phrase alludes to the fable of a snipe and a clam locked together, both unable to escape.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty work 'Hutian Lu' (壶天录) by Baiyi Jushi, where it is used to describe pointless mutual harm between contending parties. The underlying fable itself traces back to the Warring States period, recounted in 'Zhanguo Ce' (战国策). In that story, a snipe tries to peck at a clam's flesh, and the clam clamps down on the snipe's beak. Neither will let go, and a passing fisherman easily catches them both. The tale was originally used by the strategist Su Dai to persuade the King of Zhao against attacking Yan, lest Qin benefit as the third party.
example_zh: 鹬蚌相斗的结局只会让第三方得利。
example_en: When two sides stubbornly fight each other, the only outcome is that a third party benefits.

literal: constrained by text, dragged by meaning
meaning: To be overly rigid about the literal meaning of words and texts. It describes a pedantic mindset that fixates on surface-level interpretation rather than grasping the intended spirit or substance. Such literalism often leads to misreading the true intent behind what is written or said.
origin: This idiom has no single classical origin story but draws on the long-standing tension in Chinese scholarship between literalism and holistic understanding. The character 拘 means to be constrained or bound, while 牵 means to be dragged or entangled, together conveying the image of someone trapped by the letter of a text. Confucian scholars across dynasties debated whether to interpret the classics strictly by their words or to seek their underlying spirit. The phrase reflects the critique that excessive attachment to textual details obscures genuine comprehension.
example_zh: 读书若拘文牵义，便难得其真意。
example_en: If one reads while rigidly fixating on literal wording, the true meaning will remain elusive.

meaning: A magnificent and spectacular sight. It describes a rich, diverse, and abundant display of fine things, evoking a sense of grandeur and overwhelming variety.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Daoist text Zhuangzi, in the chapter 'Heaven and Earth' (《庄子·天地》), where the Dao is described as that which covers and sustains all things, 'vast and grand indeed' (洋洋乎大哉). Over time, the expression was condensed into the four-character idiom 洋洋大观, used to characterize scenes or collections of remarkable abundance and splendor. It is commonly applied to art, literature, exhibitions, and any gathering of numerous noteworthy items.
example_zh: 这场艺术展览汇集了各国大师的精品，令人觉得洋洋大观。
example_en: This art exhibition gathers masterpieces from around the world, presenting a truly magnificent and varied spectacle.

meaning: To promote upright and clean conduct while inspiring the moral standards of society. It describes the act of championing integrity to positively influence public customs and values.
origin: This idiom originates from classical Chinese moral philosophy, reflecting the Confucian ideal that virtuous individuals should actively elevate societal standards. The phrase combines the concepts of 'raising up the clear' (promoting integrity) and 'encouraging customs' (motivating public morals). Though no single definitive literary source is recorded, it embodies the long-standing tradition in Chinese culture of using personal righteousness to reform and uplift community values.
example_zh: 他一生为官清廉，立志扬清厉俗，深受百姓敬重。
example_en: Throughout his life as an official he remained uncorrupted, resolving to promote integrity and inspire public morals, earning the deep respect of the common people.

meaning: To strut around looking cocky and self-important, displaying an arrogant and smug demeanor. It describes someone who acts as though they are extraordinary and wants everyone to notice.
origin: This idiom comes from modern Chinese literature, specifically from the short story 'One Autumn Evening' (一个秋天晚上) by the Sichuanese writer Sha Ting (沙汀), active in the 20th century. In the story, the author remarks on the most peculiar thing being those swaggering ruffians who behaved just like dogs. The phrase captures the theatrical, boastful display of people who think highly of themselves. Over time it became a common expression for anyone showing off with an air of superiority.
example_zh: 他刚升了小组长，就神气活现地对大家指手画脚。
example_en: He just got promoted to team leader and is already swaggering around, bossing everyone about.
