example_en: After retirement, the old gentleman tended flowers and sipped tea in his courtyard, savoring a touch of leisurely elegance.

meaning: A metaphor for harboring a secret, ulterior motive or guilty conscience. It describes someone who conceals something they dare not reveal to others, often because of wrongdoing or improper intentions.
origin: This idiom originates from the Ming Dynasty collection 'Er Ke Pai An Jing Qi' (二刻拍案惊奇) by Ling Mengchu (凌濛初). In one story, the character Su Mei harbored a guilty secret she could not share with anyone, and could only sigh and look distressed before quietly retiring to her room. The phrase vividly compares a hidden guilty conscience to carrying a ghost fetus inside—one's heart.
example_zh: 他心怀鬼胎，不敢直视我的眼睛。
example_en: Harboring a guilty conscience, he didn't dare to look me in the eye.

meaning: This idiom is a vivid metaphor for expressing the utmost loyalty and sincere devotion. It describes someone willing to sacrifice everything—even their own blood and vital organs—to demonstrate their absolute faithfulness and earnest commitment. It is synonymous with the expression '沥血叩心' (dripping blood and striking the heart).
origin: The idiom does not have a single definitive origin story documented in classical texts. It belongs to a family of Chinese idioms that use visceral body imagery—blood, liver, heart—to convey absolute sincerity and loyalty. The imagery of baring one's liver and dripping blood draws on the ancient Chinese cultural belief that one's inner organs represent one's truest self, and revealing them symbolizes complete honesty and devotion. Related expressions such as '披肝沥胆' (baring liver and dripping gall) appear in texts dating back to the Han and Tang dynasties, where officials and scholars used such language to declare unwavering allegiance to their rulers or causes.
example_zh: 他对国家沥血披肝，毕生奉献于民族复兴事业。
example_en: He devoted himself to the nation with unwavering loyalty, dedicating his entire life to the cause of national rejuvenation.

meaning: Originally, the saying describes someone who, because a person choked to death while eating, wanted to forbid everyone in the world from eating—an absurd notion. As a metaphor, it means giving up an entire endeavor simply because of a minor mishap or fear of potential problems. It criticizes the overreaction of abandoning worthwhile work due to a small setback.
origin: This idiom originates from the Lüshi Chunqiu (《吕氏春秋》), specifically the chapter 'Dang Bing' (荡兵, 'On Military Affairs'), compiled during the Warring States period under the patronage of Lü Buwei. The text observes that if someone chokes to death, wanting to ban all food in the world would be a paradoxical and absurd response. The author uses this analogy to argue against abolishing armies and warfare merely because conflicts occasionally cause harm. Over time, the phrase came to broadly describe abandoning a worthwhile pursuit due to an isolated mishap.
example_zh: 我们不能因为一次失败就因噎废食，放弃整个计划。
example_en: We must not abandon the entire plan after a single failure—that would be like refusing to eat for fear of choking.

meaning: Describes artistic skill or craftsmanship so extraordinary that it appears to have been wrought by supernatural forces rather than human hands. It is used to praise workmanship so exquisite it seems beyond mortal capability.
origin: This idiom originates from the poem 'Cloud Gorge' (《云峡》) by Yuan Haowen (元好问), a prominent poet of the Jin Dynasty (金朝). In the poem, Yuan marvels at a wondrous natural object, asking how many such masterpieces exist between heaven and earth — carved by ghosts and chiseled by gods. The phrase emphasizes that nature's creations are so breathtakingly refined they appear to be the handiwork of supernatural beings rather than any human artisan.
example_zh: 这座石窟的造像精美绝伦，真可谓鬼刻神劖，令人叹为观止。
example_en: The statues in this grotto are so exquisitely carved — truly the work of ghosts and gods — that one cannot help but marvel.

meaning: Striking the grass startles the snake hidden within. It originally meant that punishing one party alerts another to become cautious. It now mostly describes acting carelessly and inadvertently putting the opponent on guard. It is a variant of the more common idiom 打草惊蛇.
origin: The phrase originates from the Song dynasty Chan Buddhist text 《景德传灯录》, in the record of Zen Master Shengnian (省念禅师). When asked by a monk what teaching he expounded while surrounded by the four assemblies of followers, the master replied simply '打草蛇惊' — beating the grass startles the snake. The Song dynasty philosopher Zhu Xi later used the phrase in a letter, expressing concern that seeing another reprimanded would put people on guard and make them afraid to act.
example_zh: 警方在调查此案时务必谨慎，以免打草蛇惊让嫌疑人提前销毁证据。
example_en: The police must investigate this case carefully, so as not to beat the grass and startle the snake, letting the suspect destroy evidence in advance.

meaning: Describes someone talking incessantly and with animated agitation, arguing passionately about right and wrong. The vivid image evokes lips flapping open and a mustache bristling as one pontificates at length.
origin: This idiom originates from Yan Fu's (严复) late Qing essay '论中国分党' (On Chinese Factions). Yan Fu, a renowned reformist translator, criticized ultra-conservative scholars who, despite their esteemed reputations, refused to genuinely engage with Western knowledge. When confronted with Western science and technology, these conservatives would superficially cite classical texts to justify their positions, arguing endlessly without shame. The phrase paints a vivid portrait of such a person—lips flapping and mustache standing—as they pontificate.
example_zh: 他在会上张唇植髭，滔滔不绝地反驳新方案，却提不出半点建设性意见。
example_en: At the meeting, he talked on and on with animated agitation, rebutting the new proposal yet unable to offer a single constructive suggestion.

meaning: To formulate strategy and make decisive plans from behind the lines rather than on the battlefield. It describes directing military or important affairs from a rear command position, emphasizing strategic thinking over frontline action.
origin: This phrase originates from the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) by Sima Qian, set during the founding of the Han Dynasty. After defeating his rival Xiang Yu and unifying China, Emperor Gaozu (Liu Bang) credited his three great ministers, singling out the strategist Zhang Liang (courtesy name Zifang). Liu Bang admitted that when it came to devising plans inside the command tent and securing victory a thousand li away, he was no match for Zhang Liang. The idiom thus celebrates the power of masterful behind-the-scenes strategic planning.
example_zh: 将军运筹帷帐，制定了周密的作战计划。
example_en: The general devised strategy in the command tent and drew up a thorough battle plan.

meaning: Refers to all kinds of trades and professions. The numbers 'nine' and 'eight' are used figuratively to indicate a wide variety of occupations. It is often used to describe the diverse range of work people do across society.
origin: This idiom appears in Gu Xiaoyan's novel 'What Are You Thinking About' (《你在想什么》). In the passage, the author describes the mine as the most fascinating place outside of mythological fairylands, and states that among the three teachings and nine schools, the nine trades and eight professions, miners are the most noble occupation. The phrase builds on the traditional Chinese rhetorical pattern of using numbers like nine and eight to denote comprehensiveness and variety.
example_zh: 这座城市里九行八业的人都有，热闹非凡。
example_en: In this city there are people from all kinds of trades and professions, and it is bustling with activity.

literal: Shen star, Shang star, of, worry
meaning: 参 (Shen) and 商 (Shang) are two stars that rise and set alternately, never appearing together in the sky. 虞 means worry or apprehension. This idiom describes the anxiety of being permanently separated from someone and unable to meet, or the concern that a relationship may become strained and discordant.
origin: The names 参 and 商 refer to two of the twenty-eight lunar mansions in ancient Chinese astronomy. 参 (Shen) sits in the west while 商 (Shang, also known as the Heart mansion) sits in the east; as one rises the other sets, so the two can never be seen together. This celestial phenomenon was immortalized by the Tang poet Du Fu in his famous line '人生不相见，动如参与商' (In life, people fail to meet, moving like Shen and Shang). The addition of 虞 (worry) forms the idiom, expressing the sorrow of irreparable separation or the fear of estrangement between once-close people.
example_zh: 两人虽情深意重，却因战火分隔两地，常有参商之虞。
example_en: Though deeply devoted to each other, the two were separated by war and often feared they would never meet again, like the stars Shen and Shang.

meaning: Refers to a foolishly naive person who shows misplaced mercy to evil people. Named after Mr. Dongguo, who rescued a wolf only to nearly be eaten by it. Used to criticize blind kindness that endangers oneself.
origin: The idiom originates from the Ming dynasty tale 'The Tale of the Wolf of Zhongshan' (《中山狼传》) attributed to Ma Zhongxi. In the story, a scholar named Mr. Dongguo rescues a wolf being hunted by Zhao Jianzi, hiding it in his book bag. Once the danger passes, the wolf turns on him and attempts to eat him. He is saved only by a passing farmer who tricks the wolf back into the bag and kills it.
example_zh: 你对这些骗子大发善心，简直是东郭先生。
example_en: Showing mercy to these scammers makes you a regular Mr. Dongguo.

meaning: This idiom describes someone who speaks with complete frankness and directness, concealing nothing. The moment they open their mouth, their true inner character is as plainly visible as the gallbladder within the body. It is synonymous with the idiom '开口见心' (to speak with an open heart).
origin: The idiom '开口见胆' conveys the idea of speaking with absolute sincerity and transparency, leaving nothing hidden. It is closely related to the similar expression '开口见心,' both using the metaphor that when a person begins to speak, their innermost thoughts are fully exposed. In traditional Chinese medicine and culture, the gallbladder (胆) was associated with courage and one's true nature, so 'seeing the gallbladder' symbolizes perceiving a person's genuine character. No single definitive historical anecdote is tied to its origin; it emerged as a figurative expression of forthright honesty in speech.
example_zh: 他这个人开口见胆，从不隐瞒自己的真实想法。
example_en: He is the kind of person who speaks with complete frankness and never conceals his true thoughts.

meaning: To wrap something in multiple layers and carefully store it away, indicating that one treasures and cherishes the item greatly. It describes the act of preserving something with the utmost care and reverence, as if it were an invaluable treasure.
origin: The idiom originates from a story recorded in the lost ancient text 'Kanzi,' preserved in the 'Taiping Yulan' (Imperial Readings of the Taiping Era), compiled by Li Fang during the Northern Song dynasty. The tale tells of a foolish man from the state of Song who found a worthless stone from the state of Yan near Wutai and treasured it as a great treasure. When a visitor from the state of Zhou came to see it, the host dressed in formal attire to reveal the treasure, which was stored in ten layers of ornate boxes and wrapped in ten layers of fine red silk. The phrase describing these ten layers of boxes and ten wrappings of silk gave rise to the idiom, originally conveying the practice of carefully wrapping and treasuring items before storage.
example_zh: 这件祖传的玉器被他什袭而藏，从不轻易示人。
example_en: He wrapped the heirloom jade in many layers and stored it away carefully, never showing it to anyone lightly.

meaning: Superficial and trivial; fragmented and lacking substance. Used to describe arguments, writings, or discussions that touch on a topic only at the surface level and fail to reach any coherent or meaningful conclusion.
origin: This phrase originates from the Qing dynasty scholar Fang Bao's work 'Afterword on Liu's Writings' (书柳文后). Fang Bao, a leading figure of the Tongcheng School of classical prose, critically evaluated another writer's philosophical discussions. He wrote that the author's remarks touching on the Way (Dao) were 'mostly superficial and fragmented, with no real conclusion to rest upon.' The critique targeted arguments that lacked both depth and coherence, scattering across trivial details without arriving at any substantive insight.
example_zh: 这篇文章论点肤末支离，缺乏有力的论证支撑。
example_en: The article's arguments are superficial and fragmented, lacking forceful reasoning to support them.

literal: hundred million bitter, ten thousand hardship
meaning: This idiom describes extreme toil, suffering, and hardship. The exaggerated numbers 'hundred million' and 'ten thousand' emphasize that the suffering is beyond measure. It is used to convey that someone has endured tremendous difficulties in accomplishing something.
origin: The phrase originates from the essay '大哀篇' (Essay on Great Sorrow) by Li Dazhao, one of the co-founders of the Chinese Communist Party, written during the early Republic of China period (early 20th century). In the essay, Li Dazhao discusses the responsibilities of those who govern, arguing that since the people place their trust and shelter under their leadership, those in power ought to bear the corresponding duties. He uses the phrase to say that no matter how immense the hardship, there is no room for excuses. The essay reflects Li Dazhao's deep concern for the suffering of ordinary people.
example_zh: 父母亿辛万苦将我们养大成人，我们理应好好报答他们。
example_en: Our parents endured untold hardships to raise us, so we ought to repay them properly.

meaning: Literally meaning a horse or an ox wearing human clothes. It is a metaphor for a person who lacks manners and does not understand etiquette or propriety. It can also refer to a well-dressed person who is morally bankrupt, akin to a beast in human clothing.
origin: This idiom originates from a poem by the Tang dynasty scholar Han Yu, titled 'Fu Reading in the Southern City' (《符读书城南》). In the poem, Han Yu writes that a person who does not understand both ancient and modern knowledge is like a horse or ox wearing human garments. The lines critique those who, despite appearing civilized on the outside, lack the inner cultivation and moral understanding that education and learning provide. Han Yu used this vivid image to urge his son to study diligently and not become someone undeserving of human dignity.
example_zh: 此人虽衣着华贵却毫无礼义，诚马牛襟裾之辈。
example_en: Though dressed in finery, this person is utterly devoid of courtesy and righteousness—truly a beast in human clothing.

meaning: Describes a person whose eyes and gaze are so expressive and captivating that they radiate brilliance and charm. It conveys an alluring, spirited appearance full of vitality. It is synonymous with 顾盼生姿.
origin: The phrase appears in 《二刻拍案惊奇》(Slapping the Table in Amazement, Volume Two), a collection of short stories compiled by the Ming dynasty writer Ling Mengchu (凌濛初). In Volume 22, the passage depicts a wealthy young master surrounded by abundance—surplus grain, extra horse fodder, servants answering his every command—and his proud, radiant bearing as he is flattered and honored by all around him. The line reads: '一呼百诺，顾盼生辉。此送彼迎，尊荣莫并。' The idiom was later used to describe anyone whose glance and bearing are strikingly attractive.
example_zh: 她一登上舞台，顾盼生辉，顿时吸引了全场观众的目光。
example_en: As soon as she stepped onto the stage, her radiant gaze captivated the entire audience.

meaning: A variant of 胡思乱想. It refers to thinking without any basis or engaging in unrealistic, groundless speculation. The phrase describes letting one's imagination wander aimlessly rather than reasoning from facts.
origin: The phrase comes from the Song Dynasty work 'Longchuan Biezhi' (龙川别志) by Su Zhe, brother of the famous poet Su Shi. In the story, Empress Dowager Cisheng was displeased, and imperial relatives mocked her for 'seeking a rabbit in an old nest.' Those who heard were frightened and stepped back several paces. Only the minister Han Qi remained unmoved and said, 'The Empress Dowager should not engage in wild speculation.' The idiom thus became a rebuke against unfounded, anxious overthinking.
example_zh: 他总是胡思乱量，把简单的事情想得很复杂。
example_en: He is always letting his imagination run wild, overcomplicating simple matters.

meaning: To delay and be detained or held up somewhere. It describes lingering or remaining stuck rather than moving forward. The phrase is equivalent to the variant 迁延稽留.
origin: No specific literary origin is recorded for this idiom. It is a compound of two classical Chinese terms: 迁延, meaning to delay or procrastinate, and 羁留, meaning to detain or hold someone back. The combination emphasizes both the act of stalling and the state of being unable to proceed. It is commonly listed as a synonym of the more frequently encountered 迁延稽留.
example_zh: 他因事务繁杂而迁延羁留，未能及时返回。
example_en: He was delayed and held up by numerous affairs and could not return in time.

meaning: To sing praise of someone's achievements and extol their virtues. The phrase typically describes excessive flattery or sycophantic praise of a ruler's or leader's accomplishments and moral character. It often carries a negative connotation, implying the praise is undeserved or motivated by self-interest.
origin: This phrase originates from the 'Records of the Grand Historian' (史记), specifically the 'Annals of Zhou' (周本纪), compiled by Sima Qian during the Han dynasty. The original text reads, 'The people all sang of him with joy and praised his virtue,' referring to the common people of Zhou celebrating their benevolent ruler's good governance. Over centuries, the expression evolved to describe the act of lavishing praise on someone's merits and virtues, often with an implication of excessive or self-serving flattery rather than genuine admiration.
example_zh: 这篇文章通篇歌功颂德，毫无客观可言。
example_en: This article is filled from beginning to end with praise of merits and virtues, with no objectivity whatsoever.

meaning: Refers to Changbai Mountain (长白山) and the Heilongjiang River (黑龙江), collectively symbolizing Northeast China. It is commonly used to describe the northeastern region of China, its landscape, and its cultural heritage.
origin: The phrase originates from the 'History of Jin' (《金史·世纪》), which records the birthplace of the Jurchen people as having the Huntong River and Changbai Mountain. The Huntong River was also called the Heilongjiang (Black Dragon River), giving rise to the expression 'white mountain and black water.' The term has since become a poetic shorthand for the Manchurian homeland and the broader Northeast China region.
example_zh: 白山黑水之间孕育了无数英勇的儿女，他们为保卫家园付出了巨大牺牲。
example_en: Between the white mountains and black waters, countless brave sons and daughters were nurtured, who made great sacrifices to defend their homeland.

meaning: This idiom refers to the legendary Emperor Yu the Great's diligence in controlling floods and his deep appreciation of time. It uses 'cun yin' (an inch of a sundial's shadow, i.e., a brief moment) to emphasize the importance of valuing every second. It serves as praise for those who are tireless and devoted to their work.
origin: This idiom originates from the legend of Yu the Great (大禹), a sage king of ancient China who devotedly tamed the great floods. During his thirteen years of flood control, Yu was said to have passed his own home three times without entering, so consumed was he by his mission. The phrase captures how Yu treasured even the smallest unit of time—represented by 'cun yin,' an inch of a sundial's shadow—to accomplish his monumental task. The idiom celebrates Yu's virtue of diligence and has been used throughout Chinese history to encourage treasuring time.
example_zh: 他常以禹惜寸阴自勉，珍惜每一分每一秒。
example_en: He often encouraged himself with the example of Yu cherishing every inch of time, treasuring every minute and second.

meaning: To wash one's neck clean and stretch it under the executioner's blade. It is a metaphor for passively awaiting destruction or death without any resistance. The phrase vividly depicts someone resigned to their fate, making no effort to fight back.
origin: No single classical text is credited as the definitive origin of this idiom. The imagery draws upon ancient execution customs, where a condemned prisoner would have their neck washed before being beheaded. Over time, the phrase became a literary metaphor used in historical novels and vernacular fiction to describe those who surrender to inevitable doom. It appears in various Ming and Qing era works depicting scenes of battle and capitulation.
example_zh: 面对强敌压境，守军若不积极备战，无异于洗颈就戮。
example_en: Facing an overwhelming enemy at the gates, the garrison that fails to prepare for battle is essentially washing its neck for the executioner.

literal: gaze, then, give rise to, fear
meaning: To feel fear or awe upon seeing something. It describes a person or thing that appears intimidating or forbidding at first sight, inspiring a sense of dread or reverence in those who behold it.
origin: The phrase traces back to the 'Analects of Confucius' (论语), specifically the chapter 'Yao Yue' (尧曰), compiled during the Spring and Autumn period. Confucius described how a gentleman should conduct himself with dignified appearance and bearing, so that people would feel a respectful awe upon seeing him. He noted that this would make the gentleman commanding yet not cruel. Over time, the expression evolved into a common idiom used to describe anyone or anything that inspires fear or intimidation at first glance.
example_zh: 他那严厉的目光和冰冷的面孔，让人望而生畏。
example_en: His stern gaze and cold expression made people feel intimidated the moment they saw him.

meaning: To eliminate chaos and restore normal order. It is a variant of the more common idiom 拨乱反正 (bō luàn fǎn zhèng). The phrase describes the act of correcting a disorderly situation and bringing back stability and proper governance.
origin: The phrase originates from the Yuan dynasty play 'Chen Tuan Lies Down' (陈抟高卧) by Ma Zhiyuan (马致远), where the Daoist sage Chen Tuan observes the chaos of the Five Dynasties period and expresses his aspiration to dispel disorder and restore governance. The Five Dynasties were a time of extreme turmoil and suffering. Chen Tuan, though a recluse, harbored this ambition despite his withdrawal from worldly affairs. The expression later appeared in Qing dynasty scholarly works such as He Zhuo's 'Yimen Dushu Ji' discussing governance and political restoration.
example_zh: 新君即位后励精图治，立志拨乱反治，使天下重归太平。
example_en: After ascending the throne, the new ruler strove diligently to dispel chaos and restore order, bringing the realm back to peace.

meaning: This idiom describes working or exerting oneself day and night without interruption. It conveys relentless, round-the-clock effort sustained over an extended period. The emphasis is on endurance spanning both daylight and dark hours.
origin: This is a classical Chinese compound phrase with no single literary source attributed to it. It is formed by combining 弥日 (filling the days, i.e., all day long) with 累夜 (accumulated nights, i.e., successive nights), a parallel structure common in classical Chinese. Such binomial constructions were widely used in scholarly and official contexts to describe diligent labor. It appears in various historical commentaries and essays where authors praised tireless dedication.
example_zh: 为完成这部著作，他弥日累夜地伏案写作。
example_en: To finish this work, he wrote at his desk day and night without rest.

literal: grain god, wasp, earth shrine, rat
meaning: A metaphor for people who commit evil deeds while relying on the protection of powerful patrons. Just as wasps nesting in the grain god's temple and rats in the earth god's shrine are left unharmed because of the sanctity of their shelter, villains find safety behind influential figures. It describes those who exploit their connection to authority to act with impunity.
origin: From the Han dynasty text Han Shi Wai Zhuan (韩诗外传) by the scholar Han Ying, Volume 8. The original passage observes that wasps in the Ji shrine—the temple of the grain god—are not attacked, and rats in the She shrine—the temple of the earth god—are not smoked out. This is not because these creatures possess any divine power of their own, but because they take shelter in sacred places that people dare not violate. The observation became a vivid metaphor for wrongdoers who escape punishment by hiding behind the powerful institutions or figures that shelter them.
example_zh: 这些稷蜂社鼠倚仗权贵的庇护横行乡里，百姓敢怒不敢言。
example_en: Like wasps in a shrine and rats in a temple, these scoundrels run rampant in the countryside under the protection of the powerful, while the common people seethe in silence, afraid to speak out.

meaning: To close one's door and cut oneself off from the outside world. It describes a person who deliberately isolates themselves from society and refuses all contact with others.
origin: This phrase originates from the Book of Han (汉书), in the commentary on the biographies of Zhang Liang, Chen Ping, Wang Ling, and Zhou Bo. During the reign of Empress Lü, the political situation was highly turbulent. Wang Ling openly argued in court against Empress Lü's attempt to grant noble titles to members of the Lü clan. After being demoted, he shut his door and completely severed himself from public life, refusing to serve the regime. The historian noted that each person followed their own convictions.
example_zh: 他遭到排挤后杜门自绝，从此不再参与任何社交活动。
example_en: After being marginalized, he shut his door and cut himself off from the world, never participating in any social activities again.

literal: 嫁, transfer, 祸, disaster, 于, to, 人, others
meaning: To shift one's own misfortune or blame onto another person. The idiom describes the act of making someone else bear the consequences of one's own mistakes or troubles. It carries a clearly negative connotation of evading responsibility.
origin: The phrase originates from the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) by Sima Qian of the Han dynasty, in the chapter on the Hereditary House of Zhao. During the Warring States period, the state of Han, facing pressure from the powerful state of Qin, deliberately chose not to submit to Qin in the hope of redirecting the threat onto its neighbor Zhao. The historian records that Han's refusal to join Qin was an attempt to 'shift the disaster onto Zhao.' Over time, the expression came to denote any act of deflecting blame or harm onto others.
example_zh: 出了问题不能嫁祸于人，要勇于承担自己的责任。
example_en: When problems arise, you must not shift the blame onto others; you should bravely take responsibility yourself.

meaning: To win people's submission and loyalty through virtuous conduct and moral character, rather than through force or coercion. It emphasizes that true leadership relies on moral authority to make others willingly follow and respect you. The phrase is often contrasted with ruling by brute strength or intimidation.
origin: The concept originates from classical Chinese political philosophy, most notably articulated by Mencius (孟子) during the Warring States period. Mencius distinguished between winning hearts through virtue (王道, the kingly way) and conquering through force (霸道, the hegemonic way), arguing that a benevolent ruler naturally attracts the people's allegiance. This idea became a cornerstone of Confucian governance theory and was cited by emperors and ministers throughout successive dynasties as the ideal model of rule, standing in contrast to tyrannical methods.
example_zh: 真正的领导者懂得以德服人，而非用权势压人。
example_en: A true leader knows how to win people over with virtue, rather than crushing them with power.

meaning: Describes someone who talks endlessly and in a forceful, overblown manner. It conveys the image of a person chattering on verbosely while pressing their points with excessive intensity. The phrase paints a portrait of garrulous, self-important speech that tires both speaker and listener.
origin: The phrase originates from the Daoist text Zhuangzi (《庄子》), specifically the 'Discussion on Making All Things Equal' (齐物论) chapter, written by the philosopher Zhuang Zhou of the Warring States period. In the original line, '大言炎炎，小言詹詹' (great words are fierce, petty words are verbose), the scholar Cheng Xuanying of the Tang dynasty glossed '炎炎' as 'fierce and vehement' and '詹詹' as 'wordy and wasteful of speech.' Over time the two descriptors were combined into the four-character idiom '詹詹炎炎' to characterize people who ramble on interminably. The example from early twentieth-century revolutionary Zhu Zhixin shows it being used to criticize needless rhetorical excess in political discourse.
example_zh: 他一开口便詹詹炎炎，说个没完，旁人都听得不耐烦了。
example_en: Once he started talking he went on and on, rambling so relentlessly that everyone around him grew impatient.

meaning: This idiom describes people running about to share important news with one another. It conveys a sense of urgency and excitement when significant information spreads quickly through a community.
origin: The phrase originates from the 'Guoyu' (Discourses of the States), a text from the Spring and Autumn period compiled in the Warring States era. In the section 'Discourses of Lu,' it records the phrase '士有陪乘，告奔走也,' referring to the practice of attendants accompanying a ruler and reporting urgent matters by running to relay the news. Over time, the expression evolved to describe the common scene of people hurrying to spread major news among themselves.
example_zh: 胜利的消息传来，人们奔走相告，街头巷尾一片欢腾。
example_en: When the news of victory arrived, people rushed about telling one another, and the streets were filled with jubilation.

meaning: This idiom describes someone who is fair and upright in handling affairs, honest and incorruptible in conduct, and does not bend the rules for personal gain. It is most commonly used to praise officials or leaders who serve the public interest without seeking private benefit.
origin: The phrase appears in Qing dynasty scholar Zhao Lian's work 'Xiaoting Zalu' (Notes from the Howling Pavilion), in the chapter on the histories of the Jin and Yuan dynasties. In the text, an official was first accused of various charges of corruption and cruelty, but subsequently defended with testimony describing him as fair, honest, incorruptible, cherishing of official titles, and respectful of scholars' integrity. The phrase thus encapsulates the traditional Confucian ideal of a virtuous public servant.
example_zh: 他一辈子都要求自己公正廉洁地为百姓办事。
example_en: Throughout his life, he demanded of himself to serve the people with fairness, honesty, and incorruptibility.

meaning: To abandon fame and discard profit. It describes a person who voluntarily relinquishes worldly reputation and material gain in pursuit of a higher moral or spiritual ideal. The idiom conveys a spirit of detachment from worldly desires.
origin: The phrase originates from the Tang dynasty scholar Lu Zhao's (卢肇) inscription 'Stele Inscription for Xinxing Temple in Yizhou' (《宜州新兴寺碑铭》). In the text, Lu Zhao laments that scholars are unable to restrain their desires and greed, and thus cannot leave behind fame and discard profit. The inscription reflects a Buddhist-inspired critique of worldly attachment, urging practitioners to transcend the pursuit of name and gain.
example_zh: 他晚年遗名去利，归隐山林，过着恬淡的生活。
example_en: In his later years, he abandoned fame and fortune, retreating to the mountains to live a tranquil life.

meaning: Orioles sing and swallows chatter. It describes the beautiful and vibrant scene of spring, filled with the pleasant sounds of birds. The idiom evokes a harmonious and lively springtime atmosphere.
origin: This idiom has no single definitive literary source but draws on imagery deeply rooted in classical Chinese poetry. Orioles (莺) and swallows (燕) are both iconic symbols of spring in Chinese literary tradition, celebrated in Tang and Song dynasty verse. The phrase combines the singing of orioles with the chattering of swallows to paint an auditory picture of spring's arrival. Such bird imagery appears frequently in the works of poets like Du Fu and Bai Juyi, who used spring birds to convey renewal and beauty.
example_zh: 春天的公园里莺歌燕语，让人心旷神怡。
example_en: In the park in spring, orioles sing and swallows chatter, filling one's heart with delight.

meaning: Literally refers to a tall, large horse. Figuratively, it is also used to describe a person who is tall and powerfully built. The phrase conveys an impression of imposing size and strength.
origin: The phrase appears in the Qing dynasty novel Sui Tang Yanyi (Romance of Sui and Tang) by Chu Renhuo, in the eleventh chapter. In the scene, a character is described as wearing all new clothes, having neatly packed bedding, carrying weapons, and riding a tall, large horse (高头大马). The vivid description underscores the character's imposing and well-equipped appearance, and over time the phrase came to be used both for magnificent horses and for tall, sturdy people.
example_zh: 那员大将骑着一匹高头大马，威风凛凛地走在队伍最前面。
example_en: That general rode a tall, powerful horse at the very front of the column, looking every inch the picture of martial grandeur.

meaning: Literally referring to the leftover cosmetics—fragrance and rouge—remaining after a woman has applied her makeup. It is used metaphorically to denote literary works composed in the women's quarters, typically delicate and elegant in style. The idiom evokes the refined atmosphere of the inner chambers where educated women wrote poetry and prose.
origin: This idiom draws its imagery from a woman's dressing table, where 剩馥 (remaining fragrance) and 残膏 (leftover rouge) are the cosmetic remnants of her beauty routine. In classical Chinese literary criticism, the phrase was employed to characterize poetry and prose written by women in the inner quarters (闺中). The metaphor suggests that such compositions, like the delicate traces of powder and scent, carry a subtle and refined beauty. No single historical anecdote is associated with the idiom; it belongs to the broader tradition of using cosmetic imagery to evoke women's literary output.
example_zh: 这些闺中诗作虽是剩馥残膏，却也别有一种婉约风致。
example_en: Though these poems from the women's quarters are but leftover fragrance and rouge, they possess a graceful and delicate charm all their own.

meaning: This idiom is a cryptic riddle (隐语) for the two characters "绝妙" (absolutely wonderful). In the riddle, "yellow silk" decomposes into 色丝 which combines into the character 绝, and "young woman" decomposes into 少女 which combines into the character 妙. It is used to praise writing or work as exquisitely done.
origin: The story is recorded in Liu Yiqing's "Shishuo Xinyu" (A New Account of the Tales of the World), chapter "Jiewu" (Quick Understanding), from the Southern Dynasties (Liu Song). The Han scholar Cai Yong inscribed eight characters—"黄绢幼妇，外孙齑臼"—on a stele. When the warlord Cao Cao and his advisor Yang Xiu passed by, Yang Xiu decoded it as a wordplay riddle: yellow silk (色丝) forms 绝, young woman (少女) forms 妙, daughter's son (女子) forms 好, and a mortar receiving spices (受辛) forms 辞, together reading "绝妙好辞" (exquisitely wonderful writing).
example_zh: 先生的书法堪称黄卷幼妇，令观者无不叹服。
example_en: The gentleman's calligraphy is truly a masterpiece of exquisite artistry, leaving all who see it in admiration.

meaning: Similar to the more common idiom 千疮百孔 (a thousand holes and a hundred perforations), this phrase describes something riddled with flaws, defects, or problems. It also conveys that something has been severely damaged or devastated, covered in countless wounds and injuries.
origin: This idiom is a variant of the well-known expression 千疮百孔. The character 痍 means wound or sore, so the phrase literally evokes an image of a body or surface covered with countless wounds and scars. Metaphorically, it came to describe systems, institutions, or places that are full of defects or have suffered extensive destruction. Unlike many classical idioms, it does not trace back to a single specific text or historical anecdote, but emerged organically as a vivid descriptive phrase in Chinese literary usage.
example_zh: 经过这场战争，这座古城已是千疮百痍。
example_en: After the war, the ancient city was left riddled with wounds and devastation.

meaning: A trifling or insignificant matter. The reduplication 区区 emphasizes how small or negligible something is. It is commonly used to downplay an issue or to modestly dismiss one's own contribution.
origin: The expression traces back to the Zuo Zhuan (《左传·襄公十七年》), where the state of Song is described as 区区, meaning small and weak. Over time, the doubled form 区区 came to denote anything slight or negligible. Combined with 小事, it conveys a matter too trivial to warrant concern.
example_zh: 这点忙不过是区区小事，不用专门来谢我。
example_en: Helping out with this is just a trifle—no need to thank me specially.

meaning: To know something as well as if one were pointing at the lines on one's own palm. It describes a person who has an extremely thorough and detailed understanding of a subject. The idiom conveys complete familiarity and clarity about a matter.
origin: The idiom originates from the Analects of Confucius (论语·八佾). When someone asked Confucius about the ritual of the imperial di sacrifice, Confucius replied that he did not know, but added that whoever truly understood this ritual could govern all under heaven as easily as looking at something in the palm of their hand. He then pointed at his own palm to illustrate. The Han-era commentator Bao Xian (包咸) explained that Confucius meant someone who grasped the meaning of the di ritual would understand the affairs of the world as clearly as showing an object resting in one's palm.
example_zh: 他在这个街区住了三十年，对每条小巷都了如指掌。
example_en: He has lived in this neighborhood for thirty years and knows every alley like the back of his hand.

meaning: To abandon both sleep and food. It describes a state of extreme anxiety or intense concentration, where one is so preoccupied that they neglect basic needs like eating and resting.
origin: This idiom originates from the Song dynasty work 'Yijian Zhi' (夷坚志) by Hong Mai (洪迈). In the chapter 'Shen Sees Ghosts' (沈见鬼), it describes a person who, during the summer, suffered from a severe eye inflammation causing such pain that they could neither sleep nor eat. Over time, the phrase came to be used metaphorically for extreme anxiety, grief, or intense dedication to work and study.
example_zh: 得知母亲病危的消息后，他寝食俱废，日夜守在病房外。
example_en: After learning that his mother was critically ill, he was so distraught that he could neither eat nor sleep, keeping watch outside the ward day and night.

meaning: Flowers in a mirror and the moon in the water. It refers to illusions or visions that appear beautiful but are unreal and unattainable. The idiom is used to describe things that look attractive yet have no true substance.
origin: The phrase originates from the Ming dynasty scholar Xie Zhen's work 'Simao Shihua' (Four Mists Poetry Talks), where he discussed how some poetic meanings can be understood, cannot be understood, or need not be understood, comparing them to flowers in a mirror and the moon in the water. He advised readers not to rigidly cling to surface traces of a poem's imagery. The metaphor draws on the classical Buddhist idea that reflections seen in water or a mirror are illusory and intangible. Over time, the expression came to denote any beautiful but unreal or fleeting vision.
example_zh: 那些虚浮的名利不过是水月镜花，何必苦苦追求。
example_en: Those superficial fame and fortune are nothing but moon in the water and flowers in a mirror—why chase them so obsessively?

meaning: Describes someone with outstanding literary talent, especially referring to women. The phrase evokes the image of willow catkins drifting on the wind as a poetic metaphor for snow, symbolizing a gifted and imaginative mind.
origin: During the Southern Dynasties period, Liu Yiqing recorded a story in 'Shishuo Xinyu' (A New Account of the Tales of the World). One snowy day, the statesman Xie An asked his young relatives what the falling snow resembled. His nephew Hu Er suggested it was like salt scattered in the air. His niece, the celebrated poet Xie Daoyun, replied that it was more like willow catkins rising on the wind. Xie An laughed with delight at her superior poetic comparison. The phrase came to symbolize exceptional literary talent, particularly in women.
example_zh: 她自幼饱读诗书，柳絮才高，在文坛上颇负盛名。
example_en: Having read widely since childhood, she possesses extraordinary literary talent and is quite renowned in literary circles.

meaning: To blend or merge into a single whole. It describes how different things combine so seamlessly and naturally that they form one unified entity, as if they were always one. Often used for relationships, styles, or elements that harmonize perfectly.
origin: The phrase traces back to the pre-Qin period, specifically to Guan Zhong's work "Guanzi·Qifa" (《管子·七法》), which discusses governance as an integrated whole. The text states that when governance operates as one unified system, orders can be issued and laws clarified effectively. Over time, the expression evolved beyond political theory to describe any seamless fusion of distinct elements into a cohesive unity.
example_zh: 音乐与画面融为一体，营造出震撼人心的氛围。
example_en: The music and visuals blended into one, creating a breathtaking atmosphere.

meaning: A metaphor for having limited desires and being content with little. Just as a wren needs only one branch to nest on and a mouse drinks only enough to fill its belly, one's needs in life are modest. It conveys the Daoist ideal of simple contentment.
origin: The idiom derives from the Warring States period text 《庄子·逍遥游》by the Daoist philosopher Zhuang Zhou. The original passage states that the wren (鹪鹩) nests in a deep forest yet uses only a single branch, and the mole (偃鼠) drinks from a river yet only fills its belly. Zhuangzi used these images to argue that one's true needs are naturally limited and that seeking more is unnecessary. Over time, the two images were condensed into the four-character idiom 鼷腹鹪枝.
example_zh: 鼷腹鹪枝，吾人所求本不为多，何必营营于名利之间。
example_en: My desires are like a mouse's belly and a wren's branch—I ask for little, so why fuss over fame and fortune?

meaning: Literally describing bizarre rain and blinding wind, this idiom refers to a fierce and sudden storm. It is used metaphorically to depict a swift, violent, and intense struggle or turmoil.
origin: The idiom originates from a Song dynasty ci poem by Liu Kezhuang titled 'Man Jiang Hong,' written to send off his friend Bochang. In the poem, Liu uses the imagery of strange rain and blinding wind to describe the harsh conditions that could not detain his friend's departure by the river. Over time, the phrase came to symbolize any rapid and fierce upheaval, whether natural or social.
example_zh: 黄昏蜃气忽成楼，怪雨盲风引客舟。
example_en: At dusk the mirage suddenly formed a tower, as strange rain and blinding wind drove the traveler's boat onward.

meaning: To flatter and cater to bad people while encouraging and abetting their wrongdoing. It describes someone who panders to evildoers and actively helps perpetuate bad deeds rather than stopping them.
origin: The phrase originates from the 'History of Ming' (明史), in the biography of Zhang Wenming (张文明传). The text criticizes Jiang Bin (江彬), a powerful and corrupt official during the Ming Dynasty, accusing him of catering to evil and abetting wrongdoing, and arguing he should be executed without delay. It also condemns court officials for failing to correct or remonstrate against the situation, suggesting they too deserved punishment. Jiang Bin was a notorious favorite of Emperor Zhengde who abused his power and was eventually executed after the emperor's death.
example_zh: 那些逢恶导非的小人，最终必将受到法律的严惩。
example_en: Those petty men who cater to evildoers and abet their misdeeds will ultimately face severe punishment under the law.

meaning: A metaphor for absurd, far-fetched, or fantastic claims that seem like fiction rather than reality. The phrase draws on the fantastical nature of the Arabian Nights tales. It is typically used to dismiss an idea as wildly improbable.
origin: The phrase literally refers to 'One Thousand and One Nights' (《一千零一夜》), the celebrated collection of Arabic folk tales. 天方 was the traditional Chinese name for Arabia, derived from the Kaaba (天房). The tales—featuring stories such as 'Aladdin's Lamp' and 'Sinbad the Sailor'—were said to be told by Scheherazade to King Shahryar over one thousand and one nights. In modern Chinese, the term came to be used metaphorically for any wildly improbable or incredible statement.
example_zh: 他说不用任何投资就能月入百万，简直是天方夜谭。
example_en: He claimed you could earn a million a month with zero investment—that's pure fantasy.

meaning: Literally meaning 'writing is to convey the Way.' It expresses the classical view that literature and essays should serve to elucidate moral principles and ideas. The phrase holds that literary form is a vehicle for expressing substantive thought or ethical truths.
origin: The phrase originates from the Song dynasty philosopher Zhou Dunyi (周敦颐), specifically in his work 'Tongshu: Wenci' (通书·文辞), where he wrote that writing serves to convey the Way, just as a decorated carriage is useless if it carries nothing. He argued that ornate writing without substantive moral content is like an empty cart — no matter how well decorated, it has no practical value. This became a foundational principle in classical Chinese literary criticism, emphasizing that content and moral purpose should take precedence over rhetorical flourish. The idea later influenced generations of scholars and writers throughout Chinese intellectual history.
example_zh: 古人主张文以载道，认为文章的首要任务是阐明道理。
example_en: The ancients advocated that writing should convey the Way, believing the primary task of an essay is to elucidate moral principles.

meaning: Describes writing or poetry that flows seamlessly from beginning to end, complete and natural, with no visible signs of forced craftsmanship. It conveys a sense of artistic wholeness where every part connects organically as if created in a single breath.
origin: This idiom originates from Ming dynasty poet and critic Xie Zhen's work 'Siming Shihua' (Four Seas Poetry Talks), volume four. Xie Zhen described composing a farewell poem composed on the theme of 'autumn,' where he took up his brush and completed it in a single sitting. The verse flowed forth in one uninterrupted current of inspiration, naturally whole and unified without any seams or forced effort.
example_zh: 这篇文章从头到尾一气浑成，毫无雕琢之痕。
example_en: This essay flows seamlessly from beginning to end, without any trace of forced craftsmanship.

meaning: Originally referring to ascending the hall and entering the inner chamber of an ancient Chinese house. It is used metaphorically to describe someone whose scholarship or skill has progressed from a superficial level to a profound and accomplished level, reaching a very high standard.
origin: This idiom originates from the Analects of Confucius (《论语·先进》), a text compiled during the Spring and Autumn period. Confucius used it to evaluate his disciple Zhong You (子路) for his mastery of music and learning, saying that Zhong You had ascended the hall but had not yet entered the inner chamber—meaning his understanding was solid but not yet at the deepest level. Over time, the phrase came to be used positively to praise someone who has attained a high degree of mastery in study or skill.
example_zh: 他苦练书法二十年，如今已登堂入室，自成一家。
example_en: Having practiced calligraphy for twenty years, he has now attained a high level of mastery and formed his own distinctive style.

meaning: This idiom describes a lively and enthusiastic atmosphere during conversation or discussion, where people talk with high spirits and energy. It paints the image of words flowing as freely and vigorously as a rising wind.
origin: The phrase originates from 'Xin Qixie' (New Tales of the Strange), a collection of supernatural stories by the Qing dynasty scholar Yuan Mei (袁枚). In one tale, two scholars named Zhao and Li encounter a young scholar who invites them to sit down and converse. The stranger speaks with such animation and eloquence that the conversation is described as '言论风生'—words flowing like a lively breeze. The expression has since been used to depict spirited, engaging discourse.
example_zh: 酒过三巡，大家言论风生，气氛十分融洽。
example_en: After a few rounds of drinks, everyone conversed with great animation and the atmosphere was very harmonious.

meaning: To study and investigate the profound and subtle aspects of principles and phenomena. It describes a deep, meticulous approach to scholarship that penetrates the finest details of a subject. The phrase is synonymous with the idiom 研精阐微.
origin: The phrase appears in the writings of the Qing dynasty diplomat and scholar Xue Fucheng (薛福成), specifically in his 'Diary of a Mission to Four Countries' (出使四国日记), dated the twenty-first day of the eleventh month of the sixteenth year of the Guangxu reign (1890). In the original passage, Xue Fucheng argues that the study of profound and subtle truths is a universal principle of the cosmos, and that one need not quibble over who first transmitted or inherited such knowledge. The idiom thus reflects a late-Qing intellectual's appreciation for rigorous, disinterested scholarship as a shared human endeavor.
example_zh: 他对这门学问研精究微，终于取得了重大突破。
example_en: By delving deeply into the subtle intricacies of this field of study, he finally achieved a major breakthrough.

meaning: To deliberately enhance or magnify people's visual and auditory impressions, typically through grand spectacle or ostentatious display. It often carries a critical undertone, suggesting the impression created is superficial rather than substantive.
origin: From the Ming dynasty story collection 'Stories to Awaken the World' (醒世恒言) by Feng Menglong, in the tale 'Li Daoren Walks Alone to Yunmen.' The passage discusses the ancient Feng and Shan sacrificial ceremonies performed by rulers at Mount Tai. It notes that while seventy-nine rulers before the Xia dynasty, along with Qin Shi Huang and Emperor Wu of Han, all performed these grand rites, they were not necessarily virtuous rulers. The ceremonies merely served to whitewash the appearance of peace and awe the public with grand spectacles—hence '侈人观听.'
example_zh: 这些排场不过是为了侈人观听，并无实际意义。
example_en: These ostentatious displays are merely to impress people's senses, with no real substance behind them.

meaning: The crimes are so grave that even the death penalty is insufficient to atone for them. It describes wrongdoing so extreme that no punishment can adequately address the offense.
origin: This phrase comes from Ming dynasty scholar Shen Defu's work 'Ye Huo Bian' (Unofficial Gleanings), in a section discussing the Hanlin Academy's top scholars. Shen criticized the carelessness of official historiographers, noting that accounts drawn from various sources matched only one or two out of ten facts. He concluded that such negligence in compiling history was a sin that even execution could not adequately punish.
example_zh: 这个恶徒残害无辜百姓，真是罪不胜诛。
example_en: This villain harmed innocent people; his crimes are beyond what any punishment can atone for.

literal: turn the sun, return the sky
meaning: To possess immense power capable of reversing an extremely difficult or seemingly hopeless situation. The imagery evokes someone who can turn the sun and move the heavens, suggesting authority that overrides natural order.
origin: The phrase originates from a poem by the Tang dynasty poet Lu Zhaolin titled 'Song of Old Chang'an' (《长安古意》). In the poem, Lu describes the arrogance and unchecked power of powerful generals and ministers in the capital, who vie with one another for dominance without yielding. The line describes how these grandees wield power so great it can 'turn the sun and return the sky,' yet they refuse to concede to one another. The idiom later came to symbolize overwhelming influence capable of overturning desperate circumstances.
example_zh: 他权倾朝野，转日回天之力无人能及。
example_en: His power dominated the court; his ability to reverse the irretrievable was matched by no one.

meaning: Literally means going from door to door with an alms bowl begging for food or donations. It is used metaphorically to describe soliciting help, favors, or financial support from everyone one encounters, regardless of the closeness of the relationship. The term carries a tone of self-degradation and desperate pleading.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Ernü Yingxiong Zhuan' (Tales of Heroic Sons and Daughters) by Wen Kang, Chapter 12. In the original passage, a character warns against borrowing an excuse to go begging among relatives and friends regardless of the depth of the friendship, wagging one's tail and pleading for pity. The imagery evokes a Buddhist monk walking from house to house with an alms bowl, which became a metaphor for indiscriminate and shameless solicitation of aid.
example_zh: 他宁愿沿门讬钵度日，也不愿回头求助于那些势利的亲戚。
example_en: He would rather go begging from door to door for a living than turn back and seek help from those snobbish relatives.

meaning: The idiom draws on the image of dodder vines (松萝) that cling to and lean upon pine trees. It serves as a metaphor for a husband and wife living together in harmony, mutual affection, and interdependence.
origin: This idiom draws on the natural imagery of 松萝 (pine vine), a clinging plant that grows by attaching itself to pine trees. In classical Chinese poetry and literature, the relationship between vine and tree was a familiar metaphor for conjugal love and mutual reliance. The phrase evokes two beings leaning on each other, symbolizing a harmonious and devoted marriage. No specific historical source, dynasty, or figure is recorded for this phrase.
example_zh: 他们夫妻二人松萝共倚，携手走过了半个世纪。
example_en: Husband and wife leaned on each other like pine and vine, walking hand in hand through half a century together.

meaning: Ji Bu was a historical figure renowned for always keeping his word and never breaking a promise. The idiom refers to a promise that is absolutely trustworthy and will certainly be honored.
origin: During the late Qin and early Han Dynasty, Ji Bu was a man from the Chu region celebrated for his unwavering integrity. A popular proverb of the time declared, 'Rather have Ji Bu's single promise than a hundred pieces of gold.' When the scholar Cao Qiu visited Ji Bu, he cited this proverb to explain how Ji Bu's reputation for trustworthiness had spread throughout Liang and Chu. The story was recorded in Sima Qian's 'Records of the Grand Historian' (史记), cementing Ji Bu as the archetype of a person whose word is as good as gold.
example_zh: 他在商界素有季布一诺的美誉，客户都非常信任他。
example_en: He has long enjoyed a reputation in the business world as someone whose promise is as good as gold, and clients trust him completely.

meaning: When you see someone of virtue and talent, you should strive to emulate them and reach their level. It encourages self-improvement by learning from those who are morally or professionally superior.
origin: This idiom originates from the Analects of Confucius (《论语·里仁》), compiled during the Spring and Autumn period. Confucius taught that upon meeting virtuous people, one should aspire to equal them, and upon meeting those lacking virtue, one should reflect inwardly on one's own shortcomings. The phrase embodies the Confucian emphasis on continuous moral self-cultivation through observation of others. It has served as a guiding principle in Chinese ethical thought for over two millennia.
example_zh: 看到同学的优秀成绩，他见贤思齐，决心更加努力学习。
example_en: Seeing his classmate's excellent grades, he was inspired to emulate them and resolved to study even harder.

meaning: Literally meaning 'unable to see the light of the sun,' this idiom is a metaphor for a society or situation so dark and oppressive that no trace of light or justice can be found. It describes circumstances where people live in misery with no hope of relief or fairness.
origin: The phrase originates from 'Dongxuan Biji' (东轩笔录), a notebook by Wei Tai of the Song Dynasty. In the text, the people of Fuzhou lamented that they would go their entire lives without seeing the light of day, suffering under oppressive governance. The expression captured the despair of common people living under corrupt officials who denied them any justice or hope.
example_zh: 在那不见天日的牢房里，他度过了整整十年。
example_en: He spent ten full years in that pitch-dark cell where no daylight ever reached.

meaning: This idiom compares the grief of a filial child who can no longer care for their deceased parents to the wind blowing through trees. It expresses the deep sorrow and regret of a child whose parents have passed away before they could provide for them. The imagery evokes the helplessness of nature's forces against human longing.
origin: The phrase originates from the Han Dynasty text 'Han Shi Wai Zhuan' (韩诗外传) by Han Ying, which records the saying: 'The tree wishes to be still, but the wind will not cease; the child wishes to care for their parents, but the parents will not wait.' This lament reflects the sorrow of Kongzi's disciple Qiu Yu (丘吾子), who cried by the roadside upon realizing his parents had aged and passed before he could fulfill his filial duties. Over time, the image of wind and trees became a metaphor for the grief of losing one's parents.
example_zh: 自父亲去世后，他每每念及养育之恩，便觉风木含悲，泪不能禁。
example_en: Since his father passed away, whenever he recalls the grace of being raised, he feels the wind-and-tree sorrow and cannot hold back his tears.

meaning: To inwardly grasp the essence or main idea of something. It refers to deeply understanding the core meaning of a text or the key principles of a skill, beyond mere surface reading. The phrase emphasizes intuitive comprehension that is difficult to convey to others.
origin: This phrase originates from the 'Records of the Grand Historian' (史记), specifically the 'Basic Annals of the Five Emperors' (五帝本纪) by Sima Qian of the Han dynasty. Sima Qian wrote that since ancient records were incomplete and fragmented, one could only grasp their true meaning intuitively, yet such understanding was hard to explain to those with shallow knowledge and limited experience. The expression highlights that true comprehension of classical wisdom requires both depth of insight and breadth of learning.
example_zh: 读经典著作不可囫囵吞枣，须心知其意方能有所得。
example_en: One must not swallow classical texts whole; only by grasping their inner meaning can one truly benefit from them.

meaning: An honorific term referring to the spirit or soul of the deceased in heaven. It is used to show respect when speaking of someone who has passed away. The phrase conveys reverence and remembrance for the departed.
origin: This phrase appears in Lu Xun's essay collection 'Er Yi Ji' (And That's That), in the piece 'Huanghuajie de Zagan' (Miscellaneous Thoughts on Huanghua Festival), written during the Republican era. Lu Xun argued that people need not weep daily to mourn the martyrs' 'spirit in heaven'—remembering them once a year suffices. The Huanghua Festival commemorates the 72 martyrs of the 1911 Guangzhou Uprising against the Qing dynasty. The phrase has since become a standard honorific for the souls of the departed.
example_zh: 告慰父亲的在天之灵，我终于完成了学业。
example_en: To comfort my late father's spirit in heaven, I have finally completed my studies.

meaning: An old term referring to someone who is well-versed in the Confucian classics and whose personal conduct is upright and principled. It describes a scholar whose academic mastery of the classics is matched by their moral integrity and exemplary behavior.
origin: This phrase originates from the 'Biography of Gao Rou' in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), specifically the Book of Wei. Gao Rou, a minister of the Cao Wei state during the Three Kingdoms period, used this expression to praise the court's scholars. He stated that the current doctors (academic officials) were all '经明行修' — thoroughly versed in the classics and of refined conduct — representing the finest selections of the entire realm.
example_zh: 他一生经明行修，深受乡里敬重。
example_en: Throughout his life he was well-versed in the classics and upright in conduct, earning deep respect from his community.

meaning: Literally referring to powerful bows and sturdy crossbows. The idiom describes formidable weapons and, by extension, overwhelming military strength or force. It conveys the image of an unstoppable, well-armed force.
origin: The phrase originates from Feng Menglong's 'Chronicles of the Eastern Zhou Kingdoms' (明·冯梦龙《东周列国志》), Chapter 90. The text notes that the Han state, covering over nine hundred li with hundreds of thousands of armored soldiers, was the source of the most powerful bows and crossbows in the realm. This highlighted Han's renown for manufacturing superior weaponry during the Warring States period.
example_zh: 城上守军备有强弓劲弩，令攻城之敌寸步难行。
example_en: The defending troops on the city walls were equipped with powerful bows and crossbows, making it impossible for the attackers to advance a single step.

meaning: Literally 'nine out of ten households are impoverished.' It describes a scene of widespread poverty among common people caused by natural disasters, war, or social upheaval. The idiom conveys the devastating economic toll such hardships inflict on ordinary families.
origin: The idiom originates from the Song dynasty historian Ouyang Xiu's 'New Book of Tang' (新唐书), in the section 'Biographies of the Western Regions: Gaochang.' The passage recounts how after the Tang court launched military campaigns to conquer the Gaochang kingdom, the Hexi region was forced to supply provisions and labor for the royal army. The burden was so crushing that nine out of ten households fell into destitution, and it was said the region would not recover even within five years. The phrase thus depicts the ruinous economic cost of war borne by ordinary people.
example_zh: 连年战乱使得这片土地十室九匮，百姓生活十分艰难。
example_en: Years of continual warfare left this land so devastated that nine out of ten households were impoverished, and the people's lives became extremely difficult.

meaning: Completely mistaken and not at all the case. It describes a situation where someone's assumption or belief is entirely wrong and far from the truth. Used to emphatically deny or correct a misconception.
origin: This phrase originates from a letter by the Han dynasty historian Sima Qian, titled 'Letter to Ren Shaoqing' (报任少卿书). Sima Qian, after suffering the humiliation of castration, wrote to his friend Ren An to explain his reasons for choosing to live on despite such disgrace. In the letter he laments that things often turn out to be utterly contrary to expectations, using the phrase 大谬不然 to express that reality is completely at odds with what one had hoped or assumed.
example_zh: 他以为自己稳操胜券，结果却大谬不然，输得一塌糊涂。
example_en: He thought victory was certain, but it turned out to be completely mistaken — he lost miserably.

meaning: To rise or soar suddenly into the sky or high air. It describes something ascending rapidly upward from the ground, often used for objects, animals, or even abstract forces lifting off with great energy.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty novel Sui Tang Yanyi (Romance of Sui and Tang) by Chu Renhuo, in its third chapter. In the story, Li Jing attempts to detain a mysterious woman, but she turns her horse around and the horse immediately soars into the air, vanishing in an instant. The vivid image of the horse launching skyward gave rise to this expression.
example_zh: 火箭点火后腾空而起，直冲云霄。
example_en: After ignition, the rocket soared into the sky, shooting straight through the clouds.

meaning: To be utterly resolved and unwavering in one's decision, with no intention of ever changing course. It describes someone who has made up their mind completely and will not be swayed by any persuasion or circumstance. It is a variant of the more common form 死心塌地.
origin: This idiom is a variant writing of 死心塌地, which appears in classical vernacular fiction of the Ming and Qing dynasties. The expression likens a person's determination to something heavy laid flat on the ground — immovable and settled. It was frequently used in novels such as Water Margin and Journey to the West to depict characters who had given up all hesitation or second thoughts. Over time, 死心搭地 emerged as an alternate orthography in some regional texts and editions.
example_zh: 他既然死心搭地要走，谁也拦不住他。
example_en: Since he has made up his mind to leave, no one can stop him.

meaning: A general term for places of song, dance, and entertainment, most often referring to brothels. 'Qin tower' and 'Chu hall' historically denoted pleasure quarters associated with the ancient states of Qin and Chu, famed for music and courtesans.
origin: The phrase appears in the Yuan dynasty zaju play 'Xue Rengui' by Zhang Guobin. In the third act, a parent grieves that after finally raising their child to adulthood, the child has gone off and treated his parents as though they were as far apart as heaven and earth, losing himself in the Qin towers and Chu halls without any thought for the deep grace of being raised. The line captures the era's association of Qin and Chu establishments with sensual entertainment.
example_zh: 他自幼不务正业，终日流连于秦楼楚馆，把祖传的家产挥霍一空。
example_en: From his youth he refused to do honest work, spending his days loitering in brothels and squandering every bit of his family's inherited fortune.

literal: deceive the sovereign, harm the country
meaning: To deceive the monarch and bring ruin to the nation. The idiom describes treacherous officials who mislead the ruler and cause national disaster. It is used as a grave condemnation of political betrayal and corruption at the highest level.
origin: The idiom originates from the Ming dynasty play "Mingzhu Ji" (明珠记) by the playwright Lu Cai (陆采), specifically in the scene titled "Jianmou" (奸谋, "Treasonous Plot"). In the scene, the villain Liu Zhen is described as domineering and ruthless; he had previously impeached the speaker on the charge of "deceiving the sovereign and harming the state," demanding that the offender be beheaded and the severed head publicly displayed. The phrase thus entered the literary lexicon as a severe accusation of political treachery.
example_zh: 历史上不少奸臣欺君误国，最终落得身败名裂的下场。
example_en: Throughout history, many treacherous officials deceived the sovereign and harmed the state, ultimately ending in total disgrace and ruin.

meaning: To care only about profit and nothing else. It describes someone who is driven solely by self-interest and disregards all other considerations such as ethics, duty, or the greater good.
origin: This phrase originates from the 'Book of Jin, Biography of Wen Qiao' (《晋书·温峤传》). Wen Qiao, a Jin dynasty official and general, described Su Jun's subordinates as people who only cared about profit, being cruel, arrogant, and suspicious. The phrase later became a common expression for describing those who prioritize personal gain above all else. It appears in Qing dynasty writings such as Xue Fucheng's memorials on foreign affairs.
example_zh: 盖彼之商人惟利是视，不顾大体。
example_en: Those merchants care only about profit and disregard the larger picture.

meaning: This idiom describes a journey that is arduous and exhausting, involving the physical hardship of climbing over mountains and crossing through waters. It conveys the difficulty and toil of traveling across rough terrain. It is commonly used to depict long, grueling trips or expeditions.
origin: The phrase appears in Fan Jinbiao's essay 'In Memory of Our Beloved Premier Zhou,' which recounts experiences during the Long March. The author describes how, on the frequently embattled Long March route, over the course of more than a year, Vice Chairman Zhou Enlai climbed mountains and waded through waters alongside the soldiers, braving wind and rain just as they did. The idiom thus evokes the resilience and shared hardship of revolutionary travel.
example_zh: 科考队员们爬山涉水，终于到达了人迹罕至的原始森林。
example_en: The expedition team climbed mountains and waded through waters before finally reaching the remote primeval forest.

meaning: "母难之日" literally means "the day of the mother's hardship." It refers to one's birthday, reminding us that the day we were born was a day of great pain and danger for our mother. The idiom encourages gratitude and filial piety rather than self-centered celebration.
origin: The concept stems from traditional Chinese filial piety (孝), rooted in Confucian values. In ancient times, childbirth was extremely perilous, so a person's birthday was regarded not as a day for self-celebration but as a day to honor the mother who endured suffering to bring them into the world. Classical texts and folk tradition emphasized that one should feel indebted to one's parents on this day rather than rejoicing selfishly. The phrase reflects the deep cultural importance placed on repaying parental love and remembering one's origins.
example_zh: 每逢母难之日，他都不忘给母亲打个电话表达感恩。
example_en: On each of his birthdays, he never forgets to call his mother to express his gratitude.

meaning: A metaphor for steadfast and unwavering loyalty or resolve. It compares the heart to a stone that cannot be rolled or moved, signifying an unchanging determination that external forces cannot sway. The idiom conveys firm moral commitment that remains constant regardless of circumstances.
origin: The idiom originates from the Classic of Poetry (诗经), specifically the ode 'Bai Zhou' (柏舟) in the Bei Feng (邶风) section, dating to the Zhou Dynasty. The original line reads, 'My heart is not a stone; it cannot be rolled away' (我心匪石，不可转也). The poem expresses a person's resolute moral stance that cannot be shaken by adversity or opposition. In the Five Dynasties period, Wang Dingbao quoted this phrase in 'Tang Zhi Yan' (唐摭言) to describe an official's unwavering integrity despite setbacks.
example_zh: 他面对重重诱惑，始终坚守匪石之心，不为所动。
example_en: Facing myriad temptations, he held fast to an unwavering heart and refused to be swayed.

meaning: A single oversight in a hundred careful precautions. It describes a situation where despite thorough and meticulous planning, one small detail is overlooked, leading to an unexpected flaw or failure.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty scholar Wei Yuan's work 'Yong Yi Tong Yi' (《庸易通义》), where he discussed the relationship between knowledge and action in Confucian learning. Wei Yuan pointed out that even in the most systematic approaches to study and self-cultivation, separating 'reviewing the old' from 'exploring the new' could reveal a minor flaw in an otherwise comprehensive framework. The idiom later gained wider literary usage, notably appearing in Mao Dun's novel 'Midnight' (《子夜》), where the protagonist Wu Sunfu fails to see through Du Zhuzhai's true intentions despite his usual shrewdness.
example_zh: 比赛前他反复检查了装备，却百密一疏忘了带地图。
example_en: He checked his equipment repeatedly before the race, but in a hundred precautions overlooked one thing—he forgot to bring the map.

meaning: To follow the circumstances of the times and preserve oneself in obscurity. Originally praising King Wu of Zhou for顺应时势 and biding his time before acting, it now means to temporarily retreat into seclusion and wait for the right opportunity.
origin: The phrase originates from the 'Classic of Poetry' (诗经), in the Zhou Odes section, poem 'Zhuo' (酌): '于铄王师，遵养时晦' — 'Oh, splendid was the royal army; it followed the times and preserved during obscurity.' The original context glorified King Wu of Zhou's wisdom in顺应时势, conserving strength and waiting for the right moment before overthrowing the Shang dynasty. Over centuries the wording shifted to 遵时养晦, and its usage broadened to describe anyone who temporarily withdraws from public life to await a favorable moment.
example_zh: 面对强敌，他选择遵时养晦，暗中积蓄力量。
example_en: Facing a formidable enemy, he chose to follow the times and lie low, quietly building up his strength.

literal: 怀, harbor, carry, 璧, jade, 其, its, 罪, crime, guilt
meaning: Originally meant that possessing a precious jade could bring disaster upon an innocent person, implying that wealth itself can be a cause of trouble. It later came to metaphorically describe someone who is persecuted out of jealousy because of their talent, beauty, or possession of something desirable. The idiom warns that having what others covet can make one a target.
origin: The idiom originates from the Zuo Zhuan (左传), specifically the tenth year of Duke Huan of Lu (桓公十年). A commoner named Yu Shu (虞叔) owned a fine piece of jade that the ruler coveted. When asked to surrender it, Yu Shu initially complied but later regretted it, saying that an ordinary man is innocent until he harbors a treasure—'匹夫无罪，怀璧其罪.' The phrase illustrates how possessing something valuable can itself become a crime in the eyes of the powerful.
example_zh: 他才华出众却遭同事排挤，真可谓怀璧其罪。
example_en: He was ostracized by colleagues for his outstanding talent—a true case of harboring jade and thus incurring guilt.

meaning: This idiom describes construction, architecture, or arrangements so exquisitely wrought that they seem beyond human capability, as if crafted by divine hands. It praises the extraordinary ingenuity and beauty of a structure or design.
origin: The phrase combines 神工 (divine craftsmanship) and 天巧 (heavenly ingenuity), both evoking supernatural skill beyond mortal ability. It has been used in classical Chinese literature to marvel at palaces, gardens, and monuments whose beauty seems to defy human limits. No single definitive textual source is recorded; the expression evolved from a broader tradition of praising extraordinary craftsmanship in imperial and literary writings.
example_zh: 这座千年古刹依山而建，雕梁画栋，堪称神工天巧。
example_en: This thousand-year-old temple was built into the mountainside, its carved beams and painted rafters so exquisite that it seems divinely crafted.

meaning: To feel deeply anxious and unsettled, unable to find peace of mind. It describes a state of inner fear and unease, often caused by uncertainty or threatening circumstances. The reduplication of 惶 emphasizes the intensity of the anxiety.
origin: The phrase traces back to the 'Book of Han' (汉书), specifically the biography of Wang Mang. In the text, the people were described as being in a state of panic, not knowing what to do. The Tang dynasty scholar Yan Shigu annotated this passage, explaining that the term '正营' meant '惶恐不安' — frightened and ill at ease. Over time, the expression evolved into the four-character form 惶惶不安 used today.
example_zh: 战争爆发后，城中百姓惶惶不安，纷纷收拾财物准备逃难。
example_en: After war broke out, the people in the city felt deeply anxious and uneasy, hurriedly packing their belongings to flee.

meaning: One's reputation and social status increase tenfold. It describes a dramatic rise in fame and standing. The idiom conveys how a person's prestige can soar dramatically due to favorable circumstances or powerful endorsement.
origin: This idiom originates from a letter written by the Tang dynasty poet Li Bai titled 'Letter to Prefect Han of Jingzhou' (《与韩荆州书》). In the letter, Li Bai compares meeting a powerful patron to climbing the Dragon Gate, stating that once one ascends the Dragon Gate, one's reputation increases tenfold. The 'Dragon Gate' refers to the legendary gateway that, when crossed by a carp, transforms it into a dragon. Li Bai used this metaphor to express how the endorsement of a dignitary like Prefect Han could dramatically elevate a person's social standing and reputation.
example_zh: 他得到那位名家的推荐后，声价十倍，很快成为业内炙手可热的人物。
example_en: After receiving a recommendation from that renowned expert, his reputation soared tenfold, and he quickly became a highly sought-after figure in the industry.

meaning: The chrysanthemum (黄花) blooms in late autumn when other flowers have withered, symbolizing noble conduct in one's declining years. This idiom praises a person who maintains high moral integrity and virtue even in old age. It celebrates the steadfastness of character that endures like the chrysanthemum's fragrance through the cold.
origin: This idiom originates from a poem by Han Qi (韩琦), a prominent statesman and poet of the Song Dynasty, titled 'Ninth Day in the Small Pavilion' (《九日小阁》). The poem contains the line: 'Do not mind that the old garden's autumn appearance is pale; just look at how the cold flowers keep their fragrance in the late season.' Han Qi used the chrysanthemum, which blooms in cold late autumn when other flowers have faded, as a metaphor for maintaining one's moral integrity in one's later years. The image of the resilient late-autumn flower became a lasting symbol of noble character in old age.
example_zh: 这位老科学家一生廉洁，晚节黄花，令人敬仰。
example_en: This elderly scientist lived a life of integrity and maintained noble virtue in his later years, commanding deep respect.

meaning: Describes a person whose character and conduct are extraordinary, upright, and open. It conveys someone who stands out from the ordinary with a noble and unconstrained spirit. The imagery combines rugged mountain terrain with a sense of distinct individuality.
origin: This idiom originates from a letter by Hao Jing of the Yuan dynasty, titled 'To Miao Dazhi, a Talented Scholar' (寄缪大质茂才). In the letter, Hao Jing writes about laughing heartily and reflecting that all the world's traps and schemes are exhausted. He describes a person as truly '崎嵚历落' — extraordinary and open-minded — a laughable yet remarkable individual. The term fuses imagery of rugged, steep mountain paths with the idea of a distinct, unconstrained character.
example_zh: 他为人崎嵚历落，从不随波逐流。
example_en: He is extraordinary and upright in character, never going along with the crowd.

meaning: A colloquial expression meaning to die or breathe one's last. The term 呜呼 (wū hū) was originally an exclamation of lament commonly found at the end of ancient sacrificial and funerary texts, which over time became a euphemism for death. The full phrase vividly conveys that a person's single life has come to an end.
origin: The phrase combines 一命 (one life) with 呜呼, an ancient exclamation of grief traditionally placed at the conclusion of elegies and sacrificial odes. Over the centuries, 呜呼 evolved from a mere lament into a metonym for death itself. The complete expression 一命呜呼 was popularized in modern usage, notably appearing in Mao Zedong's 1927 'Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan,' where a local tyrant named Tang Junyan reportedly had two beggars killed to inaugurate his brutal reign, and the two beggars 'thus breathed their last.' Today it is used in both serious and humorous contexts to indicate that someone has died.
example_zh: 那个贪官作恶多端，最终一命呜呼了。
example_en: That corrupt official committed countless evils and ultimately breathed his last.

meaning: A metaphor for preparing rare and exotic delicacies. It also describes dishes that are extraordinarily lavish and precious, evoking imagery of legendary feasts.
origin: This idiom comes from the Ming dynasty collection "Yushi Mingyan" (Stories to Enlighten the World) by Feng Menglong, in Volume 11. The text includes a "Zhegu Tian" ci poem depicting a grand city tavern: the towers reach into the sky, dragon and phoenix are cooked for rich and fresh flavors, and a nobleman dismounts his horse, intoxicated by the aroma, drinking freely without regard for spending ten thousand coins.
