meaning: A place where one can stand or plant one's feet. Metaphorically, it refers to a place or position where one can live, survive, or establish oneself in society. It often implies having even the most basic foothold or standing.
origin: This phrase originates from 'Xuān Tíng Yuān' (轩亭冤), a Qing dynasty work by Xiānglíng Zǐ. In the text, a character confronts a group of arrogant individuals, demanding to know whether they still have any place left to stand. The idiom subsequently gained broader literary usage, notably appearing in Cao Xueqin's classic novel 'Dream of the Red Chamber' (红楼梦), where it conveys a character's sense of having lost all ground beneath them.
example_zh: 在竞争激烈的行业中，这家公司已经没有立足之地了。
example_en: In this fiercely competitive industry, the company no longer has any foothold to stand on.

meaning: This idiom literally means playing the Jie drum to hasten the blooming of flowers. It originates from a story about Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, who so loved the Jie drum that his playing seemed to coax apricot flowers into early bloom. Metaphorically, it refers to using one's power, art, or skill to urge natural processes along, often carrying an elegant and refined connotation.
origin: During the Tang Dynasty, Emperor Xuanzong was deeply fond of the Jie drum, a two-headed drum with a narrow waist. According to Nan Zhuo's 'Jie Gu Lu' (Record of the Jie Drum), the Emperor once played the drum in the inner palace and personally composed a tune called 'Spring Light Good' (春光好). At that very moment, apricot flowers in the courtyard happened to open, and the Emperor laughed, remarking that for such a feat he might well be called the Heavenly Lord. The tale of imperial artistry seemingly commanding nature gave rise to this enduring idiom.
example_zh: 古人以羯鼓催花，寄望春光早至。
example_en: The ancients played the Jie drum to urge the flowers to bloom, hoping spring would arrive early.

meaning: Like a wolf glancing back menacingly and an owl perching watchfully. A metaphor for fierce, violent people who lie in wait, watching for an opportunity to strike or seize power. It vividly conveys a tense atmosphere of lurking treachery.
origin: This idiom comes from the History of the Northern Dynasties (北史), in the appraisal of the Northern Wei annals. It describes the early reign of Emperor Mingyuan of the Northern Wei dynasty, when the empire was just beginning to be pacified after conquest. At that time, ambitious and violent figures still harbored designs on power—glaring like wolves and perching like owls—watching for any chance to usurp authority. The phrase captures the treacherous political atmosphere of the early Northern Wei period, further compounded by severe internal strife in the final years of the Tianci era.
example_zh: 乱贼狼顾鸱踤，妄图趁机窃取权柄。
example_en: The rebels glared like wolves and perched like owls, scheming to seize power at the first opportunity.

meaning: Long sleeves make it easier to dance gracefully. Originally meaning that with the right advantages or resources, success comes more easily. Now it describes people with wealth and influence who are skilled at networking, maneuvering, and exploiting connections to get ahead.
origin: The phrase originates from the work Han Feizi, written by the Legalist philosopher Han Fei during the late Warring States period. In the chapter 'The Five Vermin,' Han Fei wrote 'Long sleeves aid the dance; much money aids trade' to illustrate that having resources makes success easier. The metaphor was originally neutral, describing how favorable conditions help one accomplish goals. Over time, the phrase acquired a negative connotation, referring to those who use wealth and influence to curry favor and manipulate social connections.
example_zh: 他长袖善舞，在商界和政界都积累了深厚的人脉。
example_en: He is a master at working the room, having built deep connections in both business and political circles.

meaning: Describes a complete lack of vitality or spirit, appearing listless and lifeless. The phrase uses the ironic contrast of 'dead' and 'alive' to emphasize a dull, energyless demeanor that drains all sense of liveliness from a person or atmosphere.
origin: This is a colloquial idiom from vernacular Chinese with no specific classical literary origin. It draws on the paradoxical pairing of 'dead' (死) and 'alive' (活) to describe a state devoid of energy. Such contrasting-character constructions are common in spoken Chinese, where the rhetorical tension heightens the sense of lifelessness being conveyed.
example_zh: 看他那死样活气的样子，连说话都提不起劲来。
example_en: Look at his listless, lifeless manner—he can't even muster the energy to speak.

meaning: To execute one person in order to warn and deter a hundred others. It is a variant of the more common 杀一儆百, describing the practice of making a severe example of a single wrongdoer to discipline the rest.
origin: This idiom is a variant form of 杀一儆百, which itself draws on an ancient Chinese governance philosophy recorded in texts such as the Han Dynasty's histories. The idea of using harsh punishment against one individual to frighten the many into obedience was a standard tool of magistrates and military commanders. The character 砺 (to whet or sharpen) stands in for 儆 (to warn), preserving the same sense of sharpening discipline through exemplary punishment. No single classical source is tied specifically to the 杀一砺百 spelling. It reflects the broader Confucian and Legalist debate over whether severity or virtue better maintains order.
example_zh: 为了整顿军纪，将军决定杀一砺百，严惩了带头闹事的人。
example_en: To restore military discipline, the general decided to make an example of the ringleader by severely punishing him.

meaning: Describes being diligent and cautious from morning to night, never allowing the slightest negligence or slackness. It conveys a relentless work ethic paired with constant vigilance and care.
origin: Originates from the Book of Changes (周易), specifically the Qian hexagram (乾卦): 'The superior man is diligent all day long, and at night remains cautious as if facing danger—then there will be no blame.' The phrase embodies the Confucian ideal of ceaseless self-improvement combined with unremitting vigilance. It later crystallized into the four-character idiom 朝乾夕惕, widely used to praise tireless and conscientious dedication to one's duties.
example_zh: 他朝乾夕惕，勤于政事，终于使国家繁荣昌盛。
example_en: Diligent and cautious from morning to night, he devoted himself to governance and eventually brought the nation to prosperity.

meaning: This idiom describes people who share a common hatred or abhorrence mutually aiding each other to confront their shared enemy. It reflects the principle that those united by a common grievance naturally form alliances and support one another against what they jointly despise.
origin: This idiom is a classical Chinese expression closely related to the similar phrase '同恶相助' (mutual aid among those who share the same hatred). It embodies ancient Chinese political and military philosophy, particularly the strategic insight that shared enmity creates natural coalitions. The concept recurs in classical discussions of statecraft and alliance-building, where common hatred is recognized as a powerful motivator for cooperation. No single definitive textual source has been recorded for this exact formulation.
example_zh: 他们同恶相恤，联手对付共同的敌人。
example_en: They shared a common hatred and aided one another, joining forces against their mutual enemy.

meaning: To be left far behind someone and stare helplessly, unable to catch up. It describes falling hopelessly behind others in skill, achievement, or progress.
origin: The idiom originates from the work Zhuangzi (庄子), specifically the chapter 'Tian Zifang' (田子方), written during the Warring States period. In the original passage, the disciple Yan Hui describes his teacher Confucius as running so swiftly and gracefully that he leaves everyone behind in the dust, while Hui himself can only stare helplessly from far behind, unable to keep pace. The phrase captures the vast gap between master and student.
example_zh: 他的棋艺精湛，我只能瞠呼其后。
example_en: His chess skills are so superb that I can only stare helplessly behind him.

meaning: Refers to outstanding and distinguished scholars serving at the imperial court. The term combines '金闺' (golden court, denoting the imperial palace or high government offices) with '国士' (national-level talents). It conveys high esteem for someone's exceptional abilities and esteemed position in service to the state.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty poet Gong Zizhen's (龚自珍) collection '已亥杂诗' (Poems of the Year Ji Hai), poem number 260. The verse reads '勉求玉体长生诀，留报金闺国士知' — seeking the secret of longevity, to share with the distinguished court scholars. Gong Zizhen was a prominent late-Qing intellectual renowned for his reformist ideas and sharp social commentary. The phrase '金闺国士' here refers to the talented scholars at the imperial court whom the poet wished to inform of his findings.
example_zh: 他才华横溢，被誉为金闺国士，深受朝廷器重。
example_en: Endowed with extraordinary talent, he was regarded as a distinguished court scholar and was highly valued by the imperial government.

meaning: Literally meaning to return the jade intact to the State of Zhao. It is a variant of the more common idiom 完璧归赵, used to describe returning something borrowed in perfect condition to its rightful owner.
origin: During the Warring States period, the State of Qin demanded the legendary He Shi Bi jade from the State of Zhao in exchange for fifteen cities. The Zhao diplomat Lin Xiangru was sent to Qin with the jade, but upon realizing the Qin king had no intention of honoring the deal, he cleverly retrieved the jade and secretly sent it back to Zhao intact. This story is recorded in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (Shi Ji). The variant form 全璧归赵 emphasizes the completeness (全) of the returned item.
example_zh: 借了朋友的书，我读完之后全璧归赵，没有一点折损。
example_en: After borrowing my friend's book, I returned it in pristine condition without a single crease.

meaning: A general term for the various schools of religion and academic thought. It also refers to people from all walks of life and all kinds of professions in society. The phrase encompasses the diversity of beliefs, doctrines, and social callings.
origin: The phrase traces back to Song dynasty scholar Zhao Yanwei's work 'Yunlu Manchao' (云麓漫钞), Volume 6, which records that Emperor Wu of Liang asked about the three teachings, nine schools, and the affairs of the Han dynasty, knowing them as if they were right before his eyes. The 'three teachings' refers to Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism, while the 'nine schools' denotes the nine major philosophical schools of ancient China. Over the centuries the expression broadened to mean all religious and academic sects, and by extension all kinds of people across society.
example_zh: 这座城市的集市上，九流三教的人都有，热闹非凡。
example_en: People from all walks of life gather at this city's marketplace, making it extraordinarily lively.

meaning: To hide a sharp blade inside a scabbard. It is a metaphor for concealing murderous intent or hostile designs beneath a calm exterior. The phrase describes someone who appears harmless but secretly harbors lethal intentions.
origin: This idiom does not derive from a single classical text but is formed from the literal image of a blade concealed within its sheath. It draws on the long-standing Chinese metaphorical tradition of associating hidden weapons with concealed malice. Unlike related idioms that trace to specific historical anecdotes, this phrase is a descriptive compound built from common characters. Its usage reflects the cultural wariness toward those who mask aggression behind a placid facade.
example_zh: 他表面和善，实则鞘里藏刀，令人难以防备。
example_en: He seems friendly on the surface, but in reality he hides a knife in his scabbard, making him impossible to guard against.

meaning: Describes a situation where official documents and meetings proliferate to disastrous excess, like mountains of paperwork and seas of conferences. It is a pointed critique of bureaucratic red tape and institutional inefficiency.
origin: This is a modern Chinese idiom with no classical literary origin. It emerged in the late twentieth century to satirize the bureaucratic phenomenon of drowning in endless paperwork and meetings. The metaphor pairs 'mountain' (山) for towering piles of documents with 'sea' (海) for the flood of conferences, vividly conveying the overwhelming scale. It became widely used in critiques of formalism and administrative bloat in government and corporate settings.
example_zh: 基层干部苦于文山会海，难以集中精力抓落实。
example_en: Grassroots cadres, burdened by mountains of documents and seas of meetings, struggle to focus on getting things done.

meaning: To compete in showing off beauty and fragrance. It describes flowers or women vying with one another to display their splendor and charm.
origin: This phrase originates from the Qing Dynasty folk song collection Baixue Yiyin (白雪遗音), specifically in the piece 'Yu Qingting · You An' (玉蜻蜓·游庵). The original line reads, 'Competing in beauty and fragrance are only the powder and paint, when in those years both elder and younger admired Lord Qiao.' The idiom draws on the imagery of flowers blossoming together, each striving to outshine the others in color and scent, and was later extended to describe people—especially women—contending in attractiveness.
example_zh: 春日百花斗艳争芳，将整座园林装点得如诗如画。
example_en: In spring, a hundred flowers compete in beauty and fragrance, adorning the entire garden like a painting come to life.

meaning: To quote from classical texts and historical records as authoritative support for one's argument. It describes someone who grounds their reasoning in established scriptures and ancient writings. The idiom conveys a scholarly, well-read approach to making a point.
origin: The idiom draws upon the long Chinese tradition of revering classical texts—particularly the Confucian canon and standard histories—as the ultimate authority in debate and governance. Scholars throughout the imperial era were expected to support their arguments with citations from works such as the Book of Documents, the Analects, and the Records of the Grand Historian. Over time, the phrase came to describe anyone who habitually invokes ancient sources to justify a position, whether in scholarly disputation, political counsel, or literary composition.
example_zh: 他在辩论中引经据古，令对手无从反驳。
example_en: In the debate, he quoted from the classics and ancient histories, leaving his opponent unable to rebut.

meaning: To deliberately confuse black and white, calling the black white and the white black. It is a metaphor for intentionally distorting right and wrong to create chaos and deception. The phrase criticizes those who twist the truth to serve their own purposes.
origin: The idiom originates from the 'Book of Later Han' (后汉书), specifically in the biography of Yang Zhen (杨震). The original text states '白黑溷淆，清浊同源' — white and black are confounded, the clear and the turbid share the same source. Yang Zhen was an upright Eastern Han official known for his integrity, and the phrase lamented the moral confusion of his era when honest and corrupt officials were treated alike.
example_zh: 他黑白混淆，颠倒是非，终将遭到众人的唾弃。
example_en: He deliberately confounded right and wrong, distorting the truth, and will ultimately be despised by all.

literal: startle the eyes, shock the heart
meaning: To see something so startling and dreadful that it shocks both one's eyes and one's heart. It describes a sight or scene that is visually horrifying and emotionally unsettling. Often used for scenes of destruction, danger, or violence that leave a deep disturbing impression.
origin: The idiom originates from the Qing dynasty collection 'Yetan Suilu' (Night Tales Recorded) by He Bang'e, in the chapter titled 'Xiu Lin.' The original passage depicts a catastrophic flood where the ground is suddenly submerged under water several zhang deep, seaweed and water plants drape from treetops, and boat rudders are pressed against rooftops—a scene of devastation horrifying to witness. It later appeared in the Qing novel 'Sanxia Wuyi' (Three Heroes and Five Gallants), where a character is so startled by the sight of a blade that he cries out in alarm.
example_zh: 这场惨烈的车祸现场令人骇目惊心，久久不能平静。
example_en: The gruesome scene of the car accident was so horrifying to witness that one could not calm down for a long time.

meaning: A metaphor for things that possess a name or appearance but lack any real substance or practical utility. Like a clay chicken that cannot crow or a pottery dog that cannot bark, it describes entities that are utterly useless despite their superficial resemblance to the real thing. It is synonymous with 土鸡瓦犬.
origin: The idiom draws on an old metaphor comparing clay (土) chickens and tile (瓦) dogs to worthless things that merely resemble the real creatures but serve no actual purpose. The imagery appears in classical Chinese writings that critique boastful but incompetent people. Over time it became a stock expression for anything hollow and impractical, often used to mock false bravado or empty titles.
example_zh: 别看他吹得天花乱坠，其实不过是土鸡瓦狗，真遇到事一点用都没有。
example_en: Don't be fooled by his grandiose boasting; he's really just a clay chicken and pottery dog—utterly useless when it truly matters.

meaning: To analyze matters point by point and break down their underlying logic. It describes speech or writing that is exceptionally well-organized, thorough, and penetrating, revealing deep insights in a structured manner.
origin: This idiom originates from Song dynasty scholar Wang Dang's 'Tang Yulin,' which records a meeting between the Tang dynasty chancellor Li Deyu (Duke of Wei) and a scholar named Shouliang. Li Deyu was initially unimpressed upon first seeing Shouliang. However, when Shouliang began to speak, he analyzed each point with remarkable clarity and depth, illuminating even the most obscure subtleties. Whenever Li Deyu was about to raise a question, Shouliang had already anticipated and explained it, leaving the chancellor astonished and leaning forward in his seat.
example_zh: 他在会议上的发言分条析理，令在座所有人都心服口服。
example_en: His remarks at the meeting were so well-organized and incisive that everyone present was thoroughly convinced.

meaning: This idiom describes eating in a ravenous and hurried manner, devouring food with great speed and intensity. It paints a vivid picture of someone eating as fiercely as a wolf or tiger pouncing on its prey.
origin: This phrase is a variant of the more common expression 狼吞虎咽, both using the imagery of wolves and tigers to depict gluttonous, hasty eating. Such animal-based metaphors for eating habits have appeared in Chinese vernacular literature since the Ming and Qing dynasties. No single classical source is attributed as its definitive origin.
example_zh: 他饿了一整天，回到家便狼吞虎餐地吃起了饭菜。
example_en: Having gone hungry all day, he came home and wolfed down his food ravenously.

meaning: This idiom describes the policy of reducing corvée labor obligations and lowering tax burdens on the common people. It reflects a classical Confucian ideal of benevolent governance in which rulers minimize demands placed on the peasantry to promote social stability and prosperity.
origin: The phrase embodies a core principle of benevolent governance advocated throughout Chinese political philosophy by Confucian thinkers. The practice of lightening labor and tax burdens was championed by enlightened rulers such as Emperor Wen of Han and Emperor Taizong of Tang, whose reigns were marked by prosperity and low taxation. It became a standard formula in imperial edicts advocating reduced hardship on the common people, appearing repeatedly in historical policy discussions.
example_zh: 新帝即位后推行轻繇薄赋，百姓的生活渐渐好转。
example_en: After the new emperor ascended the throne, he implemented policies of lightened corvée and reduced taxes, and the people's lives gradually improved.

meaning: Short hair signifies old age, while a long heart signifies deep cunning. The idiom describes an elderly person who possesses great wisdom and shrewdness. It highlights how age and experience can bring profound strategic insight.
origin: This idiom originates from the Zuo Zhuan (左传), a classical Chinese historical text covering the Spring and Autumn period, specifically from the third year of Duke Zhao's reign. The original passage states that someone whose hair is thin from age yet whose mind is deeply calculating may pose a hidden threat. The remark was made to warn of an elderly figure whose outward frailty belied sharp strategic thinking. Over time, the phrase evolved into the four-character idiom 发短心长, emphasizing the combination of old age and deep wisdom.
example_zh: 这位老者发短心长，谋略深远，令众人不敢轻视。
example_en: The old man's thinning hair belied a deeply calculating mind, commanding respect from all.

meaning: To glare at someone with wide-open, angry eyes. It describes the fierce expression of a person who is on the verge of losing their temper. The idiom conveys intense anger and hostility directed at a specific target.
origin: The idiom originates from the Ming Dynasty novel 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms' (三国演义) by Luo Guanzhong. In the third chapter, the scheming minister Dong Zhuo has seized power and considers deposing the young emperor. When the official Ding Yuan opposes him, Dong Zhuo's advisor Li Ru notices a formidable warrior standing behind Ding Yuan—Lü Bu, who cuts an imposing figure with his halberd in hand and glares furiously at Dong Zhuo. This vivid scene of Lü Bu's menacing stare gave rise to the idiom, symbolizing barely restrained rage.
example_zh: 听到这番无理指责，他怒目而视，拳头攥得咯咯作响。
example_en: Hearing these unreasonable accusations, he glared furiously, his fists clenching tight.

meaning: This idiom means to advance and retreat together in complete unison. It describes a group acting in perfect coordination, sharing the same direction and pace. It is often used in military or team contexts to emphasize solidarity and mutual dependence.
origin: The character 旅 (lǚ) in classical Chinese carries the sense of 'together' or 'jointly,' as seen in compounds such as 旅力 (combined strength). The phrase depicts troops or companions advancing and retreating in lockstep, never abandoning one another. It reflects the classical military ideal of unified action and collective solidarity in coordinated effort. No single literary source is definitively attributed to this idiom, but it draws on the broader classical tradition of valuing coordinated, communal movement.
example_zh: 全军将士退旅进旅，始终协同作战，终破敌阵。
example_en: The entire army advanced and retreated as one, fighting in perfect coordination until they finally broke through the enemy lines.

meaning: To calculate and devise strategies; to plan and make strategic decisions. The phrase evokes the image of turning counting rods while formulating battle plans or policies.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Records of the Three Kingdoms' (三国志), in the biography of Zhuge Ke (诸葛恪) of Eastern Wu. Pei Songzhi's annotation quotes Guan Chen's 'Biography of Zhuge Ke' (魏·管辰《诸葛恪别传》). Sun Quan (孙权), ruler of Wu, once asked Zhuge Ke how he compared to Teng Yin (滕胤). Zhuge Ke replied that in matters of ceremony and etiquette, he was no match for Teng Yin, but in the art of planning and strategy-making, Teng Yin was inferior to him.
example_zh: 面对敌军压境，主帅回筹转策，制定了周密的防御方案。
example_en: Facing the invading enemy army, the commander devised strategies and formulated a thorough defense plan.

meaning: To persuade someone by using various reasons and approaches, alternating between different tactics. It describes repeatedly trying to convince or mediate through both gentle and firm arguments. The phrase literally means 'acting good, acting bad,' reflecting the shifting strategies used in persuasion.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Jinghua Yuan' (Flowers in the Mirror), Chapter 11, written by Li Ruzhen. In the story, a dispute arises between a clerk and a merchant over a transaction. Two old men passing by step in and mediate using various arguments from different angles. Through their persistent persuasion, the parties finally agree to settle the goods at an eighty percent discount, completing the deal peacefully.
example_zh: 邻居们作好作歹，总算劝住了这场争吵。
example_en: The neighbors persuaded and mediated in every way they could, and finally managed to settle the quarrel.

meaning: This idiom describes a nation or society whose enterprises are flourishing and growing increasingly wealthy and powerful. It conveys the ideal state of a country achieving both economic prosperity and national strength. It is commonly used in patriotic and aspirational contexts.
origin: This idiom appears in the modern literary work《壮志录》(Records of Lofty Aspirations) by the contemporary Chinese writer 峻青 (Jun Qing, pen name of Sun Junqing, 1922–2019). In the passage, the author expresses the aspiration to build the motherland into an even more prosperous and powerful nation. Unlike many classical idioms rooted in ancient historical texts, this phrase emerged from modern Chinese literature and reflects the national sentiment of building a strong, thriving country. It has since become a common expression in political and patriotic discourse.
example_zh: 全国人民团结一心，把祖国建设得更加繁荣富强。
example_en: The people of the whole nation unite as one to build the motherland into an even more prosperous and powerful country.

meaning: Literally meaning a thousand mountains and ten thousand rivers, this idiom describes a long and arduous journey across vast distances. It conveys the hardship and remoteness of travel through rugged terrain and across countless waterways. It is often used to express how far apart people or places are from one another.
origin: The phrase originates from a Tang dynasty poem titled 'To an Old Friend in Weiyang' (寄维阳故人) by the poet Zhang Qiao (张乔). In the poem, the poet bids farewell to a dear friend by a riverbank where willow branches are tied as a token of parting, and laments that a thousand mountains and ten thousand waters now separate him from his distant companion. The imagery evokes the vast, difficult distances that lie between the parted friends. Over time, the expression became a common way to describe any long, difficult journey or the great distance separating two people.
example_zh: 他历经千山万水，终于回到了阔别多年的故乡。
example_en: After crossing a thousand mountains and ten thousand rivers, he finally returned to the hometown he had been away from for many years.

meaning: This idiom describes a state of extreme poverty where one has no grain to cook with, leaving the cooking pot empty. The vivid image of fish appearing in an empty pot conveys destitution and hunger. It evokes the helplessness of having nothing to eat despite needing to sustain oneself.
origin: The idiom originates from a poem by the Song Dynasty poet Lu You (陆游), titled '独立' (Standing Alone). The line reads '羊踏寒蔬新少梦，鱼生空釜久谙穷' — sheep trample the cold vegetables, bringing fewer dreams; fish in an empty pot, long accustomed to poverty. Lu You, a patriot and poet who lived through political frustration and material hardship, used this imagery to express his deep familiarity with destitution and the melancholy of a life in want.
example_zh: 他晚年穷困潦倒，鱼生空釜，连一碗稀粥也难得温饱。
example_en: In his later years he fell into poverty, his cooking pot empty and bare, unable even to afford a bowl of thin porridge.

meaning: A lamp coated in black lacquer that blocks out all light. It is used metaphorically to describe someone who is completely ignorant, obtuse, and impervious to reason. The image evokes a person so thoroughly closed off that no light of understanding can penetrate.
origin: This idiom comes from Ming dynasty writer Feng Menglong's vernacular story collection "Xingshi Hengyan" (Stories to Awaken the World), volume 35. In the original passage, the character Xiao Yingshi is described as not being a "black lacquered leather lamp" or a "mud-clogged bamboo tube" — that is, not someone who is utterly clueless and impossible to enlighten. The metaphor likens a hopelessly ignorant or unreasonable person to a lamp so thickly coated with black lacquer that not a single ray of light can pass through it.
example_zh: 他简直是个黑漆皮灯，怎么解释都不明白。
example_en: He's like a black-lacquered lamp — no matter how you explain it, he just doesn't understand.

literal: hair, stand up, anger, pierce, crown
meaning: Describes hair standing on end from extreme rage, so much so that it seems to pierce through one's hat or crown. It is synonymous with the idiom 发上冲冠 (hair rising to push up the crown). The expression conveys fury so intense that it physically manifests.
origin: The phrase originates from Cao Zhi (曹植), a prince and celebrated poet of the Cao Wei kingdom during the Three Kingdoms period. In the fifth of his 'Five Drum Dance Songs' (鼙舞歌五首), he wrote the line '张目决眦，发怒穿冠' — 'eyes wide open until the corners split, hair standing in anger piercing the crown.' The imagery depicts a warrior or figure consumed with righteous indignation, eyes bulging and hair bristling against his headgear.
example_zh: 听闻此言，他顿时发怒穿冠，拍案而起。
example_en: Upon hearing these words, he flew into such a rage that his hair seemed to pierce his hat, and he slammed the table and stood up.

meaning: To acknowledge the kindness one has received and repay it in kind. It describes a person of moral integrity who remembers favors and returns them. The phrase emphasizes gratitude as a foundational virtue.
origin: The phrase traces back to Yuan dynasty playwright Wang Shifu's 'Romance of the Western Chamber' (Xixiang Ji), Act Five, Scene Three, where the line reads 'In a household of good faith, one who knows kindness repays kindness.' The idiom reflects a deeply rooted Confucian value that receiving a favor creates a moral obligation to return it. Over the centuries it became a standard expression for gratitude and reciprocity in Chinese literature.
example_zh: 他受人资助完成学业，如今事业有成，自然要知恩报恩。
example_en: Having been supported financially through his studies, now that he has a successful career, he naturally wants to repay the kindness he received.

meaning: A metaphor for speaking with directness and power. It describes someone whose words are so clear and decisive that they cut through hesitation like wind being parted and water being cleaved. The phrase emphasizes forceful, unambiguous communication.
origin: This idiom appears in the late Qing dynasty novel 'Xu Niehaihua' (续孽海花, a sequel to Niehaihua), Chapter 42. In the story, a character praises another person's straightforward and decisive manner of speaking, remarking that such words are truly 'splitting wind and cleaving streams.' The remark was used to commend the resolute and powerful quality of the speaker's words, after which a decision was promptly finalized. The idiom has since been used to describe speech that is crisp, forceful, and leaves no room for ambiguity.
example_zh: 他分风劈流地说出了自己的决定，让在场的人都心服口服。
example_en: He stated his decision with such forceful directness that everyone present was convinced.

meaning: Zhong refers to ancient musical bells and ding to ancient cooking cauldrons. The idiom depicts nobles dining with bells struck and cauldrons arrayed before them. It describes the lavish, ostentatious lifestyle of the aristocracy.
origin: The phrase originates from Sima Qian's 'Records of the Grand Historian' (Shiji), specifically the 'Biographies of Money-Makers' (Huozhi Liezhuan) written during the Western Han dynasty. Sima Qian recounts how people with even humble trades—such as a knife-sharpener named Zhi and a horse doctor named Zhang Li—amassed great wealth through diligence and lived in extravagant luxury. Zhang Li was said to strike bells and dine with cauldrons, a privilege normally reserved for nobility. The passage illustrates how commerce and skill could elevate commoners to aristocratic levels of opulence.
example_zh: 古时贵族击钟陈鼎，尽显奢华排场。
example_en: In ancient times, nobles struck bells and arrayed cauldrons, displaying the height of lavish extravagance.

meaning: Time passes like flowing water, never to return. It describes the fleeting and irreversible nature of the passage of time. The idiom conveys a sense of nostalgia and the inevitability of aging.
origin: This idiom originates from 'The Peony Pavilion' (《牡丹亭》), a famous play by the Ming dynasty dramatist Tang Xianzu (汤显祖). In the tenth scene, the line reads, 'For you, a beautiful companion like a flower, and years that flow away like water.' The phrase poetically laments the transient beauty of youth and the relentless passage of time, themes central to the play's exploration of love and mortality.
example_zh: 回首往事，似水流年，青春岁月一去不复返。
example_en: Looking back on the past, time flows away like water, and the years of youth are gone forever.

meaning: To use improper or unscrupulous means to gain personal advantage. It also refers to relying on petty cleverness to reap benefits without putting in honest effort. The term carries a negative connotation, criticizing those who seek shortcuts rather than working diligently.
origin: This idiom does not trace back to a single classical text or historical figure. It emerged as a colloquial expression in modern Chinese, reflecting a cultural disdain for those who exploit loopholes and circumvent honest labor. The phrase combines '投机' (seizing opportunities, often opportunistically) with '取巧' (resorting to clever tricks), encapsulating the idea of gaining advantage through cunning rather than merit. It is commonly used in educational and moral contexts to caution against dishonest shortcuts. Over time it has become a standard term in both everyday speech and formal writing.
example_zh: 做生意要讲诚信，靠投机取巧终究不会长久。
example_en: In business you must act with integrity; relying on opportunistic tricks will never last.

meaning: This idiom describes a relationship where two people both love and resent each other at the same time. It is commonly used in classical Chinese novels and operas as an affectionate yet teasing term for lovers or children. The contradiction between '欢喜' (joy) and '冤家' (enemy) captures the bittersweet nature of such close bonds.
origin: The phrase originates from Yuan dynasty literature, specifically the work of Tongtong Xueshi (童童学士) titled 'Xinshuiling · Niannuan' (《新水令·念远》). The original lines read: 'Born because of him, die because of him, loving person, enemy.' Here the word '冤家' (enemy) is used ironically to express deep, inescapable affection rather than genuine hatred. Over time, '欢喜冤家' became a popular expression in vernacular novels and operas for lovers or family members who constantly bicker yet care deeply for one another.
example_zh: 他们俩是一对欢喜冤家，吵了一辈子却谁也离不开谁。
example_en: The two of them are a pair of bickering lovers who have quarreled all their lives yet cannot bear to be apart.

literal: bore the liver, cut the kidney
meaning: This idiom metaphorically describes exhausting one's mental faculties and putting in painstaking effort. It is commonly used to characterize the arduous dedication one devotes to undertakings, work, or artistic creation. It is synonymous with the idiom 鉥心刿目.
origin: This idiom uses the vivid imagery of boring into the liver and cutting the kidneys to convey the painful intensity of deep thought and mental exertion. The characters 鉥 and 刿 both carry the sense of piercing or cutting, employed metaphorically in classical Chinese literary tradition to emphasize how consuming intellectual labor can feel. It does not trace to a single specific historical anecdote but belongs to a family of expressions in Chinese letters that equate extreme mental effort with visceral, bodily suffering. Such imagery was favored by literati to convey the seriousness and suffering behind scholarly or artistic achievement.
example_zh: 为了完成这部学术著作，他鉥肝刿肾地工作了整整五年。
example_en: To complete this academic work, he devoted himself to it with painstaking effort for five full years.

meaning: A solemn entrustment of an orphaned child to someone's care. It refers to the grave responsibility of raising a deceased friend's or ruler's young child, symbolizing utmost trust and moral duty.
origin: The phrase derives from the Analects (论语), compiled during the Spring and Autumn period. Confucius stated that a true gentleman is one who can be entrusted with a six-chi-tall orphan and charged with the fate of a hundred-li domain. The 'six-chi orphan' refers to a young child, typically around fifteen years old or younger by ancient reckoning, who has lost their father. Over time, 'six chi entrustment' came to denote the weighty responsibility of nurturing and protecting an orphan left in one's care.
example_zh: 他临终前将幼子托付于我，这六尺之讬，我岂敢有负？
example_en: Before he died, he entrusted his young son to me—how could I betray such a solemn charge?

meaning: To fail to distinguish between black and white, i.e., to confuse right and wrong. It describes someone who cannot tell good from evil or truth from falsehood and acts without discernment. The phrase uses 'blue-green and white' as a variant of 'black and white,' symbolizing right and wrong.
origin: This idiom is a variant of the more common phrase 不分皂白 (not distinguishing black from white). The character 皂 (zào) means black, and 白 (bái) means white; together they represent right and wrong. In 不分青白, the character 青 (qīng, blue-green) replaces 皂 as a near-synonym in colloquial usage. The expression has been used in vernacular literature since the Ming and Qing dynasties to criticize people who act rashly without examining the facts.
example_zh: 他办事不分青白，把好人坏人都骂了一顿。
example_en: He handles things without distinguishing right from wrong, scolding both the good and the bad alike.

meaning: Literally describing a pair of birds that perch and roost together. It is a metaphor for a devoted couple who are inseparable, spending their lives side by side like mandarin ducks on a pond.
origin: The idiom originates from the Song dynasty scholar You Mao's work 'Quan Tang Shi Hua' (Talks on Complete Tang Poetry), volume six, which quotes a poem comparing oneself to mandarin ducks: 'Better to be mandarin ducks on a pond, roosting and flying together for a lifetime.' In Chinese culture, mandarin ducks symbolize faithful, inseparable lovers. The Ming dynasty playwright Ye Xianzu later employed the phrase in his play 'Luanbi Ji' (The Phoenix Hairpin Tale) to depict a well-matched couple.
example_zh: 他们结婚三十年来双栖双宿，从未分开过。
example_en: Married for thirty years, they have lived side by side and never once been apart.

meaning: Not worth caring about; not worth taking seriously. It describes a situation where something is so trivial or minor that one need not be concerned or bothered by it.
origin: This phrase originates from a letter by the Ming dynasty statesman Zhang Juzheng, titled 'Reply to Zheng Fanxi.' In the letter, Zhang advised Zheng to stay true to his conscience and uphold fairness and integrity, telling him that the various rumors and criticisms from others were not worth worrying about. The idiom conveys the idea of remaining undisturbed by trivial or malicious talk while staying focused on what is right.
example_zh: 这些闲言碎语不足为意，你只管做好自己的事。
example_en: These idle rumors are not worth worrying about; just focus on doing your own work well.

meaning: To use 'yellow' in parallel with 'white,' referring to the pursuit of neat antithetical couplets in writing. It describes a literary style focused on matching words and tones precisely rather than conveying substance.
origin: The phrase originates from the Tang dynasty writer Liu Zongyuan's essay 'Qi Qiao Wen' (乞巧文), where he criticized the ornate and fragmented writing style of his time. He described how writers obsessed over trivial parallelism, drawing 'yellow' to match 'white' in elaborate but empty prose. The term later came to denote the overemphasis on formal rhetorical symmetry at the expense of genuine content.
example_zh: 其文章笔力沉雄，直追汉魏，非抽黄对白之辈所能企及。
example_en: His writing is powerful and vigorous, directly continuing the tradition of the Han and Wei dynasties, beyond the reach of those who merely pursue ornate parallelism.

meaning: To abandon evil ways and return to the righteous path. It describes a person who reforms from wrongdoing and embraces a proper, moral life. The phrase emphasizes a genuine change of heart and conduct.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Three Kingdoms period, recorded in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (三国志). In a decree issued by Liu Shan, the second emperor of Shu Han, he called upon those who would abandon evil and join the righteous cause to welcome the royal army with food and drink. The edict promised rewards and titles according to established regulations. Later literary works, such as Yuan dynasty playwright Liu Yuanqing's 'Sangshen,' used the phrase to urge warriors to forsake wrongdoing and become loyal generals serving the state.
example_zh: 他决心去邪归正，重新做一个对社会有用的人。
example_en: He resolved to abandon his evil ways and return to a righteous path, becoming a useful person to society once more.

meaning: Literally meaning 'ten-character street crossing,' this idiom refers to a crossroads or intersection where two streets cross each other. It is commonly used to describe a bustling junction in a city or town. Figuratively, it can also suggest being at a critical juncture where one must choose a direction.
origin: The phrase appears in Ming dynasty author Shi Nai'an's classic novel 'Water Margin' (水浒传), Chapter 40, where it describes a scene of fierce battle at a crossroads: 'They went to the crossroads and, sparing neither officer nor commoner, slaughtered until corpses lay everywhere and blood flowed in streams.' The term vividly depicts a central intersection in a town. Modern writer Ding Ling also used it in her novel 'The Sun Shines over the Sanggan River,' cementing its place in literary Chinese.
example_zh: 人群在十字街口四散开来，各自奔向不同的方向。
example_en: The crowd scattered at the crossroads, each person rushing off in a different direction.

meaning: The wounds are deep and the grief endures for a long time. It describes a person who has suffered profound trauma and whose sorrow persists long after the event. The phrase emphasizes both the severity of the injury and the lasting nature of the pain.
origin: This idiom originates from a Tang dynasty work by the eminent scholar-official Liu Zongyuan (柳宗元), specifically his inscription 'Inscription on the Filial Gate at Anfeng County, Shouzhou' (《寿州安丰县孝门铭》). The original line reads '创巨痛仍，号于穹昮,' meaning 'the wounds are deep, the pain endures, crying out to heaven.' Liu used it to depict the enduring grief of a filial son mourning his parent. Over time the phrase came to be used more broadly for any situation of severe and lasting suffering.
example_zh: 丧子之痛，创巨痛仍，数年未消。
example_en: The grief of losing a child left wounds deep and pain enduring, unfaded even after several years.

meaning: Times change and the world changes along with them. It describes how eras and social conditions shift over time, so that past customs and norms no longer apply to the present.
origin: This phrase originates from '钱神论' (On the God of Money), a satirical essay by Lu Bao of the Jin Dynasty. In the essay, Lu Bao critiques the money-worshipping culture of his era, arguing that with times changing and customs evolving from ancient to modern, empty philosophical discourse (清谈) is useless for solving urgent practical problems. The work is a sharp commentary on how shifting social conditions render old intellectual habits obsolete.
example_zh: 时易世变，我们不应再用旧标准衡量今天的事物。
example_en: Times change and the world moves on; we should no longer judge today's affairs by old standards.

meaning: An exquisite orchid growing in a secluded mountain valley, symbolizing something rare and precious. It is commonly used as a metaphor for a person of noble character and refined elegance who stands apart from the crowd. The image evokes purity, solitude, and unappreciated beauty.
origin: The phrase appears in chapter 5 of 'The Travels of Lao Can' (老残游记), a novel by the Qing dynasty writer Liu E (刘鹗). In the story, the narrator encounters a remarkably accomplished person in an unexpected, remote place and exclaims that finding such a master there is like discovering a hidden orchid in an empty valley. The orchid has long been a symbol of virtue and refinement in Chinese literary tradition, and its image growing unseen in a deep valley underscores both its rarity and its untarnished nobility.
example_zh: 她虽身处繁华都市，却如空谷幽兰般淡泊名利。
example_en: Though living in a bustling metropolis, she remains as indifferent to fame and wealth as a secluded orchid in an empty valley.

meaning: In the marketplace there are no two prices for the same good — commerce is fair, honest, and free from cheating. It describes a healthy social atmosphere where merchants conduct business with integrity and buyers need not worry about being overcharged.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Book of Han' (汉书), specifically the 'Biography of Wang Mang.' When Wang Mang held power during the late Western Han dynasty, he implemented a series of economic reforms aimed at standardizing market prices so that no seller could charge two different prices for the same item. The full passage reads, 'He also petitioned that there be no double prices in the market and no lawsuits in government offices,' reflecting an idealized vision of fair governance and social order.
example_zh: 这条街上店铺信誉极好，真正做到市无二价，顾客买得放心。
example_en: The shops on this street have excellent reputations, truly practicing fair pricing, so customers can shop with peace of mind.

literal: separated by, wall, there is, ear
meaning: Literally meaning 'there are ears on the other side of the wall,' this idiom warns that even private conversations may be overheard. It is commonly used to caution someone to speak carefully and guard secrets, as hidden listeners may be nearby.
origin: This idiom originates from the Spring and Autumn period text 'Guanzi: Lord and Minister, Part II' (《管子·君臣下》), attributed to the renowned Qi statesman Guan Zhong. The original passage reads, 'Walls have ears, hidden enemies are at your side,' explaining that secretly plotted schemes can leak out as though someone were eavesdropping through the wall. Over the centuries, it evolved into a popular cautionary phrase reminding people to be discreet with sensitive information.
example_zh: 他压低声音提醒道："小心点，隔墙有耳。"
example_en: He lowered his voice and warned, "Be careful—walls have ears."

meaning: A Buddhist term referring to the Western Paradise or Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, the realm of Amitabha Buddha. It represents the ideal afterlife destination where sentient beings are freed from suffering and reborn from lotus flowers. The term is commonly used to describe a place of ultimate peace and spiritual liberation.
origin: The term originates from Buddhist scriptures describing the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss ( Sukhavati ), the paradise of Amitabha Buddha. It was notably referenced by the Tang dynasty poet Li Bai in his work 'Praise of the Gold and Silver Painted Transformation Tableau of the Western Pure Land.' In later Ming dynasty novels such as Fang Ruhao's 'Chan Zhen Yi Shi,' emperors and laypeople aspired to be reborn in this Pure Land after death, reflecting the deep influence of Pure Land Buddhism on Chinese religious culture.
example_zh: 他晚年笃信佛法，日夜诵经，唯愿身后往生西方净土。
example_en: In his later years he devoutly embraced Buddhism, chanting sutras day and night, hoping only to be reborn in the Western Pure Land after death.

meaning: Refers to a marriage conducted through formal and legitimate procedures. In modern usage, it denotes a lawful marriage that complies with marriage regulations. It emphasizes the openness and legality of the union.
origin: The phrase originates from the Yuan dynasty playwright Guan Hanqing's play 'Jiu Feng Chen' (Rescuing the Prostitute), specifically the fourth act. In the play, the line contrasts a proper, openly conducted marriage with behavior that flagrantly violates social customs. The expression has since been used to distinguish legitimate, formally recognized marriages from informal or illicit unions.
example_zh: 他们是明婚正娶的夫妻，谁也无权干涉他们的生活。
example_en: They are a legitimately married couple, and no one has the right to interfere with their life.

meaning: To seek temporary peace in a small corner. It describes a ruler or government that avoids resisting foreign invasion and instead settles for security in a small territory. The term criticizes a cowardly complacency that ignores the larger threat.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel *Shuo Yue Quan Zhuan* (The Complete Story of Yue Fei) by Qian Cai, Chapter 59. In the story, officials remonstrate that treacherous ministers control the court and advocate for peace negotiations, while the emperor listens to their words and seeks temporary safety in a corner with no will to wage war. The phrase critiques the Southern Song court's refusal to resist the Jin invasion, settling for survival in the south rather than fighting to reclaim lost territory.
example_zh: 南宋朝廷不思北伐，偏安江南，不过是苟安一隅罢了。
example_en: The Southern Song court, refusing to launch a northern campaign and content to remain south of the Yangtze, was merely seeking temporary peace in a corner.

meaning: This idiom describes someone whose spirit is vigorous and courage is great, making them fearless and intrepid. It characterizes a person who faces challenges or dangers without hesitation or trepidation, projecting both outward confidence and inner resolve.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a single classical text or specific historical anecdote. It is a compound expression formed by joining '气壮' (spirit is strong) and '胆粗' (courage is bold), both established descriptors of bravery in vernacular Chinese. The pairing simultaneously emphasizes outward demeanor—projecting vigor and confidence—and an inner state of fearlessness. Such compounds frequently appear in vernacular fiction, storytelling traditions, and colloquial descriptions of heroic or audacious behavior throughout late imperial Chinese literature.
example_zh: 面对强敌，他气壮胆粗，毫不退缩。
example_en: Facing a formidable enemy, he stood fearless and undaunted, refusing to back down.

meaning: To pursue personal interests and seek selfish profit at the expense of public duty. It describes those who exploit their position for private gain rather than serving the collective good. The term carries a strong sense of moral condemnation.
origin: The phrase originates from Liang Qichao's late Qing dynasty work 'On the Origins of China's Weakness' (《中国积弱溯源论》), Section Four. Liang argued that once a minister dedicates himself to the nation, he should weigh only the interests of the people, not his own personal gain. He explicitly stated that seeking private profit (营私罔利) was inexcusable for public servants, reflecting his reformist critique of corrupt officialdom in the declining Qing empire.
example_zh: 他身居要职却营私罔利，最终受到了法律的严惩。
example_en: He held a high office yet sought private profit at public expense, and ultimately faced severe legal punishment.

meaning: To distinguish even the smallest weight with perfect clarity. It is a metaphor for being extremely accurate and precise in judgment or calculation. The '两' refers to a small unit of weight, and the '星' refers to the tiny marks on a steelyard beam indicating weight.
origin: The phrase originates from the Yuan dynasty play 'Wu Yuan Blows the Flute' (伍员吹箫) by Li Shouqing, in its third act. In the scene, a character declares he will question someone with painstaking precision—splitting two and dividing stars—to get a complete account from beginning to end. The expression thus became associated with discerning even the finest distinctions with absolute clarity.
example_zh: 他对账目擘两分星，从不放过任何一笔差错。
example_en: He scrutinized the accounts with exact precision, never overlooking a single discrepancy.

meaning: To be unexpected or beyond imagination; something that one did not anticipate. It describes a situation or outcome that catches a person completely by surprise, whether pleasantly or unpleasantly.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Jinghua Yuan' (镜花缘) by Li Ruzhen. In the second chapter, a fairy visits a mountain on a bitterly cold, snowy day, and the host remarks that such an unexpected visit is truly beyond imagination. The phrase has since become a common expression for any surprising or unforeseen event in everyday Chinese.
example_zh: 他竟然放弃了高薪工作去乡下种田，真是意想不到。
example_en: He unexpectedly gave up his high-paying job to farm in the countryside—truly beyond imagination.

meaning: This idiom literally means 'to say a thousand things and mention ten thousand.' It describes talking at great length or enumerating countless reasons, excuses, or arguments. The phrase emphasizes the abundance and variety of what is said, often implying that despite all the words, the core point remains unchanged.
origin: This idiom does not have a specific classical literary origin and is considered a folk or colloquial expression. It uses the numbers 'thousand' and 'ten thousand' as hyperbole to emphasize the sheer volume of words spoken. A common variant form is '说一千道一万' (saying one thousand and mentioning ten thousand). The expression reflects a traditional Chinese rhetorical pattern of employing large numbers to convey abundance or excess.
example_zh: 说千道万，关键还是看实际行动。
example_en: Say all you want, but in the end, what matters is actual action.

literal: draw water from well, guide up, forget, fatigue
meaning: This idiom describes recommending and promoting talented individuals with such tireless dedication that one forgets about fatigue. The term '汲引' literally means drawing water from a well, used metaphorically for lifting up and advancing worthy people. It conveys an unwavering commitment to identifying and elevating talent without regard for personal exhaustion.
origin: This idiom originates from the Tang Dynasty writer Luo Binwang's letter '上衮州刺史启' (Letter to the Prefect of Yanzhou). Luo Binwang was a renowned poet and one of the Four Eminent Poets of Early Tang. In this letter, he praised a local official's dedication to discovering and promoting capable individuals, noting that the official drew up talent tirelessly and commended and guided without wearying. The phrase became a lasting expression of selfless devotion to nurturing and advancing worthy people.
example_zh: 这位老教授毕生汲引忘疲，为学术界培养了大批优秀人才。
example_en: The elderly professor spent his entire life tirelessly promoting talent, cultivating a great number of outstanding scholars for academia.

literal: dyed by wind, accustomed to customs
meaning: To be influenced by local customs and gradually acquire their habits. It describes how a person's behavior and character are shaped by the prevailing practices of their environment. The idiom emphasizes the subtle but pervasive power of cultural surroundings.
origin: This phrase originates from the Song Dynasty Daoist encyclopedia Yunji Qiqian (《云笈七签》), compiled by the scholar Zhang Junfang around 1019 CE under imperial order. Volume 56 discusses the five qi (五气), stating that they follow one's destiny to form one's nature and shift with external things, and that people are influenced by prevailing customs — hence the infinite variety of human change. The text uses the idiom to illustrate how environmental and cultural forces continuously shape human behavior. It reflects a Daoist understanding that human nature is not fixed but endlessly molded by external influences.
example_zh: 人处异地，染风习俗，言行举止难免随当地习惯而改变。
example_en: Living in a different region, one is inevitably influenced by local customs, and one's words and behavior naturally change to follow local habits.

meaning: Literally referring to silk dyed cyan becoming cyan and dyed yellow becoming yellow, then flipping back and forth. It metaphorically describes situations or people that are changeable and inconstant, shifting unpredictably like colors changing in dyeing. The idiom conveys a sense of instability and capriciousness.
origin: The idiom originates from 'Mozi·Suo Ran' (《墨子·所染》) of the Spring and Autumn period, where the philosopher Mozi (墨翟) of the state of Lu, upon seeing silk dyers, sighed: 'Dye it cyan and it becomes cyan; dye it yellow and it becomes yellow.' This illustrated how environment shapes a person. Later, the Southern Dynasties Qi dynasty writer Kong Zhigui (孔稚珪) used the phrase in his famous essay 'Northern Mountain Protest' (《北山移文》), lamenting the inconstancy of a reclusive scholar who flip-flopped between hermit life and officialdom, writing 'How could one expect such inconsistency from beginning to end, the colors flipping and overturning.'
example_zh: 世事苍黄翻覆，谁能料定明日之局。
example_en: Worldly affairs shift and change unpredictably; who can foretell tomorrow's outcome?

meaning: This idiom describes a situation where a great deal of effort is expended but the payoff is minimal. It indicates an inefficient or counterproductive approach to a task. The phrase serves as a caution against working hard without working smart.
origin: The idiom traces back to the Mencius (《孟子·公孙丑上》), where the philosopher Mencius observes that by doing half the work of the ancients, one can achieve twice the results—a notion of efficiency later crystallized in the positive idiom 事半功倍. The expression 力倍功半 inverts this ideal, describing the undesirable opposite: expending double the effort yet reaping only half the reward. It has been used in Chinese literature and discourse to criticize wasteful, poorly conceived methods.
example_zh: 如果不讲究方法，一味蛮干，往往是力倍功半，白白浪费了时间和精力。
example_en: If you ignore proper methods and just work blindly, the result is often doubled effort for half the outcome, wasting time and energy for nothing.

meaning: Like duckweed drifting on water and waves leaving no permanent mark. It describes a person who wanders from place to place without a fixed home or settled abode.
origin: The idiom originates from the Ming dynasty playwright Tang Xianzu's famous work 'The Peony Pavilion' (牡丹亭), Scene 20. The original line '恨恠恠，萍踪浪影，风剪了玉芙蓉' evokes the image of wandering without a trace, like duckweed and ripples cut by the wind. Over time the phrase was refined into the four-character form '萍踪浪迹' and became a vivid metaphor for a rootless, drifting life. It also appears in Ling Mengchu's 'Slapping the Table in Amazement' (二刻拍案惊奇), a Ming dynasty story collection.
example_zh: 他一生萍踪浪迹，从未在一个地方长住过。
example_en: He wandered aimlessly all his life, never settling anywhere for long.

meaning: An exclamation of astonishment at something absurd or contrary to reason. It describes bizarre, incomprehensible events that defy common sense and normal expectations. Used to express shock at a situation that simply should not have occurred.
origin: From 'A New Account of the Tales of the World' (世说新语·黜免) by Liu Yiqing of the Southern Dynasties, Liu Song period. Yin Hao, a prominent military commander of the Eastern Jin dynasty, was dismissed from office and exiled to Xin'an. All day long he would trace characters in the air with his finger. When local officials secretly observed what he wrote, they found he only repeatedly wrote the four characters '咄咄怪事' (absurd! absurd!), expressing his bewilderment and quiet indignation at his unjust downfall.
example_zh: 他明明考了第一名，却被取消了资格，真是咄咄怪事。
example_en: He clearly ranked first, yet his qualification was revoked—what an absurd turn of events.

meaning: A woman of peerless beauty, unparalleled in her time. The phrase describes the most beautiful woman of a given era, someone whose looks are unmatched by anyone else.
origin: The idiom originates from a song by Li Yannian, a court musician of the Western Han dynasty, as recorded in the 'Book of Han: Biographies of Imperial Relatives.' Li Yannian sang before Emperor Wu of a woman from the north who was peerless and stood alone in her beauty. The emperor was captivated and later discovered this referred to Li Yannian's sister, who became the celebrated Consort Li. The phrase has since been used to describe a woman of extraordinary, unmatched beauty.
example_zh: 她容貌出众，才华横溢，堪称绝世佳人。
example_en: With her outstanding looks and brilliant talent, she can be called a peerless beauty.

meaning: Describes having bizarre, whimsical, or fanciful ideas that are detached from reality. It conveys imagination that borders on the absurd or impractical. The phrase is closely related to the more common idiom 异想天开.
origin: This idiom is a variant form of the well-known expression 异想天开 (yì xiǎng tiān kāi), which dates back to vernacular Chinese fiction of the Qing dynasty. The phrase combines 妙想 (ingenious or fanciful thoughts) with 天开 (heaven opening apart), painting a picture of ideas so extraordinary they seem to split the sky. No single classical text is definitively credited as the origin of this particular variant. It has been used colloquially in modern Chinese to characterize unrealistic or overly creative thinking.
example_zh: 他总是妙想天开，觉得不努力也能一夜暴富。
example_en: He always has wild fantasies, believing he can strike it rich overnight without any effort.

literal: select, the worthy, appoint, the capable
meaning: To select and appoint people of virtue and talent to positions of responsibility. It emphasizes the importance of merit-based selection in governance and management. The phrase advocates choosing the wise and capable rather than relying on personal connections or favoritism.
origin: This idiom appears in the 'Jiu Tang Shu' (Old Book of Tang), specifically in the 'Treatise on Food and Commodities' (食货志). The text discusses the proper establishment of government offices and assignment of duties, stating that selecting worthy and capable officials brings benefit to the state, while appointing the wrong people brings harm to the common people. The phrase reflects the long-standing Confucian ideal of meritocratic governance. A later usage appears in Qing dynasty scholar Wang Fuzhi's 'Du Tongjian Lun' (Reading the Comprehensive Mirror), where he invokes the concept in discussing the public duty of supporting the state.
example_zh: 治理国家必须选贤任能，方能国泰民安。
example_en: To govern a country, one must select the worthy and appoint the capable; only then can the nation enjoy peace and prosperity.

meaning: Born without encountering a good time. An old expression indicating bad fate or being born at the wrong time. It laments that one's life circumstances did not align with favorable conditions.
origin: This idiom originates from the Book of Odes (诗经), specifically the poem 'Sang Rou' (桑柔) in the 'Da Ya' (大雅) section, dating to the Western Zhou dynasty. The original line reads '我生不辰，逢天僤怒' — 'I was born at an ill time and met with Heaven's fierce wrath.' The poem is attributed to King Li of Zhou's era, lamenting political chaos and natural disasters. Over time, the phrase evolved into the four-character idiom '生不逢辰,' used to describe someone born into unfortunate circumstances.
example_zh: 他才华横溢却生不逢辰，一生郁郁不得志。
example_en: He was full of talent but born at the wrong time, living his whole life in unfulfilled frustration.

meaning: This idiom means to eliminate chaos and disorder and restore normal order and correctness. 拨 means to remedy or set right, 乱 refers to a chaotic situation, 反 (通返) means to return, and 正 means proper order. It is commonly used to describe correcting past wrongs and reestablishing stability.
origin: This idiom originates from the Gongyang Commentary (《公羊传》) on the Spring and Autumn Annals, from the 14th year of Duke Ai of Lu. The original text states: 'To remedy the chaotic world and return it to proper order, nothing comes closer than the Spring and Autumn Annals.' It refers to Confucius compiling the Spring and Autumn Annals as a guide for restoring justice and order to a troubled world during the late Spring and Autumn period. The phrase later came to describe the act of correcting past errors and reestablishing correct governance.
example_zh: 新政府成立后，着力拨乱反正，恢复社会秩序。
example_en: After the new government was established, it focused on correcting past wrongs and restoring social order.

meaning: To pass by one's own door without entering. It describes someone who is so devoted to their duties that they neglect personal matters, exemplifying selfless dedication to public service. The phrase originates from the legend of Yu the Great, who passed his home three times without stopping while working to control the floods.
origin: This idiom originates from the Mencius (孟子·离娄下), written by Mencius during the Warring States period. It refers to the legendary figure Yu the Great (大禹), who was tasked with controlling the great floods in ancient China. According to the story, Yu was so dedicated to his flood-control work that he passed by his own home three times without entering to check on his family. Mencius cited this as a model of selfless public service. The phrase became a lasting symbol of devotion to duty over personal concerns.
example_zh: 大禹治水十三年，三过家门过门不入，终平水患。
example_en: Yu the Great spent thirteen years taming the floods, passing his own door without entering three times, and ultimately brought the disaster under control.

meaning: This idiom means to annihilate or exterminate completely. It evokes the imagery of attacking from all directions—cutting down on the right and slaughtering on the left—to eliminate enemies thoroughly with no survivors left behind.
origin: This idiom has no single documented literary origin. It is built from two parallel structures pairing directional words with verbs of destruction: 翦 meaning to cut down or exterminate, and 屠 meaning to slaughter. Together they convey the totality of annihilation, as if no enemy on either side is spared.
example_zh: 敌军来犯，将军下令右翦左屠，不留一个活口。
example_en: When the enemy invaded, the general ordered complete annihilation, sparing not a single life.

meaning: To withdraw from society and live in seclusion, avoiding public office and worldly affairs. It describes someone who chooses a reclusive life away from politics and social engagement.
origin: This phrase originates from the Han dynasty divination text 'Yi Lin' (Forest of Changes) by Jiao Gan, specifically from the hexagram combination 'Ge zhi Lü' (Revolution to Travel). The text states that one who withdraws from the world and lives in seclusion ultimately never meets the right time or opportunity. It reflects the ancient Chinese philosophical ideal of reclusion, where scholars disenchanted with corrupt governance would retreat to the mountains to pursue a life of virtue and simplicity.
example_zh: 他看透官场腐败，毅然选择遁世隐居，从此不问世事。
example_en: Having seen through the corruption of officialdom, he resolutely chose to withdraw from society and live in seclusion, never again concerning himself with worldly affairs.

meaning: To extensively search and gather materials from all sides while inheriting and carrying forward the traditions of distant ancients. It describes a thorough, wide-ranging approach to scholarship that draws broadly from sources and connects to classical heritage.
origin: This idiom is a variant form of '旁搜远绍' (páng sōu yuǎn shào), where the character 蒷 is an alternate writing of 搜 (to search). The phrase reflects traditional Chinese scholarly ideals, emphasizing both the breadth of inquiry—searching widely on all sides—and the depth of lineage—inheriting knowledge from remote antiquity. It is commonly associated with classical literary criticism and historiography, where scholars were praised for casting a wide net while maintaining continuity with ancient traditions.
example_zh: 他治学旁蒷远绍，终成一代经学大家。
example_en: He pursued his scholarship by broadly searching and distantly inheriting from the ancients, ultimately becoming a master of classical studies in his generation.

meaning: Trouble, disputes, or misunderstandings caused by careless or provocative speech. It refers to quarrels and gossip that arise from what people say, often needlessly. The phrase emphasizes how words alone can stir up conflict.
origin: This idiom originates from Ming Dynasty writer Feng Menglong's collection Stories Old and New (古今小说), in the tale 'Judge Teng's Ghostly Settlement of a Family Estate.' The original passage argues that fighting over inherited land can destroy sibling affection, suggesting that a destitute man with nothing to inherit is better off, since he avoids endless quarrels and verbal disputes. The phrase thus came to describe the trouble stirred up by loose talk and bickering.
example_zh: 他不愿卷入同事间的是非口舌，只想安静地做好自己的工作。
example_en: He did not want to get drawn into the gossip and disputes among his coworkers; he just wanted to quietly do his job well.

meaning: Feeling persistently depressed and seldom cheerful; having a gloomy state of mind that leaves little room for joy. It describes someone who is chronically downcast and rarely experiences happiness.
origin: This idiom has no single canonical origin in classical literature; it is a descriptive compound formed from common Chinese vocabulary. The word '抑郁' means pent-up or depressed in mood, while '寡欢' means having few moments of joy. Together they naturally characterize a persistently melancholic disposition. The phrase appears in modern Chinese literary and everyday usage to denote someone who is chronically unhappy and withdrawn.
example_zh: 自从失去亲人后，他变得抑郁寡欢，很少与人交谈。
example_en: Since losing a loved one, he has become depressed and withdrawn, rarely speaking with others.

meaning: The most outstanding person among the younger generation. It refers to a junior who stands out as a leader or exemplary figure among later scholars and newcomers. The term praises exceptional talent and promise in someone of junior standing.
origin: The idiom originates from the 'Book of Jin' (晋书), in the Biography of Pei Xiu. Pei Xiu was a brilliant scholar-official of the Cao Wei and early Jin period, renowned for his map-making and administrative talent. Contemporaries praised him with the saying 'Pei Xiu is the leader of the younger generation' (后进领袖裴秀). The Southern Qi's 'Biography of Liu Hui' later echoed the phrase, describing Liu Hui as the leader of the younger generation, clever and multi-talented.
example_zh: 他才华出众，被誉为同辈中的后进领袖。
example_en: With outstanding talent, he was praised as the leader among his peers.

literal: 通(mutual) 共(share) 有(have) 无(lack)
meaning: To share resources and help each other by exchanging what one has for what one lacks. It refers to mutual assistance and the pooling of assets between parties. The idiom emphasizes cooperation and reciprocity in meeting each other's needs.
origin: The concept of mutual exchange of goods and resources has deep roots in classical Chinese economic thought, dating back to texts such as the Book of Changes and early discussions of trade. The phrase reflects the traditional ideal of communities supporting one another by sharing surpluses and filling deficits. While no single definitive literary source is cited, the expression embodies longstanding Confucian values of reciprocity and mutual aid.
example_zh: 邻里之间应当通共有无，共同渡过难关。
example_en: Neighbors should share resources and help one another to get through difficult times together.

meaning: It refers to the glint and shadow of swords and blades faintly visible. It describes an atmosphere fraught with danger and menace, where conflict or violence lurks beneath the surface. Used both literally for battlefields and metaphorically for tense rivalries.
origin: The imagery traces to the Southern Dynasties period, during the Liang dynasty, in Wu Yun's 'Four Poems on Battling South of the City,' which depicts battle with lines such as 'sword light flashes like night lightning, horse sweat soaks the day and night mud.' Over time the phrase evolved into the four-character idiom '刀光剑影' to evoke the flashing blades and shifting shadows of combat. It came to be used figuratively for any setting thick with peril and hidden hostility.
example_zh: 谈判桌上看似平静，实则暗藏刀光剑影。
example_en: The negotiating table appears calm, but in reality it conceals the flash of blades and shadows of swords.

meaning: A blind person holding a candle to light the way. It metaphorically refers to an action or effort that is completely useless and serves no purpose, since the light cannot help someone who cannot see.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel 《野叟曝言》by Xia Jingqu, chapter 75. In the original passage, scholars fiercely debated whether Chen Shou's 'Records of the Three Kingdoms' (三国志) improperly legitimized the Wei dynasty over Shu. The author dismissed these critics' arguments as being like a blind person holding a candle — illuminating nothing and accomplishing nothing. The metaphor underscores that their discussions were entirely futile.
example_zh: 他对音乐一窍不通，却要去指导乐团排练，简直是盲人把烛。
example_en: He knows nothing about music, yet he tries to direct the orchestra's rehearsal — it's like a blind person holding a candle.

meaning: This idiom refers to bad people seeking out and colluding with each other. It describes how wrongdoers naturally gravitate toward one another and form alliances for mutual benefit. The phrase carries a strongly negative connotation, condemning such partnerships of the wicked.
origin: The phrase originates from the Zuo Zhuan (左传), specifically from the 13th year of Duke Zhao (昭公十三年), a chronicle of the Spring and Autumn period. In the original passage, the analogy is drawn to merchants in a marketplace who naturally gather together—the wicked likewise seek each other out, making collusion effortless. The Zuo Zhuan is one of the earliest and most important historical texts of ancient China, traditionally attributed to Zuo Qiuming of the Lu state.
example_zh: 这两伙贪官同恶相求，共同侵吞国库钱财。
example_en: The two groups of corrupt officials colluded together, jointly embezzling money from the state treasury.

meaning: It is widely known by everyone; a fact that is common knowledge to all. Used to introduce information that the speaker assumes the audience already agrees upon or is aware of.
origin: The phrase appears in the classical novel "Yu Jiao Li" (《玉娇梨》), Chapter 20, a work from the late Ming to early Qing dynasty. In the passage, a character remarks that the city is too noisy and difficult to live in, suggesting instead settling in the well-known Stone Village (石村) as a neighbor of Mr. Bai. Over time, the expression evolved into a standard way to refer to facts that are common knowledge among the general public.
example_zh: 众所周知，长期熬夜会对身体健康造成严重影响。
example_en: As is widely known, staying up late for extended periods can seriously harm one's physical health.

meaning: One's heart blooms like a flower in full blossom, describing a state of being extremely happy or overjoyed. It conveys an outward, visible burst of delight from within.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty novel '文明小史' (A Brief History of Civilization) by Li Baojia, in its sixtieth chapter. In the scene, the official Ping Zhongcheng is so delighted that his heart blooms like a flower, repeatedly praising someone with the words '难为他了' (he really outdid himself). The expression likened inner joy to a flower suddenly bursting into full bloom, and it has since become a common way to describe ecstatic happiness.
example_zh: 听到自己考上理想大学的消息，她心花怒放地跳了起来。
example_en: Hearing the news that she had been admitted to her dream university, she leapt up with her heart blooming with joy.

meaning: Flesh presses against flesh and bones join with bones. This idiom describes the extreme intensity of close-quarters combat where soldiers fight body to body. It conveys a battle so fierce that combatants are physically pressed together in the struggle.
origin: This phrase originates from the 'History of Yuan' (元史), specifically the biography of Hao Jing (郝经), a scholar and diplomat of the Yuan dynasty. The original passage describes a siege in which attacking soldiers pressed so closely together in assault that their flesh and bones were mashed against one another, yet they persisted until the enemy's fortified walls were breached. The vivid imagery of bodies crushed together captures the brutality of the assault. It has since been used to characterize any extraordinarily fierce and desperate battle.
example_zh: 两军在城下肉薄骨并，战况极为惨烈。
example_en: The two armies clashed in brutal close combat beneath the city walls, and the fighting was extraordinarily fierce.

meaning: Refers to attaining high official rank and great wealth. It describes the worldly success of holding government office and becoming rich. The phrase is often used to denote the pursuit or possession of fame, power, and fortune.
origin: The phrase appears in the Tang dynasty poet Li Bai's work '江上吟' (Song on the River), where he writes that if fame and fortune could last forever, even the Han River would flow northwest—implying such things are transient. The Ming dynasty writer Hong Yingming also cited it in '菜根谭' (Tending the Roots of Wisdom), advising that viewing fame and fortune from the perspective of their inevitable decline diminishes one's attachment to them. The idiom thus carries both literal and philosophical connotations about worldly success.
example_zh: 他一生追逐功名富贵，到头来不过是一场空。
example_en: He spent his whole life pursuing fame and fortune, only to find it all amounted to nothing in the end.

meaning: To invite disaster and bring trouble upon oneself through reckless or meddlesome behavior. It describes a person who unnecessarily courts calamity by acting imprudently or stirring up matters best left alone.
origin: The phrase originates from the Yuan dynasty playwright Gao Ming's famous drama 'The Lute' (琵琶记), specifically in the scene 'Niu Xiaojie Admonishes Her Father' (牛小姐谏父). In the dialogue, a character warns that persisting in a certain course will inevitably lead to ruin, saying 'you are inviting disaster and gathering misfortune.' The expression was later adopted in Ming dynasty literature, appearing in the novel 'Haoqiuzhuan' (好逑传) by an anonymous author, where bystanders avoid speaking out for fear of courting trouble themselves.
example_zh: 他这样做无异于招灾揽祸，迟早要吃大亏。
example_en: By acting this way he is simply courting disaster, and sooner or later he will pay dearly for it.

meaning: Refers to virtuous conduct and good deeds that remain unknown or unacknowledged by others. It describes someone who quietly practices morality without seeking fame, praise, or public recognition for their goodness.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a single specific classical text but is composed from traditional Chinese moral vocabulary. The character 潜 (qián) means hidden or submerged, 德 (dé) means virtue, 隐 (yǐn) means concealed, and 行 (xíng) means conduct or behavior. The phrase embodies the longstanding Confucian ideal of practicing virtue privately and doing good without expectation of reward or renown. Similar sentiments appear throughout Chinese classical literature, where scholars praised gentlemen whose worthy deeds went unnoticed by the world.
example_zh: 他一生默默行善，潜德隐行，从不张扬。
example_en: He spent his life quietly doing good, practicing hidden virtue and concealed conduct, never seeking to draw attention to himself.

literal: bend, upper arm, and, rest head on
meaning: Resting one's head on a bent arm while sleeping. It describes a life of contentment and tranquility, free from worldly worry. The idiom conveys finding joy in simplicity regardless of material hardship.
origin: The phrase originates from the Analects (论语), in which Confucius describes his own contentment: eating coarse food, drinking plain water, and resting his head on a bent arm, yet finding happiness therein.
