meaning: Literally 'accumulating years and piling up years,' this idiom describes something that has continued or built up over a very long period of time. It is equivalent to the more common phrase 积年累月 (jī nián lěi yuè). It emphasizes the great length of time involved rather than any specific outcome.
origin: The phrase appears in 'Erke Paian Jingqi' (二刻拍案惊奇, Slapping the Table in Amazement, Second Collection), a collection of vernacular short stories compiled by the Ming Dynasty writer Ling Mengchu (凌濛初). In Volume 5, a captured thief finally confesses the truth: that over many long years (积年累岁), whenever festive seasons and celebrations arrived, he would go out far and wide to plunder and steal, and in ordinary times he trafficked in children and took lives. The idiom thus originally described the prolonged, habitual nature of the criminal's wrongdoing.
example_zh: 这项工程积年累岁才得以完成。
example_en: This project was completed only after many long years of accumulated effort.

meaning: Literally 'like falling into a sea of smoke.' It describes being completely lost and disoriented, unable to find one's bearings or grasp the essentials of a situation. The idiom is used when someone is overwhelmed by complexity and cannot find a clear direction or clue.
origin: This idiom originates from 'A New Account of the Tales of the World' (世说新语) by Liu Yiqing of the Southern Dynasties (Song). The story recounts how Wang Zhongzu and Liu Zhenchang visited Yin Zhongjun (general of the central army) for a conversation, and after the talk they rode away together. Liu praised Yin, saying he was truly impressive, but Wang replied, 'You have fallen into his clouds and mist.' Wang's remark implied that Liu had been so captivated by Yin's rhetoric that he was lost in confusion, unable to see clearly.
example_zh: 面对堆积如山的数据，他如堕烟海，一时竟不知从何下手。
example_en: Facing mountains of data, he felt as if lost in a sea of smoke, unsure for a moment where to even begin.

meaning: To have lost all sense of conscience and morality. It describes someone whose wickedness has reached an extreme, completely devoid of any moral compass or decency. The phrase is used to condemn utterly ruthless and heartless behavior.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty work 'Lüyuan Conghua' (履园丛话) by Qian Yong, specifically in the chapter 'Yilun·Liji' (臆论·利己). Qian Yong observed that people of his time, already wealthy and arrogant, had further abandoned all conscience in their pursuit of self-interest. The expression has since become a severe condemnation of those who act without any moral restraint whatsoever.
example_zh: 这些丧尽天良的商人竟在婴儿奶粉里掺假，害了无数家庭。
example_en: These utterly conscienceless merchants actually adulterated baby formula, harming countless families.

meaning: The sea turns into mulberry fields, and mulberry fields turn into the sea. It is a metaphor for the immense changes and transformations that occur in worldly affairs over time. It is equivalent to the idiom 桑田沧海.
origin: This idiom shares its origin with 桑田沧海. According to 神仙传 (Biographies of Divine Immortals) by the Jin dynasty scholar 葛洪, the immortal maiden 麻姑 once told 蔡经 that since her last reception of an invitation, she had already witnessed the eastern sea turn into mulberry fields three times. This striking image of seas and farmland endlessly transforming into one another became a vivid metaphor for the vastness of worldly change across the ages.
example_zh: 几百年过去，桑田碧海，当年的繁华小镇如今只剩一片荒凉。
example_en: Hundreds of years have passed; seas have turned to mulberry fields, and the once prosperous town is now nothing but desolation.

meaning: Even a rat at least has skin. This idiom uses the rat as a metaphor to remind people that even the lowliest creature possesses a covering and a sense of decency, so humans must likewise uphold shame and propriety. It is employed to criticize those who act without manners or moral integrity.
origin: This idiom originates from the poem 'Look at the Rat' (相鼠) in the 'Odes of Yong' (鄘风) section of the Classic of Poetry (诗经), China's oldest extant poetry anthology, compiled during the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 11th century–771 BCE). The poem satirizes people who lack ritual propriety and shame, declaring that even a rat has its skin, yet a person may be devoid of manners—and such a person deserves no better than death. The work reflects the Zhou-era conviction that ritual propriety (礼) is the bedrock of a civilized, moral society.
example_zh: 他做出这种背信弃义的事，真是连相鼠有皮的道理都不懂。
example_en: By committing such an act of treachery, he shows he does not even grasp the basic principle that even a rat has its skin.

meaning: Like a dragon hibernating and an inchworm bending its body, this idiom metaphorically describes someone who lives in seclusion and declines to take public office. It conveys the wisdom of withdrawing from the world to preserve oneself during unfavorable times.
origin: The phrase derives from the 'Xi Ci' (Appended Remarks) chapter of the Yijing, or Book of Changes, a foundational text of the Zhou dynasty. The original passage states: 'The inchworm bends its body so that it may stretch forward; the dragon and snake hibernate so that they may preserve themselves.' This observation of natural creatures adapting to adversity was later distilled into the four-character idiom. During the Ming dynasty, Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng employed it in his letter 'Reply to Minister of Works Lu Wutai,' using it to describe a person of talent who chose to remain in obscurity rather than serve in government.
example_zh: 他才华横溢却龙蛰蠖屈，隐居山林不问世事。
example_en: Though full of talent, he chose to live in seclusion like a hibernating dragon and bending inchworm, withdrawing to the mountains and ignoring worldly affairs.

meaning: Like clouds dissipating and fog lifting away. It is a metaphor for things vanishing completely and cleanly, leaving no trace behind. Often used to describe worries, doubts, or misunderstandings that fully disappear.
origin: This idiom originates from a Tang dynasty imperial edict. Emperor Taizong of Tang (Li Shimin) issued the 'Edict Appointing Zhangsun Wuji as Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs' (授长孙无忌尚书右仆射诏), in which he declared that wherever weapons were directed, enemies would scatter and vanish like clouds and fog dispersing. The phrase thus originally described the overwhelming military power that could make opposition melt away entirely.
example_zh: 听了老师耐心的解释，她心中的疑虑顿时云消雾散。
example_en: After hearing the teacher's patient explanation, the doubts in her mind instantly vanished like dissipating clouds.

meaning: A metaphor for achieving sudden success or a dramatic rise in status through passing a difficult trial. It originates from the legend that carp which could leap over the Dragon Gate waterfall would transform into dragons. It is commonly used to describe someone who passes an important examination or attains a lofty position.
origin: According to the 'San Qin Ji' by Xin Shi, the Yellow River passes through a narrow gorge at Hejin called Longmen (Dragon Gate), carved open by the legendary Emperor Yu. Each spring, yellow carp would swim upstream against the current, and any that managed to leap over the gate would transform into a dragon. The Tang dynasty scholar Yuan Bi composed a famous rhapsody titled 'Fu on the Fish Leaping the Dragon Gate,' cementing the tale in literary tradition. Over time the image became a standard metaphor for passing the imperial examinations and rising in social rank.
example_zh: 十年寒窗苦读，他终于金榜题名，如鱼跃龙门般改变了命运。
example_en: After ten years of diligent study, he finally passed the imperial examination and, like a fish leaping the Dragon Gate, changed his fate.

meaning: Like flies buzzing restlessly about and rats peering around in search of openings. A metaphor for someone who ingratiates and schemes everywhere for personal gain, behaving in a greedy and shameless manner.
origin: This idiom originates from the Ming dynasty writer Wu Cheng'en, in his preface 'He Xue Bo Wei Qi Tao Shi Ying Jiang Xu' congratulating a scholar-official. In the text, Wu Cheng'en lamented the decline of academic integrity, describing how people schemed and plotted in countless ways—buzzing about like flies and peeping like rats, chasing profit like a lurking crossbow-fish. He compared such base conduct to the haggling of merchants in the marketplace, sorrowing that it had now infiltrated the schools meant for learning.
example_zh: 他蝇营鼠窥，到处巴结权贵，最终被人识破了真面目。
example_en: He buzzed about and snooped around, currying favor with the powerful everywhere, until his true face was finally exposed.

meaning: Literally not a single grain is harvested. It describes a total crop failure, typically caused by drought, flood, or other disasters. Used to emphasize the severity of an agricultural disaster.
origin: This idiom has no specific classical literary origin but is a modern descriptive compound. The phrase combines 颗粒 (each individual grain) with 无收 (no harvest), forming a vivid image of complete agricultural failure. It gained widespread use in the context of reporting on famines and natural disasters in modern Chinese. The expression reflects the agrarian foundation of Chinese society, where crop failure meant existential threat.
example_zh: 去年大旱，庄稼颗粒无收，农民们苦不堪言。
example_en: Last year's severe drought caused total crop failure, leaving the farmers in bitter hardship.

meaning: Refers to the twelve gold-lettered tablets sent in a single day by the Song court to recall General Yue Fei from the battlefield. Used as a metaphor for an extremely urgent and irresistible command or order.
origin: During the Southern Song Dynasty, General Yue Fei was winning victories against the Jin invaders and pressing toward the enemy capital. The court minister Qin Hui, fearing Yue Fei's growing power and seeking peace with the Jin, persuaded Emperor Gaozong to order his withdrawal. In a single day, twelve gold-lettered tablets bearing urgent military decrees were dispatched, commanding Yue Fei to halt his advance and return. Forced to comply, Yue Fei withdrew and reportedly lamented that ten years of effort had been destroyed in a single day. The phrase thereafter symbolized urgent, peremptory orders from above.
example_zh: 前线战事吃紧，朝廷连下十二金牌，命他即刻撤军。
example_en: With the front line under intense pressure, the court sent twelve gold tablets in succession, ordering him to withdraw his troops immediately.

meaning: To flaunt one's seniority or advanced age to assert superiority over others. It describes someone who uses their age and experience as leverage to boast, lecture, or act condescendingly. The idiom conveys disapproval of this behavior as arrogant and tiresome.
origin: The idiom appears in Cao Yu's 1940 play 'Beijing Man' (《北京人》), Act One. In the scene, a character encounters older colleagues who throw their weight around based on seniority, and has no choice but to play along with flattering agreement. The phrase captures a common social phenomenon in traditional Chinese culture, where age and rank were deeply respected, sometimes to the point of abuse. Though the expression gained literary recognition through Cao Yu, the underlying concept predates the play.
example_zh: 他总爱在年轻人面前以老卖老，实在让人受不了。
example_en: He always likes to flaunt his seniority in front of young people, which is really unbearable.

meaning: To harm public interests for personal gain. It describes corrupt behavior where someone exploits their position to profit at the expense of the collective or organization they serve. The idiom is typically used to criticize selfish and unethical conduct in government or corporate settings.
origin: The idiom reflects a long-standing moral principle in Chinese culture that dates back to ancient Confucian teachings about public service and integrity. Throughout Chinese dynastic history, officials were expected to prioritize the welfare of the state and people above personal enrichment. The phrase encapsulates the recurring problem of corruption that dynasties faced, where greedy officials would embezzle public resources for private benefit. It became a standard criticism in both historical commentary and bureaucratic reform movements.
example_zh: 他利用职务之便损公肥私，最终被纪检部门查处。
example_en: He exploited his position to embezzle public resources for personal gain, and was eventually investigated by the disciplinary authorities.

meaning: This idiom describes a situation where errors occur due to a combination of coincidental or accidental factors. It implies that things go wrong not because of deliberate intent, but through a series of unexpected twists of fate. The phrase uses the concepts of yin and yang to emphasize how opposing forces can coincidentally align to produce an unintended outcome.
origin: The phrase originates from the Ming Dynasty work 'Lihai Ji' (蠡海集) by Wang Kui, in a section discussing the calendar and numerology. Wang Kui explained that the sixty-year sexagenary cycle could be divided into four segments, with certain days designated as yin or yang positions, leading to what he termed 'yin errors and yang mistakes.' Over time, the term evolved from its technical calendrical origins into a common metaphor for accidents caused by coincidence.
example_zh: 他阴差阳错地坐错了火车，却意外遇到了多年未见的老朋友。
example_en: By a twist of fate, he boarded the wrong train but unexpectedly ran into an old friend he hadn't seen in years.

meaning: To escape from death and return to life; also used in the sense of braving mortal danger, akin to the idiom 出生入死. It describes someone who passes through life-threatening peril and survives.
origin: The phrase originates from the Tang dynasty writer Huang Tao's (黄滔) stele inscription 'Record of the Baoen Dingguang Duobao Pagoda in Fuzhou of the Great Tang' (《大唐福州报恩定光多宝塔碑记》). The original text reads: 'Such is the power of the Great Hero, bringing forth from death into life; such is the spirit of utmost sincerity, moving heaven and earth.' It originally praised the transcendent power of Buddhist faith to deliver beings from death and restore them to life. Over time it came to also describe braving deadly danger in the course of duty.
example_zh: 战士们出死入生，为保卫家园浴血奋战。
example_en: The soldiers braved death itself, fighting desperately to defend their homeland.

meaning: This idiom describes the situation where information, policies, or intentions from those in higher positions are successfully communicated to those at lower levels. It emphasizes the importance of smooth top-down communication in governance and organizational management, ensuring that directives are understood by all.
origin: This concept originates from Guanzi (《管子·明法》), a text from the Spring and Autumn period attributed to Guan Zhong, a renowned statesman of the Qi state. The original text states '下情不上通，谓之塞' (when lower-level situations cannot reach the top, it is called blockage), emphasizing the importance of unobstructed two-way communication between rulers and subjects. Over time, the complementary pair '上情下达' and '下情上达' became established idioms representing smooth communication in both directions within governance and organizations.
example_zh: 好的管理者能保证上情下达，让每位员工都了解公司的决策方向。
example_en: A good manager ensures that information from above reaches those below, so every employee understands the company's strategic direction.

meaning: When a person falls into poverty or desperate circumstances, their mind becomes sluggish and their options diminish. It describes how hardship can dull one's resourcefulness and problem-solving ability.
origin: The phrase traces to the Song Dynasty poet Chen Wuji (陈无己), who wrote '人穷令智短' (when a man is destitute, his wisdom falls short), as recorded by Zhuang Jiyu in 'Ji Lei Bian' (《鸡肋编》). A parallel expression appears in Wei Bai's 'Jianzhong Jingguo Xudeng Lu' (《建中靖国续灯录》): '人贫智短，马瘦毛长' — when a person is poor, wisdom falls short; when a horse is thin, its hair grows long — drawing a vivid analogy between human destitution and animal frailty.
example_zh: 创业失败后他负债累累，做什么决定都出错，真是人穷智短。
example_en: After his business failed and he was drowning in debt, every decision he made went wrong — truly a case of poverty dulling the mind.

meaning: To make virtue known and illustrious while putting an end to wrongdoing and corrupt practices. The phrase describes the duty of a leader to promote moral excellence and suppress evil, thereby guiding others by example.
origin: The phrase originates from the Zuozhuan (左传), in the section covering the second year of Duke Huan of Lu (708 BCE). The text states that a ruler should manifest virtue and block wrongdoing in order to oversee all officials. The Tang dynasty scholar Kong Yingda (孔颖达) explained in his subcommentary that '昭德' means to make good virtue increasingly illustrious and widely known, while '塞违' means to block evil violations so that disobedience ceases. Together the phrase encapsulates the Confucian ideal of governance through moral example.
example_zh: 政府表彰清廉官员，意在昭德塞违，端正社会风气。
example_en: The government commends honest officials, intending to manifest virtue and block wrongdoing, thereby rectifying social conduct.

meaning: To behave as if nothing were happening, remaining calm and composed in an emergency or crisis. It can also describe someone who turns a blind eye to bad behavior or wrongdoing, appearing unconcerned. The phrase conveys an attitude of unflappable composure.
origin: The idiom traces back to the Mencius (《孟子·离娄下》), a text from the Warring States period. Mencius praised the legendary sage-king Yu for controlling the floods by following the natural flow of water, acting as though nothing extraordinary were being done. Over time, the phrase came to describe a person who remains unruffled in pressing situations, and by extension someone who treats serious matters with apparent indifference.
example_zh: 大火蔓延时，他行若无事地指挥众人撤离，丝毫不见慌乱。
example_en: As the fire spread, he calmly directed everyone to evacuate, showing no sign of panic.

meaning: In traditional Chinese opera, 'chū cǎi' referred to the technique of smearing red liquid on stage to simulate bleeding during a killing scene. The idiom metaphorically means to have one's secret exposed or to be publicly embarrassed in front of an audience.
origin: This idiom originates from 'Erke Paian Jingqi' (二刻拍案惊奇), a renowned collection of vernacular short stories compiled by Ling Mengchu during the Ming Dynasty. In Volume 30, a character suggests privately settling a matter rather than letting it be publicly exposed. The theatrical imagery of simulated bloodshed on stage became a metaphor for the public revelation of secrets or loss of face.
example_zh: 他撒的谎被揭穿，当场出彩，满脸通红。
example_en: After his lie was exposed, he was publicly embarrassed, his face turning bright red.

meaning: This idiom refers to understanding the times and adapting to circumstances, living a carefree and leisurely life. It evokes an image of bathing in the Yi River and enjoying the breeze at the rain altar, symbolizing a contented, untroubled attitude toward life.
origin: The phrase originates from the Analects (Lunyu), chapter 'Xian Jin' (Advanced), where Confucius asked his disciples about their aspirations. Zeng Xi (Zeng Dian) replied that in late spring he wished to bathe in the Yi River, enjoy the breeze at the rain altar (Wuyu), and return home singing. Confucius sighed in admiration, saying he shared Zeng Xi's ideal. The idiom thus came to represent a carefree, refined enjoyment of life in harmony with nature.
example_zh: 他向往沂水舞雩的逍遥生活，不愿为名利奔波。
example_en: He yearns for the carefree life of bathing in the Yi River and enjoying the breeze at the rain altar, unwilling to toil for fame and wealth.

meaning: To lower one's aspirations and conform to prevailing vulgar customs. It describes someone who abandons their personal standards or ideals in order to accommodate commonplace trends and expectations.
origin: The phrase reflects a classical Chinese philosophical concern with the tension between personal integrity and societal conformity. While no single definitive source is recorded, the expression draws on the broader tradition of Confucian and Daoist debates about whether a person should uphold high principles or adapt to worldly norms. The term 降心 appears in early texts denoting the humbling of one's ambitions, and 顺俗 connotes yielding to popular habits. Together they capture the act of compromising one's resolve for the sake of social acceptance.
example_zh: 面对官场的腐败，他不愿降心顺俗，毅然辞官归隐。
example_en: Faced with corruption in officialdom, he refused to lower his standards and conform to vulgar customs, resolutely resigning to live in seclusion.

meaning: A family that for generations has prized literary learning and proper etiquette. '诗' refers to the Book of Songs (Shijing) and '礼' to the classic ritual texts (Rites of Zhou, Book of Etiquette, Book of Rites). It denotes a cultured household steeped in Confucian scholarship and moral propriety.
origin: The phrase comes from Volume 16 of 'Qi Xiu Lei Gao' (七修类稿), a Ming dynasty miscellany by the scholar Lang Ying (郎英). In the passage, Lang Ying laments that people cling to petty frugality while forgetting greater moral principles, and sighs that even families of poetic and ritual tradition have fallen to such behavior. The idiom encapsulates the Confucian ideal of a household that transmits literary refinement and ritual decorum across generations.
example_zh: 他出身于诗礼之家，自幼便举止温文尔雅。
example_en: Born into a family of scholarly and ritual tradition, he carried himself with refined grace from a young age.

meaning: This idiom describes speech or writing whose content is profound but whose language is simple and easy to understand. It praises the ability to explain complex ideas in plain, accessible terms, preserving depth of thought while keeping expression clear.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a single classical text or specific historical anecdote. It emerged as a descriptive phrase in Chinese literary criticism, reflecting the ideal that the best writing combines profound substance with plain expression. Over time it became a standard compliment for educators, authors, and speakers who can make difficult subjects accessible. No particular dynasty or figure is uniquely associated with its coinage.
example_zh: 李老师的讲解深入浅出，连初学者都能听懂。
example_en: Teacher Li's explanation is profound yet easy to understand—even beginners can follow along.

meaning: Refers to a person whose name and deeds endure through the ages, leaving a lasting legacy for posterity. It praises figures whose contributions are significant enough to be remembered for eternity.
origin: The phrase combines 千秋 (a thousand autumns, a metaphor for eternity or the passage of ages) with 人物 (a personage or notable figure). Unlike many classical idioms, it does not originate from a single canonical text or specific historical anecdote, but rather evolved as a descriptive compound expressing admiration for individuals of enduring renown. It has been used in literary and commemorative contexts to honor those whose achievements merit remembrance across generations.
example_zh: 这位将军战功赫赫，堪称千秋人物。
example_en: This general's illustrious military exploits make him truly a figure for the ages.

meaning: Literally cutting the long legs of a crane to lengthen the short legs of a wild duck. It is a metaphor for acting against natural laws and attempting things that cannot succeed. The idiom warns against forcing changes that contradict the inherent nature of things.
origin: This idiom originates from the philosophical text Zhuangzi (庄子), specifically the chapter '骈拇' (Webbed Toes), composed during the Warring States period by the Daoist philosopher Zhuang Zhou. In this passage, Zhuangzi observes that a crane's legs are long and a duck's legs are short by nature, and argues that one should neither shorten the crane's legs nor lengthen the duck's, as doing so would violate the natural order. He uses this imagery to critique artificial interference with the way of nature. The idiom thus embodies the Daoist principle of wuwei (non-action) and respecting the inherent qualities of all things.
example_zh: 教育应因材施教，断鹤继凫只会适得其反。
example_en: Education should be tailored to each student's aptitude; forcing everyone into the same mold will only backfire.

meaning: Profound yet clearly evident. It describes ideas, observations, or expressions that are both deeply insightful and plainly obvious to understand. The phrase is a variant of the more common '深切著明'.
origin: This idiom is a variant of '深切著明,' a phrase rooted in classical Chinese philosophical literature, particularly associated with the Book of Changes (易经) and the Great Treatise (系辞传) tradition. The sages of antiquity were said to convey wisdom that was both profoundly deep and vividly clear, so that moral and cosmic truths could be grasped by all. Over the centuries, the phrase was adopted by scholars and commentators to praise writing or reasoning that combined depth with lucidity. The variant form '深切着白' uses '白' (white, bright) in place of '明' (clear), emphasizing the luminous, self-evident quality of the insight.
example_zh: 他对这一社会现象的分析深切着白，令在场听众豁然开朗。
example_en: His analysis of this social phenomenon was both profound and strikingly clear, leaving the audience suddenly enlightened.

meaning: Describes a state of poverty where one's dwelling is old and dilapidated. Rain leaks in from above and wind blows in from the sides, leaving the house with no proper shelter from the elements.
origin: This idiom originates from a stele inscription by the Tang dynasty scholar Han Yu (韩愈), one of the Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song. In his text for a sea deity temple stele, he wrote that the building was exposed to rain from above and wind from the sides, with nothing to serve as a proper cover or barrier. The phrase vividly portrays a structure so weathered and broken that it can barely protect its occupants.
example_zh: 他家境贫寒，所居之屋上雨旁风，难以遮蔽。
example_en: He lived in poverty, his dwelling so dilapidated that rain and wind came freely through it, offering little shelter.

meaning: Originally referred to Buddhist monks going from house to house with their alms bowls to beg for food. It is now used metaphorically to describe begging from door to door, or living in destitution and relying on charity.
origin: The phrase first appears in the Qing dynasty anonymous work "杜诗言志" (Words Expressing Ambition through Du's Poetry), Volume 1. The passage warns readers to carefully distinguish the poet Du Fu's true circumstances, lest they mistake him for someone who wanders about seeking patronage like a monk begging from door to door. Over time the expression shed its literary context and became a general metaphor for begging house to house.
example_zh: 他破产之后，不得不沿门托钵，靠乞讨度日。
example_en: After going bankrupt, he had no choice but to go begging from door to door to make a living.

meaning: Describes something that has completely vanished or been wiped out, with not a single trace left behind. It conveys a total loss where everything is gone and nothing remains.
origin: This phrase comes from a decree written by the Liang dynasty scholar Ren Fang titled 'Decree on Compiling Books for Emperor Wu of Liang.' A devastating fire had broken out at the imperial library and spread to the archives, reducing ancient bamboo slips and silk-bound manuscripts to ashes. The phrase originally described how the entire collection of precious classical texts was utterly destroyed in the blaze, leaving nothing behind.
example_zh: 一场大火过后，他多年的积蓄荡然无存。
example_en: After the fire, his years of savings vanished without a trace.

meaning: The compass (规) draws circles and symbolizes Heaven; the square (矩) draws squares and symbolizes Earth. Together, the idiom means to model oneself on or emulate the order and patterns of Heaven and Earth. It often describes architecture, governance, or conduct that follows cosmic principles.
origin: The phrase originates from Zhang Heng's 'Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital' (东京赋), collected in the Wen Xuan (文选), a renowned literary anthology of the Eastern Han dynasty. In the passage, Zhang Heng describes the construction of ritual palaces where round structures imitate Heaven and square ones imitate Earth. The commentator Xue Zong explained that palace decorations followed this cosmological symbolism—round elements representing Heaven and square ones representing Earth, reflecting the ancient Chinese belief in a round heaven and square earth (天圆地方).
example_zh: 古代宫殿建筑多取天圆地方之意，规天矩地，以示法象自然。
example_en: Ancient palace architecture often adopted the concept of a round heaven and square earth, modeling itself on the cosmos to symbolize harmony with nature.

meaning: Every word is like a precious pearl. It describes writing or speech whose every word is exquisitely chosen and beautiful. The idiom is used to praise the elegance and refinement of an article or speech.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Ernü Yingxiong Zhuan' (儿女英雄传) by Wen Kang. In the text, a passage remarks that even if essays were each a piece of brocade and every word a precious pearl, one still might not pass the imperial examination to become a jinshi. The expression thus originally conveyed the frustration that literary brilliance alone could not guarantee official success, but over time it came to be used purely as high praise for beautifully written prose.
example_zh: 这位作家的散文字字珠玑，令人读后回味无穷。
example_en: This writer's prose is so beautifully crafted that every word feels like a gem, leaving readers with a lasting impression.

meaning: To suffer humiliation and lose one's moral integrity or chastity. It describes a person whose virtue and reputation have been destroyed, either through coercion or circumstance. The phrase emphasizes both the physical violation and the loss of moral standing.
origin: This phrase appears in Lu Xun's work 'Notes on Old Fiction: Dream of the Red Chamber,' where he comments on the tragic character Miaoyu from the classic novel 'Dream of the Red Chamber.' Despite Miaoyu's reclusive purity and devotion to a life of Buddhist austerity, she is kidnapped by bandits and subjected to disgrace. Lu Xun notes that the author further burdened her with accusations of losing her virtue and integrity, as well as slanders about greed and bribery. Lu Xun expressed deep sympathy, recognizing the author's profound grief over her fate.
example_zh: 她宁死不屈，绝不愿丧身失节。
example_en: She would rather die than submit and lose her virtue and integrity.

meaning: Literally 'like treading on thin ice.' It describes someone acting with extreme caution and vigilance, fully aware that a single misstep could bring disaster. The idiom conveys a sense of wariness and carefulness in delicate or dangerous situations.
origin: The phrase originates from the Shijing (Book of Odes), specifically the 'Minor Odes' section in the poem 'Xiao Min' (小旻), dated to the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 1046–771 BCE). The poem portrays a loyal minister's anxious devotion while serving his ruler, declaring: 'Trembling with fear, as if approaching a deep abyss, as if treading on thin ice.' These lines became one of the most quoted expressions of prudent vigilance in classical Chinese literature, later adopted by scholars and officials throughout history to describe the mindset required when navigating political or personal peril.
example_zh: 他在公司里如履薄冰，生怕一句话说错就会被辞退。
example_en: He felt like he was walking on thin ice at the company, terrified that one wrong word would get him fired.

meaning: An emphatic expression meaning "as large as can be" or "incredibly vast." The double negative construction intensifies the claim that nothing could possibly exceed it in size. It is used to stress the extremity of something's magnitude.
origin: This idiom is a classical Chinese emphatic construction that does not trace to a single specific source text. Its rhetorical structure—"nothing is big, [yet] not big"—uses a layered negation to assert that no comparison can surpass the thing described. Such double-negative intensifiers appear scattered across various vernacular and literary writings without one definitive origin. It remains a relatively rare and archaic expression.
example_zh: 这片海洋无大不大，一眼望不到尽头。
example_en: This ocean is as vast as can be, with no end in sight.

meaning: Long-standing habits accumulated over time are extremely difficult to eliminate or change. It describes deeply ingrained practices that resist correction despite awareness of their flaws. The idiom emphasizes the stubborn persistence of old customs or behaviors.
origin: The phrase appears in modern Chinese literature, notably in Guo Moruo's preface to 'The White-Haired Girl' (序〈白毛女〉), where he reflects on the difficulty of transforming old literary habits despite early calls for people's art. Guo Moruo (1892–1978) was a prominent poet, historian, and intellectual of the Republican era. The expression builds on the classical notion that accumulated practices (积习) become deeply rooted over time. It is a variant of the more common idiom 积习难改, conveying the same idea that entrenched habits are hard to break.
example_zh: 他抽了几十年烟，积习难除，戒了好几次都没成功。
example_en: He has smoked for decades, and the habit is so deeply ingrained that he has tried to quit several times without success.

meaning: Witty or amusing remarks that make people smile or laugh out loud. It describes speech so clever and humorous that listeners cannot help but break into a grin.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Book of Han (汉书), in the biography of Kuang Heng (匡衡), a renowned scholar of the Western Han dynasty. The text notes that when Kuang expounded on the Classic of Poetry, he could make people laugh heartily. The Tang scholar Yan Shigu (颜师古), in his annotations, quoted Ru Chun (如淳) as explaining that Kuang's interpretations were so delightful they left listeners unable to stop laughing. Over time, '解颐' came to refer to anything that brings a joyful smile.
example_zh: 老先生讲起笑话来妙语解颐，满座宾客无不捧腹。
example_en: The old gentleman's jokes were so witty that everyone in the room broke into laughter.

meaning: To embellish a story or account by adding details that were not originally present. It describes someone who, when narrating or recounting events, invents extra elements to make the tale more vivid or dramatic. The phrase uses the metaphor of a tree: just as adding branches and leaves makes a tree fuller, adding fabricated details makes a story more elaborate.
origin: The idiom originates from the Ming dynasty novel 'Jin Ping Mei Chuanqi' (The Plum in the Golden Vase), specifically Chapter 13. In the story, a character named Tang Biaobei boasts about his skill in forging paintings, claiming that even Wang Shu himself could not distinguish the forgery after enough time had passed. He then 'added branches and leaves'—embellishing the account with fabricated details about how he terrified someone with accusations of deceiving the emperor and harming the state, causing her to faint on the spot. The metaphor of adding branches and leaves to a tree illustrates how a bare narrative can be fleshed out with invented particulars.
example_zh: 他讲故事时总爱加枝添叶，把一件小事说得天花乱坠。
example_en: Whenever he tells a story, he loves to embellish it with invented details, turning a minor incident into something spectacular.

meaning: All day and all night; day and night without cease. It describes continuous, unbroken activity or existence spanning the full hours of day and night.
origin: This expression appears in the modern literature of early twentieth-century China. The writer Yu Dafu used it in his 1921 novella 'Sinking' (《沉沦》), describing a protagonist who shut himself away in his small study all day and all night. The phrase compounds the character 镇 (meaning 'whole' or 'entire') with both 日 (day) and 夜 (night) to emphasize unbroken duration. A later usage appears in Duanmu Hongliang's 'The Torrent of the Hunhe River,' where it describes the ceaseless flow of river water.
example_zh: 他镇日镇夜地守在母亲病床前，寸步不离。
example_en: He kept watch at his mother's bedside all day and all night, never leaving for a moment.

meaning: Grand and magnificent buildings are reduced to earthen mounds and rubble. It metaphorically describes the swift alternation of rise and fall, where prosperity and glory are quickly lost to ruin and decay.
origin: This idiom originates from a poem by Cao Zhi (曹植), a prince and poet of the Cao Wei state during the Three Kingdoms period. In his 'Song of the Konghou' (箜篌引), Cao Zhi wrote that those born in splendid mansions ultimately fall and return to the hills as dust. The lines lament the impermanence of worldly glory and the inevitability of decline. Over time, the phrase came to symbolize how rapidly prosperity can turn to ruin.
example_zh: 昔日繁华的宫殿如今已成华屋丘墟，令人唏嘘不已。
example_en: The once-prosperous palace has now been reduced to ruins, leaving one to sigh with sorrow.

meaning: Describes a state of mind where one's spirit and soul are unsettled, feeling dazed and unable to gather one's thoughts. It conveys a sense of emotional or mental disturbance where one loses composure and focus. The idiom can also describe being deeply moved or entranced by something.
origin: This idiom derives from classical Chinese descriptions of mental and emotional states, where the spirit (神) and soul (魂) are depicted as being tossed or swayed like an object in the wind. It appears in various literary works throughout Chinese history as a way to vividly portray psychological disorientation. Related forms include 神摇魂荡, 神魂荡扬, and 神魂飘荡. The imagery reflects the traditional Chinese belief that the mind and spirit could be physically disturbed by powerful emotions or external stimuli.
example_zh: 听了这番话，他顿时神魂摇荡，不知如何是好。
example_en: Hearing these words, he was instantly thrown into a daze, not knowing what to do.

meaning: After climbing to a high place, remove the ladder behind you. It signifies that all retreat has been cut off, leaving no option but to advance. Used to describe a situation of no return or a firm resolve to see something through to the end.
origin: This idiom originates from 'The Art of War' (《孙子·九地》) by Sun Tzu of the Spring and Autumn period. The text states that when a commander sets a time and place for battle with his troops, it is like climbing to a height and then removing the ladder — leaving the soldiers with no way back. It illustrates the military strategy of cutting off retreat to force determination and courage. The Tang dynasty writer Li Han later cited it to describe a commitment to a cause with no possibility of turning back.
example_zh: 他登高去梯，誓要与敌人决一死战。
example_en: He burned his bridges behind him, vowing to fight the enemy to the death.

meaning: To alarm and mobilize a large number of people for a task. It implies making an unnecessary commotion or fuss over something that could be handled more simply. It is a variant of the idiom 惊师动众.
origin: This idiom comes from a letter by Yuan Hongdao, a prominent Ming dynasty literatus, titled 'To Huang Pingqian' (与黄平倩书). In the letter, Yuan advises that all matters should be handled in an ordinary, straightforward manner without unnecessarily alarming and mobilizing many people. The phrase reflects the literati's preference for simplicity and calm deliberation over grand displays of effort.
example_zh: 这点小事不必惊群动众，我们几个人就能解决。
example_en: There's no need to alarm everyone and mobilize a crowd over such a small matter; the few of us can handle it.

meaning: The entire course of events and the underlying reasons behind them. It refers to understanding or recounting the full story from start to finish, including why things happened as they did.
origin: Originates from the Yuan dynasty playwright Ma Zhiyuan's zaju play Qing Shan Lei (Tears of the Blue Shirt), Act 4. The original line reads, 'You must tell the whole story and its reasons in detail, without concealing anything.' The phrase combines '始末' (beginning and end, i.e., the whole process) with '缘由' (cause and reason) to describe a complete account of what happened and why.
example_zh: 老管家将此事的始末缘由细细说了一遍。
example_en: The old steward recounted the entire course of events and its causes in detail.

meaning: Beacon fires rising to fill the sky. It is a metaphor for war and warfare spreading across the land. The idiom describes a situation where conflict has engulfed many regions at once.
origin: The phrase originates from a memorial by the Han dynasty scholar Cai Yong, recorded in his collected works. During that period, the Xianbei people repeatedly invaded the border commanderies of Yunzhong and Wuyuan. Within a single month, the border beacon fires never ceased and the dust they raised reached the sky. The imagery of unbroken beacon fires reaching the heavens came to symbolize widespread warfare.
example_zh: 连天烽火中，百姓流离失所，苦不堪言。
example_en: Amid beacon fires reaching the sky, the common people were driven from their homes and suffered beyond words.

meaning: This idiom describes a person who has become emaciated or thin. It refers to clothing and belts becoming loose because the wearer has lost weight. It is typically used to depict the physical toll of longing, grief, or lovesickness.
origin: The phrase originates from Wang Shifu's 'Romance of the Western Chamber' (西厢记), a famous Yuan dynasty dramatic work. In the second part, fourth scene, the text reads: 'Word by word, the night drags on; sound by sound, clothes grow wide and belts grow loose.' The lines express the sorrow of separation and lovesickness, where grief causes one to waste away physically, resulting in loose-fitting garments.
example_zh: 自他远行后，她终日思念，日渐衣宽带松，形容憔悴。
example_en: Since he went away, she pined for him day and night, growing thin and haggard until her clothes hung loose.

meaning: Literally meaning to take up an axe to chop and carve, this idiom by extension refers to the careful polishing and refinement of a literary work. It evokes the image of a craftsman shaping wood, applied metaphorically to the writer's deliberate revision and chiseling of prose.
origin: No single classical source is recorded for this idiom. It draws on the familiar imagery of a craftsman wielding an axe to shape and carve wood, a metaphor with deep roots in Chinese literary tradition. Over time, the expression came to describe the painstaking process of revising and refining one's writing, much as a woodworker chips away at rough material. It reflects the traditional Chinese appreciation for treating literary composition as a form of skilled craftsmanship. The phrase thus bridges the worlds of manual artistry and literary endeavor.
example_zh: 他在修改文稿时弄斤操斧，反复推敲每一个字。
example_en: When revising his manuscript, he chiseled away at every word with meticulous care, revising over and over again.

meaning: The peacock screen was hit and one was chosen. It refers to being selected as a son-in-law through a competitive process. The phrase originates from a story where a father tested suitors by having them shoot arrows at peacocks painted on a door screen.
origin: During the Sui Dynasty, Dou Yi, father of a talented daughter, painted two peacocks on a door screen and promised her hand to any suitor who could shoot both peacocks in the eyes with two arrows. Dozens of young nobles tried and failed. Li Yuan, who later became Emperor Gaozu of the Tang Dynasty, arrived and hit each peacock in one eye with his two arrows. Delighted, Dou Yi gave his daughter to Li Yuan in marriage, and she became Empress Dou of the Tang Dynasty.
example_zh: 前来求婚的人很多，最终小李凭借出众的才华雀屏中选，成为王家的女婿。
example_en: Many suitors came to propose, but in the end Xiao Li was chosen as the son-in-law thanks to his outstanding talent.

literal: hit the ground, cry to heaven
meaning: This idiom describes a person hitting their head against the ground and crying out to heaven in extreme grief. It portrays overwhelming sorrow expressed through dramatic physical action. The image conveys the most intense form of despair and lamentation.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Officialdom Unmasked' (官场现形记) by Li Baojia (李宝嘉), Chapter 14. In the story, when a shop owner's wife discovers that her daughter-in-law has died, she is so devastated that she throws herself to the ground, cries out to heaven, and weeps without end. The phrase vividly captures her uncontrollable grief at the sudden loss.
example_zh: 得知儿子遇难的消息，她抢地呼天，痛哭不止。
example_en: Upon hearing the news of her son's death, she threw herself to the ground, cried out to heaven, and wept without ceasing.

meaning: Literally 'red mouth and poisonous tongue,' describing someone whose words are vicious and hurtful. It refers to speech that is biting, cruel, and designed to wound others. The redness evokes fire and aggression, while the venom suggests deliberate malice in what is said.
origin: The phrase originates from a poem by the Tang dynasty poet Lu Tong (卢仝) titled 'Lunar Eclipse' (《月蚀》). In the poem, Lu Tong describes a bird that acts as a host yet goes unnoticed, greedily entering people's homes and wielding a 'red mouth and poisonous tongue.' The imagery compares the bird's destructive chatter to venomous creatures, vividly conveying how malicious words can be as harmful as physical poison.
example_zh: 他那人赤口毒舌，几句话就把同事气得当场落泪。
example_en: He has a red mouth and poisonous tongue; just a few words from him left his colleague in tears on the spot.

meaning: Literally 'rinsing with a stone and pillowing on a stream,' this idiom refers to living in seclusion and withdrawing from worldly affairs. It originated from a witty slip of the tongue that was cleverly explained away, and came to symbolize the hermit's life.
origin: From 'A New Account of the Tales of the World' (世说新语·排调) by Liu Yiqing of the Southern Dynasties Song period. Sun Chu intended to say '枕石漱流' (pillow on stone, rinse with stream) to express his wish for a reclusive life, but accidentally reversed it to '漱石枕流.' Wang Wu teased him, asking whether one could really pillow on a stream or rinse with a stone. Sun cleverly retorted that he pillowed on the stream to wash his ears and rinsed with the stone to whet his teeth, turning the error into a graceful defense of his hermit ideal.
example_zh: 他厌倦了官场的纷争，决心漱石枕流，归隐山林。
example_en: Weary of officialdom's strife, he resolved to withdraw into seclusion among the mountains and forests.

meaning: The path of true advancement may appear like retreating. It expresses the Daoist philosophical idea that genuine progress often looks like backward movement to the untrained eye. The idiom is a variant of '进道若退' (jìn dào ruò tuì).
origin: This idiom stems from Daoist philosophy, closely related to the passage in the Laozi (Daodejing) of the Spring and Autumn period, where Laozi describes how the great way appears contrary to ordinary perception. The concept that 'the way of advance seems like retreat' reflects the Daoist dialectical view that apparent regression can signify true progress. The variant character '踡' (quán, to curl up) conveys a sense of contracting or drawing back, reinforcing the imagery of seeming retreat. It has been used in later literary and philosophical writings to describe situations where strategic withdrawal or humility leads to forward advancement.
example_zh: 老将军深知进道若踡的道理，主动撤兵十里以诱敌深入。
example_en: The old general, well versed in the principle that true advance may look like retreat, deliberately withdrew his troops ten li to lure the enemy deeper.

meaning: A difference as vast as that between heaven and earth. Used to describe an enormous gap or extreme contrast between two things. The idiom emphasizes that two things are worlds apart in quality, condition, or nature.
origin: From 'Baopuzi' (抱朴子·内篇·论仙) by Ge Hong of the Jin Dynasty (晋代葛洪). The original text discusses how people's preferences and desires differ enormously, stating that such differences are already as vast as the gap between heaven and earth and as incompatible as ice and charcoal. Ge Hong used this comparison to illustrate the extreme divergence in human pursuits and values. Over time, the phrase '天壤之别' became a standalone idiom denoting a fundamental, unbridgeable difference.
example_zh: 城乡教育资源的分配存在着天壤之别。
example_en: There is a world of difference in the distribution of educational resources between urban and rural areas.

meaning: A literary technique where the depiction of environment and atmosphere is tightly integrated with the expression of characters' thoughts and feelings. It describes works of art in which emotion and setting enhance and reflect each other so seamlessly that they become inseparable.
origin: This idiom has no single definitive origin story or literary source. It is a critical term from traditional Chinese literary aesthetics describing the artistic technique where scenic description and emotional expression are woven together as one. The concept became central to Chinese poetics, particularly in the evaluation of classical poetry and prose where natural imagery is used to mirror or evoke inner feeling. It reflects a core Chinese aesthetic ideal that external landscape and internal sentiment should resonate and illuminate each other rather than stand apart.
example_zh: 好的诗篇必然是情景交融，理在其中。
example_en: A fine poem inevitably blends emotion with scenery, with deeper meaning embedded within.

meaning: To be wrapped in a horse hide after death on the battlefield. It refers to dying heroically in combat and having one's body returned wrapped in horse skin. The idiom symbolizes a warrior's resolve to sacrifice his life for his country rather than die peacefully at home.
origin: This idiom originates from the biography of Ma Yuan (马援) in the Book of Later Han (后汉书). Ma Yuan was a famous general of the Eastern Han dynasty. He declared that a true man should die on the frontier battlefield and have his corpse wrapped in horse hide for burial, rather than lying in bed surrounded by wives and children. His words expressed a determination to serve the nation with ultimate sacrifice, and the phrase became a lasting symbol of martial heroism.
example_zh: 将士们抱定马革裹尸的决心，义无反顾地冲向敌阵。
example_en: The soldiers, resolved to die on the battlefield wrapped in horse hide, charged toward the enemy lines without hesitation.

meaning: From knowing one thing, one can deduce knowledge of ten thousand things. It describes the ability to infer broader truths and universal patterns from a single point of knowledge, emphasizing the power of logical reasoning and extrapolation.
origin: This idiom originates from the Warring States period text 'Xunzi: Against Physiognomy' (《荀子·非相》) by the philosopher Xunzi (荀子). In the original passage, Xunzi writes that a wise person can know the distant from the near, know the many from the one, and know the obvious from the subtle. The phrase reflects the rationalist epistemology of early Chinese philosophy, where grasping fundamental principles allows one to comprehend a vast range of phenomena.
example_zh: 他善于以一知万，总能从细微之处发现问题的本质。
example_en: He excels at deducing the whole from a single clue, always able to uncover the essence of a problem from its subtlest details.

meaning: To turn inward and examine oneself for the causes of failure or conflict, rather than blaming others. It emphasizes personal responsibility and self-reflection as the path to improvement. The phrase encourages looking at one's own shortcomings before criticizing external circumstances.
origin: This idiom originates from the Mencius (《孟子·公孙丑上》), a foundational Confucian text from the Warring States period. Mencius taught that a noble person, when facing defeat or adversity, should not resent those who surpass them but instead reflect upon their own conduct. The phrase encapsulates the Confucian ideal of moral self-cultivation through honest introspection. It was later widely cited by Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song dynasty, such as the Cheng brothers, as a guiding principle of personal cultivation.
example_zh: 项目失败后，他没有推卸责任，而是反求诸己，认真总结自己的不足。
example_en: After the project failed, instead of shifting blame, he reflected on himself and carefully summarized his own shortcomings.

meaning: A metaphor for precious things being broken, scattered, and destroyed. It evokes the sorrowful image of once-treasured items reduced to fragments and lost over time.
origin: The idiom originates from the Yuan dynasty work《萱堂记》by the scholar 同恕 (Tong Shu). The text recounts how inscriptions and poems were once composed to praise and celebrate virtue, with scrolls piled brilliantly. Yet after seventy years had passed, the precious writings had scattered like fallen pearls and jade, with nothing left surviving. It laments how even the most treasured creations inevitably succumb to ruin and loss over the passage of time.
example_zh: 历经战乱，那些珍贵的典籍珠零玉落，再难寻觅。
example_en: After years of war, those precious texts were scattered and destroyed, never to be found again.

meaning: Describes being both lazy and habitually procrastinating, putting things off through slothfulness. It characterizes a person who is indolent and fails to act or make progress because of habitual delay.
origin: This phrase originates from a letter by the Tang dynasty scholar Han Yu titled 'Reply to Yin Shiyu' (答殷侍御书). Han Yu expressed his desire to fully pursue his learning, but his official duties kept him entangled and prevented him from continuing his intellectual pursuits. He lamented that he had become lazy and procrastinating, unable to strengthen himself. The phrase thus conveys the regret of wasting time through idleness and delay.
example_zh: 他因怠惰因循，错过了许多大好机会。
example_en: Due to his laziness and procrastination, he missed many great opportunities.

meaning: A metaphor for having exhausted all combat power and resources, leaving no options remaining. It describes a situation where one's strength is completely depleted and no further action is possible. The image is that of a warrior whose bow has snapped and whose blade is worn out.
origin: The phrase originates from the Song Dynasty text 'Jingde Chuandeng Lu' (景德传灯录) compiled by the monk Shi Daoyuan. In the original passage, someone remarks that they intended to attack Mount Luoshan's stronghold, but found their bow broken and their knife spent. The expression was later adopted in Chan (Zen) Buddhist discourse to illustrate the point where all conventional means and effort have been exhausted, leaving one with no recourse. It conveys a sense of complete depletion of strength or strategy.
example_zh: 敌军久攻不下，已是弓折刀尽，只得下令退兵。
example_en: The enemy army, having failed to take the city after a long siege, found its strength completely exhausted and had no choice but to order a retreat.

meaning: Literally refers to the simple, everyday meals served at home. Figuratively, it describes something that is so common or routine that it is unremarkable. It often conveys that an occurrence has become an expected, everyday matter.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Tang dynasty text 'Nü Lunyu' (女论语) by Song Ruohua and Song Ruozhao, which advises wives to diligently prepare 'home-style tea and meals' for their husbands. Song dynasty scholar Luo Dajing later wrote in 'Helin Yulu' (鹤林玉露) that 'ordinary officials are easy to serve, and home-style meals are easy to eat,' reinforcing the idea of simple, familiar fare. Over time, the expression evolved from describing humble household meals into a metaphor for anything commonplace or routine.
example_zh: 加班到深夜对他来说早已是家常便饭了。
example_en: Working overtime until late at night has long been a matter of routine for him.

meaning: Not understanding the reason why something is the case. It describes a state of being puzzled or bewildered about the cause of an event. The phrase conveys a sense of confusion when one cannot figure out why something has happened.
origin: This phrase originates from the Tang dynasty work 'Fa Shu Yao Lu' (Records of Calligraphy) by Zhang Yanyuan, specifically in the chapter 'Gu Lan Ting Xu' (Purchasing the Lanting Preface). The passage recounts the story of Emperor Taizong of Tang, who coveted Wang Xizhi's masterpiece calligraphy 'Lanting Xu' (Preface to the Orchid Pavilion). When the monk holding the scroll was suddenly confronted, the text describes him as 'not knowing the reason why' he was being pursued. The phrase has since come to describe anyone who is at a loss to explain or understand why something has occurred.
example_zh: 听到这个突如其来的消息，他一时不知所以，愣在了原地。
example_en: Hearing this sudden news, he was momentarily bewildered and could not figure out why, frozen where he stood.

meaning: This idiom means "for thousands of ages and ten thousand generations," equivalent to 千秋万代. It emphasizes the extreme longevity and eternity of time, often used to describe something that lasts forever.
origin: The idiom originates from a poem by the Tang dynasty poet Lu Zhaolin (卢照邻), one of the "Four Eminences of Early Tang" (初唐四杰). In his poem "Huai Xian Yin" (《怀仙引》), he wrote the line "天长地久时相忆，千龄万代一来游," expressing a longing for immortals and the hope that across vast ages, friends might still meet to wander together. The phrase was later adopted as a set idiom denoting eternity.
example_zh: 古人的智慧结晶将流传千龄万代。
example_en: The crystallized wisdom of the ancients will be passed down for thousands of generations.

meaning: The cries of orioles and the chatter of swallows. It vividly describes the beautiful scenery of spring, when birds sing and the season is at its finest. The idiom evokes the lively, harmonious sounds of nature in springtime.
origin: This idiom originates from a Tang Dynasty poem titled 'Spring Thoughts' (春思) by the poet Huangfu Ran (皇甫冉). The line reads: 'Orioles cry and swallows chatter announcing the new year, while the road to Mayi and Longdui stretches thousands of li.' The poem contrasts the joyful arrival of spring at home with the distant, perilous frontier where a loved one serves. Over time, the phrase came to represent the idyllic beauty of spring.
example_zh: 春风送暖，莺啼燕语，江南的田野一片生机盎然。
example_en: As the spring breeze brings warmth and orioles sing while swallows chatter, the fields of Jiangnan are brimming with vitality.

meaning: This idiom refers to a large, bustling metropolis that is well-connected and accessible from all directions. It describes a major commercial and cultural hub with extensive trade and transportation networks. It is a variant form of the more common idiom '通都大邑' (tōng dū dà yì).
origin: The phrase is a rearrangement of the classical expression '通都大邑,' which appears in Chinese historical and literary texts describing major cities linked by roads and waterways. The terms '通邑' (accessible city) and '大都' (great metropolis) both connote urban centers of commerce and administration. Such cities served as economic and political hubs throughout China's dynastic history. The expression reflects the traditional Chinese emphasis on connectivity and urban prosperity.
example_zh: 这座城市自古便是通邑大都，商贾云集，繁华无比。
example_en: This city has been a great metropolis since ancient times, bustling with merchants and extraordinary prosperity.

meaning: Literally 'spinning a cocoon to bind oneself.' It means doing something that ultimately traps or restricts oneself. The idiom describes how a person's own actions create the very predicament they suffer from.
origin: The phrase appears in Tao Xingzhi's work 'On Mass Education in China' (1930s), where he criticized those who helped enemies form a united front against themselves. He compared such people to silkworms that spin cocoons around their own bodies, thereby trapping themselves. The metaphor draws on the well-known image of a silkworm sealing itself inside its cocoon. The underlying idea — that one's own actions become one's prison — echoes the older classical idiom 作茧自缚, of which 造茧自缚 is a variant form.
example_zh: 他订立了太多繁文缛节，结果造茧自缚，什么事都办不成。
example_en: He created so many red-tape rules that he ended up binding himself in his own cocoon, unable to get anything done.

meaning: Literally meaning to apply ink at the major points. Originally referring to the practice in painting or writing of concentrating effort on the most important parts. It is used metaphorically to mean handling matters with an eye on the big picture, focusing on what truly matters rather than minor details.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty novel 'Guanchang Xianxing Ji' (Revelations of Officialdom) by Li Baojia, Chapter 20. In the story, a character praises another for knowing how to spend money lavishly, calling him someone who 'applies ink at the big places' — a person who acts on a grand scale and focuses on major matters rather than petty concerns. The phrase draws on the artistic metaphor of a painter concentrating brushstrokes where they matter most.
example_zh: 做战略规划应当大处落墨，把握全局方向。
example_en: When making strategic plans, one should focus on the big picture and grasp the overall direction.

meaning: To depend on each other for survival. It describes a relationship where two parties rely on one another so deeply that neither can live without the other. Often used for family members or close companions sharing a difficult life together.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Petition Expressing My Feelings' (陈情表), a famous memorial written by Li Mi of the Jin Dynasty. Li Mi was raised by his grandmother after his father died and his mother remarried. In the memorial, he wrote that without his grandmother, he could not have survived to this day, and without him, she could not live out her remaining years. The grandmother and grandson thus relied on each other for survival, giving rise to the phrase 相依为命.
example_zh: 父子俩在山村中相依为命，度过了无数艰难岁月。
example_en: Father and son depended on each other for survival in the mountain village, enduring countless difficult years together.

meaning: This idiom refers to an unexpected and unprovoked calamity that strikes without cause or warning. It describes disasters that fall upon someone seemingly out of nowhere, with no apparent reason. The phrase emphasizes the sudden and unjust nature of such misfortune.
origin: The phrase originates from Yuan dynasty dramatist Zhang Guobin's play 'He Han Shan' (The Sweat Shirt), in its third act. The story involves a family that suffers ruin after the patriarch once took in a disreputable man as a sworn brother. This villain eventually brings destruction upon the entire household, illustrating how a single poor judgment can lead to calamity. The idiom also appears in Qin Jianfu's Yuan drama 'Zhao Li Rang Fei' (Zhao Li Yields the Fat), where a character laments being struck by sudden, inexplicable disaster.
example_zh: 他平生行善积德，却遭这场横祸非灾，实在令人扼腕。
example_en: He had lived a life of virtue and good deeds, yet suffered this sudden, unprovoked calamity—truly heartbreaking.

meaning: People die and the family is ruined. It describes the tragic state of a household that has suffered both death and financial destruction. A variant of the more common form 家破人亡.
origin: The phrase originates from the 'Book of Jin' (晋书), in the Biography of Wen Qiao (温峤传). During the Jin Dynasty, the loyal general Liu Kun (刘琨) fought against northern invaders but was ultimately killed by Duan Pidi (段匹磾). Wen Qiao, who had served under Liu Kun, submitted a memorial to the emperor praising Liu Kun's loyalty, writing that although his great deeds went unfulfilled, his family was broken and his people perished, and he therefore deserved posthumous honor to satisfy the hopes of the realm. The expression later became a common idiom for complete household ruin accompanied by loss of life.
example_zh: 那场战乱使得许多家庭人亡家破，失去了往日的安宁。
example_en: That war caused many families to lose their loved ones and be ruined, losing their former peace.

meaning: To deliberately put on an act or pretend in order to impress others. It describes someone who behaves in an affected, artificial manner rather than naturally. The idiom conveys a sense of phoniness and insincerity.
origin: This idiom originates from the Qing dynasty playwright Li Yu's work 'Shenzhong Lou: Shuang Ding' (蜃中楼·双订). In the scene, a character remarks on how two people who previously adored someone now act stiff and pretentious upon meeting that person face to face. The phrase vividly captures the contrast between genuine feeling and affected behavior. Over time, it became a common expression for describing deliberate posturing or affected conduct.
example_zh: 她明明不懂装懂，在专家面前妆模作样，结果当场被识破了。
example_en: She clearly knew nothing yet pretended to be an expert, putting on airs in front of the specialists, only to be exposed on the spot.

meaning: Literally means to push the waves and stir up billows. It is used metaphorically to describe abetting evil deeds, fanning emotions, and deliberately stirring up trouble or incidents. The phrase conveys a negative connotation of someone who inflames situations rather than calming them.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a specific classical text or historical anecdote. It is a later-formed expression built from the vivid imagery of the sea, where one pushes the waves and raises the swell. Over time it came to be used figuratively for those who fan the flames of trouble and abet wrongdoing.
example_zh: 他不仅不劝阻，反而推涛作浪，让事情变得更糟。
example_en: Instead of dissuading them, he fanned the flames and made things worse.

meaning: A general term for letters and written correspondence. It combines two classical allusions: a letter discovered inside a fish's belly and a message tied to a goose's foot, both legendary methods of delivering mail in ancient China. The phrase is often used in the context of longing between separated loved ones.
origin: From the Ming dynasty song suite '醉罗歌·题情' (Drunken Luo Song — On Love) by Shi Shukao, with the line '泪痕一线罗裙绣裾，相思两字鱼笺雁书' — a line of tear stains on an embroidered skirt, and the word 'lovesickness' carried by fish letters and goose mail. The idiom draws on two ancient legends: '鱼传尺素,' from a Han dynasty poem about finding a silk letter concealed inside a carp, and '雁足传书,' from the story of Han envoy Su Wu, who while detained by the Xiongnu tied a letter to a goose's foot to send word back to the Han court.
example_zh: 自从他远赴边疆，两人便断了鱼笺雁书，彼此音信全无。
example_en: Since he departed for the distant frontier, the two exchanged no more letters, and all news between them ceased.

meaning: Describes someone swaggering and eager to show off, like a beast raising its tail and sharpening its horns. It conveys an arrogant, competitive attitude of trying to dominate others. Used to depict people who are boastful and combative in demeanor.
origin: The phrase originates from a preface by the Qing dynasty scholar Qian Qianyi (钱谦益), titled 'Preface to the Poems of Feng Sicao' (《冯巳苍诗序》). Qian describes how at banquets and gatherings, debates would flare up with guests citing ancient texts to prove their points, each raising their tail and sharpening their horns — swaggering with self-importance — claiming to represent the singular learning of the Feng family, while critics found nothing to challenge them. The imagery of an animal puffing itself up captures the boastful, combative spirit of intellectual one-upmanship.
example_zh: 他在会上矫尾厉角地炫耀自己的见解，旁人都不愿搭理他。
example_en: At the meeting he swaggered and showed off his opinions, and no one else wanted to engage with him.

meaning: The mountains and rivers are as beautiful as a painting. It describes natural scenery so magnificent that it resembles a landscape painting. Often used to express admiration for stunning vistas.
origin: This phrase originates from the Song dynasty poet Su Shi's famous ci poem 'Nian Nu Jiao: Reflections at Red Cliff' (念奴娇·赤壁怀古). In the poem, Su Shi stands at the site of the historic Battle of Red Cliff and marvels at the breathtaking scenery, writing 'The land is like a painting, how many heroes lived in that era.' The idiom combines the grandeur of nature with a sense of historical reflection.
example_zh: 登上泰山之巅，只见江山如画，令人心旷神怡。
example_en: Reaching the summit of Mount Tai, one sees the land as beautiful as a painting, filling the heart with joy and tranquility.

meaning: This idiom refers to the decadent music favored by King Zhou of the Shang dynasty, historically regarded as the sound of a doomed nation. It symbolizes vulgar and declining music that foretells the fall of a state.
origin: The phrase originates from the Treatise on Music in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (史记·乐书). It describes how King Zhou of Shang (殷纣) favored music from the northern rustic region of Zhaoge. The text explains that 'north' signifies defeat and 'rustic' signifies vulgarity. Because the king loved such music, he alienated the feudal lords and the common people, ultimately leading to his death and the destruction of his kingdom.
example_zh: 此曲调低沉颓靡，颇有北鄙之音的意味。
example_en: This melody is low and decadent, carrying the flavor of the sound of a doomed nation.

meaning: This idiom refers to the persistent winds and rains that occur during the transition from late summer to autumn. It is also used more broadly to describe continuous, unrelenting stormy weather. It is a variant of the idiom 阑风长雨.
origin: This idiom is a traditional Chinese expression describing the lingering winds and rains characteristic of late summer and early autumn. It is closely related to the variant 阑风长雨, where 阑 suggests the wind lingering or waning and 伏 suggests the rain lying hidden yet persistent. The phrase has been used in classical Chinese literature to evoke the imagery of endless storms during the seasonal transition.
example_zh: 阑风伏雨连日不绝，秋收的庄稼怕是要遭殃了。
example_en: The unrelenting winds and rains continued day after day, and the autumn harvest was likely to suffer.

meaning: This idiom describes a relaxed, carefree mood and pleasant, unhurried interests. It refers to the state of enjoying life's simple pleasures at a leisurely pace, free from worry or pressure. It is synonymous with the more common variant 闲情逸致.
origin: The idiom conveys the traditional literati ideal of cultivating a tranquil, unhurried spirit away from worldly concerns. It is a close variant of the more widely cited phrase 闲情逸致, which appears in classical writings extolling a life of refined leisure. No single definitive source story is attached to 闲情逸趣 specifically; it emerged as a parallel expression in later literary usage. The sentiment reflects the long-standing Chinese cultural appreciation for detached, elegant repose.
example_zh: 退休后，他在乡间种花养鸟，享受着闲情逸趣。
example_en: After retiring, he moved to the countryside to grow flowers and keep birds, enjoying a life of leisurely pleasures.

meaning: A metaphor for accepting small bribes. '蹄' (hoof) refers to animal meat given as a gift, while '缣' (fine silk) refers to cloth given as a gift. Together they represent trivial gifts or minor bribes received by officials.
origin: The phrase originates from Qing dynasty scholar Wu Weiye's work 'Meicun Shihua' (Plum Village Poetry Talks). The original passage criticizes a judicial paradox: corrupt officials who plunder recklessly go unpunished, yet those who accept even trifling gifts—a small hoof or a bit of silk—are immediately arrested and prosecuted. The idiom thus came to symbolize minor bribes or petty corruption.
example_zh: 这位官员虽未收受大额贿赂，却因寸蹄尺缣而被御史弹劾。
example_en: Though the official had not accepted any large bribes, he was impeached by the censor for accepting even the smallest gifts.

meaning: Rare and extraordinary precious treasures. Refers to valuables that are unusual and hard to come by. Often used to describe objects of great rarity and worth.
origin: This phrase appears in the Song dynasty scholar Hu Zi's work 'Tiaoxi Yuyin Conghua Houji' (苕溪渔隐丛话后集), specifically in the section on Su Dongpo. Hu Zi sighs that the world does not lack wondrous and rare treasures, but rather lacks people capable of recognizing their true value. The idiom highlights the idea that extraordinary treasures exist everywhere, but discerning eyes are rare. It is a variant ordering of the more common phrase 奇珍异宝.
example_zh: 博物馆里陈列着各国的异宝奇珍，令人叹为观止。
example_en: The museum displays rare and wondrous treasures from various nations, leaving visitors in awe.

meaning: Originally referring to talented people from the State of Chu being employed by the State of Jin. It is now used as a metaphor for a country's or organization's talent draining away to work for another, benefiting a rival instead of its origin.
origin: This idiom comes from the Zuo Zhuan (左传·襄公二十六年), set in the Spring and Autumn period. When a Chu minister named Shengzi compared officials of Chu and Jin, he noted that while Jin lacked top ministers, its capable officers were all Chu material, like fine timber and leather flowing from Chu to Jin. He concluded: 'Though Chu has talent, Jin actually uses it.' The phrase became a lasting metaphor for domestic talent being put to work abroad.
example_zh: 公司花重金培养的骨干纷纷跳槽到对手那里，简直是楚材晋用。
example_en: The key staff the company spent heavily to train have jumped ship to its rivals one after another — a clear case of talent being used by others.

meaning: The true situation has been exposed to the enemy, and one's position has become disadvantageous. Originally a military term describing a state where one's conditions are known to the opponent while one holds the weaker hand.
origin: This idiom originates from Sima Qian's 'Records of the Grand Historian' (史记), specifically the biography of Han Xin, the Marquis of Huaiyin, during the Western Han dynasty. The advisor Kuai Tong warned Han Xin that if he led his exhausted troops to besiege the heavily fortified city of Yan, the campaign would drag on, supplies would dwindle, and his disadvantageous position would become apparent to all—allowing Yan to resist and Qi to strengthen its defenses.
example_zh: 敌军情见势屈，只得弃城而逃。
example_en: The enemy forces, their situation exposed and their position weakened, had no choice but to abandon the city and flee.

meaning: "Fāng tóu" (square head) colloquially refers to someone who is out of touch with the times and inflexible; "bù liè" means stubborn and unyielding. The idiom describes a person with a stubborn, obstinate personality who refuses to yield or adapt to circumstances.
origin: This idiom originates from the Yuan dynasty playwright Guan Hanqing's play "Qian Dayin Zhikan Feiyi Meng" (钱大尹智勘绯衣梦, "Prefect Qian's Clever Investigation of the Crimson Robe Dream"), in the fourth act. In the play, a character mentions someone named Pei Yan, describing him as "好生方头不劣" — exceptionally stubborn and unruly. The expression reflects the colloquial speech of the Yuan period, where "square head" metaphorically characterized someone rigidly unaccommodating and defiant.
example_zh: 他性格方头不劣，旁人怎么劝都不听。
example_en: He is so stubborn and obstinate that no matter how others try to persuade him, he refuses to listen.

meaning: Describes a scene of utter disorder and disarray, with people or things lying about haphazardly in all directions. It conveys a sense of untidiness and confusion.
origin: This idiom originates from the poem 'Dawn' (《晓》) by the modern Chinese poet Liu Fu (刘复). In the poem, the narrator looks back inside a vehicle and sees everyone lying about in complete disarray, snoring loudly. The vivid image of passengers sprawled in every direction during early morning travel gave rise to this expression describing chaotic, disorderly scenes.
example_zh: 那间宿舍好久没打扫，衣物东横西倒堆得到处都是。
example_en: That dorm room hadn't been cleaned in ages, with clothes piled everywhere in total disarray.

meaning: To be of one heart and one mind, sharing both courage and purpose. It is equivalent to the idiom 同心同德, emphasizing unity, mutual trust, and a shared sense of resolve among people working toward a common goal.
origin: This phrase originates from the Tiandihui (Heaven and Earth Society), a secret fraternal organization active during the Qing dynasty. It appears in their song 'Common Harmony Song' (《共同和合歌》), which includes the line 'With harmony, brothers naturally gather; sharing courage and one heart, they worship the five.' The song was part of the society's initiation rituals, emphasizing brotherhood and mutual loyalty. The Tiandihui was a significant underground organization that played a role in anti-Qing resistance throughout Chinese history.
example_zh: 众人合胆同心，终于度过了这场难关。
example_en: United in heart and courage, the group finally overcame the crisis together.

meaning: Literally 'raising the eyes to see a thousand li.' It describes a vast, far-reaching field of vision where one can see great distances. Used metaphorically for broad perspective or wide-open, unobstructed views.
origin: The phrase originates from a Song dynasty work, 'Songjiang Shaobian' (松江哨遍) by the scholar Liu Xueji (刘学箕). He depicted the landscape where the Songjiang River meets Lake Tai, writing that 'raising one's eyes, one can see a thousand li; the wind and waves are still, and the water surface is as flat as a whetstone.' The expression evokes the boundless, tranquil expanse of water under calm conditions.
example_zh: 登上泰山之巅，举目千里，群山尽收眼底。
example_en: Reaching the summit of Mount Tai, one can see a thousand li at a glance, with all the mountains spread out below.

meaning: Feeling dissatisfied and unhappy; sulking because things did not turn out as one wished. It describes a resentful, discontented mood when expectations are not met.
origin: This phrase originates from Sima Guang's 'Ying Zhao Lun Ti Yao' (Reply to the Emperor on Essential Principles) written during the Song Dynasty. In the text, Sima Guang warned that when those in charge are made to feel dissatisfied and unhappy, they will not work wholeheartedly to assist in planning or cooperate to accomplish tasks. The idiom has since been used to describe a sulking, resentful attitude born of dissatisfaction.
example_zh: 他因为没能升职，整天怏怏不悦的。
example_en: He was sullen and resentful all day because he didn't get the promotion.

meaning: Describes the extravagant dining customs of ancient aristocrats, who ate with bronze bells chiming and food served in ceremonial tripods. It symbolizes a lavish, opulent lifestyle of the nobility.
origin: The phrase traces back to Sima Qian's "Records of the Grand Historian" (史记·货殖列传) in the Han dynasty, where he observed that even those with humble trades, like the Zhi family of knife-sharpeners, could rise to aristocratic dining customs with bells and tripods. The expression was later immortalized by the Tang dynasty poet Wang Bo in his famous "Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Teng" (滕王阁序), where he described prosperous families whose bells rang and tripods were arrayed at mealtimes.
example_zh: 昔日鼎食钟鸣的豪门，如今已家道中落。
example_en: The once lavishly dining noble family has now fallen into decline.

meaning: A thirsty person finds any drink sweet. In classical usage, it metaphorically describes how people who have long endured harsh governance are most grateful when benevolent rule finally arrives. The idiom highlights that those in greatest need appreciate relief the most.
origin: This idiom originates from the book 'Mencius · Gongsun Chou I' (《孟子·公孙丑上》), a Warring States period text. Mencius, the Confucian philosopher, stated to his disciple Gongsun Chou: 'The hungry find food easy to eat, the thirsty find drink easy to drink.' He was arguing that when the people have suffered under a tyrannical ruler, even modest acts of benevolent governance will be received with overwhelming gratitude. The passage illustrates how suffering heightens appreciation, and how a wise ruler can win hearts simply by ending oppression.
example_zh: 经过多年苛政，百姓如渴者易饮，对新君的德政感恩戴德。
example_en: After years of harsh rule, the people, like the thirsty who find any drink sweet, were deeply grateful for the new ruler's benevolent governance.
