He collectively refers to these as 'the four objects of the study,' gathered from mountains and seas in the most exquisite selections across the land.
example_zh: 他的书房里整齐地陈列着一套精致的文房四物。
example_en: In his study, an exquisite set of the four scholarly objects was neatly displayed.

meaning: A humble euphemism for one's own wife, literally meaning 'the servant of the dustpan and broom.' It originally referred to the person who handled household sweeping chores and became a self-deprecating way to speak of one's spouse in classical Chinese.
origin: This idiom originates from 'Han Shi Wai Zhuan' (韩诗外传), Volume 9, compiled during the Han Dynasty. King Zhuang of Chu sent an envoy bearing a hundred catties of gold to recruit the scholar Mr. Beiguo (北郭先生). The scholar replied, 'I have a servant of the dustpan and broom — I wish to go in and consult with her,' humbly referring to his wife. His willingness to seek his wife's counsel before accepting a royal appointment demonstrated deep respect for her. The phrase subsequently became a classical humble term for one's own wife.
example_zh: 他谦称妻子为箕帚之使，凡事必先与她商议。
example_en: He humbly referred to his wife as his 'servant of the dustpan and broom,' consulting her first on all matters.

meaning: This idiom describes talented people emerging continuously, generation after generation. It conveys that a society, institution, or era produces a steady stream of capable individuals.
origin: The phrase appears in the 'Xu Zizhi Tongjian' (Continuation of the Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance), compiled by the Qing dynasty scholar Bi Yuan. It is recorded in the section on the Yuan dynasty under Emperor Shizu's twenty-eighth year of the Zhiyuan era (1289), where it was said that if someone like Left Minister Xu Heng were to teach the National Academy, talented people would emerge in successive waves. Xu Heng was a prominent Confucian scholar and official who played a key role in establishing Yuan-era education. The idiom thus praises the continuous cultivation and emergence of capable talent.
example_zh: 我们这个时代人才辈出，各行各业都有杰出人物。
example_en: In our era, talented people emerge in every generation, with outstanding figures in every field.

meaning: Describes a scene of busy, disordered activity where many people work together at once. It conveys the chaotic energy of everyone pitching in simultaneously, with hands and feet all in motion.
origin: This idiom appears in Li Chang's memoir 'Recollections of the People's Vanguard Team' (回忆民先队), which documents the activities of the People's Vanguard Team during the wartime period. The author describes a tense moment when members were hastily organizing documents and packing belongings before police arrived at the courtyard. The phrase vividly captures the frantic, collective effort of everyone scrambling to act at the same time. It is also written as '七足八手'.
example_zh: 大家七脚八手地把家具搬进了新房子。
example_en: Everyone pitched in hands and feet, hastily moving the furniture into the new house.

meaning: To rely on one's strength to oppress and bully those who are weaker. It describes the behavior of powerful individuals or groups who use their advantage to mistreat the vulnerable. The phrase condemns the abuse of power.
origin: The phrase originates from Ming Dynasty author Feng Menglong's collection 'Jingshi Tongyan' (Stories to Caution the World), Volume 3. The text discusses the notorious tyrants Jie and Zhou, noting that their crimes amounted to nothing more than relying on nobility to oppress the humble and using strength to bully the weak. It concludes that such behavior is merely an abuse of power. The idiom has since been used to criticize those who exploit their strength to dominate others.
example_zh: 他恃强凌弱的行为遭到了众人的谴责。
example_en: His behavior of bullying the weak was condemned by everyone.

meaning: To seize every moment and strive to achieve a goal in the shortest possible time. The characters 朝 (morning) and 夕 (evening) together denote a brief span of time. It conveys a sense of urgency and determination to make the most of each day.
origin: This idiom originates from Mao Zedong's 1963 poem 'Man Jiang Hong — Reply to Comrade Guo Moruo' (《满江红·和郭沫若同志》). The famous lines read: 'The world turns, time presses. Ten thousand years is too long—seize the day and the night.' The poem was composed in response to a verse by the scholar Guo Moruo and reflects a revolutionary spirit of urgency and resolve. The phrase urges people not to wait idly but to act promptly and purposefully. It has since become widely used to express the importance of making every moment count.
example_zh: 面对激烈的市场竞争，我们必须只争朝夕，加快研发进度。
example_en: Facing fierce market competition, we must seize every moment and accelerate our R&D progress.

meaning: This idiom describes someone who sleeps on coarse firewood and tastes bitter gall to endure hardship and spur themselves on. It portrays extreme self-discipline and determination to suffer in the short term in order to achieve future success or revenge.
origin: During the Spring and Autumn period, King Goujian of Yue was defeated and captured by the State of Wu. After his release and return to Yue, he refused comfort: he slept on rough firewood and tasted bitter gall each day to keep the shame of defeat fresh in his mind. This relentless self-remembrance drove him to rebuild his kingdom's strength until, years later, he finally defeated Wu and restored Yue's power. The story, recorded in Sima Qian's 'Records of the Grand Historian,' became a lasting symbol of patient, painful determination.
example_zh: 为了报仇雪耻，他尝胆卧薪整整十年。
example_en: To avenge his humiliation, he endured hardship—sleeping on firewood and tasting gall—for ten full years.

meaning: The sound shakes the roof tiles of a house. It describes a shout or cry that is extremely loud, powerful, and overwhelming. The idiom conveys a sense of tremendous vocal force that can physically vibrate buildings.
origin: This idiom originates from Sima Qian's "Records of the Grand Historian" (史记), in the biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru during the Warring States period. When the Qin army encamped west of Wu'an, they drilled their troops with thundering war drums so intense that the roof tiles of every house in Wu'an were set vibrating. The phrase later became a vivid metaphor for any overwhelmingly loud and forceful voice or outcry.
example_zh: 将士们齐声高呼，声振屋瓦，气势如虹。
example_en: The soldiers shouted in unison, their voices so thunderous they shook the roof tiles, their morale soaring like a rainbow.

meaning: The finest lacquer from She County and the best glue from Dong'e—both renowned for their tenacious adhesive power. Used metaphorically to describe a deep, inseparable bond of affection or friendship between people, as though their hearts were joined like glue and lacquer.
origin: This idiom comes from a couplet in the Ming Dynasty work 'Jiandeng Yuhua' (Tales After the Lamp) by Li Changqi, in the story 'Tian Zhu Meets Xue Yuan.' The verse reads: 'Even She lacquer and Dong'e glue suddenly come apart—how can clear dust and muddy water ever meet again?' She County in Anhui produced the finest lacquer and Dong'e in Shandong the finest gelatin, both prized for their powerful adhesion and thus symbolizing an unbreakable bond. The poet ironically laments that even the strongest of ties can be severed, comparing it to the impossibility of clear dust and muddy water ever reuniting.
example_zh: 他们二人歙漆阿胶，情谊深厚，纵经患难也不曾疏远。
example_en: The two shared a bond like She lacquer and Dong'e glue—a friendship so deep that even hardship could never drive them apart.

meaning: This idiom refers to the increase and decrease, growth and decline of things — essentially the ebb and flow of fortune and circumstance. It is synonymous with the idiom 进退消息. It captures the cyclical shifting of power, influence, or vitality over time.
origin: The phrase appears in the preface to the collected writings of Zhuang Zongbo of Wujin, written by the Qing dynasty scholar Wei Yuan. The text describes how, during the late Qianlong reign, the gentleman served at court alongside the powerful Grand Secretary Heshen but was deeply at odds with him and unhappy. Wei Yuan notes that in his studies of the Book of Odes and the Book of Changes, the scholar often reflected on the advance, retreat, decline, and growth of noble and petty men, expressing indignation and sorrowful sighs. The phrase thus encapsulates the cyclical contest between virtuous and corrupt factions at court.
example_zh: 历朝历代的政治格局都在进退消长之间不断演变。
example_en: The political landscape of every dynasty evolves ceaselessly through cycles of advance, retreat, decline, and growth.

meaning: Having broad and abundant talent can sometimes backfire and harm oneself. It warns that being too capable may invite jealousy or trouble, and that one should not rely solely on one's abilities.
origin: This idiom originates from a sanqu (散曲) suite titled 'Dou Anchun·Ziwu' (《斗鹌鹑·自悟》) by the Yuan dynasty writer Zhou Wenzhi (周文质). In the piece, the author reflects on how heroes ruin their lives pursuing fame and military glory, quoting the common saying '才广妨身，官高害已' — broad talent harms oneself, high office harms oneself. The work expresses a philosophy of detachment, cautioning that exceptional ability and high status can be sources of danger rather than blessings.
example_zh: 历史上才广妨身的例子不少，杨修便是一例。
example_en: History offers many cases where abundant talent brought ruin; Yang Xiu is one such example.

meaning: To have fully experienced every kind of hardship and suffering. It describes someone who has endured all forms of difficulty and adversity in life. The idiom emphasizes the completeness and depth of the suffering one has gone through.
origin: This idiom originates from the Zuo Zhuan (Chronicle of Zuo), in the 28th year of Duke Xi's reign, which states that despite dangerous obstacles and hardships, all were fully experienced. The Tang dynasty scholar Han Yu later used the phrase in his Veritable Records of Emperor Shunzong, describing how the emperor personally held bow and arrow, leading troops as a vanguard guard, having fully endured hardships. Over time the expression became a standard way to convey that one has suffered through every kind of adversity.
example_zh: 他在创业的道路上备尝艰苦，但始终没有放弃。
example_en: He experienced all kinds of hardships on his entrepreneurial journey, but never gave up.

meaning: A great pig and a long snake; a metaphor for the rapacious and cruel. It describes greedy tyrants or aggressive invaders who devour and destroy like a giant boar and a massive serpent.
origin: This phrase originates from the Zuo Zhuan (Commentary of Zuo), compiled during the Spring and Autumn period. In the record of Duke Ding's fourth year, the state of Wu is compared to a great pig and a long snake, constantly encroaching upon and consuming the central states. The imagery of two insatiable beasts was used to condemn Wu's relentless aggression against its neighbors.
example_zh: 侵略者如封豕长蛇，步步蚕食邻国领土。
example_en: The invaders, like a great boar and a giant serpent, devoured neighboring territories step by step.

meaning: Originally a legend about an immortal who could chew ink and spit it onto paper to form meaningful writing. It is now used to describe someone with exceptional literary talent who writes with remarkable skill and fluency.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Shen Xian Zhuan' (Biographies of Divine Immortals) by Ge Hong of the Jin Dynasty. The text describes a figure named Ban Meng, whose origins are unknown. Ban Meng possessed extraordinary abilities, including the power to swallow ink. When he spread paper before him, chewed the ink, and sprayed it out, every drop turned into legible characters, filling the entire page with meaningful text.
example_zh: 这位作家文思敏捷，犹如嚼墨喷纸般一气呵成。
example_en: This writer's thoughts flow so swiftly that he composes with the effortless brilliance of one who could chew ink and spray it into words.

literal: Fenghu and Emo (nicknames of the Xie nephews Xie Shao and Xie Yuan)
meaning: A metaphor for outstanding young men or excellent descendants of a noble family. It originally praised the talented nephews of the illustrious Xie clan of the Eastern Jin dynasty, and is now used to commend exceptional youth.
origin: The phrase originates from 'A New Account of Tales of the World' (世说新语) compiled by Liu Yiqing of the Liu Song dynasty (Southern Dynasties). Xie Daoyun, a celebrated talented woman of the Eastern Jin period and niece of the powerful minister Xie An, was so disappointed by her mediocre husband Wang Ningzhi that she returned to her parents' home in distress. When Xie An asked the reason, she lamented that her own family was full of brilliant men—uncles like 'Ada' and 'Zhonglang,' and cousins like 'Fenghu' (Xie Shao) and 'Emo' (Xie Yuan)—and she never imagined that in all the world there could be someone like her husband Wang. The combined nicknames thus became a metaphor for outstanding young men of a family.
example_zh: 谢家子弟个个封胡遏末，皆为青年才俊。
example_en: The young men of the Xie family are all outstanding talents, every one of them brilliant youth.

meaning: To be crooked oneself yet try to straighten others. It describes a hypocrite whose own conduct is improper but who presumes to correct or guide other people. The idiom implies that moral authority over others requires first being upright oneself.
origin: The phrase originates from Mencius (《孟子·万章上》), a text of the Warring States period. In dialogue with his disciple Wan Zhang, Mencius discusses whether a person of virtue should seek office through improper means. Mencius declares, 'I have never heard of one who is crooked himself yet can correct others' (吾未闻枉己而正人者也), arguing that compromising one's own integrity disqualifies a person from reforming anyone else. The saying became a classic admonition against moral hypocrisy in leadership and self-cultivation.
example_zh: 身为领导若自身贪腐，却要求下属廉洁奉公，岂非枉己正人？
example_en: If a leader is corrupt yet demands integrity from subordinates, is that not a case of being crooked oneself while trying to correct others?

meaning: To confuse black with white, turning right and wrong upside down. It describes a situation where truth and falsehood are deliberately or carelessly reversed, making the innocent appear guilty and wrong appear right. The idiom condemns the perversion of justice and moral order.
origin: This idiom originates from the Biographies of Exemplary Women (列女传) compiled by Liu Xiang of the Western Han dynasty. In the chapter on Zheng Mao of Chu, the text criticizes a ruler who fails to investigate matters clearly and unjustly punishes the innocent, calling it a case where black and white are reversed and the order between high and low is thrown into confusion. The metaphor of mixing up black and white vividly denounces the distortion of truth and the subversion of justice.
example_zh: 他为了个人私利，经常白黑颠倒、混淆是非。
example_en: For his own personal gain, he frequently confounds right and wrong, blurring the line between truth and falsehood.

meaning: Having the same ideals, principles, and ambitions as another person. It describes a deep mutual understanding and shared sense of purpose between individuals. The phrase emphasizes that true partnership arises when people walk the same path and hold the same aspirations.
origin: The phrase originates from the memorial 'Chen Shen Ju Biao' (Memorial Recommending Shen Ju) by Cao Zhi of the state of Wei during the Three Kingdoms period. In the text, Cao Zhi reflects on how Yi Yin, though once a lowly attendant, and Lü Shang, though once a humble butcher, were ultimately elevated by Tang of Shang and King Wen of Zhou respectively. He attributes their remarkable success to the fact that ruler and minister were 'dao he zhi tong' — united in the Way and shared in aspiration, achieving extraordinary things through this profound alignment. The phrase thus celebrates the power of kindred spirits joining forces.
example_zh: 他们二人道合志同，合作多年从未有过分歧。
example_en: The two shared the same ideals and aspirations, and their years of collaboration never saw a single disagreement.

meaning: The crookedness or straightness follows the form. This idiom expresses the philosophical idea that consequences naturally correspond to one's nature or actions, just as a shadow's shape is determined by the object that casts it. Good and evil outcomes follow inevitably from good and evil deeds.
origin: This idiom has no single definitive literary source but draws from the ancient Chinese philosophical tradition of using the relationship between an object and its shadow as a metaphor for causality. The concept parallels ideas found in early texts where shadow imagery illustrates how moral qualities produce corresponding results. The term reflects the broader classical Chinese worldview that justice and consequence are inherent in the natural order, not imposed externally.
example_zh: 他深知枉直随形的道理，因此一生行事坦荡从不做亏心事。
example_en: Understanding the principle that consequences follow one's actions like a shadow, he lived openly and never did anything against his conscience.

literal: cut the stump, dig the root
meaning: To cut down the stump and dig out the root, meaning to eradicate something completely and thoroughly. It conveys the idea of removing an evil or threat at its source so that it can never grow back. The idiom emphasizes thoroughness in eliminating dangers.
origin: The phrase originates from 'Zhanguo Ce' (Strategies of the Warring States), a text compiled during the Han Dynasty that records the political strategies and diplomatic rhetoric of the Warring States period. In the Qin Strategies section, it advises rulers to eliminate threats completely—cutting the stump and digging out the root—so that no remnants remain to cause future trouble. The counsel warns that only by removing a problem at its foundation can one avoid neighboring disaster. It became a metaphor for the principle that evil must be uprooted entirely.
example_zh: 对待腐败问题必须削株掘根，绝不能留下任何隐患。
example_en: Corruption must be eradicated root and branch, leaving no hidden dangers behind.

meaning: Literally 'washing away dirt to search for scars.' It is a metaphor for deliberately seeking out and magnifying the faults and shortcomings of others in a nitpicking manner. It is a variant of the idiom 洗垢求瘢.
origin: This idiom is a variant of 洗垢求瘢, rooted in classical Chinese literary criticism traditions. The metaphor likens excessive fault-finding to washing dirt off a surface only to search for scars underneath—an act of over-scrutiny. The phrase reflects the traditional Chinese cultural disdain for those who deliberately magnify minor flaws rather than appreciating overall merit. No single definitive textual origin has been recorded for this specific variant.
example_zh: 评审专家对这篇论文洗垢索瘢，连标点符号都不放过。
example_en: The reviewer nitpicked the paper relentlessly, not even sparing the punctuation marks.

meaning: Speaking and acting in contradictory ways. It describes someone whose words do not match their deeds, revealing a fundamental inconsistency between what they profess and what they actually do.
origin: This idiom does not originate from a single classical text or historical anecdote. It is a compound formed from the common terms 言行 (words and deeds) and 相悖 (mutually contradictory), both deeply rooted in Chinese philosophical tradition. The ideal of unity between words and actions was a recurring theme throughout Chinese intellectual history, from Confucius's emphasis on sincerity in the Analects to later Neo-Confucian moral philosophy, which stressed that a person of integrity must never say one thing and do another.
example_zh: 他整日高谈诚信，自己却言行相悖，实在令人失望。
example_en: He talks endlessly about integrity, yet his own words and deeds contradict each other, which is truly disappointing.

meaning: To embrace and retain things of different content and nature at the same time. It describes an inclusive attitude toward diverse ideas, cultures, or materials. Equivalent to the more common phrase 兼收并蓄.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a single classical text or historical figure. It is a variant of the well-known phrase 兼收并蓄, whose spirit originates from the inclusive scholarly tradition championed by Tang dynasty literatus Han Yu. The underlying philosophy reflects the Confucian and later Neo-Confucian ideal of gathering and preserving diverse schools of thought without prejudice.
example_zh: 这座图书馆兼包并畜，收藏了古今中外的各类典籍。
example_en: This library embraces and retains all kinds of texts, collecting classics both ancient and modern, Chinese and foreign.

meaning: Refers to the skirts and fans used in dancing and singing, and by extension to singing and dancing entertainments themselves. It can also denote people who are skilled at singing and dancing. A close variant is the phrase 舞衫歌扇 (dance gown, song fan).
origin: This is a descriptive compound pairing 'dance skirt' with 'song fan' as parallel objects representing the accouterments of entertainment, rather than a phrase tied to a single historical anecdote. Such parallel pairings were a common rhetorical device in classical Chinese poetry and prose describing banquets, court life, and pleasure quarters. The closely related variant 舞衫歌扇 appears in Tang and Song dynasty verse. Together the two forms circulated through later literary descriptions of lavish song-and-dance gatherings.
example_zh: 当年的歌楼里，舞裙歌扇，丝竹之声不绝。
example_en: In the music halls of those days, there were dance skirts and song fans, and the sound of strings and flutes never ceased.

meaning: Describes dramatic and violent changes in circumstances. The imagery evokes the earth growing old and the sky turning dark, conveying a sense of profound upheaval and transformation.
origin: From the Ming Dynasty playwright Tang Xianzu's 'The Peony Pavilion' (牡丹亭), specifically the scene 'Thinking of My Daughter' (忆女). In this passage, a grieving mother laments the overwhelming changes in her world, having nowhere to settle herself and reflecting on her total lack of kin to rely on. The phrase uses the imagery of earth aging and sky darkening to express the magnitude of the upheaval she experiences.
example_zh: 政局骤变，地老天昏，百姓流离失所。
example_en: The political situation shifted dramatically, the world was turned upside down, and the people were displaced from their homes.

meaning: Describes something vast and boundless, as if filling the entire sky and spanning across the sea. It conveys a sense of immensity and limitlessness, often used to depict grand natural scenery or sweeping scope that seems to have no end.
origin: No specific literary origin is documented for this idiom. It draws on the imagery of the sky and sea—two of nature's most expansive elements—to evoke a feeling of boundlessness and infinite reach. The phrase likely emerged from folk or literary usage inspired by classical descriptions of vast, majestic landscapes. Unlike the similarly pronounced stratagem '瞒天过海' (deceiving the heavens to cross the sea), this idiom emphasizes spatial vastness rather than cunning or deception.
example_zh: 登上高山之巅，只见云海翻涌、漫天过海，仿佛天地之间再无边界。
example_en: Reaching the mountain summit, one sees clouds surging and spreading across sky and sea, as if there were no boundary left between heaven and earth.

meaning: To abandon old customs and conventions in favor of new trends and ideas. It describes a deliberate choice to break from tradition and embrace innovation. The idiom conveys a progressive attitude toward social change and modernization.
origin: This idiom originates from the essay 'Paying New Year Visits' in Ye Shengtao's collection 'The Unwearied Collection: Hardship' (未厌集·苦辛), published during the early Republican era. Ye Shengtao, a prominent 20th-century Chinese writer and educator, questioned the significance of the traditional New Year greeting custom, calling it a superficial formality. He wrote that people collectively stopped paying New Year visits as a way of showing their intention to discard old customs and pursue new ways of thinking.
example_zh: 年轻人应当避俗趋新，勇于接受新事物。
example_en: Young people should abandon old customs and embrace new ideas, having the courage to accept new things.

meaning: To shut one's mouth and stop in one's tracks. It describes someone who, out of fear or concern, dares neither to speak nor to approach, keeping at a safe distance. The idiom conveys how people avoid a situation entirely when they perceive danger or risk.
origin: This idiom originates from 'Zhan Guo Ce' (Strategies of the Warring States), in the chapter on the Strategies of Qin. The statesman Fan Sui (范雎) warned King Zhao of Qin that if loyal ministers who served the state faithfully were met with suspicion or ruin, others would see their fate and be terrified. Consequently, talented people would shut their mouths and refuse to step forward, depriving the ruler of able counsel. The phrase thus captures the chilling effect that punishing the loyal has on recruiting talent.
example_zh: 面对权贵的威压，百姓们杜口裹足，不敢直言时弊。
example_en: Under the pressure of the powerful, the common people shut their mouths and kept their distance, not daring to speak openly about the abuses of the times.

meaning: This idiom describes people rubbing their fists and wiping their palms, indicating a state of eager excitement and readiness for action. It portrays the enthusiasm and high spirits of people preparing for a contest, battle, or labor. It is a variant of the more common idiom 摩拳擦掌.
origin: This idiom is a variant form of the well-known expression 摩拳擦掌 (mo quan ca zhang), which appears in classical vernacular novels of the Ming and Qing dynasties. The imagery of rubbing fists and palms conveys the physical eagerness of fighters or workers about to begin. While 摩拳擦掌 became the standard form, the variant 擦拳抹掌 appears in some literary works with the same meaning and usage. No single definitive origin story is associated with this particular variant.
example_zh: 比赛还没开始，队员们已经擦拳抹掌，准备大显身手。
example_en: The competition hadn't even started yet, but the team members were already rubbing their fists and wiping their palms, ready to show their skills.

meaning: To hide one's traces and conceal one's form. It describes someone who goes into hiding so completely that no sign of their presence can be detected. The phrase emphasizes remaining entirely out of sight and undetected.
origin: The phrase originates from the Yuan dynasty playwright Gao Wenxiu's work 'Hei Xuanfeng' (The Black Whirlwind), specifically in the first act. In the play, a character expresses enduring humiliation silently by hiding away and concealing all traces of himself. The expression has since been used to describe someone who disappears completely from public view, leaving no clue to their whereabouts.
example_zh: 罪犯作案后匿迹潜形，警方多方追查仍无结果。
example_en: After committing the crime, the culprit went completely into hiding, and despite extensive investigation, the police found no trace of him.

meaning: The numbers three and four represent disorder and confusion. The idiom describes speech or actions that are jumbled, incoherent, or topsy-turvy. It conveys a sense of things being done in the wrong order or in a chaotic manner.
origin: The phrase originates from the Ming dynasty novel Investiture of the Gods (封神演义) by Xu Zhonglin. In the forty-fourth chapter, after several days of continuous ritual worship, the character Jiang Ziya is described as being turned topsy-turvy and unable to sit or rest peacefully. The expression uses the numbers three and four to convey the sense of things being thrown into disorder. Over time it became a common idiom for describing confused or jumbled speech and behavior.
example_zh: 他喝醉了酒，说话颠三倒四，谁也听不懂他在说什么。
example_en: He got drunk and spoke in such a jumbled, incoherent way that nobody could understand what he was saying.

meaning: To be genuinely convinced both inwardly and outwardly. It describes a situation where someone not only verbally agrees but also truly believes in their heart, showing sincere submission or acceptance. The phrase emphasizes authentic conviction rather than forced compliance.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Daoist text Zhuangzi (《庄子》), specifically the chapter 'Fable' (寓言). In the original passage, Zhuangzi discusses how presenting arguments about right and wrong may only win people's verbal agreement, but true persuasion must make them submit in their hearts without daring to oppose. The idea is that superficial persuasion only convinces the mouth, while genuine virtue and truth convince the heart. This concept was later condensed into the four-character idiom '心服口服' to express wholehearted conviction.
example_zh: 听了他的详细分析后，大家都心服口服，不再有异议。
example_en: After hearing his detailed analysis, everyone was genuinely convinced and raised no further objections.

meaning: A metaphor for collecting all valuable things, regardless of whether they are large or small. It conveys the idea of gathering every piece of goodness, even fragments of something precious. Used to describe thorough and comprehensive collection or preservation.
origin: This idiom originates from the Tang dynasty treatise 'Shu Yi' (书议) by the calligrapher and scholar Zhang Huaiguan. He wrote that even a single hair of the qilin and phoenix, or a single piece of shell from the turtle and dragon, should all be recorded without omission. The turtle and dragon were revered as symbols of longevity and wisdom in ancient Chinese culture, so even a fragment of them was considered precious. The phrase thus came to represent the thorough collection of anything of value.
example_zh: 这部文集搜罗宏富，龟龙片甲皆有所录。
example_en: This collected anthology is rich and comprehensive, recording even the smallest fragments of value.

meaning: One's spirit and morale soar beyond the clouds and the Milky Way. It describes someone possessing tremendous courage, boldness, and commanding presence. The term 霄汉 refers to the high heavens—the clouds and the galaxy.
origin: This idiom does not trace to a single specific text but is built from classical Chinese literary components. The word 霄汉, meaning the clouds and the Milky Way, has been used since the Han dynasty to evoke the highest reaches of the sky. The character 逾 conveys surpassing or exceeding. Together the phrase paints a vivid image of noble spirit rising above the firmament, a motif common in Tang and Song poetry celebrating heroic resolve and moral courage.
example_zh: 面对强敌，将士们气逾霄汉，誓死保卫家园。
example_en: Facing a formidable enemy, the soldiers' spirit soared beyond the heavens as they vowed to defend their homeland to the death.

meaning: To not know which direction to follow or what course to take. It describes a state of bewilderment and indecision, where one is unable to determine which path to pursue or which authority to obey.
origin: This idiom is a classical variant of the more common 无所适从. In classical Chinese, 靡 (mǐ) functions as a negation equivalent to 无 (wú), meaning 'without' or 'not having,' so the phrase conveys having nowhere to turn and no direction to follow. It appears in classical literature to describe situations where a person faces conflicting circumstances or commands and cannot decide what to do. Over time the variant with 无 became the standard form, while 靡所适从 retained a more archaic, literary flavor.
example_zh: 面对众人各不相同的意见，他靡所适从，不知如何是好。
example_en: Faced with everyone's differing opinions, he was at a loss and did not know what to do.

meaning: Describes a person who is warm-hearted and straightforward in temperament. It conveys both genuine enthusiasm for helping others and an open, candid disposition that does not hide behind pretense.
origin: This idiom originates from the modern Chinese writer Ke Yan's essay collection 'Strange Letters — The Pearl of the East III' (《奇异的书简·东方的明珠三》). In the original passage, the author describes a woman whose warm and forthright nature makes her a natural confidante — whenever people in the community face problems, they instinctively seek her advice and assistance. Unlike many classical idioms rooted in ancient historical anecdotes, this phrase emerged from 20th-century literary writing and reflects everyday virtues of sincerity and helpfulness.
example_zh: 她热心快肠，邻居遇到困难总爱找她帮忙。
example_en: She is warm-hearted and straightforward, so neighbors always turn to her for help when they run into difficulties.

meaning: To hang one's head and droop one's wings. It describes a person who is dispirited and dejected after suffering a setback or defeat, like a bird that has lost its vigor and confidence.
origin: This idiom comes from a proclamation written by Chen Lin during the late Eastern Han dynasty, titled 'Proclamation to Yuzhou on Behalf of Yuan Shao.' Chen Lin wrote on behalf of the warlord Yuan Shao to denounce Cao Cao, describing how even the most capable officials within the capital region hung their heads and drooped their wings, with nothing to rely on. The phrase vividly depicted the demoralized state of court officials during the chaotic power struggles of that era.
example_zh: 比赛失利后，他垂头搨翼，好几天都提不起精神。
example_en: After losing the competition, he hung his head and drooped his wings, unable to muster any energy for days.

meaning: This idiom describes someone with an extraordinary physique and bearing, comparing their bone structure to a phoenix and their posture to a dragon. It conveys a noble, striking appearance that suggests a person of exceptional refinement and spiritual elevation. The phrase is typically used to praise someone's regal or immortal-like demeanor.
origin: The phrase originates from the Daoist text 'Yunji Qiqian' (云笈七签), a Song dynasty compilation by Zhang Junfang, which is an encyclopedia of Daoist scriptures. In the passage, a celestial being observes a worthy person and remarks that their essence is brilliantly radiant and luminous, with a phoenix-like bone structure and dragon-like posture, and a glowing mind. The imagery draws on the phoenix and dragon—two of the most auspicious creatures in Chinese mythology—to convey an otherworldly, elevated quality of body and spirit.
example_zh: 这位少年生来凤骨龙姿，众人皆言日后必成大器。
example_en: The youth was born with the bearing of a phoenix and the posture of a dragon; everyone said he would achieve greatness in the future.

meaning: Advancing or retreating both leads to hitting a fence. It describes being caught in a dilemma where every direction is blocked by obstacles. It is equivalent to the variant 进退触藩.
origin: The idiom evokes the image of being hemmed in by a fence on all sides, unable to move forward or backward without obstruction. The variant form 进退触藩 uses 藩 (hedge or fence) and draws on imagery common in classical Chinese literature depicting entrapment. It captures the predicament of having no viable path, whether advancing or retreating. No single definitive origin story is recorded for this expression.
example_zh: 公司资金链断裂，进退触篱，只能寻求外部融资。
example_en: The company's capital chain broke, leaving it in a dilemma with no way forward or back, so it could only seek outside financing.

meaning: Literally the top of a hundred-foot pole. It is used as a metaphor for reaching a very high level of achievement in one's career, studies, or official position. The phrase is often paired with '更进一步' (to advance one more step), urging one to keep improving even after attaining great success.
origin: The phrase originates from a poem by the Tang dynasty poet Wu Rong titled 'The Merchant' (商人), which contains the line 'At the top of a hundred-foot pole, the wind pennant slants; where in this life is not a home?' The imagery draws on the tall poles used in acrobatic performances or as ship masts. Over time it became a metaphor for reaching the pinnacle of achievement. Buddhist texts later extended the expression with '更进一步' to encourage further progress beyond the summit.
example_zh: 他在学术上已取得百尺竿头的成就，却仍然孜孜不倦地探索新领域。
example_en: He has achieved the pinnacle of academic success, yet he continues to explore new fields with tireless dedication.

meaning: Everything that should be present is present. It describes a situation where a place or collection is complete and well-stocked, lacking nothing that one would expect to find.
origin: This phrase originates from the 'Book of Song' (宋书), specifically the biography of Jiang Zhiyuan (江智渊), a scholar-official of the Southern Dynasties period. A contemporary praised him, saying: 'What a person should have, he has in full; what a person should not have, he has none of at all—surely this describes Jiang Zhiyuan!' The remark highlighted both his abundant virtues and his freedom from undesirable traits. Over time, the first half of the quotation evolved into the idiom '应有尽有,' used to describe completeness or comprehensiveness.
example_zh: 这家商场里的商品品种丰富，应有尽有。
example_en: The products in this shopping mall are so diverse that they have everything one could possibly want.

meaning: Refers to two legendary swords forged by the master swordsmith Ganjiang and his wife Moye during the Spring and Autumn period. Used as a metonym for exceptionally sharp, precious blades. Can also metaphorically denote outstanding talent or skill.
origin: According to legend, during the Spring and Autumn period, the master swordsmith Ganjiang and his wife Moye forged two legendary swords for King Helü of Wu, naming the swords after themselves. The phrase first appears in the 'Zhan Guo Ce' (Strategies of the Warring States), where the diplomat Su Qin warned King Min of Qi that even swords like Ganjiang and Moye cannot cut without human strength. Over time, the names of these swords became a byword for exceptionally sharp, precious blades. The idiom can also metaphorically denote outstanding talent or skill.
example_zh: 这把宝剑锋利无比，堪称干将莫邪。
example_en: This precious sword is incredibly sharp, truly worthy of being called Ganjiang and Moye.

meaning: This idiom describes something that is incomplete, unfinished, or done only halfway. It often refers to tasks, speech, or efforts that have been left in a partial state without reaching completion. The reduplicative structure emphasizes the ragged, uneven quality of the unfinished work.
origin: The phrase appears in Zhu Ziqing's essay 'On How Much to Speak' (《论说话的多少》), a modern Chinese literary work from the Republic of China era (early 20th century). Zhu Ziqing describes the awkward situation when speaking before a large group: if one's words trail off halfway, listeners lose interest and drift into their own private conversations, doze off, or look around restlessly. The expression captures the communicative failure of incomplete speech and, by extension, any endeavor left half-done.
example_zh: 这件工作做得半半拉拉的，实在让人不满意。
example_en: This job has been done in a half-baked, incomplete manner, which is really unsatisfying.

meaning: To accumulate and endure bitterness and hardship over a long period. It describes someone who has experienced considerable difficulty and suffering. A variant of the idiom 停辛伫苦.
origin: This idiom belongs to the tradition of Chinese four-character expressions describing endurance through adversity. The characters 停 (to linger or remain) and 贮 (to store or accumulate) both convey the sense of hardship persisting and accumulating over time. It is a variant form of 停辛伫苦, with similar meaning and usage. No specific literary origin or associated historical figure is recorded for this particular variant.
example_zh: 父母停辛贮苦一辈子，只为供孩子们读书成才。
example_en: Their parents endured a lifetime of hardship, all so their children could study and succeed.

literal: hang up, carriage, retire from, office
meaning: To hang up one's carriage and retire from government office, referring to an official retiring in old age. In ancient times, officials were expected to retire at seventy, symbolized by putting away their carriage to show they would no longer serve. It conveys the idea of gracefully stepping down to make way for the next generation.
origin: The phrase originates from Ban Gu's Bai Hu Tong (白虎通) of the Han dynasty. It records that a minister at age seventy should retire, because by then his hearing and sight decline and he can no longer serve effectively. Hanging up the carriage symbolized that it would no longer be used for travel to court. This practice of retiring at seventy was seen as a way to preserve integrity and modesty, yielding one's post to more capable successors.
example_zh: 他年逾七十，上书悬车致仕，归隐故里。
example_en: Over seventy years old, he petitioned to retire from office and returned to his hometown in seclusion.

meaning: To walk with extremely light and careful footsteps, moving cautiously so as not to make any noise. It describes someone acting with great care and timidity, often to avoid being noticed or disturbing others.
origin: This idiom originates from Ming dynasty literature. It appears in Shi Nai'an's 'Water Margin' (水浒传), Chapter 21, where the character Tang Niu'er creeps upstairs using cautious, quiet steps. It also appears in Feng Menglong's 'Awakening the World' (醒世恒言), Volume 13, where an official approaches Lady Han's window with hushed, delicate movements. Both usages depict characters moving stealthily and gingerly to avoid detection.
example_zh: 他捏脚捏手地走进婴儿房，生怕吵醒熟睡的孩子。
example_en: He tiptoed into the nursery, terrified of waking the sleeping baby.

meaning: The gentleman has three prohibitions to observe throughout life. In youth he guards against lust; in his prime, against quarrels and aggression; in old age, against greed and covetousness. It teaches moral self-restraint appropriate to each stage of life.
origin: This idiom originates from the Analerta (论语·季氏), a record of Confucius's sayings compiled by his disciples during the Warring States period. Confucius taught that a gentleman (君子) must restrain himself against the dominant temptation of each stage of life: lust in youth, strife in adulthood, and avarice in old age. The teaching reflects the Confucian emphasis on lifelong moral self-cultivation. It has been cited for over two thousand years as guidance for ethical conduct at every age.
example_zh: 孔子告诫弟子要谨守君子三戒，方能修身养性。
example_en: Confucius admonished his disciples to observe the gentleman's three prohibitions so as to cultivate virtue and character.

meaning: Half of one's body is already buried in the earth. This idiom is a metaphor meaning that a person does not have long to live, as their life is nearly at its end. It is often used to describe someone who is getting old and approaching death.
origin: This idiom originates from 'Dongpo Zhi Lin' (Dongpo's Notes), Volume 12, by the Song Dynasty literatus Su Shi (Su Dongpo). In the original passage, Su Shi remarks that someone is already half-buried in the earth yet still arguing about who is superior. The vivid image of a person half in the grave but still caught up in petty disputes gives the phrase its enduring force.
example_zh: 爷爷常说自己是半截入土的人了，什么风浪没见过。
example_en: Grandpa often says he's a man already half in the grave—what storms hasn't he weathered?

meaning: To gird one's robe and bind up one's hair in a formal topknot. This describes the act of dressing formally to take up an official position. It symbolizes leaving seclusion to enter government service.
origin: The phrase comes from the Tang Dynasty scholar Han Yu's essay 'Zheng Chen Lun' (On the Contending Official). In it, Han Yu describes how hermits and worthy men living in mountain retreats, upon hearing of a virtuous and just government, would formally dress and bind their hair, eager to present themselves at the palace gates to offer their service. The image evokes the Confucian ideal that talented scholars should emerge from obscurity to serve when the state is worthy of their loyalty.
example_zh: 古代读书人束带结发，皆盼望能入仕报国。
example_en: In ancient times, scholars would gird their robes and bind their hair, all hoping to enter government service and serve their country.

meaning: This idiom describes things being neatly organized, orderly, and methodical. It conveys the idea that every item has its proper place and everything is arranged in a tidy, systematic fashion. It is often used to describe someone's belongings or work being well-organized.
origin: The idiom originates from a modern literary work — the song-and-dance drama 'Little Red Army Soldier' (《小红军》) by Bai Chengren and He Jiguang. In the story, a character is described carrying both a red-tasseled spear and a hand grenade, with everything arranged neatly and in order, looking just like a seasoned Red Army soldier. The phrase vividly captures the sense of military tidiness and disciplined organization.
example_zh: 他把房间收拾得归十归一，每样东西都放在该放的位置上。
example_en: He tidied up the room so that everything was neatly in order, with every item placed exactly where it should be.

meaning: When happiness reaches its extreme, sorrow inevitably follows. It describes the transition from peak joy to sadness, reflecting the idea that emotions and fortune are cyclical in nature. It is a variant of the more common idiom 乐极生悲.
origin: This idiom is a variant expression of the well-known phrase 乐极生悲 (extreme joy begets sorrow), a concept rooted in classical Chinese philosophy about the balance and cyclicality of emotions. The underlying idea appears in texts dating back to the Han dynasty and earlier, where philosophers observed that extremes naturally reverse. No single definitive origin story is attributed to this exact phrasing. It conveys the same wisdom found in Daoist and Confucian thought about moderation and the interplay of yin and yang.
example_zh: 庆功宴上众人欢声笑语，谁知乐尽悲来，一场意外打破了所有的喜悦。
example_en: Everyone was laughing and cheering at the celebration banquet, but joy turned to sorrow when an unexpected accident shattered all the happiness.

meaning: Answering questions as fluently and smoothly as flowing water. It describes someone who responds quickly, articulately, and without hesitation in conversation. The idiom conveys both nimbleness of mind and eloquence of speech.
origin: This idiom originates from the Book of Jin (晋书), in the Biography of Zhang Hua. Zhang Hua was a renowned scholar-official of the Western Jin dynasty, celebrated for his encyclopedic knowledge and quick wit. The text records that 'Hua responded as fluently as flowing water, and those who listened forgot their weariness,' praising his ability to answer any question swiftly and eloquently. The phrase later became a standard expression for articulate and agile repartee.
example_zh: 面对记者的提问，她应答如流，展现出深厚的学识。
example_en: Faced with the reporters' questions, she answered as fluently as flowing water, demonstrating her profound erudition.

meaning: An expression used to emphasize that something is absolutely true and beyond any doubt. It conveys complete certainty about the accuracy or authenticity of a claim or situation.
origin: The phrase appears in modern Chinese literature, notably cited by the writer Ying Xiuren in the work 'Jinzi Ta Yinbao Ta,' where a southern villager insists that a piece of news is absolutely true. It also appears in Mao Dun's novel 'Ziye' (Midnight), where a character vouches for the reliability of information about a military officer's concubine fleeing to the county town. The idiom compounds '千' (a thousand) and '万' (ten thousand) to signify an overwhelming degree of certainty.
example_zh: 这件事千真万确，我亲眼所见。
example_en: This matter is absolutely true; I saw it with my own eyes.

meaning: This idiom uses broken weapons—an axe (斧) and a chisel (斨)—as a metaphor for the inevitable sacrifices and costs endured during war. It describes the heavy toll that warfare exacts upon those who fight in it.
origin: The idiom originates from the Book of Songs (诗经), specifically the poem '破斧' (Broken Axe) in the 豳风 (Bin Feng) section. The original lines read '既破我斧，又缺我斨'—'My axe is broken, and my chisel is notched.' The poem is traditionally associated with the Duke of Zhou's (周公) eastern military campaigns to suppress rebellions during the early Western Zhou dynasty. The imagery of damaged weapons symbolizes the sacrifices and hardships suffered by soldiers in these campaigns.
example_zh: 经过数年征战，将士破斧缺斨，终得凯旋归乡。
example_en: After years of campaigning, the soldiers endured broken axes and notched chisels before finally returning home in triumph.

meaning: This idiom describes changes that are so wondrous, varied, and unpredictable that they seem to involve the supernatural. It conveys transformations that are impossible to fathom or grasp. It is often used to praise writing, art, or strategy for its extraordinarily varied and mysterious quality.
origin: This idiom originates from a poem by Song Zhiwen (宋之问) of the Tang Dynasty titled 'Song of the Heavenly Gate of Mount Song' (《嵩山天门歌》). The original lines describe mountain scenery: pines shifting and peaks turning, changing left and right; winds arising and clouds gathering, 'going out like ghosts and entering like gods.' The phrase was later adopted by Ming Dynasty scholar Hu Yinglin (胡应麟) in his work 'Shisou' (《诗薮》) to praise Li Bai's poems such as 'Hard Road in Shu' (蜀道难) for their supernatural, unfathomable changes.
example_zh: 这篇文章构思奇巧，出鬼入神，令人叹为观止。
example_en: This article is ingeniously conceived with wondrous, unpredictable changes that leave one in awe.

meaning: The Jinwu was the official responsible for guarding the capital city during the Qin and Han dynasties. The idiom originally referred to the Lantern Festival, when the night curfew was lifted for three days so people could view lanterns all night. It now broadly means there is no night curfew and people may come and go freely around the clock.
origin: During the Tang dynasty, Wei Xu recorded in his Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital that the streets of the capital were patrolled by Jinwu officials who called out at dawn and dusk to prohibit night travel. However, an imperial decree permitted the Jinwu to relax the curfew on the night of the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, along with one day before and after, allowing citizens to enjoy the lantern displays throughout the night. This practice gave rise to the idiom, which later came to signify the absence of any night restriction.
example_zh: 元宵佳节，金吾不禁，满城灯火辉煌。
example_en: On Lantern Festival night the curfew was lifted, and the whole city blazed with brilliant lanterns.

meaning: Those who know when they are content will not suffer disgrace. It advises people to avoid greed and be satisfied with what they have. The saying emphasizes that contentment protects one from humiliation and ruin.
origin: This phrase originates from Chapter 44 of the Daodejing (《老子》), written by the ancient philosopher Laozi during the Spring and Autumn period. Laozi wrote, 'He who knows contentment will not be disgraced; he who knows when to stop will not encounter danger; thereby one can endure long.' The idea was later echoed in the Book of Han (《汉书·疏广传》), where the Han dynasty official Shu Guang quoted it to justify his retirement from public life. It became a widely cited maxim on the virtue of moderation.
example_zh: 常言知足不辱，你既已功成名就，何必再贪求无厌？
example_en: As the saying goes, contentment avoids disgrace—having already achieved success and fame, why keep coveting more?

meaning: Advancing and retreating both follow a fixed pattern or law. It describes acting with discipline, proper timing, and a steady rhythm rather than impulsively. The idiom conveys that all actions should accord with natural rules and order.
origin: This idiom originates from the text He Guan Zi (鹖冠子), a work from the Warring States period attributed to the philosopher He Guan Zi. In the chapter 'Tai Hong Shi' (泰鸿十), the author observes that the sun rises and sets reliably and the moon waxes and wanes on schedule, stating that they 'advance and retreat with regularity.' The passage uses these celestial cycles as metaphors to illustrate that natural phenomena follow fixed laws, and by extension human affairs should also observe proper order and timing.
example_zh: 他为人处世进退有常，从不贸然行事。
example_en: He conducts himself with steady discipline, never acting rashly.

meaning: Literally 'thus have I heard,' this phrase is the traditional opening of Buddhist scriptures. It is attributed to Ananda, the Buddha's disciple, who claimed to have personally heard the teachings directly from the Buddha. It is used to affirm the authenticity of a transmitted teaching or account.
origin: This phrase originates from Buddhist scripture tradition. According to legend, Ananda, the Buddha's cousin and close disciple, recited the Buddha's sermons from memory at the First Buddhist Council. He prefaced each sermon with '如是我闻' to indicate that he had personally heard the teaching from the Buddha. The phrase appears in the 《佛地经论》, which explains that the transmitter of the Dharma declares 'such things I once heard.' It subsequently became the standard opening line for nearly all Buddhist sutras translated into Chinese.
example_zh: 如是我闻，当年他在山中修行时，曾得高僧指点。
example_en: Thus have I heard: when he practiced in the mountains, he once received guidance from an eminent monk.

meaning: To roam far and wide in all directions; to travel extensively between north and south. It conveys the idea of wandering across great distances without a fixed destination, similar to journeying everywhere.
origin: This idiom is a folk expression without a single definitive literary origin. It draws on the traditional Chinese spatial pairing of south (上) and north (落) to describe movement across vast territories. Historically, merchants, travelers, and laborers who crisscrossed the empire were said to move 'up south and down north.' Over time it became a colloquial way to characterize a life of extensive travel and wandering.
example_zh: 他年轻时上南落北，走遍了大半个中国，见识了各地的风土人情。
example_en: In his youth he roamed far and wide, traveling across more than half of China and experiencing the customs and culture of every region.

meaning: Literally 'to return with white hair and empty hands.' It describes someone who has grown old without achieving anything, especially after years of study. The idiom conveys the sorrow of wasted effort and unfulfilled ambition in old age.
origin: The phrase comes from the 'Book of the Later Han' (后汉书), in the 'Chronicle of Emperor Xian' (献帝纪). It describes elderly Confucian scholars over sixty who left their hometowns seeking food and resources, unable to devote themselves to learning. The text laments that they entered school as children yet returned in old age with nothing accomplished. The saying highlights the tragedy of a lifetime of study yielding no success.
example_zh: 少年若不努力求学，只怕到头来白首空归，悔之晚矣。
example_en: If one does not study diligently in youth, one may end up returning empty-handed in old age—too late for regrets.

meaning: Literally 'dog-stealing and rat-pilfering,' referring to petty thieves who steal like dogs and mice. Metaphorically, it describes insignificant rebels or petty criminals who lack the power to achieve anything of consequence. It is used to dismiss someone as beneath serious concern.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Han Ji' (汉纪) by the Han dynasty scholar Xun Yue, in the 'Annals of Emperor Hui.' Xun Yue argued that with a wise sovereign ruling above and clear laws established below, true rebels could not arise. Those who caused trouble were merely 'dog-stealing rat-pilfering' petty criminals, not a genuine threat to the state. The phrase thus came to denote would-be insurgents too insignificant to matter.
example_zh: 这些不过是狗盗鼠窃之徒，成不了什么气候。
example_en: These are merely petty thieves and pilferers who will never amount to anything.

meaning: To hear of someone's reputation and yearn to meet them. It describes admiring and longing for a person of renown whom one has not yet encountered. The idiom emphasizes the power of a good name to inspire admiration from afar.
origin: The idiom originates from the ancient text Guiguzi (《鬼谷子·内揅》), a work attributed to the legendary strategist Guiguzi of the Warring States period. The passage discusses the paradoxical nature of ruler-minister relationships: some are distant yet close, some near yet alienated. It observes that a minister may be passed over when standing right before the ruler, yet when his reputation reaches the ruler from afar, the ruler longs for him deeply. The phrase '遥闻声而相思' captures this idea that hearing of a worthy person's name from a distance can inspire greater admiration than daily proximity.
example_zh: 他对这位学者闻声相思，盼望能当面请教。
example_en: Hearing of the scholar's reputation, he yearned to meet him in person and seek his guidance.

meaning: Everything is completely settled and finished. It describes a situation where all matters have been thoroughly resolved, leaving nothing outstanding. The idiom conveys a sense of total completion and tidiness.
origin: This idiom is a folk expression formed by pairing the numbers 'thousand' and 'hundred' with the character '了' (to finish or complete), emphasizing thoroughness and totality. Similar in structure to other number-paired idioms like '千了百当', it reflects the Chinese rhetorical device of using large numbers to signify completeness. No single literary source is definitively credited as its origin; it circulated as a colloquial phrase conveying that all affairs are neatly concluded.
example_zh: 他把所有事务都安排得千了百了，终于可以安心退休了。
example_en: Having arranged all affairs to be completely settled, he could finally retire with peace of mind.

meaning: Describes a restless and uncontrolled mind, likened to a galloping horse and a leaping monkey. It refers to someone whose thoughts are scattered and cannot concentrate. The phrase emphasizes the difficulty of taming one's wandering attention.
origin: The metaphor originates from Han-dynasty alchemist Wei Boyang's commentary on the Cantong Qi, where he wrote that the 'mind-ape' is restless and the 'will-horse' gallops in all directions. Tang poet Xu Hun later used the imagery in his poem 'For Layman Du,' writing that when the mind is exhausted the heart-ape is subdued, and when the spirit is at ease the will-horse roams. Over time the phrase became a stock Buddhist and literary metaphor for mental restlessness.
example_zh: 打坐修行须先降伏意马心猿，方能入定。
example_en: To enter deep meditation through seated practice, one must first tame the restless mind.

meaning: Free from all worries, attachments, and burdens. It describes a state of mind where one is unencumbered by worldly concerns or emotional ties, living with complete ease and inner peace.
origin: This idiom has roots in Buddhist philosophy, where the term refers to mental attachments and hindrances that obstruct enlightenment. In the Heart Sutra tradition, being free from attachments is described as a prerequisite for achieving ultimate liberation. Over the centuries the phrase entered everyday Chinese usage, shifting from its religious context to describe anyone living a carefree, unburdened life.
example_zh: 退休后他过上了无挂无碍的生活，每天读书散步，怡然自得。
example_en: After retirement, he lived a carefree life free from all worries, spending his days reading and taking walks, perfectly content.

meaning: When going out to handle affairs, one should be as careful and respectful as if receiving an honored guest. It describes conducting oneself with earnestness and prudence in all endeavors. The phrase emphasizes a principled, reverent attitude toward daily responsibilities.
origin: This phrase originates from the Zuo Zhuan (左传), a foundational historical text of the Spring and Autumn period, specifically from the record of Duke Xi's thirty-third year (僖公三十三年). A minister quotes the saying 'when going out, act as though receiving a guest; when handling affairs, act as though conducting a sacrifice—this is the way of benevolence.' The saying encapsulates the Confucian ideal that everyday conduct should carry the same gravity and sincerity as ceremonial occasions. It became a lasting moral precept about earnestness and respect in one's actions.
example_zh: 他做事出门如宾，从不敢有半点懈怠。
example_en: He handles every task as carefully as receiving an honored guest, never daring to be the least bit negligent.

meaning: In ancient China, when a boy was born, an archer would shoot arrows made from a mulberry-wood bow and grass stems toward heaven, earth, and the four cardinal directions. The ritual symbolized the wish that the boy would grow up with far-reaching ambition and achieve great things in the world.
origin: The idiom originates from the Book of Rites (礼记·内则), a Confucian classic compiled during the Zhou dynasty. The text describes an ancient birth ceremony in which, upon the birth of a son, an archer shot six arrows from a mulberry-wood bow and grass-stem arrows at heaven, earth, and the four directions. This expressed the hope that the boy would carry lofty ambitions and roam the world to accomplish great deeds. The ritual reflects the early Chinese emphasis on instilling aspiration from the very moment of birth.
example_zh: 他自幼胸怀大志，正如桑弧蓬矢，立志走遍四方建功立业。
example_en: From a young age he harbored great ambitions; like the mulberry bow and grass arrow, he was determined to travel far and wide to build a career.

meaning: Something that is very much worth seeing or worth paying attention to. It describes matters, achievements, or amounts that are considerable in scale and should not be overlooked. Often used to indicate that a situation or result is impressively significant.
origin: This idiom does not trace back to a single classical text but emerged as a common expression in vernacular Chinese literature. It appears in Qing dynasty novels such as Li Baojia's 'Wenming Xiaoshi' (A Brief History of Civilization), where it was used to describe sums of money or situations of notable scale. Over time it became a standard phrase for anything warranting serious attention or admiration.
example_zh: 这次展会的规模比往年都大，确实大有可观。
example_en: This exhibition is larger than in previous years and is truly worth seeing.

meaning: Originally meant 'you walk slowly, I walk slowly; you walk fast, I walk fast.' It now describes someone who lacks independent judgment and blindly imitates or follows others in everything they do. The term carries a negative connotation of having no original ideas.
origin: This idiom comes from the Zhuangzi (庄子), specifically the chapter 'Tian Zifang' (田子方), a text from the Warring States period. It records the words of Yan Hui (颜回), the favorite disciple of Confucius (孔子), who described his attempts to follow his master: 'When the Master walks, I walk; when he hurries, I hurry; when he gallops, I gallop; when he races ahead leaving no dust behind, I can only stare blankly in his wake.' Over time the phrase evolved from a disciple's humble admiration into a criticism of mindless imitation.
example_zh: 这家公司只会亦步亦趋地模仿竞争对手，毫无创新可言。
example_en: This company merely slavishly imitates its competitors, with no innovation to speak of.

meaning: Describes a situation that has descended into complete chaos with no way to restore order. The vivid imagery evokes disorder spreading everywhere like mud smeared across the ground. It conveys total, unmanageable collapse.
origin: This idiom originates from the essay 'On Guan Zhong' (管仲论) by Su Xun of the Song Dynasty. Su Xun discusses the statesman Guan Zhong, who served Duke Huan of Qi during the Spring and Autumn period. When Duke Huan died, the state of Qi fell into total chaos because Guan Zhong had already passed away without cultivating a capable successor. Su Xun wrote that upon the duke's death everything collapsed into utter disorder — a situation that was entirely predictable, since the state had relied solely on one man who was already dead.
example_zh: 公司失去核心管理层后，内部一乱涂地，业务全面停摆。
example_en: After losing its core management team, the company descended into total chaos, with operations grinding to a complete halt.

meaning: To see through what is obscure and illuminate the minutest details. It describes a sharp, penetrating insight that can perceive deeply hidden and subtle aspects of things. Often used to praise someone's exceptional discernment or analytical ability.
origin: The phrase originates from a preface by the Ming dynasty writer Wu Cheng'en, titled 'Preface to Lord Shao Bao's Report on Governance.' In it, Wu praises an official for possessing the clarity to perceive distant and hidden matters, alongside a composed and unhurried demeanor. The idiom highlights a rare combination of acute perceptiveness and measured judgment. It later came to be used broadly to commend those who can discern subtle truths others overlook.
example_zh: 这位老侦探洞幽烛微，仅凭案发现场的蛛丝马迹便锁定了嫌疑人。
example_en: The veteran detective, with his penetrating insight, identified the suspect from mere traces left at the crime scene.

meaning: To work or study diligently without ever feeling tired. It describes someone who devotes themselves tirelessly to a task, especially learning or scholarship. The phrase emphasizes sustained, unwavering effort over a long period.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Biography of Fan Tai' in the History of the Southern Dynasties (《南史·范泰传》). Fan Tai was a scholar-official of the Liu Song dynasty during the Southern Dynasties period. He was widely read in the classics, fond of writing essays, and took pleasure in encouraging and mentoring younger scholars. The history records that he pursued these endeavors '孜孜无倦'—diligently and without weariness. His example became a model of lifelong devotion to learning and teaching.
example_zh: 他几十年如一日，孜孜无倦地研究古典文学。
example_en: For decades he studied classical literature diligently and without tiring.

meaning: A metaphor for seeking immediate gain without considering the consequences. Just as a snake that rushes forward in greed forgets its own tail, a person too eager for profit may neglect what follows behind. It warns against shortsighted recklessness.
origin: The idiom originates from the Song dynasty work 'Yuhu Qinghua' (玉壶清话) by the literatus Wen Ying. The text states, 'A greedy snake rushing forward will inevitably forget its tail.' Wen Ying used the image of a snake hurrying ahead and losing track of its own body to illustrate the folly of pursuing gain without regard for what one leaves behind. The phrase later condensed into the four-character idiom '贪蛇忘尾' as a warning against shortsighted greed.
example_zh: 他为眼前的利益铤而走险，真是贪蛇忘尾，迟早要出事。
example_en: He takes desperate risks for immediate gain—truly like a greedy snake forgetting its tail; it is only a matter of time before trouble catches up with him.

meaning: This idiom describes someone who acts shamelessly and uses their power or position to oppress and intimidate others. It conveys both unruly, unreasonable behavior and the abuse of authority to bully people into submission. The phrase is typically used to criticize such domineering conduct.
origin: This idiom originates from the novel 'Spring Tide Urgent' (春潮急) by the modern Chinese writer Ke Fei (克非). In a vivid scene, a character known as Li Huzi (李胡子, Li the Bearded) resolves to act shamelessly and throw his weight around, snatching the worn leather cap from his head and slamming it hard onto a square table while shouting at another character, Meng Er Huzi (孟二胡子), to get out. The dramatic depiction captures the essence of someone resorting to bullying and intimidation when reason fails them. The phrase has since become a descriptive term for such oppressive, unreasonable behavior in Chinese.
example_zh: 那恶霸在集市上放泼撒豪，吓得百姓不敢吭声。
example_en: That local tyrant acted shamelessly and domineeringly in the marketplace, frightening the common people into silence.

meaning: Originally referred to throwing a stone before sneaking into a place at night to check whether anyone was around or alert. It is now used metaphorically to describe probing or testing a situation cautiously before taking further action. The idiom emphasizes gathering information through a small, low-risk move before committing.
origin: This idiom has no single definitive literary source but derives from the practical tactics of thieves, scouts, and night infiltrators in ancient China. Before entering an unfamiliar or dark compound, they would toss a stone inside and listen for any reaction—barking dogs, shouted challenges, or movement—that might reveal whether the area was guarded. Over centuries this literal precaution became a widely used metaphor for cautious probing and tentative exploration in negotiations, diplomacy, and everyday decision-making.
example_zh: 谈判前他先提了个小问题，算是投石问路。
example_en: Before the negotiation, he raised a minor question as a way of testing the waters.

meaning: This idiom refers to the age of three years old. It derives from the Confucian teaching that a newborn child remains in the parents' embrace for three years before gaining enough independence to leave it. It is used in literary contexts to describe a very young child of three.
origin: This phrase traces back to the Analerta (论语), specifically the 'Yang Huo' chapter, where Confucius stated: 'A child is born, and after three years, then is freed from the parents' embrace.' This referred to the period of infancy when a child is completely dependent on parental care. The expression was later extracted from this passage to denote the specific age of three. The concept is also closely linked to the Confucian practice of three-year mourning for parents, regarded as repayment for those three years of nurturing.
example_zh: 这孩子尚未到免怀之岁，便已能识得数百字。
example_en: This child has not yet reached three years of age, yet can already recognize hundreds of characters.

meaning: Literally describes the morning sun just rising in the east. It is used metaphorically to describe a scene or situation full of vitality, energy, and promise. The idiom conveys a sense of youthful vigor and bright prospects.
origin: This idiom draws from the universal imagery of the morning sun ascending over the eastern horizon, a symbol deeply rooted in Chinese literary tradition. Unlike many classical idioms tied to a specific historical text or figure, this phrase evolved organically from poetic descriptions of dawn found across various dynastic writings. The rising sun has long been a metaphor for renewal and flourishing potential in Chinese culture. No single definitive source text is associated with this expression.
example_zh: 这群朝气蓬勃的年轻人正如旭日初升，充满了无限可能。
example_en: This group of energetic young people is like the rising sun, full of limitless possibilities.

meaning: This idiom metaphorically refers to the great virtue, good reputation, and meritorious achievements left behind by predecessors. It describes how the legacy of excellence from earlier generations continues to shine and influence those who follow.
origin: This phrase originates from the 'Book of Song' (宋书·礼志三), compiled by Shen Yue during the Southern Dynasties period. The passage discusses how from the Zhou dynasty through the Han dynasty, refined customs and traditions persisted, and the lingering virtue and glory of former ages continued to illuminate the annals of history. It was used in the context of ritual and ceremonial discourse, reflecting on how the cultural and moral legacy of great dynasties endured long after their fall.
example_zh: 先贤虽已作古，其遗芬余荣仍泽被后世。
example_en: Though the sages of old have passed away, their enduring virtue and glory continue to bless later generations.

meaning: Like ice melting away; describes doubts, misunderstandings, or estrangements that completely dissolve and disappear. It conveys a thorough clearing up of tensions or suspicions between people. The idiom emphasizes the totality and naturalness of the resolution.
origin: This idiom is a variant of the more common 涣然冰释, both drawing from the imagery of ice melting in warm conditions. The phrase builds on classical Chinese metaphors where ice symbolizes coldness, rigidity, and barriers between people. While no single definitive origin text is cited, the expression follows a long tradition in Chinese literature of using natural phenomena to describe emotional and social reconciliation. It has been used in various literary works to depict the resolution of grudges and the restoration of harmony.
example_zh: 经过一番坦诚交谈，两人之间的误会涣如冰释。
example_en: After an honest conversation, the misunderstandings between them melted away like ice.

meaning: This idiom refers to the dual pursuit of improving one's moral character and building one's career or accomplishments. It emphasizes that personal cultivation and professional success should go hand in hand. The phrase comes from classical Confucian philosophy advocating both inner virtue and outer achievement.
origin: The idiom originates from the I Ching (Book of Changes, 周易), specifically the Wenyan commentary (文言传) on the Qian hexagram. The original passage reads: 'The superior man advances in virtue and cultivates his achievement,' explaining that loyalty and trustworthiness advance virtue, while refining one's words with sincerity establishes one's endeavors. Dating to the Zhou dynasty, the text is traditionally associated with King Wen of Zhou and later Confucian commentary. It has served as a guiding principle for scholars and officials throughout Chinese history.
example_zh: 他在学业上不断进取，正是进德脩业的体现。
example_en: His relentless pursuit of academic progress exemplifies the principle of advancing virtue and cultivating achievement.

meaning: Literally meaning 'one sings here, the other responds there,' this idiom describes mutual echoing or呼应. It is used as a metaphor for people coordinating and reinforcing each other's words or actions, often in a supportive or collusive manner.
origin: The phrase originates from the Qing dynasty scholar Chen Tian's 'Ming Shi Ji Shi' (Chronicles of Ming Poetry), in the preface to the 'Ji Qian' section. Chen described how certain poets, though separated from the 'Former Seven Masters' for decades, still echoed each other's literary voices in perfect harmony, as though following the same track. The idiom thus evokes a scene of natural, responsive agreement between parties.
example_zh: 会议上两人此唱彼和，很快就将提案通过了。
example_en: The two echoed each other at the meeting and quickly pushed the proposal through.

meaning: Baseless and unreasonable remarks or rumors. It refers to speech that has no foundation in fact or logic, often spread to confuse or mislead. The phrase emphasizes the worthlessness and unreliability of such talk.
origin: This idiom does not have a single well-documented classical origin. It combines two established terms: '流言' (liú yán), meaning rumors or words that spread like flowing water, and '混话' (hùn huà), meaning confused, nonsensical, or muddled talk. Together they form a compound that has been used in vernacular Chinese to dismiss hearsay and unfounded claims. It reflects the long-standing cultural value placed on truthful, evidence-based speech.
example_zh: 对于这些流言混话，我们不必理会。
example_en: There is no need to pay attention to such baseless rumors.

meaning: A metaphor for a person who studies with great diligence and devotion. It originates from the image of a scholar reading a book hung on an ox's horn while riding. It praises those who pursue learning tirelessly regardless of their circumstances.
origin: During the Sui Dynasty, Li Mi—who would later play a key role in the founding of the Tang Dynasty—rode an ox draped with a straw saddle. He hung a scroll of the 'Book of Han' (汉书) on one of the ox's horns and read as he traveled. The story is recorded in the 'New Book of Tang, Biography of Li Mi' (《新唐书·李密传》). The Song Dynasty poet Liu Kezhuang later immortalized this image in his ci poem 'Qinyuanchun—Answering Ye Xianliang of Jiuhua.'
example_zh: 学子们以牛角书生为榜样，勤奋读书。
example_en: Students look up to the ox-horn scholar as a role model and study diligently.

meaning: This idiom means to reveal one's sincere and innermost feelings to others. '披露' means to disclose or make known, while '腹心' refers to one's true heart and genuine intentions. It describes the act of showing complete sincerity and holding nothing back.
origin: This phrase originates from the 'Records of the Three Kingdoms' (三国志), specifically the Biography of Fa Zheng (法正) in the Book of Shu (蜀志). Fa Zheng was a brilliant strategist who served the warlord Liu Bei during the late Eastern Han dynasty and early Three Kingdoms period. The original text notes that from beginning to end, one disclosed one's true heart, concealing no feelings whatsoever. The phrase reflects the high value placed on sincerity and mutual trust in both political alliances and personal relationships during that turbulent era.
example_zh: 他向老友披露腹心，说出了多年来藏在心底的话。
example_en: He laid bare his heart to his old friend, speaking of the words he had kept hidden inside for years.

meaning: Every day and every night; continuously without interruption. It describes an action or state that persists over a long period of time.
origin: The phrase appears in modern Chinese literature, notably in Hong Shen's play 'Qinglong Tan' (青龙潭), where a character named Liu Xiu works tirelessly pumping water for three days and nights until he faints from exhaustion on the water wheel. The idiom captures the relentless, round-the-clock nature of sustained effort. It has been widely used in 20th-century poetry and prose to describe unwavering dedication.
example_zh: 母亲日日夜夜守在病床前，照顾着生病的父亲。
example_en: The mother kept watch by the sickbed day and night, caring for her ailing father.

meaning: This idiom means that everything is arranged in a thoroughly proper and satisfactory manner. The pattern 'four... eight...' conveys comprehensiveness in all directions, while both 亭 and 当 carry the sense of 停当, meaning properly settled. It describes a situation where all matters have been handled neatly and completely, leaving nothing out of place.
origin: The phrase comes from a letter by the Song Dynasty Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi (朱熹), titled 'Reply to Lü Bogong' (答吕伯恭书). Zhu Xi wrote about striving to discipline his body and mind so that they would be 'four-settled, eight-proper' — even and well-ordered in every respect — without any unevenness or rough spots. The characters 亭 and 当 here both function as variants of 停当, meaning properly arranged or settled, and the numbers four and eight emphasize thoroughness in all directions.
example_zh: 他把这次活动的各项事务安排得四亭八当。
example_en: He arranged every aspect of the event in a thoroughly proper and satisfactory manner.

meaning: A single fish scale floating in the vast ocean. It serves as a metaphor for something extremely insignificant or negligible in the grand scheme of things. The phrase conveys a sense of how trivial one's existence or possessions appear against an immense backdrop.
origin: The idiom originates from the late Qing dynasty novel 《冷眼观》(Cold-Eyed Observer), authored by Wang Jianqiu. In its seventh chapter, the passage recounts a scholar who spent ten years studying by lamplight, only to offend a powerful young official while trying to seek justice for an ordinary citizen. As a consequence, everything he had labored for was swept away in an instant, likened to a single fish scale in the boundless sea or a fleeting cloud over Mount Wu, vanishing into nothingness.
example_zh: 他的财富在富豪榜上不过是沧海一鳞罢了。
example_en: His wealth is but a single scale in the vast ocean compared to those on the billionaires' list.

meaning: This idiom describes someone who slanders their subordinates while deceiving their superiors. It characterizes a treacherous person who undermines those beneath them while hiding the truth from those above. Such behavior reveals a calculating and morally corrupt nature.
origin: The phrase originates from the Tang Dynasty essay '骂尸虫文' (Reprimanding the Corpse Worm) by the renowned literatus Liu Zongyuan (773–819). In the essay, Liu condemns a parasitic spirit believed to dwell in the human body that reports people's misdeeds to Heaven to bring them harm.
