meaning: A metaphor for an extreme disparity in weight, value, or significance between two things. It likens one thing to a swan's down feather — weightless and trivial — and the other to Mount Tai — monumental and weighty. It is a variant of the more common idiom 鸿毛泰山.
origin: This idiom originates from a poem by Guo Moruo (郭沫若), a prominent 20th-century Chinese writer and historian. In the third poem of his 'Miscellaneous Chants on Returning Home' (《归国杂吟》之三), collected in his 1937 volume 'Battle Cry Collection' (《战声集》), Guo wrote: 'For forty-six years I have been prepared to die, having long since weighed whether my death would be as light as a swan's feather or as heavy as Mount Tai.' The line echoes Sima Qian's famous reflection on the meaning of death in his 'Letter to Ren An,' where he first contrasted 鸿毛 and 泰山. Guo Moruo's variant swaps 泰山 (Mount Tai) for the synonymous 泰岱, drawing on Mount Tai's alternative name 岱宗.
example_zh: 人生取舍之间，鸿毛泰岱当自分明。
example_en: When weighing life's choices, one must clearly discern what is as trivial as a feather and what is as weighty as Mount Tai.

meaning: To overcorrect an error so much that one goes beyond the proper limit, creating a new problem in the opposite direction. It warns against the human tendency to swing too far when trying to fix a mistake, missing the balanced middle ground.
origin: This idiom originates from Yuan Kang's "Yue Jue Shu" (《越绝书》) during the Han Dynasty, in the chapter "Pian Xu Wai Zhuan Ji." The passage describes how a son's revenge and a minister's pursuit of justice, though sincere enough to move heaven, can become excessive — likened to a nursing dog feeding a tiger cub without weighing the consequences. Centuries later, the Qing-era scholar Liang Qichao used the phrase in his treatise on Chinese academic thought to describe how learning had stifled human nature to such an extreme that a correction was inevitable, though it too risked going too far.
example_zh: 改革不能矫枉过直，否则会引发新的问题。
example_en: Reform must not overcorrect, or it will give rise to new problems.

meaning: Literally 'jade amassed in the Mysterious Garden,' referring to the legendary paradise where fine jade abounds. Figuratively, it describes a grand collection of the finest things or a gathering of outstanding talents and works — a treasure trove of excellence.
origin: The idiom derives from ancient Chinese mythology, in which the 'Mysterious Garden' (玄圃) is a celestial paradise located on Mount Kunlun, the dwelling place of immortals. According to legend, this garden was filled with exquisite jade and rare treasures, making it synonymous with a repository of the finest things in the world. Over time, the phrase came to be used metaphorically to praise anthologies, collections, or assemblies of exceptional quality. No single definitive source text is recorded as its origin.
example_zh: 这次展览的作品件件精美，真可谓玄圃积玉。
example_en: Every piece in this exhibition is exquisitely crafted — it is truly a treasure trove of excellence.

meaning: To open one's heart and drink freely, without any restraint or inhibition. The idiom describes a state of complete abandon and joyous celebration, usually in the company of good friends. It conveys not just the act of drinking, but the emotional release and camaraderie that accompany it.
origin: This idiom first appeared in the third act of the Yuan dynasty play 'Shooting Willows and Beating the Pill' (《射柳棰丸》) by an anonymous author. In the play, a character orders wine and food to be prepared so that everyone can celebrate the Dragon Boat Festival together, drinking heartily without reservation. The phrase later gained wider circulation through its use in the Ming dynasty novel 'Water Margin' (《水浒传》), where the character Li Kui is described as drinking with abandon, completely forgetting the warnings given by Song Jiang.
example_zh: 老友重逢，众人开怀畅饮，直到深夜才散。
example_en: When old friends reunited, everyone drank heartily and without restraint, not parting until late into the night.

meaning: Describes grief so profound and intense that it seems to move heaven and earth themselves. The idiom conveys the idea that heartfelt, genuine sorrow resonates beyond the human realm, touching the universe with its depth.
origin: The idiom originates from the Song Dynasty Buddhist text 'Wudeng Huiyuan' (《五灯会元》), compiled by the Chan monk Shi Puji (释普济). In Volume 1 of the text, a king receives devastating news and cries out in uncontrollable grief. His sorrow is so deep and genuine that it is described as moving both heaven and earth, giving rise to this enduring expression.
example_zh: 那场葬礼上的哭声哀感天地。
example_en: The weeping at that funeral was so heart-wrenching it moved heaven and earth.

meaning: To do whatever one pleases without any restraint or consideration for rules or others. It describes a person who acts arbitrarily, following only their own whims and desires, often with a negative connotation of abusing power or freedom.
origin: This idiom is a classical expression that emerged from ancient Chinese philosophical and literary traditions. The structure follows the pattern of '惟...所...' meaning 'only that which...', a common construction in classical Chinese. While no single definitive source is cited for this exact phrase, it reflects the Confucian and Legalist critique of unchecked personal conduct. The variant '为所欲为' is more commonly attested in classical texts, appearing in works like 'Zuo Zhuan' (左传) and later historical records to describe tyrannical or lawless behavior.
example_zh: 他仗着权势，在乡里惟所欲为，无人敢管。
example_en: Relying on his power and influence, he did whatever he wanted in the village, and no one dared to stop him.

meaning: This idiom describes the flying formations of wild geese during migration. Geese fly either in a diagonal V-shape (resembling the Chinese character 人) or in a straight horizontal line (resembling the character 一), hence the name. It evokes the orderly and disciplined flight patterns of migratory birds across the sky.
origin: The idiom derives from ancient Chinese observations of wild geese migrating south in autumn. Chinese poets and scholars have long admired the disciplined formations of geese, noting how they alternate between diagonal and horizontal patterns to conserve energy. While no single classical text is credited as the definitive source, the imagery appears frequently in Chinese poetry and prose, symbolizing order, unity, and the changing seasons.
example_zh: 秋色连天，大雁斜行横阵，向南飞去。
example_en: The autumn hues stretch to the horizon as wild geese, in slanting and horizontal formations, fly southward.

meaning: Seeing a scene or landscape triggers feelings of sadness and sorrow. It describes the experience of being moved to grief by familiar or evocative surroundings, often linked to memories of loss or bygone times.
origin: This idiom originates from 'The Peony Pavilion' (《还魂记·惊梦》) by Tang Xianzu, a celebrated playwright of the Ming Dynasty. In the story, the heroine Du Liniang wanders into a rear garden where flowers are in full bloom. The beautiful spring scenery stirs deep melancholy within her, as she is struck by the contrast between nature's vitality and her own loneliness. She returns home dejected, having been wounded by the very sights that should have brought joy.
example_zh: 回到故乡的老屋，他睹景伤情，不禁潸然泪下。
example_en: Returning to the old house in his hometown, he was wounded by the familiar sights and could not hold back his tears.

meaning: To turn fatigue into rest and refreshment. It describes the strategic act of converting a state of exhaustion into one of ease and renewed energy, often through clever rotation or timing.
origin: This idiom originates from the Ming Dynasty military treatise 'Bing Jing Bai Pian' (《兵经百篇》) by strategist Jie Xuan (揭喧), specifically the chapter 'Geng' (《更字》). Jie Xuan observed that if one army forces the enemy to respond repeatedly to feints, the enemy's ease turns into exhaustion. Conversely, by rotating one's own troops so they rest in turns, fatigue is transformed back into ease — and rested troops can then strike decisively. The phrase was originally a principle of battlefield stamina management.
example_zh: 合理的轮班制度能让工人们反劳为逸，保持高效产出。
example_en: A sensible shift rotation system allows workers to turn fatigue into ease and maintain high productivity.

literal: autumn, carry out, summer, seasonal order
meaning: Doing summer things when autumn has already arrived — acting out of season. It describes behavior that is anachronistic, inappropriate for the current time, or stubbornly out of step with changed circumstances.
origin: This idiom originates from Chapter 8 of Lu Xun's satirical novella "The True Story of Ah Q" (《阿Q正传》), published in the early 1920s during China's Republican era. The story is set in late autumn in the fictional village of Weizhuang, yet certain men still wear their hair queues (braids) in a style associated with summer, clinging to a fashion that is seasonally and symbolically outdated. Lu Xun uses the phrase to mock the absurdity of holding onto old customs — specifically the queue hairstyle mandated by the fallen Qing dynasty — even as times have changed. The idiom thus carries a sharp satirical edge, criticizing those who refuse to adapt to new realities.
example_zh: 都已经深秋了你还开着空调制冷，这不是秋行夏令吗？
example_en: It's already late autumn and you're still running the air conditioner on cooling mode — isn't that just doing summer things in autumn?

meaning: To make overall plans and take all factors into consideration. It describes a holistic approach where one coordinates all aspects of a situation and balances competing needs without neglecting any part.
origin: This idiom emerged from modern Chinese political and administrative discourse rather than classical literature. It gained prominence in the mid-20th century as a guiding principle for governance, emphasizing the need to balance diverse interests in a complex society. The phrase encapsulates the dialectical method of addressing contradictions by weighing all sides simultaneously. It has no single traceable classical source but reflects the synthesis of traditional Chinese holistic thinking with modern statecraft.
example_zh: 发展经济必须统筹兼顾环境保护与民生改善。
example_en: Developing the economy must take overall planning into account, balancing environmental protection and the improvement of people's livelihoods.

meaning: To act completely contrary to the established way or previous approach. It describes someone who deliberately does the opposite of what is expected or what has been done before, often as a strategic choice or expression of defiance.
origin: No definitive classical origin is recorded for this idiom. It appears to be a condensed form of the longer phrase '反其道而行之' (to act contrary to the usual way), which has been used in Chinese literature for centuries. The construction follows the classical pattern of using '一' as an intensifier meaning 'entirely' or 'completely,' combined with '反其道' (reversing the course). Though not traceable to a single canonical source, it has entered modern usage as a concise way to describe contrarian behavior.
example_zh: 他总是喜欢一反其道，做出让人意想不到的决定。
example_en: He always likes to go completely against the grain and make decisions that catch everyone off guard.

meaning: Refers to a man and woman secretly communicating their romantic feelings for each other. It alludes to clandestine love affairs conducted behind closed doors. Synonymous with the more common variant 韩寿偷香.
origin: During the Western Jin Dynasty, Han Shou was a handsome and talented subordinate of the high official Jia Chong. Jia Chong's daughter, Jia Wu, saw Han Shou at a banquet and fell deeply in love with him. She sent her maid to convey her feelings, and Han Shou began sneaking over the wall at night to meet her secretly. Jia Wu gifted him a rare foreign incense that had been bestowed upon the Jia family by the emperor. When Jia Chong later smelled this unique incense on Han Shou, he discovered the secret affair but ultimately consented to their marriage. The idiom was later used by the Later Shu poet Ouyang Jiong in his poem 'Chun Guang Hao.'
example_zh: 那两人韩寿分香，早被众人看在眼里。
example_en: Those two were secretly courting each other, and everyone had long since noticed.

meaning: To stage a comeback after a defeat; to rally one's forces and return with renewed strength. It describes a person or group that, having suffered a setback or failure, regroups and returns more powerful than before.
origin: This idiom originates from the Tang dynasty poet Du Mu's poem "Written on the Black River Pavilion" (题乌江亭). The poem reflects on the historical figure Xiang Yu, the Hegemon-King of Western Chu, who was defeated by Liu Bang at the Battle of Gaixia and chose to take his own life at the Wu River rather than retreat. Du Mu mused that the talented young men of Jiangdong could have been rallied, and that Xiang Yu sweeping back with fresh forces was not beyond imagination. The phrase thus immortalizes the idea that defeat need not be final.
example_zh: 这次失败后，他决心卷土重来。
example_en: After this defeat, he is determined to stage a comeback.

meaning: Originally describing the vigorous dance movements in the 'Wu' music of the early Zhou dynasty, where dancers moved their limbs energetically and stamped the ground fiercely. It symbolizes the courageous, forward-marching spirit of Taigong Wang when he assisted King Wu of Zhou in overthrowing the Shang dynasty. Today it is used metaphorically to describe someone who is high-spirited, full of fighting will, and advancing with great enthusiasm.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Record of Music' (《乐记》) chapter in the Book of Rites (《礼记》), a Confucian classic compiled during the Han dynasty. It describes the ritual dance accompanying the 'Wu' (武) music, which was composed in the early Zhou dynasty to celebrate King Wu's victory over the tyrannical King Zhou of Shang. The dancers' vigorous movements — hands and feet flying, stamping fiercely on the ground — were said to embody the spirit of Taigong Wang (太公望, also known as Jiang Ziya), the legendary strategist who served as King Wu's chief advisor. The phrase was later quoted in the Qing dynasty novel 'The Complete Biography of the Flying Dragon' (《飞龙全传》) by Wu Xuan.
example_zh: 将士们发扬蹈厉，一举攻克了敌军的主城。
example_en: The soldiers, full of fighting spirit and vigor, captured the enemy's main city in one bold strike.

meaning: Refers to not having enough food to satisfy one's hunger; describes a life of extreme poverty and deprivation. It is synonymous with 食不果腹 and conveys the hardship of barely scraping by without adequate sustenance.
origin: No specific classical source is recorded for this idiom. It is a variant of the more common expression 食不果腹, which appears in ancient texts describing the plight of the poor. The phrase captures the universal experience of hunger caused by poverty, passed down through vernacular usage rather than a single literary origin.
example_zh: 战乱年代，百姓食不充饥，生活极为艰难。
example_en: During the years of war, the common people could not get enough food to fill their stomachs, and life was extremely harsh.

meaning: This idiom refers to the act of ruining or corrupting good social customs and moral standards. It describes behavior that undermines societal norms and ethical values, leading to the deterioration of public decency. The phrase is often used to condemn vulgar, immoral, or socially harmful conduct.
origin: The idiom originates from the 'Book of Jin' (《晋书》), in the 'Biography of Liu Yi' (刘毅传). Liu Yi was an upright official of the Western Jin Dynasty known for his outspoken criticism of corruption and moral decay. In a memorial to the throne, he denounced certain practices as '毁风败俗,' arguing that such behavior was harmful to moral education and social transformation. He declared that throughout history, no greater failing existed than actions that corrupt public customs and degrade societal values.
example_zh: 这种低俗的表演实在毁风败俗，必须加以制止。
example_en: This kind of vulgar performance truly corrupts social morals and must be stopped.

meaning: Using the eyes to eat and the ears to see—a vivid metaphor for confusing or reversing the proper functions of things. It describes a state of topsy-turvy disorder where one fails to grasp what should be obvious, mixing up means and ends entirely.
origin: This idiom comes from Sima Guang's work '迂书·官失' (The Book of Pedantry, chapter 'Official Failings') during the Northern Song Dynasty. Sima Guang, the renowned historian and statesman, lamented that in his time, 'few indeed are those in the world who do not use their ears to see and their eyes to eat.' He was criticizing officials who had lost their sense of proper roles and responsibilities, doing things completely backwards. The phrase captured the absurdity of people abandoning their natural faculties and duties, and it later became a set idiom for any situation of muddled confusion.
example_zh: 他做事目食耳视，完全搞错了方向。
example_en: He works in a completely topsy-turvy way, having mistaken the entire direction of things.

meaning: Refers to the governance of a nation as a grand and noble enterprise. In its original context, it especially emphasizes the vital role of writing and literature in statecraft and civilization.
origin: This idiom originates from 'Discourse on Literature' (典论·论文) by Cao Pi (曹丕), Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty during the Three Kingdoms period. Cao Pi wrote that 'literary composition is the great enterprise of governing the state, a splendid undertaking that never decays.' He elevated writing to the highest level of national importance, ranking it alongside political and military achievements.
example_zh: 他把治学视为经国大业，一生笔耕不辍。
example_en: He regarded scholarship as a great enterprise of national governance and never ceased writing throughout his life.

meaning: To be deeply saddened by the sight of a scene or landscape before one's eyes. The idiom describes how encountering familiar or evocative scenery can trigger painful memories and emotional distress, often associated with nostalgia, homesickness, or grief over lost times and people.
origin: The idiom originates from Act 3 of the Yuan Dynasty play "Wang Can Ascends the Tower" (《王粲登楼》) by the renowned playwright Zheng Dehui (郑德辉). The play follows Wang Can, one of the Seven Scholars of Jian'an, who climbs a high tower and is overcome with sorrow upon seeing the distant landscape. The original lines read: "Climbing high and gazing far, every man harbors the grief of a lost homeland; caressing the scenery and wounding the heart, everywhere one sheds tears of despair." The idiom captures this universal experience of being emotionally triggered by one's surroundings.
example_zh: 登高望远，不免抚景伤情，思念故乡。
example_en: Climbing high and looking far, one cannot help but be moved to sorrow by the scenery, longing for one's hometown.

meaning: This idiom means something is not merely a matter of a single morning and evening — it has been going on for a long time. It emphasizes that a state, effort, or aspiration has persisted over an extended period rather than being a fleeting impulse.
origin: The idiom has no single recorded classical source (出处: 无). Its earliest known literary appearance is in Pu Songling's Qing Dynasty collection 'Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio' (《聊斋志异》), in the story 'Yingning' (《婴宁》), where a character declares 'I have held this ambition not for merely a day or two' (我有志，匪伊朝夕). The phrase uses the archaic negation '匪' (a variant of 非) and the classical particle '伊', combined with '朝夕' (morning and evening, a synecdoche for a brief span of time), to express the notion of long duration.
example_zh: 他痴迷古籍匪伊朝夕，书房里早已堆满泛黄的卷轴。
example_en: His obsession with ancient texts has lasted not merely a day or two — his study is already piled high with yellowed scrolls.

meaning: To treat others with complete sincerity and trust, holding nothing back. It describes opening one's heart fully to another person as if placing it directly into their chest. This idiom conveys the deepest level of genuine, candid interaction between people.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Book of the Later Han' (《后汉书》), in the biography of Emperor Guangwu (光武帝). When Liu Xiu was still the Prince of Xiao, he had just defeated the Tongma rebel army and faced the challenge of winning over the surrendered troops. Rather than keeping them at a distance, he personally visited their camps unarmed and without guards, showing absolute trust in their loyalty. The surrendered soldiers were so moved by his sincerity that they declared, 'The Prince of Xiao pushes his red heart into our bellies — how could we not die for him?' (萧王推赤心置人腹中，安得不投死！). This act of placing his heart, figuratively, into the bellies of former enemies became the enduring metaphor for treating others with unreserved sincerity.
example_zh: 他们推心置腹地谈了一整夜，多年的隔阂终于烟消云散。
example_en: They talked heart-to-heart all night long, and years of estrangement finally melted away.

meaning: To fabricate something entirely out of thin air, with no basis in fact or evidence. It refers to the act of inventing falsehoods, rumors, or accusations without any grounding in reality, purely for one's own purposes.
origin: This idiom first appeared in the Ming Dynasty supplement to the Wanli Yehuo Bian (《万历野获编补遗》) by Shen Defu (沈德符), a late Ming scholar and official. In the section on native chieftain succession, he criticized contemporary forgers who would fabricate hereditary claims out of nothing, bribing clerks in the Ministry of War's Bureau of Appointments to rubber-stamp their fraudulent documents. The phrase described the practice of inventing genealogies and official records with no historical basis whatsoever.
example_zh: 这些指控完全是凭空捏造，毫无事实依据。
example_en: These accusations are entirely fabricated out of thin air, with no factual basis whatsoever.

meaning: Describes a state of extreme exhaustion from talking excessively, to the point where one's lips are worn out and tongue feels decayed. It conveys the idea of having argued, persuaded, or explained something so much that one's mouth is completely spent. Often used to emphasize the futility of endless speech when the listener remains unmoved.
origin: This idiom is a variant of the more common expression '唇焦舌敝' (chún jiāo shé bì), which dates back to classical Chinese literature describing the exhaustion of repeated persuasion. The character '敝' (worn, tattered) is replaced here by '腐' (rotten, decayed), intensifying the image of oral fatigue. No specific dynasty or historical figure is definitively tied to this particular variant, as it likely evolved through literary usage as a rhetorical flourish. The idiom belongs to a family of expressions that use physical deterioration of the mouth to metaphorically represent the toll of excessive speech.
example_zh: 为了劝他回头，我已说得唇敝舌腐，他却依旧执迷不悟。
example_en: I have talked until my lips are worn and my tongue is rotten trying to persuade him to turn back, yet he remains stubbornly unrepentant.

meaning: The gateway through which both calamity and blessing enter one's life. It refers to the source or origin point from which disaster and good fortune alike arise, often implying that one's own words and deeds are the door that invites either outcome.
origin: This concept originates from classical Chinese philosophical thought, particularly within the Daoist tradition. The phrase appears in the 'Huainanzi' (淮南子), a Han dynasty text compiled under the patronage of Liu An, the King of Huainan. It reflects the yin-yang worldview that opposites share a common root. The idea is that fortune and misfortune are not random external forces but emerge from the same door — one's own conduct, speech, and choices. This teaching was later echoed in various moral and philosophical works urging self-cultivation as the key to determining one's fate.
example_zh: 言行乃祸福之门，不可不谨慎对待。
example_en: Words and deeds are the very door to misfortune and fortune, and must be treated with the utmost caution.

meaning: Describes a person who drifts from place to place without a settled home, much like a broken twig carried by the wind or tumbleweed blown across the land. It conveys a sense of rootlessness and the hardship of a nomadic, unstable existence.
origin: This idiom originates from a poem by the Song Dynasty poet Lu You (陆游), titled 'The Day Before the Examination Number Is Posted' (《拆号前一日作》). In the poem, Lu You laments his wandering life, writing that drifting and scattering is his lot wherever he goes, comparing himself to a broken stem and windblown tumbleweed. Lu You was a renowned patriotic poet who himself experienced displacement during the tumultuous Southern Song period. The phrase captures the melancholy of a life without roots or permanent settlement.
example_zh: 这些年他断梗飞蓬，四处漂泊，终于在此安了家。
example_en: All these years he drifted like a broken stem and flying tumbleweed, wandering everywhere, and has finally settled down here.

meaning: Refers to a beautiful young woman from a humble or ordinary family background. The term emphasizes natural, unadorned beauty rather than noble or aristocratic refinement. It often carries a tone of gentle affection or admiration.
origin: The idiom originates from the 'Biyu Song' (碧玉歌) in the Yuefu Poetry Collection (《乐府诗集》), a compilation of folk songs and ballads from the Han to Tang dynasties. The poem tells of a girl named Biyu, a 'small-family daughter' (小家女), who felt unworthy to marry into a noble household. Moved by a man's sincere affection and sense of honor, she ultimately formed a deep, sworn bond with him. Over time, 'small-family Biyu' evolved into the set phrase '小家碧玉,' used to describe any lovely young woman of modest origins.
example_zh: 她虽是小家碧玉，却气质不凡。
example_en: Though she is a modestly born beauty, her demeanor is extraordinary.

meaning: To be so deeply moved by someone's magnanimity and virtue that one feels intoxicated without realizing it, much like drinking fine wine. It describes the natural, effortless charm of a person of great character whose company uplifts and captivates others.
origin: This idiom originates from an annotation by Pei Songzhi in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, citing the Jiang Biao Zhuan. It describes the experience of befriending Zhou Yu, the famed general of Eastern Wu during the Three Kingdoms period. Cheng Pu, an older general who initially resented Zhou Yu, remarked that associating with Zhou Yu was like drinking rich, mellow wine — one becomes intoxicated by his grace before even realizing it. The phrase celebrates Zhou Yu's broad-mindedness and personal magnetism.
example_zh: 与他相处如饮醇自醉，令人流连忘返。
example_en: Spending time with him is like drinking fine wine and becoming naturally intoxicated — it makes one reluctant to leave.

meaning: To be partly skeptical and partly convinced at the same time, unable to determine whether something is true or false. It describes a state of wavering between belief and disbelief, without reaching a firm conclusion either way.
origin: This idiom originates from the Tang dynasty poet Yuan Zhen's poem 'Ancient City-Building Song' (《古筑城曲》). In the poem, Yuan Zhen describes a frontier scenario where a peace negotiation is proposed after conflict — the defenders are half-doubting and half-believing the enemy's sincerity, so they continue building the city walls as a precaution. The phrase captured the ambivalent, cautious mindset of people facing uncertain claims, and later entered common usage as a set idiom.
example_zh: 我对他的承诺半疑半信，决定再观察一段时间。
example_en: I was half-doubting and half-believing his promise, so I decided to observe for a while longer.

meaning: The arrow strikes stone with such force that the feather fletching vanishes into it. It originally described archery of supernatural strength, and later came to refer to any superlative martial skill or concentrated power.
origin: The idiom first appears in the 'Lüshi Chunqiu' (Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals, circa 239 BCE), which records that the legendary archer Yang Youji (养由基) of the Chu state once mistook a stone for a rhinoceros and shot an arrow that buried itself completely, feather and all. A similar story is told of the Han dynasty general Li Guang (李广), who shot an arrow into a stone believing it to be a tiger. Both tales illustrate that absolute concentration and sincerity of intent can produce extraordinary power.
example_zh: 这位老将虽年过花甲，箭术依然射石饮羽，令人叹服。
example_en: Though past sixty, this veteran general can still shoot through stone and bury the feather, earning everyone's admiration.

meaning: Describes a location nestled against mountains with a river flowing beside it, enjoying a scenic and strategically favorable natural setting. It evokes the image of mountains as one's pillow and rivers as one's armrest, conveying both shelter and abundance.
origin: The idiom comes from the Song Dynasty scholar Wang Yinglin's encyclopedic work 'Yuhai' (Jade Sea), in the section on geography and prefectures. It describes Qingyuan (modern-day Ningbo in Zhejiang Province), located east of Kuaiji, as a place that 'pillows on mountains and arms the river, backs onto the vast sea, and faces Fusang.' The phrase captures the strategic and natural advantages of a settlement cradled by mountains and waterways.
example_zh: 这座古镇枕山臂江，风景如画，令人流连忘返。
example_en: This ancient town, pillowed by mountains and embraced by the river, boasts picturesque scenery that makes visitors reluctant to leave.

meaning: To remain completely unashamed and at ease despite having done something disgraceful. It describes a person who has lost all sense of moral conscience and feels no remorse for their wrongdoing, behaving as if nothing were wrong.
origin: This idiom originates from a passage in Yan Ermei's Qing dynasty essay 'On Fang Guan.' The Tang dynasty official Fang Guan suffered a military defeat and, by military law, should have been executed for dereliction of duty. Instead, he was merely dismissed from his post — a lenient punishment that was already illegal. Yet Fang Guan showed no shame whatsoever, continuing to entertain guests at his home as if nothing had happened. Yan Ermei used the phrase to condemn Fang Guan's utter lack of conscience.
example_zh: 他剽窃他人作品被揭发后，不仅不道歉，还恬不知愧地继续出席各种活动。
example_en: After being exposed for plagiarizing others' work, not only did he not apologize, but he shamelessly continued to attend various events as if nothing had happened.

meaning: Times change and circumstances shift accordingly. This idiom expresses that as eras pass, the prevailing conditions, power dynamics, and social realities inevitably transform — what once was no longer holds true. It is often used to justify adapting strategies or reassessing situations in light of new realities.
origin: The idiom first appears in the Qing dynasty scholar Hang Shijun's work "Zhiyi · Zhu Shi" (《质疑·诸史》, "Questions and Doubts · Various Histories"). In a passage discussing the harsh reforms of Shang Yang, the Legalist statesman of the Qin state during the Warring States period, Hang argues that later generations unfairly blame Shang Yang alone. He notes that as times and circumstances changed, each dynasty added its own embellishments to governance — "时移势易，踵事增华" — so it is unreasonable to single out Shang Yang for condemnation. The phrase thus originally carried a sense of historical relativism: judging past figures by present standards ignores how much the world has moved on.
example_zh: 时移势易，当年无人问津的荒地如今成了寸土寸金的核心地段。
example_en: Times have changed and circumstances have shifted — the wasteland that nobody wanted back then is now prime real estate worth a fortune.

meaning: Profound and unmistakably clear. It describes a statement, argument, or principle that is expressed in a deeply penetrating yet lucid manner, leaving no room for ambiguity. The idiom emphasizes both depth of insight and clarity of presentation.
origin: The idiom originates from Sima Qian's 'Records of the Grand Historian' (《史记》), in the 'Preface by the Grand Historian' (《太史公自序》). Confucius is quoted as saying, 'I wished to record empty words, but it is better to see deeds that are profound and evident' (深切著明). Sima Qian invoked this phrase to justify his historical method — letting events and actions speak more powerfully than abstract commentary. The idiom was later used by Qing dynasty scholar Wang Fuzhi (王夫之) in his work 'Shang Shu Yin Yi' (《尚书引义》).
example_zh: 他的文章深切著明，读后令人印象深刻。
example_en: His article is profound and unmistakably clear, leaving a deep impression after reading.

meaning: To feel completely helpless, as if one's hands are tied. It describes a situation where a person faces a problem but has no idea what to do and cannot come up with any solution at all.
origin: This idiom first appeared in the Yuan dynasty historical text 'Song Ji San Chao Zheng Yao' (《宋季三朝政要》), an anonymous work chronicling the late Song dynasty. The passage describes the aftermath of the death of Qin Hui (秦桧), the infamous chancellor who betrayed the Song. After Qin Hui died, the Jin ruler Wanyan Liang (完颜亮) launched a southern invasion, and the Song court was so panicked and unprepared that no one could devise any countermeasure — they were all utterly helpless. The image of hands being bound captures the paralysis and despair of that moment.
example_zh: 面对突如其来的洪水，村民们束手无策，只能等待救援。
example_en: Faced with the sudden flood, the villagers were completely helpless and could only wait to be rescued.

meaning: This idiom criticizes the tendency to set unrealistic, overly ambitious goals that are beyond one's practical reach. It warns against chasing lofty ideals without a solid foundation or feasible plan.
origin: The idiom originates from Qing dynasty writer Li Yu's work 'Xian Qing Ou Ji' (闲情偶寄), specifically in the chapter on utensils and playthings discussing design principles. Li Yu observed that when people first conceive a design, they often fall into the trap of being overly ambitious and impractical (未免弛高骛远). The phrase is a less common variant of the more widely used idiom 好高骛远, sharing the same figurative meaning.
example_zh: 年轻人创业切忌弛高骛远，应从实际出发。
example_en: Young entrepreneurs must avoid pursuing unrealistic ambitions and should start from practical realities.

meaning: The tail is too large to wag. Originally a metaphor for subordinates growing so powerful that superiors lose control over them. In modern usage, it describes an organization so bloated that it becomes unmanageable and unresponsive to command.
origin: This idiom comes from the Zuo Zhuan (《左传》), a classic Chinese history text, under the 11th year of Duke Zhao's reign (昭公十一年). The full passage reads: '末大必折，尾大不掉，君所知也' — meaning 'When branches grow too large, they will break; when the tail grows too large, it cannot be wagged — this Your Lordship already knows.' The speaker was warning a ruler about the dangers of allowing subordinate powers to grow unchecked.
example_zh: 公司部门尾大不掉，总部决策难以执行到位。
example_en: The company's departments have become too unwieldy to manage, making it difficult for headquarters to enforce its decisions.

meaning: To bathe and perfume oneself repeatedly as an act of utmost reverence and sincerity. It describes the elaborate ritual purification one undergoes before meeting a revered person or performing a sacred duty, signifying profound respect and solemn devotion.
origin: This idiom originates from a letter written by Han Yu (韩愈), the great Tang Dynasty essayist, to Minister Meng (孟尚书). In the letter, Han Yu expressed that he would bathe three times and fumigate himself with incense three times before visiting someone of exceptional virtue and moral character. The practice reflects ancient Chinese ritual customs where purification was a prerequisite for approaching the divine or the highly esteemed. Over time, the phrase became a fixed expression for showing extreme respect and earnestness.
example_zh: 他三沐三薰后才敢去拜见老师。
example_en: Only after bathing and perfuming himself three times did he dare to go pay respects to his teacher.

meaning: A dwelling or location that is both secure and convenient. The idiom describes a place where one feels protected and at ease while also finding it practically advantageous for daily life. It often carries a subtle irony, suggesting that what one takes for a safe haven may be perilously narrow in scope.
origin: The idiom originates from the 'Xu Wugui' chapter of the Daoist classic Zhuangzi, attributed to the philosopher Zhuang Zhou (c. 4th century BCE). In the passage, Zhuangzi describes a louse that dwells in the folds of a pig's skin — between the hoof crevices, udders, and thigh gaps — and smugly believes these spots to be 'safe chambers and convenient places' (安室利处). The louse's complacency is shattered when the butcher one day singes the pig's bristles and the louse perishes in the flames, never having grasped the true precariousness of its home. The story satirizes those who cling to narrow comforts without recognizing the broader dangers surrounding them.
example_zh: 他在这个小镇上找到了安室利处，从此不愿再漂泊他乡。
example_en: He found a safe and convenient haven in this small town and never wished to wander again.

meaning: This idiom describes the total collapse of a regime or entity caused by internal decay and civil strife rather than external attack. The bird burns its own nest, and the fish rots from the inside out — both metaphors for self-inflicted destruction.
origin: The idiom fuses two classical sources. The first half comes from the Book of Changes (《易·旅》), which describes a bird that burns its own nest after a moment of laughter turns to wailing. The second half comes from the Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals (《公羊传·僖公十九年》), which explains the fall of the state of Liang during the Spring and Autumn period — it perished not from invasion but from internal decay, like a fish rotting from within. The idiom was later used in the Old Book of Tang (《旧唐书》) to describe rebel forces that collapsed from their own corruption.
example_zh: 这个王朝鸟焚鱼烂，终因内乱而覆灭。
example_en: This dynasty collapsed like a bird burning its nest and a fish rotting from within, ultimately destroyed by internal strife.

meaning: To adapt to one's environment and remain content in any situation or circumstance. It reflects a philosophical acceptance of life's changes and the ability to find inner peace regardless of external conditions.
origin: The exact origin of this idiom is not clearly documented in classical texts. It is a variant form of the more common idiom '随遇而安' (suí yù ér ān), which shares the same pronunciation and meaning. The phrase is believed to have appeared in Song Dynasty scholar Zhu Xi's annotations on the works of Mencius, where he used it to describe the sage's ability to remain undisturbed by poverty or wealth alike.
example_zh: 无论身处何地，他都能随寓而安，从不抱怨。
example_en: No matter where he finds himself, he can always adapt and be content, never complaining.

meaning: Describes weapons that are broken and damaged, particularly axes and other bladed implements of war. The idiom conveys a state of military equipment being worn out or rendered useless after prolonged combat, often implying the exhaustion and hardship of soldiers.
origin: This idiom originates from the poem 'Broken Axes' (破斧) in the 'Odes of Bin' (豳风) section of the Classic of Poetry (诗经), the oldest existing collection of Chinese poetry dating to the Western Zhou dynasty. The poem laments the hardships of soldiers who, after following the Duke of Zhou on a three-year eastern campaign to quell a rebellion, returned home with their axes broken and their qiang-axes damaged. The imagery of shattered weapons became a metaphor for the toll of prolonged warfare on both equipment and morale.
example_zh: 连年征战，斧破斨缺，士兵们早已疲惫不堪。
example_en: After years of continuous warfare, with axes broken and weapons damaged, the soldiers were already utterly exhausted.

meaning: This idiom warns that a woman who dresses provocatively or adorns herself with excessive allure invites lustful advances and immoral behavior. It reflects a traditional Confucian admonition against vanity and the dangers of attracting unwanted attention through appearance.
origin: The phrase originates from the 'Xici Shang' (系辞上) commentary of the I Ching (周易), one of the oldest Chinese classics dating back to the Western Zhou dynasty. The full passage reads: '慢藏诲盗，冶容诲淫' — 'Carelessly hoarding valuables teaches others to steal; seductively adorning one's appearance teaches others to lust.' The saying was later referenced by Song dynasty scholar Sun Guangxian in his work 'Beimeng Suoyan' (北梦琐言).
example_zh: 她虽不认同冶容诲淫的陈旧观念，但依然讲究衣着得体。
example_en: Though she does not subscribe to the old-fashioned notion that seductive dress invites lewdness, she still values dressing appropriately.

meaning: Neither a relative nor an old acquaintance. Describes two people who share no familial ties or prior friendship — complete strangers with no connection whatsoever.
origin: The idiom first appears in a poem titled 'Sent to Jia Dao' (寄贾岛) by the Tang Dynasty poet Ma Dai (马戴). In the poem, Ma Dai writes of jade pendants and clanging gold, saying they are 'neither kin nor old friends' — using the phrase to describe two fine things that, though equally precious, have no inherent bond. Over time, the expression shifted from describing objects to describing human relationships, cementing its meaning of having no prior connection between people.
example_zh: 我与他非亲非故，实在不便开口借钱。
example_en: He and I are neither relatives nor old friends, so it's really not appropriate for me to ask him for a loan.

meaning: Describes the formal attire of ancient Chinese scholar-officials: a tall ceremonial hat and a wide waist sash. The idiom evokes the dignified, stately bearing of the literati class and is often used figuratively to suggest someone of elevated status or refined appearance.
origin: The idiom first appears in Guan Hanqing's Yuan dynasty zaju play 'Xie Tianxiang' (《谢天香》), where it describes a renowned scholar-official's noble appearance. It was later popularized by Luo Guanzhong in the Ming dynasty classic 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms' (《三国演义》), Chapter 37, where a visitor of extraordinary bearing is announced as wearing 'a high hat and broad sash.' The phrase became a stock image for the idealized Confucian gentleman-official.
example_zh: 那位峨冠博带的老先生缓步走进大厅，气度不凡。
example_en: The elderly gentleman in a high hat and broad sash walked slowly into the hall, his bearing extraordinary.

meaning: To persist in evil intentions or criminal schemes, refusing to give up one's wicked designs despite warnings or consequences. It describes someone whose bad nature remains unchanged, continually plotting or committing misdeeds without remorse.
origin: This idiom has no definitive classical literary source. It emerged from vernacular Chinese, combining '贼' (thief or evildoer) with '心不死' (the heart does not die) to form a vivid metaphor. The phrase likens a person's stubborn attachment to evil intentions to a heart that refuses to perish. It became widely used in colloquial speech and modern literature to condemn recidivists and unrepentant wrongdoers.
example_zh: 他被罚过多次，却贼心不死，仍然偷窃。
example_en: He has been punished many times, yet his thieving heart refuses to die, and he still steals.

meaning: Water slides right off a duck's back without soaking in. This idiom describes something that passes through a person's mind without leaving any impression or being retained at all. It is often used to criticize superficial learning or a total failure to absorb information.
origin: There is no recorded classical literary source for this idiom. It originates from folk observation of nature: ducks have oily, waterproof feathers, and water beads up and rolls off their backs without being absorbed. This vivid natural image was adopted into everyday speech to describe a person who hears or reads something but retains nothing, much like water that vanishes from a duck's back the moment it passes over.
example_zh: 老师苦口婆心地劝了他半天，结果全是水过鸭背，他一句也没听进去。
example_en: The teacher earnestly advised him for a long time, but it was all water off a duck's back — he didn't take in a single word.

meaning: Government affairs run smoothly and the people live in harmony. It describes a thriving, well-governed society where the administration is effective and the populace is content and united.
origin: This idiom originates from 'Record of Yueyang Tower' (岳阳楼记) by Fan Zhongyan, a renowned statesman and literary figure of the Northern Song Dynasty. The essay recounts how Teng Zijing, a demoted official, governed Yuezhou so effectively that 'the following year, governance was smooth and the people harmonious, and all previously neglected undertakings were revived' (越明年，政通人和，百废俱兴). Fan Zhongyan used this phrase to praise good governance and social prosperity. The idiom has since become a classic expression for an ideal state of political and social well-being.
example_zh: 当今社会政通人和，百姓安居乐业。
example_en: In today's society, governance is smooth and the people are harmonious, with everyone living and working in peace and contentment.

meaning: Refers to the age of seventy, when ancient Chinese officials would retire from public service and cease using their official carriages. The idiom evokes the image of hanging up one's vehicle for good, symbolizing the end of an official career and the beginning of a quiet life in retirement.
origin: This idiom originates from the ancient Chinese convention that officials should retire at seventy, a practice codified as the '悬车' (suspending the carriage) ritual. The phrase appears in '归田琐记·七十致仕' (Miscellaneous Notes on Returning to the Fields) by Liang Zhangju of the Qing dynasty, who argued that if one entered officialdom before forty, the retirement age need not be strictly seventy. Liang himself noted that he twice retired before reaching the 'age of suspending the carriage,' demonstrating the idiom's use as a cultural benchmark for retirement.
example_zh: 祖父已至悬车之岁，仍每日读书不辍。
example_en: Although my grandfather has reached the age of seventy, he still reads every day without pause.

meaning: Refers to the chief instigator or ringleader who masterminds a plot or conspiracy. It describes the person who originates and orchestrates a scheme, typically in a criminal or conspiratorial context. The idiom emphasizes the primary role of the person who conceived and initiated the wrongful plan.
origin: This idiom originates from Chapter 18 of Shi Nai'an's classic Ming dynasty novel 'Water Margin' (水浒全传). In the story, Bai Sheng is captured and brought before the authorities for his involvement in the robbery of the birthday gifts. Under interrogation, he is bound with ropes and pressed to reveal who was the mastermind behind the entire scheme, using the phrase '主情造意' to ask who the chief instigator was.
example_zh: 经过审讯，警方终于查出了这起案件的主情造意之人。
example_en: After interrogation, the police finally identified the mastermind behind this case.

meaning: To remain vigilant and on guard both day and night, never letting one's guard down. It describes a state of constant watchfulness and prudence, especially in positions of responsibility where one cannot afford a moment of carelessness.
origin: This idiom originates from the Northern Song dynasty scholar and official Shen Kuo (沈括) in his memorial 'Yanzhou Xie Dao Ren Biao' (《延州谢到任表》), submitted upon assuming office in Yanzhou. In this memorial, Shen Kuo pledged to exhaust his efforts in fulfilling the emperor's entrusted duties, and to remain vigilant day and night, ever mindful of the grace bestowed by heaven and earth. The phrase reflects the Confucian ideal of a diligent official who is ceaselessly watchful over his responsibilities.
example_zh: 边防战士昼警夕惕，守护着祖国的每一寸土地。
example_en: The border guards remain vigilant day and night, safeguarding every inch of their homeland.

meaning: The lanes and alleys are emptied of people — not because they are hiding indoors, but because everyone has poured out onto the streets. It describes a spectacular occasion, such as a celebration or welcoming ceremony, that draws an entire community out of their homes.
origin: This idiom first appeared in a poem by Su Shi (苏轼) of the Northern Song Dynasty, titled 'Revisiting the Sea-Viewing Tower on the Seventeenth of the Eighth Month.' Su Shi wrote that thanks to the tide-watching spectacle the next day, 'ten thousand people emptied the lanes, vying in their new attire.' The phrase was later popularized in Qing Dynasty literature, notably appearing in Wu Jianren's (吴趼人) novel 'Strange Events Witnessed in the Past Twenty Years.'
example_zh: 除夕之夜，烟花表演让整个城市万人空巷。
example_en: On New Year's Eve, the fireworks display emptied the entire city — everyone poured into the streets to watch.

literal: stretch, head, in order to, gaze
meaning: To crane one's neck and gaze into the distance. It describes a state of earnest, anxious anticipation — waiting for someone or something with great hope and longing.
origin: The idiom originates from two classical sources. In 'Mencius: King Hui of Liang', Mencius tells the king that if a ruler refrains from killing, the people of the world will all crane their necks and look to him with hope. It also appears in the 'New History of the Five Dynasties' in the biography of Guo Chongtao, a Tang dynasty general, where it describes how people north of the Yellow River craned their necks to gaze hopefully toward the newly established imperial proclamation, longing for success and peace after prolonged warfare.
example_zh: 灾民引首以望，等待救援物资的到来。
example_en: The disaster victims craned their necks in hope, waiting for relief supplies to arrive.

meaning: Describes walking with bold, confident strides while speaking freely and loudly. It metaphorically refers to acting and speaking without any restraint, fear, or inhibition, embodying a carefree and unconstrained spirit.
origin: The idiom originates from the Records of the Three Kingdoms (《三国志》), in the annals of Emperor Wen of Wei, Cao Pi. Pei Songzhi's annotation cites the Book of Wei (《魏书》), which records Cao Pi's aspiration to promote benevolent governance through the teachings of the Three Chapters and harmonious virtue. He wished that the common people, who had long lived in oppression and held their breath in fear, could finally 'stride freely and talk boldly' without any sense of danger or dread. The phrase captures the ideal of a liberated and peaceful life under enlightened rule.
example_zh: 几位学者阔步高谈，从广场这头走到那头。
example_en: Several scholars strode across the square, talking loudly and freely from one end to the other.

meaning: Dressed in splendid garments and riding fine spirited horses, this idiom paints a picture of ostentatious luxury and youthful swagger. It describes someone who flaunts their wealth through extravagant attire and a bold, untamed lifestyle.
origin: This idiom first appears in the Ming dynasty work 'Ye Huo Bian' (《野获编》) by Shen Defu, within a section on unjust cases under the Ministry of Justice. The passage recounts how a gang of bandits, having grown powerful and arrogant, took to wearing dazzling clothes and riding spirited horses while calling themselves wandering knights-errant. Their ringleader, a man named Zhu Guochen, had originally been a butcher before rising to notoriety.
example_zh: 他年轻时鲜衣怒马，如今却偏爱粗茶淡饭的日子。
example_en: In his youth he lived a life of splendid clothes and spirited horses, but now he prefers the simplicity of plain tea and humble meals.

meaning: The sound of drums and music is so loud that it fills the sky. It describes a scene of extremely lively celebration and joyous festivity, where the atmosphere is vibrant and bustling with sound.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'History of the Five Dynasties: Han History' (《五代史平话·汉史》), a Song dynasty historical narrative. The original text reads '笙歌聒地，鼓乐喧天,' meaning reed pipes and songs filled the earth while drums and music resounded to the heavens. The passage depicts a grand celebratory scene with music so powerful it seemed to shake both heaven and earth.
example_zh: 庙会上鼓乐喧天，舞龙舞狮的队伍穿街而过。
example_en: At the temple fair, drums and music filled the air as the dragon and lion dance troupes paraded through the streets.

literal: Bi star rain, Ji star wind
meaning: Originally referring to the common people being like stars — the Bi constellation favors rain while the Ji constellation favors wind — it metaphorically describes how the populace yearns for the benevolent grace of their ruler. Later used as a term of praise for a sovereign who broadly bestows compassionate and virtuous governance upon the people.
origin: From the 'Book of Documents' (《书·洪范》), which states that the common people are like stars, some favoring wind and others favoring rain. The Han dynasty commentator Kong Anguo (孔安国) explained that the Ji constellation (箕星) is fond of wind and the Bi constellation (毕星) is fond of rain, just as the people have their natural inclinations. The phrase later evolved into a classical expression praising rulers for administering benevolent policies that satisfy the people's heartfelt desires.
example_zh: 陛下毕雨箕风，恩泽遍及四海，万民仰德。
example_en: Your Majesty, like the Bi star bringing rain and the Ji star bringing wind, bestows grace across the four seas, and all people look up to your virtue.

meaning: Describes the scene of osmanthus flowers in full bloom around the Mid-Autumn Festival, their sweet fragrance wafting through the air. It evokes the sensory beauty and tranquil atmosphere of early autumn.
origin: The idiom originates from a line in the Tang dynasty poem 'Lingyin Temple' (《灵隐寺》) by the poet Song Zhiwen (宋之问). The couplet reads: '桂子月中落，天香云外飘' — osmanthus seeds fall as if from the moon, and their heavenly fragrance drifts beyond the clouds. The verse was inspired by the poet's visit to Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou, where osmanthus trees surrounded the sacred grounds. Over time, the imagery was condensed into the four-character idiom '桂子飘香' to capture the ethereal beauty of autumn osmanthus.
example_zh: 中秋时节，桂子飘香，满城皆是秋意。
example_en: At Mid-Autumn, the osmanthus fragrance drifts through the air, filling the whole city with the feeling of autumn.

meaning: Describes a situation so precarious it is like a thread about to snap — on the verge of collapse or extinction. It can refer to a critical political or military situation, or to the decline of a family line with few descendants remaining. The idiom conveys extreme fragility and imminent danger of being cut off entirely.
origin: The idiom first appears in the "Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals" (《公羊传》), under the fourth year of Duke Xi's reign. It describes how the southern Yi and northern Di barbarian tribes were simultaneously attacking the central Chinese states, leaving the Zhou civilization hanging by a thread — 'as if a single strand that could snap at any moment.' The phrase was later adopted by Ban Gu in the "Book of Han" (《汉书》) to describe the dwindling descendants of meritorious officials from the early Han dynasty, whose family lines were barely surviving.
example_zh: 战乱之后，这个家族人丁稀少，不绝如线。
example_en: After the war, the family had so few members left that its lineage hung by a thread.

meaning: A classical term for ordinary farmers and elderly villagers living in the countryside. It evokes rustic simplicity and the common rural folk who are far removed from officialdom or urban sophistication.
origin: The idiom first appears in the Ming dynasty scholar Jiao Hong's work 'Yu Tang Cong Yu' (《玉堂丛语》), in the chapter on virtuous conduct. It recounts how Zhou Chen (周忱), a governor patrolling the Jiangnan region, would personally walk into the countryside to speak with local farmers and rural elders, asking about their hardships. This image of a high official humbly consulting the lowliest villagers gave the phrase its enduring literary resonance.
example_zh: 他虽身居高位，却常与村夫野老促膝交谈，体察民情。
example_en: Though he held a high position, he often sat down to chat with village farmers and rural elders to understand the people's hardships.

meaning: The formal institutions, regulations, and established precedents of the imperial court and the state. It refers broadly to the codified body of dynastic laws, rites, and administrative systems that governed traditional Chinese governance. The term evokes the weight and continuity of bureaucratic tradition.
origin: The idiom appears in a preface by Lu Xun (鲁迅) in his 1935 essay collection 'Essays from the Qiejieting Studio, Part Two' (《且介亭杂文二集》). Lu Xun observed that readers of earlier eras pored over diaries and letters not merely for personal gossip, but to study '朝章国故' — the court's institutional norms and state precedents — along with elegant phrasing and the art of social maneuvering. He noted wryly that this scrutiny made prominent figures afraid to write casually even in their private journals. The phrase captures the late imperial literati's obsession with the minutiae of bureaucratic form and ritual.
example_zh: 老先生毕生钻研朝章国故，对历代典制如数家珍。
example_en: The old scholar devoted his life to studying court regulations and state precedents, knowing the institutions of every dynasty like the back of his hand.

meaning: This idiom conveys that with unwavering perseverance and diligent effort, even the most seemingly impossible tasks can eventually be accomplished. It emphasizes that sustained hard work can transform something rough and crude into something refined and useful.
origin: The story is traditionally associated with Li Bai, the renowned poet of the Tang Dynasty. As a child, Li Bai was playful and disliked studying. One day, while wandering near a stream at Mount Xiang'er, he encountered an elderly woman tirelessly grinding an iron pestle on a whetstone. When Li Bai asked what she was doing, she calmly replied that she intended to grind the iron rod into a sewing needle. Astonished by her determination, Li Bai realized that with enough persistence, any goal could be achieved, and he thereafter devoted himself to his studies.
example_zh: 只要坚持努力，磨杵作针终会成功。
example_en: As long as you persist and work hard, grinding a pestle into a needle will eventually lead to success.

meaning: To relentlessly pursue and strike down an already-defeated villain or enemy. The idiom advises against showing mercy to bad people who have temporarily lost power, because if they recover, they will strike back. It emphasizes thoroughness in eliminating evil rather than stopping halfway out of misplaced compassion.
origin: This idiom comes from Lu Xun's famous essay 'On "Fair Play" Should Be Deferred' (论'费厄泼赖'应该缓行), published in his 1927 collection 'The Grave' (坟). Lu Xun argued that when a vicious dog falls into water, one should not pity it or pull it out — instead, one should keep beating it, because if it climbs back onto land, it will bite you again. He used this metaphor to criticize intellectuals of his time who advocated for 'fair play' toward defeated warlords and reactionaries, warning that leniency toward the wicked would only lead to more harm. The essay became highly influential in modern Chinese political thought, shaping the ruthless approach to class struggle in later revolutionary discourse.
example_zh: 对于这种坏人，我们必须打落水狗，绝不手软。
example_en: When dealing with such villains, we must beat the drowning dog and show no mercy whatsoever.

meaning: To have one's mind pulled in multiple directions at once, unable to settle on a single thought or decision. It describes a state of indecision, distraction, or half-heartedness where one lacks focus and commitment.
origin: This idiom originates from Chapter 6 of the Ming dynasty novel '禅真逸史' (The True Story of the Escape of Zen) by Fang Ruhao. In the story, a character admonishes another that chanting the Buddha's name is a serious matter and should not be done with a divided mind. The phrase has since become synonymous with '三心二意', both describing a lack of concentration and wavering intent.
example_zh: 学习一门手艺不能二心三意，要专注才能学精。
example_en: When learning a craft, you cannot be half-hearted about it; you must focus to master it.

meaning: To cook sand in hopes of making a meal. This idiom describes an endeavor that is fundamentally impossible from the start — no matter how much effort one pours in, the result can never be achieved. It is a vivid metaphor for wasted labor and utter futility.
origin: The idiom originates from the Tang dynasty poet Gu Kuang's poem 'Xing Lu Nan' (行路难, 'The Hard Road'). In the poem, Gu Kuang uses the image of carrying snow to fill a well and cooking sand to make a meal as examples of completely hopeless tasks. The line '炊沙作饭岂堪吃' ('How can one eat a meal made by cooking sand?') drives home the point that some efforts are doomed from the outset. An alternate version of the text uses the character 砂 instead of 沙, giving us the form 炊砂作饭.
example_zh: 想靠死记硬背掌握一门语言，无异于炊砂作饭。
example_en: Trying to master a language through rote memorization alone is no different from cooking sand to make a meal.

meaning: A colloquial expression referring to minor ailments, everyday aches and pains, or trivial misfortunes. It describes the kind of small, passing troubles that everyone experiences from time to time and that are not worth worrying over.
origin: This idiom originates from Act 1 of the Yuan dynasty zaju play 'Kan Tou Jin' (《勘头巾》, 'Examining the Headscarf') by the playwright Sun Zhongzhang (孙仲章). In the play, a character is told that within a hundred days, should any minor illness befall someone, the responsibility would fall on them. The phrase was later popularized in modern literature by Lao She, who used it in his novel 'Four Generations Under One Roof' (《四世同堂》) to liken the city of Beiping's hardships to a person's inevitable minor ailments.
example_zh: 人上了年纪，偶尔头疼脑热是难免的，不必太过担心。
example_en: As one gets older, the occasional headache or minor ailment is inevitable, so there is no need to worry too much.

meaning: Using a cat as bait to catch mice — an absurd approach because the cat would eat the mice rather than lure them. It describes a method that is fundamentally self-defeating and doomed to fail from the start.
origin: This idiom comes from The Book of Lord Shang (《商君书·农战》), a Legalist text by Shang Yang (商鞅), the renowned statesman of the Qin state during the Warring States period. In the chapter "Agriculture and War," Shang Yang argues that seeking official promotion through flattery and personal connections, rather than offering tangible value or merit, is as futile as trying to lure mice with a cat as bait — the outcome is certain failure. The metaphor underscores the absurdity of using a means that inherently contradicts the desired end.
example_zh: 他想用这种手段解决问题，无异于以狸饵鼠，根本行不通。
example_en: Trying to solve the problem with such a method is no different from using a cat as bait to catch mice — it simply won't work.

meaning: Describes writing that flows so perfectly from the author's mind that not a single character needs to be altered. It praises both the speed and the quality of literary composition, suggesting the writer has achieved effortless mastery.
origin: This idiom originates from the "New Book of Tang" (《新唐书》) compiled by Ouyang Xiu in the Song Dynasty. The entry describes the Tang Dynasty literary prodigy Wang Bo (王勃), who would first grind a large amount of ink, drink heavily, then pull a blanket over his face and lie down. Upon waking, he would take up his brush and compose an entire essay in one stroke, without altering a single character. Contemporaries marveled at this and called his method "belly draft" (腹稿), meaning he composed the entire piece perfectly in his mind before writing it down.
example_zh: 他这篇散文一气呵成，不易一字，令人叹服。
example_en: He wrote this essay in one breath without changing a single word, leaving everyone in admiration.

meaning: Literally a wild goose cut off from its flock and flying alone. It metaphorically describes someone who lives in solitude, most commonly referring to a man who remains unmarried and without a companion.
origin: This idiom comes from the Ming dynasty drama "红拂记" (The Story of the Red Whisk) by Zhang Fengyi, in the act "杨公完偶" (Lord Yang Completes a Match). In the play, a character addresses Xu Sheng with the line: "You have long been like a severed goose, alone and solitary — have you ever sought a partner?" The image draws on the migratory behavior of wild geese, which fly in tight formations, making a lone straggler a poignant symbol of isolation.
example_zh: 他年过三十仍是断雁孤鸿，父母颇为着急。
example_en: He is past thirty and still a lone bachelor, which worries his parents quite a bit.

meaning: Describes someone who acts in a slow, unhurried, and deliberate manner, taking their time without any sense of rush or anxiety. It conveys a calm and composed demeanor where every action is measured and methodical.
origin: This idiom originates from Chapter 1 of the Qing dynasty novel 'The Tale of Heroic Sons and Daughters' (《儿女英雄传》) by the writer Wen Kang (文康). In the story, the young master is carefully checking his examination materials when he hears his father speak. He then approaches respectfully and, in a slow and unhurried manner, replies that the matter requires his father's further consideration. The phrase '漫条斯理' is a variant of the more common '慢条斯理', with '漫' carrying the same sense of leisurely slowness as '慢'.
example_zh: 他漫条斯理地泡了一壶茶，慢慢品尝起来。
example_en: He unhurriedly brewed a pot of tea and slowly began to savor it.

meaning: Describes a person who is muddle-headed, confused, or unclear about what is going on. It refers to a state of mental fog where one fails to grasp the situation or acts without proper awareness. The phrase often carries a tone of mild exasperation at someone's cluelessness.
origin: There is no specific classical origin for this idiom, as it is a colloquial expression that emerged from everyday vernacular speech. It follows the common AABB reduplicative pattern in Chinese, repeating the characters 糊 (paste-like, muddled) and 涂 (smeared, confused) to intensify the meaning. The idiom gained popularity in modern spoken Chinese and literature as a vivid way to describe someone's baffled or oblivious state of mind.
example_zh: 他糊里糊涂地签了那份合同，事后才后悔。
example_en: He signed that contract in a muddle-headed daze and only regretted it afterward.

meaning: A metaphor describing a scene of widespread suffering where victims of famine, war, or natural disasters are everywhere — displaced, starving, and crying out in misery. It evokes the image of countless suffering people scattered across the land like wailing wild geese.
origin: The idiom originates from the 'Lesser Odes' (小雅) section of the 'Classic of Poetry' (《诗经》), China's oldest collection of poetry compiled during the Zhou Dynasty. The poem 'Wild Geese' (《鸿雁》) contains the line 'The wild geese fly, their mournful cries are loud' (鸿雁于飞，哀鸣嗷嗷). The wailing of migrating geese, separated from their flock and lost, became a powerful metaphor for the cries of displaced and starving common people during times of chaos. Later generations condensed this imagery into the set phrase '哀鸿遍地' to describe scenes of mass suffering.
example_zh: 战乱之后，哀鸿遍地，百姓流离失所。
example_en: After the war, the land was filled with suffering victims, and the common people were displaced and homeless.

meaning: To stockpile scarce commodities and calculate the maximum profit from them. It describes merchants who corner the market on rare goods and manipulate supply to reap excessive gains.
origin: This idiom originates from Chao Cuo's memorial 'On the Importance of Grain' (《论贵粟疏》) during the Western Han dynasty. Chao Cuo criticized large merchants who hoarded goods to earn double interest while small traders sat in market stalls peddling wares, all 'manipulating rare goods for profit' (操其奇赢) as they idled through the cities. His essay argued that such profiteering harmed agriculture and destabilized the state, urging the emperor to prioritize grain production over commerce. The phrase was later condensed into the four-character idiom 操奇计赢.
example_zh: 那些操奇计赢的奸商最终自食其果。
example_en: Those profiteering merchants who hoarded and manipulated the market ultimately reaped what they had sown.

meaning: Describes a state of such extreme fluster or panic that one does not know where to put their hands and feet. It conveys being completely at a loss, unable to cope with a sudden or overwhelming situation, often with visible physical awkwardness.
origin: The phrase originates from the Analects of Confucius (《论语·子路》), where Confucius tells his disciple Zilu that if punishments and laws are not just and fair, the common people will not know where to place their hands and feet — meaning they will lose all sense of how to behave properly. Over time, this political observation evolved into a fixed idiom describing any scenario where a person is so flustered or panicked that they become physically awkward and unable to respond. It was later popularized in vernacular literature, such as Chen Chen's Qing dynasty novel 《水浒后传》, where a character is startled by the sudden arrival of enemy troops.
example_zh: 面对突如其来的质问，他一时手足无措，说不出话来。
example_en: Faced with the sudden interrogation, he was so flustered that he could not utter a word.

literal: prop up thunder, split the moon
meaning: Describes an astonishing voice, spirit, or creative force so powerful it seems capable of propping up thunder and splitting the moon. It conveys an overwhelming, earth-shattering presence that leaves a profound impact on those who witness it.
origin: This idiom originates from the Tang Dynasty poet and literary critic Sikong Tu (司空图) in his essay 'Evaluating Poetry with Wang Jia' (《与王驾评诗》). Sikong Tu had just compiled his own poetry collection titled 'Yiming Ji' (《一鸣集》) and remarked that his verses could 'prop up thunder and split the moon, wrenching the very liver and spleen of fellow writers.' He declared that even such bold self-praise would not cause him to blush — a testament to his unshakable confidence in his poetic power.
example_zh: 他一声长啸，撑霆裂月，震慑全场。
example_en: He let out a long howl, as if propping up thunder and splitting the moon, awing the entire audience into silence.

meaning: To operate or control something with complete ease and proficiency, as if it were second nature. It describes a state where one can maneuver or manage an object, vehicle, or situation effortlessly without any hindrance or difficulty.
origin: The idiom originates from the Ming dynasty work 'Xian Bo Zhi Shi' (《先拨志始》) by Wen Bing (文秉). The text records that the powerful eunuch Wei Zhongxian (魏忠贤) and his faction were able to 'manipulate affairs at will' (操纵如意), reflecting how they controlled the imperial court with unchecked ease. The phrase later evolved into '操纵自如', broadening its meaning to encompass any skilled and effortless handling of tools, vehicles, or situations beyond the original political context.
example_zh: 他操纵自如地驾驶着汽车，在蜿蜒山路上飞驰。
example_en: He drove the car with effortless control, speeding along the winding mountain road.

literal: each other, be apart, not, much
meaning: The two are not far apart from each other; the difference between them is negligible or insignificant. Used to express that two things are nearly the same in degree, quality, or distance.
origin: This idiom originates from the Northern Song Dynasty scholar Su Xun (苏洵) in his essay 'On the Land System' (田制), part of his 'Jiayou Collection' (嘉祐集). He argued that the tax burden under the Song Dynasty was essentially no different from that of the ancient Zhou Dynasty. The phrase was later echoed by his son, the renowned poet and statesman Su Shi (苏轼), who used it in a memorial to the emperor, criticizing two flawed policies as being equally bad.
example_zh: 这两款手机的性能相去无几，价格却差了一倍。
example_en: The performance of these two phones is not much different, yet their prices differ by double.

meaning: Describes a state of extreme fear or nervous anxiety where one is constantly on edge. The heart races in alarm and the gallbladder feels as if it is suspended, capturing the physical sensation of dread. It conveys being so frightened that one cannot find peace of mind.
origin: This idiom has no recorded classical source. It is a variant of the more common idiom 提心吊胆 (tí xīn diào dǎn), which carries the same meaning. The imagery draws on traditional Chinese medicine, where the heart governs the spirit and the gallbladder governs courage and decisiveness. When terrified, the heart palpitates and the gallbladder feels as though it is dangling — a vivid metaphor for the visceral experience of fear.
example_zh: 深夜独自穿过墓地，他一路惊心吊胆。
example_en: Walking alone through the graveyard late at night, he was frightened and on edge the whole way.

meaning: Describes a person who is firm, upright, and incorruptible — never bending to curry favor or showing partiality. It embodies unwavering moral integrity and the refusal to pander to power or influence.
origin: The idiom appears in Yu Jideng's '典故纪闻' (Records of Classical Allusions), Volume 14, from the Ming Dynasty. The original passage discusses how officials who were 'righteous and unyielding, refusing to engage in private lobbying' were unjustly deemed unworthy by those who preferred flattery and backdoor dealings. The phrase thus crystallized as a hallmark of incorruptible character in Chinese bureaucratic tradition.
example_zh: 他一生刚直不阿，从不向权贵低头。
example_en: All his life he was unyielding and upright, never bowing his head to the powerful.

meaning: To glare with wide eyes and raise one's eyebrows in an exaggerated manner. It describes someone who puts on a pretentious show of authority or self-importance, striking a pose to intimidate or impress others.
origin: This idiom originates from the Yuan dynasty play "Jian Fa Dai Bin" (剪发待宾) by Qin Jianfu (秦简夫). In the third act, a character admonishes another to remember the Confucian principle that harmony is precious in the use of propriety, instructing them to bow and fold their hands respectfully rather than adopt the haughty, posturing demeanor of "shān yǎn pū méi." The phrase later appears in Ming dynasty writer Kang Hai's (康海) play "Wang Lanqing" (王兰卿), further cementing its usage in classical drama.
example_zh: 他不过是苫眼铺眉罢了，其实什么本事也没有。
example_en: He is just putting on airs with that haughty look—in truth, he has no real ability at all.

meaning: This idiom describes work or behavior that is superficially impressive but lacks substance or genuine effort. It refers to a perfunctory,敷衍 approach where one goes through the motions, focusing on appearances rather than real results or practical outcomes.
origin: No specific classical origin is recorded for this modern idiom. It emerged from colloquial Chinese usage to criticize bureaucratic formalism and hollow posturing. The phrase gained prominence in political discourse, most notably when Deng Xiaoping used it in his 1978 speech at the National Science Conference to condemn formalism that prioritizes superficial display over actual efficiency, speed, quality, and cost-effectiveness.
example_zh: 他的工作报告全是表面文章，没有解决任何实际问题。
example_en: His work report was nothing but superficial window-dressing, solving no real problems at all.

meaning: This idiom describes unexpected complications, side issues, or obstacles that suddenly and unexpectedly arise during the course of handling a matter. It conveys the frustration of a straightforward situation becoming tangled with unforeseen difficulties, much like branches and knots sprouting chaotically from a tree trunk.
origin: The idiom originates from a memorial to the throne written by Xue Fucheng (薛福成), a prominent Qing dynasty diplomat and essayist, titled 'A Comprehensive Plan for Establishing Consular Offices in the South Sea Islands to Protect Chinese Nationals.' In this document, Xue argued that when legal cases involving foreigners occurred, consular officials from foreign powers handled them independently, often undermining the authority of local Chinese magistrates. He pointed out that this extraterritorial interference was precisely the root cause of the numerous complications and troubles that had arisen at China's various treaty ports.
example_zh: 本以为事情简单，没想到枝节横生，反而更难处理了。
example_en: I thought it would be a simple matter, but unexpected complications kept cropping up, making it even harder to handle.

meaning: Refers to disaster or conflict erupting from within one's own household or inner circle. The 'screen wall' (萧墙) was a small wall inside the gate of an ancient palace — trouble starting there means the threat comes from within, not from outside. It is used to describe internal strife, betrayal, or discord within a family, organization, or state.
origin: The idiom originates from a stele inscription written by Yu Xin (庾信) of the Northern Zhou dynasty (6th century CE), titled 'Zhou Da Jiangjun Sima Yi Shendao Bei' (Stele for the Spirit Path of Grand General Sima Yi of Zhou). The line reads: '时值乱离，衅起萧墙' — 'In times of chaos and separation, strife arose from within the screen wall.' The screen wall was a feature of noble residences, metaphorically representing the inner court or household. The phrase was later popularized as a variant of the more common '祸起萧墙', which appears in the Analects of Confucius, where Confucius warns that the real danger to a state comes not from external enemies but from internal discord.
example_zh: 家族企业衅起萧墙，兄弟反目，公司最终分崩离析。
example_en: Strife arose from within the screen wall of the family business — the brothers turned against each other, and the company ultimately fell apart.

meaning: Describes something that is well-founded, traceable, and has a clear basis or origin. It indicates that a matter is not fabricated out of thin air but has identifiable clues and evidence to support it.
origin: This idiom originates from the Ming dynasty vernacular story collection "石点头" (The Stone Nods), specifically in the tale "郭挺之榜前认子" (Guo Tingzhi Recognizes His Son Before the Examination Board). The narrator remarks that although the event was strange, it still had roots and sprouts — meaning it was traceable and could be recalled. The agricultural metaphor of roots and sprouts symbolizes something that can be followed back to its source.
example_zh: 这件事有根有苗，查起来不难。
example_en: This matter has a clear basis and trail — it won't be hard to investigate.

meaning: A horse's age can be told by its teeth, so this idiom is a humble, self-deprecating way to say one has grown older without achieving anything noteworthy. It expresses regret that time has passed while one's career or studies have made no real progress.
origin: This idiom comes from the 'Guliang Zhuan' (《谷梁传》), a commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, in the entry for the second year of Duke Xi of Lu (僖公二年). Duke Xian of Jin (晋献公) wished to attack the state of Guo but needed passage through the state of Yu, so he bribed the Duke of Yu with a precious jade disk and a fine horse. After Jin conquered Guo, it turned back and annexed Yu as well. Upon recovering his jade disk, Duke Xian remarked, 'The jade is still the same, but the horse's teeth have grown longer.' The phrase later evolved into a metaphor for aging without accomplishment.
example_zh: 回首往事，深感马齿徒增，愧对师长教诲。
example_en: Looking back on the past, I deeply feel that I have merely grown older in vain, failing to live up to my teachers' guidance.

meaning: Like clouds surging upward and dragons soaring into the sky, this idiom describes heroes and outstanding figures rising to prominence at an opportune moment. It conveys the momentum of talented individuals seizing the times and ascending to power or greatness.
origin: This idiom originates from the 'Hanshu' (Book of Han), specifically the postface to the biographical section compiled by Ban Gu in the Eastern Han dynasty.
